<meta>The cover features the supra-libros of the renowned book collector Richard Heber (1773–1833). A small white circular label with the number "6" is affixed to the top of the spine.</meta>

This volume is bound in half-leather. The spine and corners are finished in dark brown leather with gold-line tooling, while the boards are covered in a reddish-brown pebbled <term>morocco leather</term> <note>a high-quality goatskin leather known for its visible grain and durability</note>. Centered on the front board is a gold-stamped <term>supra-libros</term> <note>Latin for "above the books," referring to an owner's coat of arms or mark stamped on the outside of a binding</note>. 

The heraldic stamp features a shield depicting a diagonal stripe (a "bend") between six small crosses with pointed lower ends (known as "cross-crosslets fitchy"), with a lion standing on its hind legs in the upper-left corner. The shield is topped by a coronet and enclosed within an oval border containing the owner's inscription.

# Decorative Marbled Endpaper

This page displays a decorative <term>marbled endpaper</term> <note>A decorative paper used by bookbinders to line the inner covers of a book, created by floating pigments on a liquid surface to create patterns.</note>, which likely serves as the front pastedown—the part of the paper glued to the inner board—or a flyleaf of this bound manuscript. 

The pattern is a classic <term>peacock</term> <note>A traditional marbling pattern characterized by rhythmic, feathered arches that resemble the "eyes" of peacock feathers.</note> or <term>nonpareil</term> <note>From the French meaning "without equal"; a dense, combed marbling pattern created with a fine-toothed tool.</note> marbled design. It is characterized by rhythmic, feathered arches that repeat across the entire surface. The color palette features a deep maroon or burgundy base, accented with undulating swirls of off-white, golden yellow, and slate blue. 

A small portion of a white paper slip is visible at the left edge. It shows faint, partially obscured typed text, which appears to be modern cataloging notes or <term>folio</term> <note>original Latin: "folium," meaning leaf. In manuscripts, pages are often numbered by the leaf rather than by the individual side.</note> references added by a librarian or collector.

<keywords>marbled paper, peacock pattern, nonpareil pattern, bookbinding, endpaper, burgundy, manuscript decoration, folio references</keywords>

She stands facing forward, wearing an elaborate crown—symbolizing her royal status as a princess—and richly decorated, wide-sleeved garments featuring various geometric and floral patterns. She holds a book in her right hand, representing her great learning and status as the patroness of scholars. She rests her left hand on the hilt of a large, upright sword, the instrument of her death. To her lower left, the distinctive <term>breaking wheel</term> <note>A spiked wheel used in an attempt to torture the saint; according to legend, it shattered at her touch.</note> of her martyrdom is partially visible. # MARCH

The first day of the month joins the fourth to the end <note>original: "Prima dies menis sociat v̄ qrtā tēdā." This is a mnemonic verse regarding "Egyptian Days," which were considered unlucky. In March, the 1st and 4th were the dangerous days.</note>
March has 31 days, the moon 30.

### On the Appearance of the Moon on the 29th Day at Evening or Not.

<margin>If the day is equal to the night <note>the Equinox</note>, and truly hours are to be added to the day then according to the number of the day which is at evening.</margin>
If you ask on which day at the start of the lunar month, on the 29th at evening, the moon might be seen or not: it is to be found beyond the location of the sun and moon according to the noon of that day, with the addition of a six-hour examination. Here their place will be held according to the evening of the same day. The given place of the moon from the place of the sun which it now has is to be noted more diligently. <margin>If the moon is in the "thymele" <note>original: "thimeli"; a technical term here referring to the northern part of the ecliptic</note>—that is, in this northern part—the latitude is noted as gathered outside the moon itself. If it is in the "knees" <note>original: "genuibus"</note>—that is, from that southern or austral part—the same is subtracted and everywhere defined. Concerning the amount in the table below, we will guide you through the sign of the moon and the face of the sign, and it will be noted which of those angles were true. Thus, in that meeting, if the aforementioned distance is greater, the moon will appear on the same evening of expectation. If, however, it is smaller by 2, [it will not]. If indeed it is equal to 8, it will scarcely appear even to a sharp eye. Know also that for seven years the moon is to appear at the morning hour; with the location of the three of the sun and the moon according to the noon of the same day noted, four six-hour subtractions... will also remain in the aforementioned [calculations].</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the medieval "computus"—the science of calculating time and the dates of religious festivals. This was essential for calculating the date of Easter and predicting eclipses.</meta>

-># On the Conjunction of the Sun and Moon:<-
---

<margin>
In the era of the moon it will have the hour.
Note concerning the degree of the sun.
True conjunction <note>The moment when the sun and moon are at the same celestial longitude.</note>.
If the sun preceded the moon.
If the moon [preceded] the sun.
In the table.
So that I may know the argument <note>In astronomy, an "argument" is the mathematical value or angle used as an input to find a result in a table.</note>.
</margin>

**Concerning** the true conjunction or opposition of the sun and moon, lest this be neglected through the carelessness of incautious speech, or so that the tedious reasoning of the work may appear stable: we gird ourselves to clarify this doctrine through a very brief and learned explanation. Therefore, the positions of the sun and moon at noon of the day on which the moon is in the 28th, 29th, or 30th [day] of the ecliptic body must be found through the method of equalization. Where they are found: if their position is one and the same in signs, degrees, and minutes, you have the work of the local time of conjunction at the noon of that same day. But if it is not so, it shall be observed which of them preceded the other, and you will diligently note their distance. Once noted, you shall separate it by dividing by 12. Take one minute for every twelfth part. When this is done, you shall add that twelfth part to the adjustment <note>original: "restructioni"; likely a corruption of "restitutioni," meaning the corrected position</note>, and you will note its value for the greater motion. If therefore the sun preceded the moon, that greater adjustment must be added to the position of the moon, and the aforementioned twelfth part to the position of the sun. But if the moon preceded the sun, the same must be subtracted from them in the same manner as above. When this is executed: if their positions agree in signs, degrees, and minutes, that is the location; provided you have correctly marked the day or time of their conjunction. If indeed it happens otherwise, everything must be changed until it happens without doubt. Therefore, when you have correctly marked the positions of conjunction, the work for that calculation is not yet fully known. For if you wish to know the designated hour and minute of the conjunction of the sun and moon, it must be gathered from the table written below, which is established for the hourly motions of the sun and moon. It should be known that the hourly motion of the sun is subtracted from the hourly motion of the moon, and the remainder shall be said to be "above the moon." If therefore the adjustment of the sun and moon is reduced by one second and divided by the moon's second, you will have the hours and minutes. The entry into the table is prescribed in the line of the arguments <note>the input values</note> of whichever of them—the sun or moon—is already equalized. After you enter with the degrees of that same argument, with all of them, use that number to find the hourly motion of the sun and moon at the moment of their conjunction and opposition. Indeed, the equalization of the arguments of the sun and moon is applied to the equalization of whichever argument is used.

<margin>20.0.34.42</margin>

**First**, the mean motion of the sun must be investigated.
**Second**, the "severing" of the sun <note>original: "abscisio solis"; this likely refers to the solar apogee or the eccentricity correction</note> found according to the present time: this must be taken away from the mean motion of the sun. The remainder is to be called the **argument of the sun**.
**Third**, with that same argument, enter through the lines of the number into the table of the **equation of the sun** <note>The "equation" is a correction factor to account for the fact that the sun's apparent motion is not a perfect circle at a constant speed.</note>; and the adjustment found there should be noted.
**Fourth**, lead the argument back again: if the argument was the remainder, subtract it if it was greater, or add it if it was smaller to the mean motion. From which, by the hand <note>original: "p' manu signor'"; referring to the manual calculation or a specific diagram</note> of signs, degrees, and minutes, the junction of the argument or the lessening of the mean motion is reached. This is taken from Aries to find the true position of the sun.
Furthermore, if you have a sign in which the position of the sun [is located], which has been revolved into minutes, with one degree added to its argument, enter into the lines of the table and note the adjustment. If the adjustment was greater, it must be extended. And the smaller is taken from the greater, and the remainder is to be led into minutes. What results from this leading must be divided by 60 <note>original: "p .lx. diuidendū"; medieval astronomy used base-60/sexagesimal math.</note>. If the second adjustment was greater than the first, that which comes from the division by sixty must be added to the first adjustment. If it was smaller, it must be subtracted from the same. If the first adjustment [unclear], this must be added or subtracted from the mean motion according to the argument's reasoning, so that the true position of the sun in signs, degrees, and minutes may be held.

---

When indeed you work toward the brief equation of the sun and moon: thus concerning whatever minutes, whether more or less, you shall be refined. If in the mean motion the equation happens to fall, you shall have the argument as 20 seconds, or more for those [representing] one minute.

Because the numbers are entered into the lines, these minutes above with the added degree should be entered, and it should be rectified in every way through multiplication and division.

<summary>This page provides astronomical tables and instructions for calculating the "Mean Motion" of the sun relative to London. It outlines a four-step process to transform a mean position into a "True Position" using an "argument" and an "equation" (correction factor).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the astronomical tables for the mean motion of the sun. While the previous page dealt with "collected years" (long spans of time), this page focuses on the "expansion" of those motions into smaller increments: days, hours, and minutes. This allowed a medieval astronomer to calculate the sun's exact position for any specific moment of the year.</meta>

It should be noted that the Kalends <note>The Roman name for the first day of a month. In medieval astronomy, dates were often still calculated using the Roman system of counting backwards from the Kalends, Nones, and Ides.</note> are never to be calculated except when it is a leap year <note>original: "bissextus." The term refers to the "twice sixth" day added to February in a leap year.</note>, at which time the Kalends of March must be calculated. Then the end of February is reached at noon on the 11th Kalends of March <note>February 19th.</note>. If indeed you wish to proceed to noon on the 2nd Kalends of March <note>February 28th.</note>, take February as complete. If you wish to proceed to noon on the Kalends of March <note>March 1st.</note>, take February as complete with one [extra] day. For the remainder is moved to the noon of the Kalends.

<meta>This page follows the solar tables which corrected the Sun's position for its elliptical-like path. This specific page focuses on the "Sun's Apogee"—the point in the Sun's apparent orbit where it is furthest from the Earth. In medieval astronomy, the apogee was not fixed but shifted very slowly over time. This table allows a computer (a person performing calculations) to determine exactly where that furthest point was for any given date by adding up values for "collected" large groups of years, individual "remaining" years, months, and days.</meta>

You shall subtract the mean motion of the <term>Dragon's Head</term> <note>The North Node of the Moon.</note> from 12 signs, which are to be arranged thus: In the first house <note>The first cell or column of your calculation workspace.</note> 12 signs shall be placed; in the second, 0 degrees; in the third, 0 minutes; in the fourth, 0 seconds. Then, let the mean motion of the Dragon's Head be subtracted from them.

It should be noted that in the <term>equation of the planets</term> <note>A correction applied to find the true position from the mean position.</note>, the eighth sphere is accounted for, because the planets move within the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>; however, the Head and the Tail move with the firmament itself. Therefore, in the equation of the Head and Tail, it shows what is to be completed. <note>This refers to the phenomenon of precession, where the entire background of stars shifts slowly over time.</note>

<column-break/>

The position of the Dragon’s Head <term>caput draconis</term> <note>original: "caput draconis"; this refers to the North Node, the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's path) moving north.</note> is to be subtracted from the position of the Moon; or, let the mean course be added to the position of the Moon with the Dragon’s Head. For from either one subtraction or the other addition of the signs, degrees, and the rest of the minutes, nothing will result except what arrives: it shall be called the argument of latitude <term>argumentum latitudinis</term> <note>The angular distance of the Moon from its node, used to calculate how far it is from the ecliptic plane.</note>. Therefore, with that same argument, one must now proceed through the lines toward the Moon’s latitude; the addition must be noted. And so, when it has been added to it: that which it indicates will be the Moon's latitude <term>latitudo</term>.

At this point, if one desires to know whether that latitude is ascending or descending, or in which part it may be, one must return to the signs of the argument of latitude. If it is within the first signs <note>The first 90 degrees or first quarter of the cycle.</note>, the latitude will be northern <term>aquilonaris</term> and increasing. If however it is within the second signs, the latitude is northern but decreasing. If however it is within the third signs, the latitude which is southern <term>australis</term> is decreasing. If it is within the fourth signs, the latitude is southern but increasing.

<margin>
If the mean motion of the sun cannot be taken from the mean motion of the moon: 12 signs should be added to the mean motion of that moon, so that the mean motion of the sun may be taken from it.
</margin>

The location of the Moon is gathered by this reasoning. First, let the <term>mean motion of the sun</term> <note>The average position of the Sun if its orbit were a perfect circle.</note> be subtracted from the <term>mean motion of the moon</term> as was said above. Subtract the mean motion of the sun from the mean motion of the moon, and the remainder of these, when doubled, is called the <term>double argument</term> <note>original: "duplex argumentum"; this is a technical step in calculating the moon's "evection," or the second inequality of its motion.</note>. With this, through the rows of numbers in the center, look for the <term>equation</term> through the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>A mathematical adjustment to account for the moon's varying distance from Earth.</note> noted for each. If the <term>double signs</term> are less than six signs, add the center equation to the <term>argument of the moon</term>. If it is greater, subtract it. Thus you will know the equated argument of the moon. With this equated argument, through the rows of numbers in the equation, find the diameter of the short epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary motion.</note>, and the equation of the argument together. Then, whatever part of the number of 60 <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>Using the "sexagenary" or base-60 system common in medieval astronomy.</note> has been preserved, multiply it by that part of the second equation of the diameter, and add that part to the equation of the arguments. Or, for example, if the proportional minutes are 30, since 30 is half of the sixty-unit number, add half of the said equation to the equation of the argument. If the equation is larger, multiply the whole equation of the differing diameter by the proportional minutes and divide the total by 60. Whatever comes from that division, add to the equation as above, and here the equated argument of the moon becomes the final equation. If the equated argument of the moon is greater than six signs, add this equation of the moon to the mean motion; if it is less, subtract it. Namely, by taking the starting point from <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the zodiac, used as the zero-point for measurements.</note>, the location of the moon in signs, degrees, and certain minutes will be found as desired.

<margin>
[unclear]
</margin>

Having the mean motion of the moon, the argument is taken. When it is sought in the equation of the argument through the lines of numbers, work by the second method: reconcile it with the sun in such a way that if the argument is greater than six signs, the addition must be added to the mean motion of the moon; if it is less, it must be subtracted.

<term>Sign</term> <note>original: "Sig."</note> — A unit of astronomical measurement. The sky is divided into 12 signs (like the Zodiac), each consisting of 30 degrees.

<term>Mean Motion</term> — The average position of a celestial body, calculated as if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle, before correcting for its actual, more complex orbit.

### On the positions of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.

The positions of the superior planets—namely Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—are to be found in this manner. First, find the **mean position** <note>original: "locum medium"; the average position of a planet assuming a perfectly circular orbit</note> of whichever one you wish. From this mean position, subtract the mean motion of the Sun. The remainder is to be called its **argument** <note>original: "argumentum"; the angular distance used to enter astronomical tables</note>. If less than the mean position is subtracted, the remainder is called its **center**. With this center, enter the table through the "lines of numbers" <note>the input column of a table</note> to find the **equation of the center** <note>original: "coequationem centri"; a correction factor to account for the elliptical nature of the orbit</note>. Note the value joined to it. If the center of Mars is in 5 signs, add its correction to the center; likewise, subtract it from the argument. If it is less, subtract the same from the same, and add it to the argument. In this way, the center and the argument are equated. Since this cannot be perfected without **proportional minutes** <note>original: "minutorum proportionalibus"; values used to interpolate between the planet's nearest and farthest points from Earth</note>, once the center is equated, enter the lines of numbers for those minutes, and let the result designate the proportional parts.

If there is a smaller diminution, the higher altitude <note>referring to the planet's distance from Earth</note> is found. If they are minutes of **augmentation**, use them in the same equating of the argument, and the lower altitude is considered together as a member, and let the value joined to it be noted. Whatever sixty-part <note>original: "sexageni"; minutes or fractions based on 60</note> of the proportional minutes exists, it shall separate the total of the accepted altitude. And if it is of the greater altitude, subtract that equation from the argument; if of the lesser, add it to the same. Thus the equation of the argument is found to be equated. Or otherwise: whichever altitude you take, multiply it by the proportional minutes, and divide the product by 60. Whatever results, by the aforementioned rule, add or subtract it from the equation of the argument. If the equated argument is less than 6 signs, add that equation to the equated center; if more, subtract it from the same. Thus the final center is produced from the equated center. If you then add the **apsis** <note>original: "abside"; the point in the orbit farthest from the center</note> of that same planet to this center, it will undoubtedly correspond to the position of that planet.

The positions of the superior planets were found by eliciting their arguments from their tables. Their mean motion is the mean motion of the Sun. ### On the investigation of the latitudes of the 5 planets.

<margin>Latitude of the 5 planets.</margin>
<margin>Greater altitude.</margin>

We teach how to investigate the altitudes of the five planets in this way. With the equated argument of any of them, look up the first latitude through the lines of numbers, and note the value joined to it. Then the number of the "dragon" <note>the planetary node</note> is to be added to the equated position of that same planet. The whole is to be called the argument of latitudes. With this argument, look up the second latitude through the lines of numbers, and take the value joined to it. That value is to be divided by the first joined latitude; for that which results is what is sought. For Venus and Mercury, with the equated argument of either, look up the first latitude through the lines of numbers, and note the value joined to it. For the dragon and the altitude of their mean motion of the Sun and the argument of the latitudes of the other 5 planets...
<margin>note</margin>
...if it is from one degree up to 3 signs, they will be the northern ascending parts; as you should have through the hours, and understand the latitude of the Moon.

With the argument <note>original: "argumento"; the angle used to enter astronomical tables to find a planet's position</note> having been equated for one of them at the same time through the lines of numbers, they are to be accumulated. It is said that this represents the total of the latitude's argument. Therefore, with that argument found through the lines of numbers in latitude according to the world <note>original: "secundum mundum"; likely referring to the celestial sphere or the local meridian</note>, and its adjunct <note>a secondary value used in the calculation</note> being taken, it should be divided by the adjunct of the first latitude. For indeed, it will show that the desired result comes from the division. And if the remainder according to latitude cannot be divided by the first latitude, let the first latitude be divided by the second. For that which results: that will be the latitude of the planet itself at that same hour, where the larger number is to be placed above and the smaller number below.

## On finding the retrogradation, station, and direct motion of the planets.

It should be known in which hours the five planets <note>the five planets known since antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are found to be moving forward <note>original: "progredientes"</note>, in which they are moving backward <note>original: "regradi"; retrograde motion is when a planet appears to move backward in the sky due to the Earth's relative position</note>, and in which they are stationary. When you wish to find this, take their equated center <note>original: "centrum coequatum"</note> through the lines of numbers into the first station according to the planet's position in the world, and its adjunct must be noted. This will be the first station. Then, subtract the first station from 12 signs <note>OCR says "xv" (15), but 12 signs (360 degrees) is the standard astronomical subtraction for finding the second station; the scribe may have erred or used a specific coordinate system</note>; whatever remains is to be noted as the second station. If, therefore, the equated argument of that planet is equal to the value of those stations in signs and degrees: it will be in that station.
<margin>namely if it is less than the first and greater than the second</margin>
And if it is not so, but is notably greater than the first and less than the second, it will be moving backward in retrogradation. Otherwise, it should be judged to be moving forward in direct motion.

## On finding the Opposition of the Sun and Moon.

The opposition <note>a "Full Moon," when the Sun and Moon are 180 degrees apart</note> of the Sun and Moon is to be found by their locations in a similar way [to conjunction]. However, first one must arrive at those values for calculation. When the Moon is at 13 or 14 days of age, let its location and the location of the Sun be found through their equations. Once found, if their locations in signs, degrees, and minutes are similar through the opposite diameter <note>meaning they are exactly 180 degrees apart</note>, it is necessary to find their point of opposition in this way. If it is not so, all those things described in the instructions for conjunction <note>the "New Moon"</note> must be carried out. But it should also be known that the hours and minutes

<column-break/>

of the Sun and Moon must be shown. If it happens after the equating of the centers, the hours and minutes must be either added or subtracted. If the Sun is found to be preceding, add the hours and their minutes—collected from the demonstration of the Moon’s surplus division—to the time of noon. If the Moon has preceded the Sun, subtract them from it; thus one may recognize the determined hours and minutes of the conjunction <note>original: "coniunctionis"</note> and opposition of the Sun and Moon.

## On the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon.

The failure of the lights <note>original: "Defectus luminum"; an eclipse</note>, which in Arabic is called *al-kusuf* <note>original: "elcuzuf"</note> and in Greek is called *eclipsis*, must be discussed in this place so that the reasoning for it may be understood. First, therefore, the conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon must be skillfully noted. Their distance from the Head or Tail of the Dragon <note>original: "capite vel cauda draconis"; the lunar nodes, the two points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note> must be taken. Secondly, the daily motion of the Sun and Moon, as well as the Dragon's motion, along with half the quantity of the lunar latitude at the hour of conjunction or opposition—which is clearly the hour of the middle of the eclipse—must be investigated. By following this skillful computation, one arrives very easily and most certainly at the hour and magnitude of the eclipse. Concerning these things, I shall urge each point individually, so that I may teach in a brief discourse how these are found. If, therefore, I wish to collect the daily motion of the Sun and Moon, we can find it very easily through their hourly motions from the table of hourly motions of the Sun and Moon, as has been taught before. Having taken their hourly motions from the aforementioned table according to the hour and minute of the conjunction or opposition, let those hourly motions be multiplied by 24. That which results will show their daily motions. If you seek to find the circle of the Sun, Moon, and Dragon: take the daily motion of the Sun, reduced to seconds, then collected eleven times, and divide by 20; the result will be seconds. When divided by 60, it will establish the minutes. Whatever is less will remain as seconds. These minutes and seconds [are calculated] according to the hour.

### On the eclipse of the moon.
An eclipse is either total or partial. Total is when the solar or lunar sphere is interposed, or when the whole is blocked by the shadow so it is not visible. Partial is when a certain part is covered, but another part is left shining. And since the moon is swifter than all the other planets and stands closer as it goes through the twelve signs, its eclipse is what we must first treat. First, however: when the reason of the calculation has noted the place of opposition, and has diligently assigned the distance of the places from the head or tail of the dragon: if that distance itself is 12 degrees or less from the dragon, I affirm that very distance to be the beginning of an eclipse of the moon. But if the aforementioned distance exceeds 12 degrees from the dragon: it denies an eclipse to all climates <note>regions of the earth</note>. Unless this itself has been found in the upper daily motion: and the eclipse happens to be seen in that climate. If the latitude of the moon is greater than the half-quantity, the eclipse is denied; if it is less, it is affirmed. And if it occurs: the latitude of the moon is to be subtracted from the half-quantity, and the remainder compared to the equation of the moon. And if the equation of the moon is greater, it portends a total eclipse with a delay <note>a total eclipse where the moon stays in the shadow for a period</note>. If it is equal, it will be a total eclipse without a delay. And if it is less, it demonstrates a partial eclipse. If therefore it is a partial eclipse, and you wish to know how great a part of the moon's orb ought to be eclipsed: divide the remainder of the half-quantity (collected by 12) by the equation of the moon. That which comes from it are the "digits" <note><term>Digits</term>: A unit of measure for eclipses, where 12 digits equal the full diameter of the celestial body.</term></note>. Multiply what remains by 60 and divide the sum by the whole lunar sector; these will be the minutes. So that the digits and minutes are collected: do not doubt that as many digits and minutes of the diameter of the moon's orb are eclipsed. Thus, if the number of digits is close to twelve, the whole part of the moon to be eclipsed will be the whole lunar body. If, for example, there are 6 digits and 20 [minutes]: since 6 is a fourth part of the number twelve, a fourth part of the lunar sphere, along with a third part of one-twelfth <note>meaning 1/36th of the whole</note>, will be eclipsed without doubt.

### On the eclipse of the Sun.
A solar eclipse is at the place of conjunction, if it is 12 degrees or less from the dragon. If it happens to be seen: if the hidden latitude of the moon is greater than the half-quantity, it denies an eclipse. If it is less, it affirms it entirely. And if it occurs: the hidden latitude of the moon is to be subtracted from the half-quantity. Compare what remains to the equation of the sun. If the equation is greater than it or equal to it: it signifies a total eclipse. If it is less, it signifies a partial eclipse. Collect the remainder of the half-quantity by 12, and divide the collection by the equation of the sun; these will be the digits. Multiply what remains by 60 and divide the product by the equation of the sun as above; these will be the minutes. By these digits and minutes, we have likewise discussed the quantity of the eclipse by the most certain reason, and it can be predicted without any wandering of error, if you find the latitude of the moon according to what was taught for the northern side. For a southern latitude of the moon denies an eclipse, unless the place of conjunction or opposition is within six degrees or less from the dragon.

It defines the criteria for total versus partial eclipses using "digits" as a measure of magnitude and the 12-degree rule for proximity to the nodes.</summary>
<keywords>lunar eclipse, solar eclipse, Dragon's head and tail, lunar nodes, celestial latitude, digits of eclipse, conjunction, opposition, medieval astronomy, orbital calculations</keywords>

# Mean Motion of Jupiter

<note>original heading: "Medius cursus Iovis." Mean motion refers to the average speed at which a planet travels, as if its orbit were a perfect circle. Astronomers used these tables to calculate a planet's approximate position before applying "equations" or corrections for its actual elliptical path.</note>

This specific table calculates the corrections for Jupiter's eccentricity and its position on its epicycle (the smaller circle its orbit follows).</note>

# Equations of Jupiter

<note>original heading: "Linee Hygeris" — likely a scribal or transcription error for "Lineae Numeri" (Lines of Numbers). In medieval astronomy, "Equations" are corrections applied to the average (mean) position of a planet to find its true position as seen from Earth. This table accounts for two main factors: the eccentricity of Jupiter's orbit and its position on its epicycle (a smaller circle used to explain planetary motion).</note>

<note>original: "Locus equantis n u o e r j. Centrum equantis n u o e r j." The string "n u o e r j" is a transcription of "numeri" (of the number), referring to the input value used to look up data in the table.</note>

### Saturn's altitude and the First Station of Mars
<note>original: "Saturni q d r Alactudo q q d r Martis Stand pma". The term "Alactudo" is a scribal variation of "Altitudo" (Altitude), referring to the planet's distance from Earth. "Stand pma" is "Statio prima" (First Station).</note>

### Center of the equation: greater natural [sum], lesser total; Jupiter’s decans.
<note>original: "centru equ. nalia maior guma do minor Iovis decennas". These headers describe the various corrections for the center of the planets' orbits. "Decennas" likely refers to "decanos" (decans), 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs, or perhaps "differentias" (differences).</note>

<note>Terminology Guide:
**Equation of the Center:** A mathematical correction to account for the fact that a planet's orbit is not a perfect circle around the Earth, but rather an eccentric path.
**Equation of the Argument:** A correction for the planet’s movement on its "epicycle" (a smaller circle it travels on while orbiting).
**Proportional Minutes:** Small values used to adjust the calculations based on the planet's varying distance from the Earth.
**Variation of Diameters:** (original: diver-cio omnor / diversitas diametrorum) This accounts for the apparent change in the size of the planet’s path (the epicycle) as it moves closer to or further from Earth.
**First Station:** The point in the sky where a planet appears to stop moving forward and prepares to begin "retrograde" (backward) motion.
**Sign:** A 30-degree division of the zodiac.
</note>

# The True Argument for the Years of the Lord
<note>The "True Argument" is a specific angle used in medieval astronomy to determine the position of a planet on its epicycle—the small circle it was thought to travel along while that circle itself moved around the Earth.</note>

Year of the World 5001: 32 [Signs], 5 [Degrees], 1 [Minute], 32 [Seconds] <note>original: "Anno mundi 5001". This provides the "radix" or starting position for calculations using the Anno Mundi (Year of the World) calendar epoch.</note>

# The Argument of Mercury in Collected Years <note>The "Argument" is a specific angle used in ancient astronomy to determine a planet's position on its epicycle. "Collected years" are large intervals of time used as shortcuts in calculation.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the planetary tables of Mercury found on the previous page to a foundational treatise on the construction of the astrolabe. The author identifies himself as Hermannus—almost certainly Hermannus Contractus (Hermann the Lame), an 11th-century monk of Reichenau who was instrumental in introducing Arabic astronomical instruments to the Latin West. This text focuses on the geometric layout (the 'measurement') of the instrument’s plates.</meta>

Hermann, the lowest of Christ’s poor and a follower of the students of philosophy—indeed, a follower slower than a snail. **B.** To his friend, flourishing in judgment, greetings. Since I have been frequently asked by many friends to attempt to write more fully the rules for the measurement of the astrolabe—which among us is found in common use only in an obscure and everywhere mutilated form—I have hitherto avoided this, partly because of the ignorance of my mind and partly because of a very difficult and, alas, too familiar laziness. At last, urged on most by your insistence, and with that same laziness and habit of delay finally set aside, I have applied my hand to the work with effort. I have not aimed for charm or an elegant composition of words, but rather for an explanation of the matter discovered. In this, if any lack of skill offends, let the kindly charity of friends indulge it everywhere, and let them attribute the whole fault to their own zeal, which placed a burden on a weak back that it could not bear. You therefore, my friend, however others may feel who read these writings of mine—since, as they say, it is fitting for anyone looking down on a simple thing—receive the measurement of the instrument, so that once you have learned something of its logic in this manner, you may then dare to investigate the whole with eager leisure.

From here, the measurement for the correction of the astrolabe must be carried out very precisely, for which the hours, that is, the plane sphere <note>original: "plana spera"</note> called the astrolabe, must first find the rules for the circles <note>In emendatione; the author is explaining the geometric "rules" for drawing the circles on the instrument.</note>. The middle of these, which represents the celestial equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>, according to the variety of the book as I understand it, requires four tables to be measured to one's liking. When these have been marked by diligent calculation, point **a** is the center, and points **b**, **c**, **d**, and **e** are marked. Point **b** represents the East; **c** is opposite to it; **d** is the North; and **e** is the South. From here, a ruler is applied, and a straight line is drawn from point **b** through **a** to **c**, from one end of the table to the other—that is, from the East...

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the celestial sphere or an astrolabe plate. A vertical line bisects the circle with 'd' at the top and 'e' at the bottom. A horizontal line bisects it with 'a' on the left and 'c' on the right. The center intersection point is labeled 'b'.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

...to the West. Likewise, draw another line from North to South through **d**, **a**, and **e**. These lines, which divide the sky into four parts, the Arabs call *alacon* or *alcaton* <note>Likely corruptions of the Arabic "al-qutr," meaning diameter.</note>; we maintain they are the colures <note>The colures are the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that pass through the poles.</note>. With these lines thus arranged, divide each quadrant of the circle into 15 equal parts. From here, one should take 18 parts from each side of **c** toward **d**. To do this more easily, divide each quadrant into three, so that each third contains 15 parts... <unclear>equial</unclear>... understand these clearly. From these, by the line through **a** and **b**, mark the points above and below. Thus between **c** and the points marked, a small note should be placed... if you prefer, points **d** and **r** are placed. From there, see the path where the line drawn from East to West through **b** and **a** touches the "sky," and mark it **h**. Fix the foot of the compass in **h**... and draw the circle of the winter solstice... between the points **e** and **g**... if you place it on the aforementioned line **b**, **a**, and **c**...

<margin>
climates <note>The "Climates" were seven latitudinal zones used by ancient and medieval geographers to divide the known world.</note>
1. 15
2. 18
3. 20
4. 26
5. 41
6. 45
7. 48
</margin>
With these circles thus found, whichever climate you wish to establish, look at the degrees of climatic altitude: for example, the first of the climates is 15. The second is 18. The third is 20. The fourth is 26. The fifth is 41. The sixth is 45. The seventh is 48. Take that many parts out of 15 from **a** and **c** toward the center... and likewise from **a** and **b** toward **d**. By these means you will have the climate you desire... by the same reasoning as the others... which reach toward **c**, which holds 15 degrees... and add 25, which it takes from the sixty... from that quadrant you will have the height...

# The Construction of the Spider

**P**repare the volvelle or "rete," which the Arabs call the **spider** <note>Original: *alancabuch*, from the Arabic *al-ankabut*. This is the filigreed top plate of the astrolabe that rotates to show the positions of the stars.</note>. It should first be fashioned from a plate somewhat thicker than the underlying discs. These are three in number, corresponding to the circles of the world: the equinoctial, and the winter and summer solstices. Upon this plate, straight lines are drawn called **colures** <note>The colures are two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles.</note>. One colure divides the other, directed from north to south. From the northern point, the summer circle is located at the inner limit, extending to the opposite point where it joins the winter circle in the south. In the middle, the circle of the **zodiac** is fixed, in which the whole effectiveness of the instrument shines forth. It is shaped so that it contains the smallest circle within itself. On one side it is joined, and on the opposite side it is united by a diameter. The middle circle and the other colure intersect at individual points, and through the line of the colure itself, it is divided into two hemispheres, though not equally. Within its suitable width, the names of the signs and certain stars may be inscribed as desired, in the spaces where the locations of those signs are found.

**T**he entry for measuring the circles is divided according to each seasonal part. Then, for each part of the circles and for the center of the three circles, the zodiac circle is placed. Where it cuts the circle at each position, a line is drawn that cuts the circle into spaces that are not equal. In one hemisphere, there are six signs from Aries to Libra, arranged from right to left in the world. In the larger space, there are likewise another six signs returning to Aries. Thus, from the equinoctial circle toward the summer circle, it encompasses Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. Then, turning back toward the equinoctial, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo decline. Furthermore, toward the winter circle, it turns through Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius; and returning toward the equinoctial, it rises through Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. On the instrument, between Sagittarius and Capricorn, a certain part of the circle projects outward, which is called the **pointer** <note>Original: *calculator*, often called the *almuri* in Arabic. it is a small tooth used to point to the degrees on the outer rim.</note> in Arabic, used to indicate the parts or degrees of the signs.

<column-break/>

This same zodiac is divided into parts of the sky, following the individual parts and fractions down to the center of the circles. Then the zodiac is placed above, and according to where it touches, the signs are marked. In each sign, there are 72 effective intervals <note>The text describes a specific geometric division where 72 intervals of 5 degrees each account for the 360 degrees of the entire celestial circle.</note> encompassing the 360 degrees of the whole sky.

## It remains afterwards that the surface of the back-plate
should be measured and marked with all the degrees of the zodiac, the signs, and the days of the year. When the outer edges of the heavens have been equated by four lines drawn through the center, you should distinguish the measurements of the circle as described before. Namely, each quadrant should be divided into intervals, so that the instrument is complete. Each of these should be divided into degrees, which together complete 360.

Under these, in the first interval of the heavens, the signs are distributed in each quadrant and inscribed with their names. Starting from the western line and moving toward the southern perpendicular line, the heaven is linked: this area contains **Taurus** and **Gemini**. From there to the eastern left: **Cancer**, **Leo**, and **Virgo**. From there to the north: **Libra**, **Scorpio**, and **Sagittarius**. And from there back to the west: **Capricorn**, **Aquarius**, and **Pisces**. Thus, each sign is given thirty degrees, totaling the 360 degrees of the celestial wheel.

Under these, another interval of the heavens is drawn, where the signs are distributed according to their beginnings. Under these again, the days of the year are divided, with five additional days added to make a full year. This makes the calculation easy. From one quadrant of the heaven, exclude fifteen parts. Divide the rest of the hollow into twenty, and each of those into four. Thus, you will find 71 intervals in total, which when multiplied by five, gives the circle divided into 365 days. You will then begin the calculation from the vernal equinox, which is currently believed to be at the first degree of Aries, on the 15th day before the **Kalends of April** <note>March 18th. This aligns the solar calendar with the zodiacal year.</note>, and so on...

The paths proceed in the same manner as the fixed stars in their established signs. Furthermore, for the most certain calculation of the hours of the night, their artificial threads are used with the approximation of the calculations and the imagination <note>original: "iūginatio", likely "imaginatio"; referring to the mental projection of celestial circles onto a flat surface</note> which is fixed so that the small vessel is led toward the wandering <term>errā: referring to the planets or "wandering stars"</term> by reading the clock with a prudent mind, lest the measurement of the light depart from the truth. The calculation of the instrument's change is that which is for the clocks of the calculations according to the rules of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work formed the basis of medieval astronomy</note>; some things are more abundant than others, and it is superfluous to navigate through them all. But we speak to those seeking the power of the parts; they are not so numerous as to be unnumbered. All the following names, or other northern ones, are distinct in the "ear of the heart" <note>a metaphorical phrase meaning to hold something firmly in one's memory</note> so that they may be held tenaciously. On a small, flat, or convex surface, one should be prepared to discover them. These things are thus provided, not by the negligence of the architects or those of mechanical reason, concerning the space of those things and their names; lest I offend by writing too much, I shall speak briefly, so that no stain may fill the page.

The **Walzacora** <term>Walzacora: an early medieval term for the astrolabe's plate or tympanum</term> is a table shaped to the roundness of the heaven, with the measure of equal spaces on each surface, which presents the lines of the diameters through the center itself. It shows the columns with the northern tract included, leading to the center in the depiction of the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: the "circle of animals" or the path the sun follows through the constellations</term>, dividing the sea where the wall of the few captures passes through. When the spirit takes this up, let it select some of the intersections of the lines. Of these lines, the one at point **b** is called **almaldeb** <note>original: "almaldebc"; from the Arabic al-mashriq, meaning the East</note>, the eastern line from the rising of the stars and the day. The outer line at **u** is **almagrip** <note>original: "almagri"; from the Arabic al-maghrib, meaning the West</note>, the western line from the setting of the stars and the day. And that line which divides the East from the West, since it is designated in the first solar rising as a ray or the shadow of the **gnomon** <term>gnomon: the part of a sundial or instrument that casts a shadow</term>, is the upper line or **alstebre** <note>original: "alstēbrē"; referring to the meridian line</note> of the Walzacora; this is the meridian line, because by ascending to the marked point **y**, it effectively brings the hour of midday, and by descending toward the setting, it begins to urge onward. The lower line at **e**, however, is called **carazeuzel** <note>from the Arabic "ka'b al-uzal", referring here to the line of the nadir or midnight</note>, the line of qualities or the immediate appearance. And that line which extends from midday to the North, since the ray of the sun or the shadow of the gnomons is interpreted as the summer solstice, designates the hand of the flat plate of the circle of the Zodiac.

<column-break/>

The circles of the heaven are attributed to it, one of which is placed in the middle by the equinoctial calculation, marking the sign of **Aries** and **Libra** without deviation; this is called the **equinoctial** <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator, where day and night are of equal length</term> because in its presence the spaces of light and night are equal. It is also called the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the path of the sun</term>; when the sun and moon meet here, they are both subject to an eclipse. And from the two boundaries, one lower circle of the heaven is forced into a lower center, which, according to the observed rule, is narrower because the center is in the vicinity and requires caution. This is called the summer circle for the rest of the singers <note>likely a poetic or technical reference to those who observe the stars</note>. In the outer expansion of the table, in the hollow, the circle of **Capricorn**, or the winter solstice, is inscribed. By these means, the likeness of the celestial sphere is arranged. They include the latitude of the sign-bearer <note>the Zodiac</note> and the heaven, as well as the solstices of the planets with their light. This is from the remote orb in the northern region, positioned with artificial skill as the **hoztaralzatad** <note>likely a corruption of an Arabic term for the horizon line</note> at point **u**. Short lines of the hours are established with partitions of equal intervals, so that the narrowness of the intersections may be seen from the center according to the latitude. The middle line is the diagonal line of either midday. With each degree and similar things, it is doubled, and the limit of the **12 hours** is established for us; they are denoted individually by their Arabic names, which are seen written below in this formula:

The delineation of these hours, whether before midday or after midday, is marked for the sake of calculation. It demonstrates the winter observations when the **horoscope** <term>horoscope: here meaning the ascendant or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> is applied. In the upper middle region, circles shine forth, machined with artificial industry, which are called **alnicantaraz** <note>original: "alnicantaraz"; the Almucantars, or circles of altitude above the horizon</term>. These are solved through frequent hollowing and turning; some are for the "wanderers" <note>planets</note> and others for the quarters, crowned by a certain and necessary location in which the great efficacy of this instrument consists. In their intersections, the degrees of the ascent and descent of the sun are administered, and the miracle is doubled, being revealed by the sign of the number ten. These [lines] through the devotion of the days... the summer signs terminate in the **equinoctial line**. Much higher... and the depressed autumn days, through expanded devotion, pertain to coming to the **solstice of Capricorn**. This reduces it by the winter devotion of the remaining sign. In this part of the heaven, the diligence of the wood <note>likely referring to the material of a master model or the "limbs" of the instrument</note> distinguishes it. This sign also distinguishes the parts into five intervals; which, given six, the third part devours three in order through the gradient of the **zodiac** to fulfill the number... which the sharp engineers directed here. Which, being placed in the right places, notes the stars, through which I may know the hours of the night. This is inscribed with **Arabic** names. In the roundness of its face... placed over Capricorn... and by calculating the sum of the various inequalities... the polished surface shows the hours, which is called the **calculated [circles]** <gloss>i. calculated</gloss> <note>original: "almi"; likely an abbreviation for *almichantarat*</note>... through the rotation of the plates. ... it reaches the back of the earth... the measure of the signs... for the sake of the inscription... through the linear division of arithmetic. This denotes the zodiac through the square. ... You also have the **alidade** <gloss>i. the sighting bar</gloss> <note>original: "alehidada"; the pivoting rule on the back of the instrument used for measuring the altitude of the sun or stars</note> which we call the ray. This is extended like a rule over the plate. At its ends are two upright pinnules <note>original: "se pine", likely *pinnulae*; sighting vanes</note> for catching the ray of the sun and the stars. ... these holes demonstrate the altitude of the sun... there is also the **axis** <gloss>i. the round bolt</gloss> <note>original: "alarob"; the central pin or "horse" that holds all the plates together</note>...

...perforated in the middle to [fasten] and mark the plates of the **climates** <term>climates: geographical zones based on latitude, each requiring a specific plate on the astrolabe</term>. Its infinite usefulness is provided to anyone... which is called the **alpharaz** <note>original: "alpharaz"; from the Arabic *al-faras*, meaning "horse"</note>, that is, it is called the "horse" because it is shaped in the likeness of a horse. Again, there is a bright part... except for one triangle, concerning which I will speak in its own place whenever you wish: if the bolt clings to the inner parts, or if the paths to the [outer parts] are unknotted; for their utility, nothing is lacking to this account. If however the reader understands what has been said or is to be said... he will find that all things have been arranged with sufficient diligence. Therefore, by completing these notes in the treatises, so that I may speak with certainty, I will first speak of the **artificial hours** <term>artificial hours: also known as unequal or seasonal hours; these divide the daylight and night into 12 equal parts regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" is longer in summer than in winter</term> of the day and night.

<column-break/>

If, dearest one, you desire to know the hours of the day, or the artificial hours of the day and night, it is necessary first that you know in which sign the sun is, and in which **decan** <term>decan: a subdivision of a zodiac sign, representing ten degrees of the 30-degree sign</term> or degree of that same sign. Indeed, the calculator should know these things through similar reasoning... as I write here at the beginning, [the sun is] not in autumn... and thus it is held in the Arabic fashion. These signs are placed on one side with the names of the months set forth. Next to them, the days of the months are listed by number. In the middle of its face, the signs of the whole zodiac of heaven are arranged by degrees... so that in this way you may find the degree in which the sun is for any day. In the [inner] part, look for the line and the number for that degree; consider that sign to be where the sun resides.

**I**f you wish to know, for any day of the present month, what [degree of the zodiac] to assign to it, add 15 to the sum. Take the total collected and search from the first **degree** <term>degree: one of the 360 divisions of the celestial circle; each zodiac sign contains 30 degrees</term> of the sign pertaining to that month through the aforementioned intervals; then you will discover in what degree the sun will be. For example: if 15 days of April have passed, add 15, and by calculating the total, begin to count from the first degree of **Aries** <note>In the medieval calendar, the sun was often calculated as entering Aries in mid-March, making the first degree of Aries align roughly with the start of April in some simplified systems.</note>, which is the 1st of April, and by counting you will arrive at the 15th degree of **Taurus**. For if from Aries 15 [you add] 15, there will remain 15 of Taurus; and you will lead the method appropriately so that on that day of April the sun is in the 15th degree of Taurus.

**T**hrough the astrolabe, moreover, one will know it skillfully on its flat or solid sphere, [calculating] the days of the months and the proportions of the wood. Place the **alhidada** <term>alhidada: the pivoting sighting bar on the back of the astrolabe used for measuring the altitude of the sun or stars</term> over the present day (that is, the one you are seeking) to find the degree. Then, with the tip of the alhidada over the 15th day of April, it will mark the 15th degree of Taurus. Note that degree in its place on the other side in the **alancabuch** <term>alancabuch: from the Arabic *al-ʿankabūt*, meaning "the spider." This is the "rete," the rotating openwork plate that serves as a star map.</term>.

**A**t this point it must be advised that for any calculator, nothing [is achieved] unless the elevation of the **quadrant** <term>quadrant: an instrument for measuring angles up to 90 degrees, often engraved on the back of the astrolabe</term> of the world is solved.

...let it be done as if from right to left. For the southern <unclear>caldatura</unclear> or by calculating <unclear>it is proceeded</unclear> in this way.

**T**he degree of the sun having been thus found and marked in the **alancabuch**, the **nadair** <term>nadair: from the Arabic *nazīr*, meaning the "nadir" or the point diametrically opposite the sun on the zodiac circle</term> (that is, the opposite of the sun) ought to be found. This we call the <unclear>colcopon</unclear>, measured through the diameter of the sphere from sign to sign. From the sign of the sun, [move] through the whole fourth sign <note>The text suggests finding the point 180 degrees away; for example, if the sun is in Aries, the nadir is in Libra.</note>... it is correctly called the <unclear>achur</unclear>. Having found it thus, with the 15 days of April passed, place the **nadair** of the sun's degree (already marked in the **alancabuch**) over the lowest **almicancharath** <term>almicancharath: from the Arabic *al-muqanṭarāt*, these are the altitude circles or "horizons" engraved on the plates of the astrolabe</term> or upon the eastern line. While the previous page likely introduced the components, this page focuses on the practical application: measuring the sun's altitude to determine the time of day and using the stars for the same purpose at night.</meta>

<margin>
The <term>alidade</term> <note>The pivoting bar on the back of the astrolabe used for sighting.</note>

...just as the day closes. Indeed, it is the same and equal to the last part of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, following the sun's path.</note> that passes through the celestial <term>horizon</term> <note>The circle where the sky meets the earth.</note>, which can be determined by an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>A portable tool used by medieval astronomers to tell time and solve problems related to the positions of the sun and stars.</note>. Once these things are found, carefully record the notation for the day and night. For by the careful administration of these, all other things will easily be made clear.

Because from this one may know the hours of the day, one must find the altitude of the <term>sun</term>, which in Arabic they call the <term>elevation and height</term> <note>original: "astrabam et hemath"</note>, at whatever hour you wish. Here, moreover, the altitude of the sun is measured as it rises from its lowest point at dawn, gradually moving by the momentum of the world, ascending to the higher spaces of the heaven and then descending to the lower parts. For while it still shines, it proceeds from the east. If the <term>astrolabe</term> is held correctly, you will see the line of the <term>alidade</term> moved toward the east so that the sun's light passes through both sighting holes. From there, it visits the higher altitudes until it reaches the meridian line, and then it descends toward the west. In this way, the altitude of the sun for any hour is found through this hanging instrument.

Having taken up the <term>astrolabe</term> and holding it firmly, oppose it to the sun so that it hangs evenly by its ring in your right hand. With the back face of the <term>astrolabe</term> toward you, move the <term>alidade</term> diligently, looking through the sighting holes until the sun's rays pass perfectly through both holes. Once this is done carefully, observe the scale on the outer edge, counting the degrees from the eastern line to where the <term>alidade</term> points. This number is the total altitude of the <term>sun</term>. Record this number faithfully in your memory, then turn to the front face of the <term>astrolabe</term> and find that same number of the sun's altitude among the <term>almucantars</term> <note>The lines or circles of altitude engraved on the astrolabe's plate.</note>. You must start from the first one. If it is morning, look on the eastern side; if it is afternoon, look on the western side. Once found, place the position of the <term>sun</term> on the <term>rete</term> <note>original: "alhacabuch" — the "spider" or star-map part of the astrolabe.</note> upon that altitude.

<column-break/>

In that region, consider the <term>nadir</term> <note>original: "nadair" — the point diametrically opposite a position on the celestial sphere.</note> to find the corresponding hour. That is the present hour which you seek. Similarly, for every individual hour of the day, whether in summer or winter, the time is found by this same reasoning of the intervals. This is most worthy for the celebration of the Divine Office <note>The daily cycle of prayers and psalms recited by monks and clergy at specific times.</note> and is an extremely useful science for men. For all things proceed properly when the soul, with due reverence, judges the hours under a just rule that can never fail. By this, the Lord's work is performed without shadow.

Having thus acquired the hours of the day with care, the holy duty of the divine work requires the investigation of the altitude of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>The stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the planets.</note> to indicate the nocturnal hours. First, the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "horoskop" — the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> must be lowered. Just as the hours of the day are found through the solar altitude, so the hours of the night are found through the fixed stars. In this place, I advise those who know the holy science of the stars to include the names of the stars. But here, let the student labor so as not to be confused by too many names; the more you practice, the clearer these things will become. To take the altitude of any star: lift the <term>astrolabe</term> and adjust the <term>alidade</term> until you see the chosen star appearing through both sighting holes of the instrument. Once the altitude is demonstrated by the <term>alidade</term>, find that same altitude among the <term>almucantars</term> for that star. Having found this on the <term>almucantar</term>, place the star's marker upon it, and the degree of the sun will then show the hour. But observe this: the <term>nadir</term> of the sun indicates the hours of the day, while the degree of the sun indicates the hours of the night.

There are four quarters of the world, of which one, the North, never receives the sun. The other three—the East, the West, and the South—admit the sun, and the hours are distributed among them in four groups. These four quarters yield the hours: the East yields 1, 2, 3, and 4; the South yields 5, 6, 7, and 8; and the West yields 9, 10, 11, and 12. Thus, two hours are always under one number or measure, except for the 6th and the 12th.

--- Page 90 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical manual for the astrolabe, moving from measuring the sun's altitude to the specific methods for calculating and converting between unequal (temporal) hours and equinoctial (fixed) hours using the instrument's components like the nadir and almucantars.</meta>

For just as the highest point of the sun is taken from the earth to the sky, so the 24 parts <note>The 24 hours of a full day-night cycle.</note> of the descending weights cannot be joined or equated in a stable way. For if one is placed in the summer... the moon is seen in its setting positioned in the west.

**H**itherto he has arranged the <term>artificial hours</term> <note>Also called "unequal" or "temporal" hours. These were calculated by dividing the period of daylight into 12 equal parts, meaning an "hour" in summer was much longer than an "hour" in winter.</note>; next I shall speak of the <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>Fixed hours of 60 minutes each, where 24 hours always equal one full rotation of the sky.</note> which the twelve-fold heaven traverses. I will explain how to change the unequal into the equal, or the equal into the unequal. If you wish to know how many hours are found in this entire heaven, divide the half-circle <note>The 180 degrees of the visible sky.</note> by the 24 equinoctial hours, so that each hour contains 15 degrees. Indeed, in the full rotation of 24 equinoctial hours, there are 360 degrees. For when the sphere has revolved once, a total of 24 hours are found for the day and night. If, however, you seek how many unequal hours are made, give to each eleven or twelve parts, and you will find in the whole sky 24 hours. The equinoctial hours are only equal to the artificial hours on two days in the year: when the sun is in the first part of <term>Aries</term> or <term>Libra</term> <note>The Spring and Autumn Equinoxes, when day and night are of equal length.</note>. Furthermore, the computation of the unequal hours is shortened or lengthened by the change of the seasons. This variation is always in our view... For in the shortest days there are no more than 9 parts <note>degrees</note> for an hour, but in the longest no more than 15. These hours increase or decrease according to the equinoctial parts.

**S**i you wish to know the <term>unequal hours</term> of the day, place the <term>nadir</term> <note>The point on the zodiac directly opposite the sun's current position.</note> of the sun upon the first line of the hours. Having done this, carefully mark the part that is shown on the back... then move the nadir to the last

<column-break/>

line of those hours, and whatever parts are indicated below the limits, those are considered to be the total parts in the middle of the hours of the day.

**S**i you wish to know with the <term>nadir</term> of the sun placed upon the degree of the first line of any hour, denote the assigned place; here, having rotated to the last part, it designates how many parts are contained. But be careful to see whether the part for the diurnal <note>daytime</note> hours is said by the nadir, or the part for the total nocturnal <note>nighttime</note> hours is said by the degree of the sun itself.

**A**nd if you wish to know from the diurnal hour parts how many remain for the night, subtract the number from 24, and what remains will be the total for the nocturnal hours. Or if you subtract from the 24 nocturnal hours, the remainder will be the diurnal parts... as was said below.

**W**hen, however, you wish to calculate the equinoctial hours of the day or night, or how many equinoctial parts are necessary for a day hour, you must first investigate the length of the day and night. I say the length of the day is from the first rising of the sun until its setting, along with the revolution of the sphere. You will find it thus: place the degree of the sun upon the first <term>almucantar</term> <note>Circles of altitude engraved on the astrolabe plate.</note> in the eastern part, and carefully mark the location. Once marked, turn the degree of the sun to the last almucantar in the western part, and mark that location again. The distance from the first location to the end of the location... tells the length of the day. The night is found by the <term>nadir</term> of the sun. For as the day is found by the degree of the sun, so the night is found by the nadir of the sun. When you wish to know how many equinoctial hours there are, divide the length of the day from the first point to the second by 15 <note>Since each 15 degrees equals one equinoctial hour.</note>.

# Here begins the book of Alfraganus on Astronomy.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'N' (or stylized 'I') in red, blue, and green inks, featuring internal floral patterns and a long vertical stem with foliate scrollwork extending into the left margin.</image-desc>The number of Arab and Latin months is 12. But the Arabs begin from Muharram <note>original: "almuharam"; the first month of the Islamic lunar calendar</note>, which has 30 days. The second is Safar <note>original: "saphar"</note>, with 29 days. And thus they alternate through the months: one being 30 days, the next 29. Because of this, the total days of the year are 354 <note>This describes the Lunar Hijri year</note>. To account for the fractions of the day that accumulate, they add 11 days over a cycle of 30 years. Thus, the portion for one year becomes 354 days and roughly one-fifth and one-sixth of a day <note>original: "v · xi · partium"; referring to the 11/30 fraction used in leap year calculations</note>. This results in some years being "perfect" (leap years) and others "imperfect." The number of these days is not taken by the movement of the sun, but by the conjunction of the sun and moon <note>the New Moon</note> through their mean motion and the sighting of the new crescent moon, by which the month increases or diminishes. Because it is possible for two "perfect" months to succeed one another, they do not strictly follow the count but rely on the sighting of the moon...

It should be known that the Arab day, by which they number their months, begins at the setting of the sun. For example, the first day of the week <note>Sunday</note> begins when the sun sets on the day of the Sabbath <note>Saturday</note>. They begin from the sunset and end at the sunset. The Arabs have placed one day and its night together starting from the hour of sunset, because they take their months from the hour the moon appears, and the hour of the moon's appearing is always following the sunset. This is different from the Romans and others who live in the regions where the sighting of the new moon is not used; for them, the day with its night is from the rise of the sun until the next rise. Thus, the Arabs take their months from the moon, and others from the sun. The account of the years and months of the Egyptians and other nations is different...

<column-break/>

...and is treated elsewhere.

No division exists among the wise but that the heaven is in the likeness of a sphere <note>original: "sphaera"; Alfraganus here asserts the medieval consensus on a spherical earth and universe</note>, and that it revolves with all the stars that are in it. This sphere turns upon two immobile poles <note>the North and South celestial poles</note> which indicate the center of the world. All the stars rise in the east, elevated little by little in a uniform order in their motions according to the size of their bodies and their distance from one another, until they reach the middle of the heaven <note>the meridian</note>. From there, descending, they seek the west in that same order, moving with an equal speed. Some stars are direct <note>aligned</note> with others. The measure of their velocity and distance is not divided, as if they were moved within the sphere by one single rotation. This is proven by the signs of the heavens and the rotation of the stars... and the observations of the astronomers. Two stars that are seen... whether they be stars of the first magnitude or smaller... those stars revolve in circles... and even if they are moved in a greater or lesser circle in the heaven, their motion is relative to the magnitude of the heaven. The distance from the same point... until it reaches the same distance from that point... those stars which set... it is known that the stars... follow the same point... falling from the greater to the lesser... until it rises again. Therefore, the stars follow the same longitude... and revolve with the sphere. From this it is manifest to all that the heaven is like a sphere and that its rotation is like the rotation of a sphere. And this heaven is neither light nor heavy, but is elevated...

Because in the parts of heaven, the parts that are directly above our heads <note>the zenith</note> would be closer to us than those further away at the edge of the hemisphere, which would be at a greater distance. It should be judged that the sun, moon, and other stars at the time of their rising appear small because of their distance from our sight. Therefore, it would cease as they approached the middle of heaven <note>the zenith</note>, at which time they would be closer to our sight. And if they were seen in this way, in their descent they would gradually fall from our sight until they were hidden from view. We see that however they are when they rise, they appear larger when they set than when in the middle of heaven. And we see the sun at the time of its setting to be larger. The knowledge of its body in the middle of the hemisphere is small compared to when the end of its body sets. The same is true for the moon. The truth regarding the appearance of their magnitude in the east and west is not because they are closer to us than in the middle of heaven. It is because of the vapors which rise from the earth; here, as they fall into our sight in the distance of our atmosphere at the beginning of the hemisphere, it shows that they appear larger to us because they fall into air filled with many humid vapors, more so than in the middle of the day. Although for the moon and the sun many volumes have taken up this speech—that in setting it is of one magnitude—it is deceptive to say otherwise. Although there may be something else in the depths which might be seen clearly, the sight is deceived by the quantity of the distance. For the more clear the air is, the deeper the reason; and therefore the sight is better seen in the heavens.
