Because in the parts of heaven, the distance from us would not be uniform, as the part of heaven which is directly above our heads would be closer to us than that which is further away at the edge of the hemisphere, which would be at a greater distance. It must be judged that the sun, moon, and other stars at the time of their rising appear small <note>original: "modica"</note> because of their distance from our sight. Therefore, this effect would cease as they approached the middle of heaven <note>the zenith</note>, at which time they would be closer to our sight. And if it were so, in their descent they would gradually fade from our sight until they were hidden from view. But this is not the case at all; rather, we see them appearing differently when they rise, when they are in the middle of heaven, and they set with the same magnitude. We see that however great they are when they rise, in the coming of their setting they are larger than in the middle of heaven. We see the sun at the time of its setting is larger. Indeed, its body in the middle of the hemisphere appears smaller before the end of its body sets. The same is true for the moon. The truth regarding the increased magnitude of these bodies in the east and west is not because they are closer to us than when in the middle of heaven. Instead, it is because of the vapors which rise from the earth; as these enter our sight through the length of our atmosphere at the edge of the hemisphere, it shows that their quantity appears larger to us because they fall into air containing much humidity, more so than in the middle of the day. Although for the moon and the sun many books have discussed this—how at setting they are of a certain size—it is a deception to say otherwise. Although there may be something in the depths that can be seen clearly, the sight is affected by the quantity of the atmosphere's length. For the more clear the air, the deeper the vision; and therefore the sight is better in the heavens.

The wise have also agreed that the Earth is in the middle <note>the center of the universe</note> of the heavenly spheres. The cause of the Earth's shape being like a round sphere is shown by the fact that the sun, moon, and stars do not rise or set for all people at the same time. If the Earth were flat, they would rise for those in the east at the same time as for those in the west. This is also apparent from events that happen in the upper air, which occur differently in various regions of the Earth. For example, a lunar eclipse <note>original: "eclypsis lune"</note> which is the darkening of its light; in different regions, such as the east and the west, it is found that the eastern eclipse is seen at an earlier hour than the eclipse in the west. It is found that in the regions to the east, it is later...

for these hours of the night:

<column-break/>

...according to the quantity of the space which exists between both regions in longitude. It indicates that the increase of hours in the eastern region, which happens only there before its setting in the western region, shows that the distance between the two regions is great. It is found that the hours of the eastern regions are more than the hours of the western regions. It is found that this diversity exists across the entire habitable region of the Earth between the east and the west. This is also found regarding the quantity of space between locations far removed from each other between the north <note>original: "septentrionale"</note> and the south <note>original: "meridiem"</note>. For those who move between the north and the south, it is found that certain stars which were visible at one time are now hidden, and others which were hidden now appear; this happens in order as one moves.

<margin>The Church</margin>
It is demonstrated that the entire surface of the Earth is round. If the Earth were flat, this would not happen. As was said, the rising of the stars would be at one time across all parts of the Earth. Furthermore, for those traveling between the north and the south, the stars would not be hidden or appear in the order that they do.

<margin>Something</margin>
It can also be proven that the Earth is in the middle of heaven <note>the center of the universe</note> by the observation of the stars. The distance of each star from any part of the Earth is found to be universal in longitude. That there is an equal distance between the heaven and the earth in all parts of the earth proves that the Earth is in the middle of heaven. It is manifest that if the Earth were not in the middle of heaven, it would be closer to some parts of the heavens than others. One who lived in a place closer to the heavens would always see less than half of the sky, and one who lived in a place far from the heavens would always see more than half. But in every part of the Earth, six signs <note>the zodiac signs</note> are always visible above the horizon and six are always hidden. From this, it is understood that the Earth is like a point <term>point (puncti)</term><note>A standard medieval argument that the Earth is mathematically insignificant in size compared to the vastness of the firmament.</note> in relation to the heavens. Because if it were of great size relative to the heavens, one would not see exactly half of the sky from every part of the Earth.

And we see indeed that because of what appears from the sky, the middle of the earth's surface is never filled by any sensible division from it. <note>The author is arguing that the Earth is so small compared to the heavens that it can be treated as a geometric point with no measurable width.</note> Let it be indicated here that on the surface of the earth there is no sensible division. And a similar thing holds that in the sea, a point exists, and its significance is never such that in the sea there is a sensible quantity compared to the quantity of the heaven. Again, how should it be understood that the space of the earth is as a single point in proportion to the space of the heaven? It is either the whole or in certain divisions of the accounts of the quantity of the number of stars, for the smaller stars of the heaven are among the stars which appear to the sight to be either larger or smaller than the earth; [yet] every star of the heaven appears as a point in the sky. How much more so is the body of the earth, which in the number of stars is as nothing compared to the body of the heaven? Now, what is clear from these things we have said is that the earth is in the middle of the world <note>original: "in medio mundi"; here "world" refers to the entire universe or cosmos</note> as a point of the heaven. Again, the cause must be divided, and besides all this, consider the air in relation to the quantity of the earth as it is to the heaven: as the quantity of a point is to the heaven.

Since the narrative has been permitted to suggest the heaven and the earth by recounting what is seen from the house of the heaven, let us say that the beginnings of the motions that are seen in the heaven are two. The first is that which moves the whole, through which it is said that the sun and moon and the remaining stars revolve, rising from the east to the west in the motion of day and night once in a single, equal, and swift revolution upon two axes, which are named the axes of the first motion. One of these is the northern [axis], which I have made mention of in the preceding sections; it rules the world and follows either nature or the way stars are carried in the heavens in a straight line by the revolving of this motion. This heaven is called the heaven of the equinox of the day <note>The Celestial Equator</note>, and by this singular first motion, the space of the heaven is shown through the middle, or its length from both [poles] is in one quantity. It is called the heaven of the equinox of the day because when the sun stays upon it, the day and night are equal in every land for all inhabitants. The second motion is that which is seen of all the planets from the west to the east, which, besides the first motion, moves upon two other axes departing from those of the first motion. This is called the heaven of the zodiac <note>original: "celum zodiaci"</note>, as its distance from these extreme poles is of one quantity. This is the heaven of the second motion, or the heaven of the signs <note>The Ecliptic</note>, because it describes its whole motion from west to east; and we see its parts divided into equal portions which are called "signs." The names of these are Aries, Taurus, and so on. Each sign is divided into 30 degrees of the heaven, totaling 360 degrees, and each degree is divided into minutes, and so forth.

<column-break/>

The circle of the signs [crosses] the heaven of the equinox of the day at two opposite points; it declines from it toward the north and the south by an equal quantity. The point at which the sun is seen to ascend into the north from the equinox of the day is called the equinoctial point, which is in the sign of Aries. That point upon which it turns from the north toward the south is called the autumnal equinoctial point, which is in the sign of Libra. There are also northern signs from the equinox of the day, which are from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo <note>OCR: "lgiñ", likely Virgo</note>. Likewise, there are southern signs which are from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces. A zone is marked in the circle in latitude, directed from the north toward the south, extending upon both poles of the circles, and this whole description is lined upon both poles of the circles. From this, each of the heavens—namely the heaven of the equinox of the day and the heaven of the signs—is divided through the middle. Necessarily, the heaven of the signs is marked according to three points, which are at the final declination and length from the equinox of the day toward the north and the south. The point is called the summer solstitial point because it is in the sign of Cancer; the southern one is called the winter solstitial point because it is in the sign of Capricorn. These are connected by a line through the heaven to the equinoctial line and the solstitial point. The distance from the solstitial point directly to the equinox of the day is the quantity of the declination of the heaven of signs from the equinox of the day. This comes to <insert>23</insert> degrees and 33 minutes. This most certain measurement, which Almeon <note>Likely referring to the astronomers under Caliph Al-Ma'mun, such as Alfraganus, whose measurements were standard in the Middle Ages</note> proved, he spoke of according to his own faithful calculations... <insert>23</insert> degrees and 33 minutes. Now it is clear from these things we have said that besides this, the earth revolves <note>meaning the planets/sun revolve relative to it</note> upon the axes of the heaven of signs from west to east through its primary middle. But the first motion revolves them and the rest from east to west in the same way, because the axes of the equinox of the day are immovable, while the axes of the heaven of signs are moved by the first motion according to the equinox of the day, being inseparable from it, based on the circle described upon both axes of each heaven.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical discussion from the previous section, moving from the general division of the celestial sphere to the specific effects of solar declination on different "climates" or latitudes of the Earth. It focuses on the changing length of days and nights as the sun moves between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</meta>

Likewise, whatever occurs within one climate and for those places positioned directly along the same distance <note>latitude</note> from the equinox <note>the celestial equator</note>, the same effects are seen. If there is a great deviation in one place, or a smaller deviation in another as it approaches the equinox of the sky, it follows from what we have said that when the sun is in any of the equinoctial points, day and night will be equal across the entire earth. On that day and at midnight, the sun is in the part of the sky that divides the hemisphere into two equal halves.

When the sun is in the northern signs, the day will be longer than the night. The further it is removed from the equinox toward the north, the more the day increases over the night until it reaches its maximum distance from the equinox at the beginning of Cancer <note>the Summer Solstice</note>. Conversely, in the southern signs, the opposite of what we have said occurs: the day is shorter than the night, and its brevity increases until the sun is at the very bottom in Capricorn <note>the Winter Solstice</note>. There, the shortness of the day and the length of the night are completed according to the two celestial circles positioned directly opposite, just as the distance from the equinox is measured. 

For those living under these conditions, the quantity of the day for one is equal to the quantity of the night for the other. Thus, the longest day when the sun is in the beginning of Cancer is equal to the longest night when the sun is at the beginning of Capricorn. Similarly, the night of Cancer is equal to the day of Capricorn. This is the universal rule for all habitable places on earth.

Now, since we have narrated the properties of habitable locations in relation to the equinoctial sky, we should consider those who live in these places. At the equinox, the whole sky is elevated... <margin>declination of the zodiac</margin> ...the sun passes over the zenith <note>original: "centrum capitis", literally "center of the head"</note> once in a year. The distance of the zenith from the equinox is less than the declination of Cancer from it. In both cases, there are two places where the declination from the equinox is equal to the altitude of the stars. When the sun is in one of these two places,

<column-break/>

it passes directly over the zenith. When it moves into the northern region, which is our area, the signs of the zodiac pass toward the north of the zenith in those places where the altitude of the stars is equal to the declination of the zodiac. There, the sun passes over the zenith once a year, specifically when it is at the beginning of Cancer. In all other places where the pole is elevated further than the declination of the zodiac, the sun never passes directly over the zenith, but always passes toward the south. 

The greater the altitude <note>latitude</note> of the region, the more the sun is depressed from the zenith toward the south. The summer sunrise is removed from the winter sunrise, and the length of the day increases over those other days. If one reaches the places where the pole is elevated above the horizon by an amount equal to the distance of Capricorn and Cancer from the equator—which is 66 degrees and 33 minutes <note>the Arctic Circle</note>—the zenith's distance from the equinox is equal to the distance of the zodiac signs from it. 

In their rotation, the signs of the zodiac pass over the zenith. In the case of Cancer, it remains visible above the earth for a long time. When the sun is in that sign, it is day, and there is a 12-hour period where there is no night. Conversely, when it is in the beginning of Capricorn, there is a night of 12 hours <note>or "a full unit of time"</note> and no day. This occurs because the signs of the zodiac are tilted relative to the hemisphere. We find that Cancer is in the northern hemisphere and Capricorn is in the southern hemisphere. 

When the signs of the zodiac recede from the zenith, they move through the hemisphere through the middle... half of the zodiac signs rise in the east and sink in the west. One would see six signs at one time, from the beginning of Capricorn to the end of Gemini, and similarly the remaining six signs would set. If anyone wishes to know the zenith of these places succeeding each other until the completion of the earth, he shall know the altitude of the pole above the celestial hemisphere is equal to the distance of Cancer from the equator.

# Ascensions <note>original: "alcidiot," likely a corruption of the Arabic 'al-maṭāli’' meaning ascensions</note>

<margin>
It is by the quantity that is divided by the **direct circle** <note>The celestial equator</note> through four parts toward the middle of its signs from the **equinox** <note>The point where the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night equal</note>. The sign of the non-declining ones is equal to the **ascension** <note>original: "alcoit"</note> when it is reduced by one ascension in the **oblique** <note>original: "declinis"</note> manner.
</margin>

From the quantity of the equinoctial day, namely a quarter, which is divided into the four points of the world's **direct circle** <note>The Right Sphere, where the equator is vertical to the horizon</note>; along with the circle of **Libra** and **Capricorn**. The parts of the quarters are those of the dividers, namely the middle of their term, which teaches the visible width of all two arcs of equal signs at that point from the equinox. There are four visible **ascensions** <note>original: "alcoit"</note> of their non-declining signs; their terms are equal in the **oblique** <note>original: "declinis"</note> manner. The ascension is equal to the mid-points of the terms of the signs. With this, however, so that the width of both arcs of the signs <unclear>is equal</unclear> from each side, one of them has a point that is decreased and its ascension is increased by one—namely, the ascension of the arc following **Aries** in the oblique manner of the ascension <gloss>which follows</gloss> its own in the **ecliptic** <note>The sun's annual path</note>. In the direct ascension, however, the arcs of Libra are increased in the direct manner by the quantity of the reduction of the altitude. The arcs of the signs following <unclear>Aquarius</unclear>, namely the terms, are twenty ascensions of the two arcs of equal signs from each side of the points of **Cancer** <unclear>zauatus</unclear>, which are equal to the ascensions of the arc in the direct manner. Because they are such that where the ascension of two opposite signs is joined in the oblique manner, they will be equal ascensions in the direct manner. # The Division of Time and the Order of the Spheres

<page-num>8</page-num>

By fifteen, there will be that which results for each of the **equal hours** <note>original: "horarum diei aequalium"</note>; and similarly, when you divide this part of the night by twenty-four, that which results is the value of the hours of the night, which is a fourth part of the smallest hour of the day. This hour, however, they call **unequal** <note>original: "inequalis"; also known as seasonal or temporal hours, which vary in length depending on the season</note>, and it is one part of each day and night, both in summer and in winter. For any given six hours, the sky has been divided according to the length of the day and the shortness of the night. When the hours of the night are more numerous, the hour of the night will be longer; and similarly, when the days are shorter, their hours will be shorter. And when the arc of the day is divided by fifteen, that which results will be the quantity of the **celestial revolution** <note>the rotation of the sky</note> in each single hour. These are called the **times of the hours** <note>original: "tempora horarum"; in medieval astronomy, one 'time' equals one degree of the equator, so 15 'times' equal one hour</note>. And similarly, when the arc of the night is divided by fifteen, the result is the times of the hours of the night; but this is what diminishes the times of the hours of the day from fifteen parts. Now it is clear that these **equal hours** <note>original: "equales"</note> are such because they are not divided according to the quantity of the length or shortness of the days; for them, the times are always equal. But the **unequal hours** are those whose times are diverse, for no two such hours are identical.

But since I promised what I ought to provide concerning the nature of the division of the **climates** <note>latitudinal zones of the Earth</note> and what happens concerning the distance of the night and day, I will begin to narrate concerning the stars. For the sake of memory, I will provide a figure of the heavens and their orders, following what has been agreed upon by the ancients in all things. We say that the number of the heavens <note>spheres</note>, according to the common and immense movement of the stars, is **eight**. Of these, seven belong to the **wandering planets** <note>original: "planetarum erraticas"</note>, and the eighth is above them all: the sphere of the **fixed stars**, which is the circle of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note>. The shape of these heavens is like spheres placed one inside the other, of which the smallest and innermost of all is the first sphere, that of the **Moon** <note>original: "lune"</note>; then follow the spheres of **Mercury**, **Venus**, the **Sun**, **Mars**, **Jupiter**, and the **Saturn**. The eighth is the sphere of the **fixed stars**, which is the boundary of the heavens and the circle of the signs.

<column-break/>

The center of these spheres is always the same; even though these spheres are perceived to be distant from the center in divided parts. In each of these spheres, the twelve signs are present. The heaven carries the sphere by a double movement: from the east to the west, and also according to the movement of the sphere of the fixed stars and the union of the circle of the signs. In this way, its movement is processed through a diverse and equalizing method which is seen by all to be a plain movement from the west to the east. Because of this, the **equant** <note>original: "aequans"; a mathematical concept used to explain the observed speed changes of planets</note> is called the "equalizing heaven." These planets move in the middle of their equal circles from west to east. And in these heavens, which are called spheres, there are two opposite locations: one at a much greater distance <note>apogee</note> and one at a much closer distance <note>perigee</note> to the Earth. When the planet is in that place of the greatest longitude, it is called the **apogee** <note>original: "augis"</note> of the planet; the point at the closest longitude is the opposite of the apogee. When the planet is in the middle of its sphere at its greatest distance, its motion is seen in the circle of the signs to be **slower** <note>original: "tardior"</note>; but its motion in its own center is equal. If, however, it is in the part closest to its sphere, its motion in the circle of the signs is seen to be **faster** <note>original: "velocior"</note>. And if it is in the middle, it is always seen as the movement of the planet in its own sphere, equal to the center. It is the **equant** <note>original: "equat"</note> that reveals its entry into the middle of the signs. All this is positioned upon its sphere, and the equalizing center <note>the equant</note> is aligned with the center of the heaven of signs. The Sun moves in an equal manner; the surface of the heaven of signs does not decline from it. The other planets, however, travel through the remaining bodies upon the circuit of the equalizing center; they are placed upon smaller heavens called the **epicycles** <note>original: "celi breves"; literally "short heavens"</note>. The centers of these small heavens are placed upon the larger equalizing heavens. If one heaven declines from the surface of the signs, or from the surface of either of the heavens or the equalizing center, it is said to decline from that surface.

<meta>This page continues the technical geometric analysis of planetary latitudes and the orientation of their orbital planes (the "ecliptics of the apsides") relative to the ecliptic of the signs (the Zodiac). It builds on the previous discussion of the "cusps" or orbital axes.</meta>

The quantity always remains one for **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** <note>original: "Saturni, iouis, et martis"; transcribed as "ū, 7, y"</note>, because their motion is not upon the axes of the **ecliptic of the signs** <note>The zodiacal circle on the celestial sphere</note>, but always upon the axes of the **ecliptic of the apsides** <term>apsides (singular: apsis)</term> <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or farthest from the center of its motion</note>. These axes extend from the deeper surface of the ecliptic of the signs across the diameter of the ecliptic of the signs and decline from it toward the **North** of the world. Therefore, their latitude is divided at the surface of the signs; namely, the ecliptic of the Moon and these apsides, from there to the surface of the ecliptic of the signs, up to the **capital points**—that is, the head and the tail <note>original: "caput et cauda"; referring to the Ascending and Descending Nodes of an orbit</note>—and it declines toward the North of the world. This declination remains fixed at one quantity and does not move from it. However, the surface of the **short ecliptic** <note>original: "eclictici biuſ"; likely the epicycle's plane or a secondary orbital circle</note> is inseparable from the surface of the ecliptic of the apsis and does not decline from it; thus, it has one constant latitude and declination. Specifically, the ecliptic of the apsis relative to the ecliptic of the signs for those three—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—possesses a latitude that is not uniform, because the circle of their apsides declines from the zodiacal ecliptic and from the surface of the ecliptic of the signs across its diameter. For **Venus and Mercury**, the ecliptic of their apsides, from the surface of the zodiacal ecliptic across its diameter, declines toward the North of the world; that is, at the locations of their **apsides** <note>original: "abſationū"</note>. For these two, the location of the latitude is in the middle between the longitudes; that is, each middle longitude of the ecliptic of the apsides for Saturn. In the return to the middle of each longitude, it declines from the **longer longitudes** <note>apogee</note> of the ecliptics of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars toward the North from the zodiacal ecliptic in the longitude of the poles toward the **South** <note>original: "indiē", likely a transcription of "meridiem"</note> always unequally and in a mobile way. The declination of the ecliptics for **Venus** comes to the center of the apsides; it is not fixed, but moves across the diameter of the zodiacal ecliptic as far as the nodes with a slight motion toward the North. It returns to the position of the map once a year, while it follows the mode of the longitude—that is, the half of the longitude of the ecliptic of the apsis toward the North from the zodiacal ecliptic for Venus and toward the South for Mercury. Similarly, the half of the poles **nutates** <note>wobbles or tilts</note> toward the North of the world. I suppose the surface of the ecliptic of the apsides is above the surface of the zodiacal ecliptic at the beginning of this year; that is, its apsis is in both nodes. And when the apsis of the ecliptics of **Venus** is in either of the nodes, from the beginning

<column-break/>

of the declination of the half of the ecliptic of the apsis which follows that node toward the North, and the other half toward the South. In the beginning, however, when the apsis of the ecliptic is in the same node, then also is the beginning of the declination of the half that follows in that node toward the [North] of the world, and the other half toward the North. Thus, the node is on one part of the zodiacal ecliptic, and each declines to the other part, so that the apsis of the ecliptic for these three planets is in the surface of the zodiacal ecliptic. When it is at either of the nodes on one part of the zodiacal ecliptic, each will decline to the other part, so that the apsis of the ecliptic for **Venus** is always toward the North from the zodiacal ecliptic. **Mercury**, however, is always toward the South. Apart from what was said before, the declination of the ecliptics of the apsides for Venus is inclined from the zodiacal ecliptic toward the North of the world, and it follows that part of the short ecliptic in the **longer longitude** <note>apogee</note> of the ecliptic of the apsis. ## From these are the Mansions 
of the moon by which our people name them. I have noted them here by these names by which men know them. The **first** of these is **Anathach** <note>original: "anathach"; from Arabic 'al-natih' (the butting), referring to the horns of Aries</note>. These are two bright stars in the head of Aries, separated from each other; and it is with that northern star indeed. The **second** is **Alburain** <note>original: "alburain"; from Arabic 'al-butayn' (the little belly)</note>, which is said to be three stars formed in the likeness of a tripod. The **third** is **Althrace** <note>original: "althrace"; from Arabic 'al-thurayya' (the Pleiades)</note>, and these are small stars collected together; in Latin they are called the **Pleiades**. The **fourth** is **Aldebaran**. 
Consider the second mention of it with the mansion that the Arabs name **Balahayrech**. And there is with it indeed that star which is called **Acalonic**. The **fifth** is **Alahacab** <note>original: "alahacab"; from Arabic 'al-haqa'a'</note>, which by another name is called **Almeisen**, and it is the head of Gemini <note>original: "cap geĩ"; caput geminorum</note>, three small stars joined together. The **sixth** is **Alahanna** <note>original: "alahannaë"; from Arabic 'al-han'ah'</note>, which by another name is called **Athoraia**, and these are seven stars placed in a straight line; or like a field; 
and each one is placed individually. The **seventh** is **Aduath** <note>original: "aduath"; from Arabic 'al-dhira' (the arm)</note>. These are two divided stars, of which one, which is the northern one, is brighter; and they are at the feet of Gemini. 
The **eighth** is called **Anathera** <note>original: "anathera"; from Arabic 'al-nathrah' (the nose-hair or sneeze)</note>, which belongs to the Lion. It consists of a cloud-like point in the middle between two small stars. 
The **ninth** is named **Arpharphẽ** <note>original: "arpharphẽ"; from Arabic 'al-tarfah' (the gaze)</note> which begins at the summit of the moon. These are two stars that the Arabs name the eyes of the Lion. The **tenth** is called **Agelbab** <note>original: "agelbab"; from Arabic 'al-jabha' (the forehead)</note>, which they interpret as the forehead of the moon. These are bright stars not of equal power, as you see in the figure. It is called by the Indians the "heart of the Lion" <note>original: "caua; can' leonil"; likely a corruption of Cor Leonis, or Regulus</note>. The **eleventh** is **Acobha** <note>original: "acobha"; from Arabic 'al-zubra' (the mane)</note>. These are bright stars following the heart of the Lion; they name them **Aleharathen**. The **twelfth** is called **Alarpha** <note>original: "alarpha"; from Arabic 'al-sarfah' (the changer)</note>. And this is the star which is in the Lion's tail. The **thirteenth** is **Aloe** <note>original: "aloe"; from Arabic 'al-awwa' (the barker)</note>. These are stars in the likeness of the Arabic letter called **Aluph** <note>Aleph</note>. Seven are deposited and dispersed in the air. One is lower [than the others]. And these are among the twenty-four great [stars]. 
Next is **Almouchabahabacel** <note>original: "almochabahabacel"; from Arabic 'al-simak al-a'zal' (Spica)</note>. We have already noted these among the martial stars, which is called **Alghisece**. And these are eight stars, drawn out thin, of which two precede the others. 
The **fourteenth** is called **Alaubene** or **Alaubenei** of the Scorpion. For some it is pleasing that these are two divided stars which are the scales of the Balance <note>the constellation Libra</note>. 
The **fifteenth** is **Achit** <note>original: "achit"; from Arabic 'al-iklil' (the crown)</note>. These are three stars placed in a row.

The **sixteenth** is the **Heart of the Scorpion** <note>original: "coz scorpionil"; Cor Scorpionis, known as Antares</note>, a bright red star between two other stars. These are two small stars, of which one is northern; and a certain small hidden star is added to them, which the Arabs call **Oudt**. This mansion is called the Fortune of the Beheaded. The **twenty-eighth** is the **Belly of the Fish** <note>original: "uent' pifcal"; Latin 'venter piscium', from Arabic 'batn al-hut'</note>. These are the stars of the northern fish, and they are formed in its image. In its eastern side is a bright star which they call **Alflogi**, the heart of the fish. In this book too, let us demonstrate the properties of their risings and their settings under the rays of the sun. We say that **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** with their cardinal points <note>original: "elum cardinez"; likely referring to the pivotal points of their orbits</note> and the sun, when it is between them before the sun, the sun then approaches it, and its appearance is in the west in the evening. After it is hidden until its occultation <note>term: occultation; when a celestial body is hidden by another or by the sun's glare</note> is under the sun, then when it emerges through its own path returning from under the sun's rays, it will appear in the east in the morning. However, each of them moves in such a way that their setting is in the evening and their rising is in the morning. And on the day of their retrograde <note>term: retrograde; the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky</note> rising and setting in the morning, because they were in the velocity of the sun, one of them is smoothed out as long as it has maintained that course. One of them completes five reversals <note>original: "v. reversiones"; likely referring to synodic cycles or loops</note> out from under the sun's rays, which is its evening setting, until it comes to its greatest distance in longitude from the sun. Through this minimum, it exists in its reversal to the sun's rays, and then its occasion is in the east in the evening when it has been separated from the sun. Returning from under its rays, they would move in the morning until they reach the furthest distance from the sun. After this, it makes the celestial velocity reach the sun. Thus, its settings move in the evening. The **Moon**, however, because she is faster than the sun, then comes from the sun's retreat. Thus, she reaches the sun again in the east in the morning, and after she has exited, she moves in the evening. Regarding the fixed stars, we have already spoken at the beginning of the book. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary and lunar movements, specifically focusing on how their positions in the zodiac and their distance from the Sun affect their visibility from Earth. Since it belongs to the signs, and at that time the Moon is in direct motion while the Sun is in Virgo and Libra: and then in the evening: when for one day the Moon is among these signs and at the extent of its declination <note>term: declination; the angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator</note> from this hemisphere: the more the Moon’s distance from the Sun appears, the more its light will appear to us in its body according to its motion.

It should be known that for the three superior planets, namely **Jupiter** and **Mars**: whenever the Sun is in the lower part of this sky, such is their motion. This variation is due to the different ascensions <note>term: ascension; the rising of a zodiac sign over the horizon</note> of the signs and the different longitudes of many souls <note>original: "animarum"; possibly a scribal error for "anomalies" or "angles"</note>. Truly, they may join the Sun in the light of the sky twice or once. When it is directed through twelve minutes of the lower part of the sky while in retrograde <note>term: retrograde; the apparent backward motion of a planet</note>: the duration of their stay under the rays is doubled. This is because of the variation in the rising of the signs and the variation in latitude. If one calculates the visibility from the variation of the celestial signs and its latitude—since it lacks the other variations—one arrives at a latitude according to what is found in **Ptolemy's Almagest** <note>The "Almagest" was the most influential astronomical textbook of the Middle Ages, written by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD</note>: at six degrees, so that it moves one degree when it is in retrograde in the middle, until it is hidden under the rays of the Sun for two days before it reaches the Sun's degree. It moves with that same motion until it is seen again by the Sun. When it joins, its stay under the rays lasts until it appears in the east after sixteen days. This combination is gathered from two variations, so that it is at its furthest distance from the Sun, and note that an eclipse may occur at this distance; and this distance for an eclipse happens when it is swift toward the east.

# Treatise of Master Habhe
## On the Calculation of the Sun and Moon

### On Direct and Retrograde Motion

### On the Dragons <note>term: "draco"; in medieval astronomy, the "Dragon" refers to the orbital nodes, the two points where a planet's path crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's path). The "Head" is the Ascending Node and the "Tail" is the Descending Node</note>

To know the place of the Head of the Dragon for any of these planets: If for **Saturn**, seek the minutes from the other place, and it is in the quantity of 9 signs and 10 degrees. If indeed for **Jupiter**: the minutes from the other place are 10 signs and 5 degrees. If for **Mars**: the minutes from the other place are 3 signs and 15 degrees, and in the remainder is the Head of the Dragon. If for **Venus**: the minutes from the other place are 180 degrees. And see if any of these are within 90 degrees. The Head [of the Dragon] from its own head: up to 180 degrees, where it is descending, it is on the left. Descending from 0 to 180, it will descend on the right. And up to 360, it will ascend on the right. But the Head of the Dragon comes into the place of another, which is the same quantity as the place of the **Sun**. To the place of **Mercury**, add 6 signs, and you will have the Head of the Dragon. If in the adjustment the Head of the Dragon comes into Mercury, it is properly determined whether the latitude is to the right or the left, by the proper art which is given above. Thus it is according to the rule.

### On the latitude and the median altitude of the sun for a location.

On the 19th day of March in a non-leap year <note>original: "anno n̄ bissextili"; the author is providing a method for the spring equinox</note>. In a leap year, or for the preceding year, or if you wish to cross-reference with an astrolabe <note>term: "astrolabium"; a portable medieval instrument used to solve problems relating to time and the position of the sun and stars</note>, they shall teach you thus. Take the minimum altitude and subtract it from 90 degrees <note>original: "g’"; abbreviation for gradus/degrees</note>; the remainder will reveal the latitude of the location. For the altitude of the sun on that day is called the altitude of the start of Aries or Libra <note>These represent the equinoctial points where the sun crosses the celestial equator</note>. If you seek the latitude of any location on another day, take the altitude of the sun on that day at midday. On the astrolabe, create the midday shadow at noon. Above the median altitude: treat the declination <note>term: "declinatio"; the angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the sun on that same day. It was less from the 19th day of March until the 14th day of September, and it was right-handed <note>meaning southerly</note> from the 14th day of September until the 19th of March. Add the declination to that same midday altitude, and it is joined to the true altitude of the start of Aries and Libra. Subtract that from 90 degrees and the remainder will be the sought-after latitude. If the result is finished, subtract the declination from the altitude and the remainder will be found from 90.

### On shadows.

Shadows are of three kinds...

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin>
...and they are called digits <note>term: "digiti"; a standard medieval unit for measuring shadows, usually 1/12th of the height of the gnomon</note>. This is truly called the vertical shadow <note>original: "umbra recta"; the shadow cast on a horizontal plane by a vertical gnomon</note> because it has a body fixed upright and orthogonally <note>meaning at a right angle</note> to something. Otherwise, it is called a foot-measure <note>original: "pedale"</note>. Not because it is equal to the vertical shadow or the prior one, but here it is named by the measure of the portions of light. For it was decided to divide it into 12 ordered measures of feet, because by diligent investigation they find the measure to be equal to as much as the foot above. There is another kind of shadow which is called the horizontal shadow <note>original: "iacente"; literally "lying," cast by a horizontal gnomon onto a vertical wall</note>. This is produced by a body held in some frame orthogonally to a plane to make a right angle. This is your shadow, or a body raised in the air that is equidistant from the ground.
<margin>h</margin>

### On finding the foot-measure shadow from the vertical shadow.

<margin>ata</margin>
**B**y knowing only the digits, you shall find the foot-measure. Multiply the digits by 4 and divide the product by 9, and the feet will come out. The remainder will be in ninths; multiply that by 6 and let it be divided so it stands, and the sixtieths of a foot will come out. If you have a digit measure and want to operate from the digital to the foot-measure, multiply by 4 and divide by 9, and the measure of feet will come out. And for the remaining measure made from the division of the digits, add it to those, and from 6 make a foot.

### Foot-measure for vertical [shadow].

<margin>S</margin>
**I**f one wishes to make a vertical shadow from a foot-measure, or having a foot-measure: multiply the quotient by 9 and divide by 4, and the measure of the digit will come out. If one has a measure of a foot-measure: multiply it by 9 and divide by 4, and the measure of the digit will come out.

### On the horizontal shadow.

### Through the horizontal [to find] the vertical, etc.

Multiply the remainder by 6 and divide by the same divisor, and the measure will come out. In this way, having the digits, you have found the proportion of the unknown shadow.

## On the Diameter of the Right Shadow
<note>"Right shadow" (umbra recta) refers to the shadow cast on a horizontal surface by a vertical gnomon</note>

And if the sun is in the northern signs, add the whole declination to the altitude of the head of Aries, and the sum is the midday altitude of the sun. If it is in the southern signs, subtract the whole declination from the altitude of the head of Aries; the remainder will be the midday altitude of the sun. <margin>i</margin> Conversely, take the chord <note>original: "cordam" - a trigonometric value used in medieval astronomy, similar to the modern sine function</note> of that sum and save it. Then take the altitude which is the hour of the day by the astrolabe <note>original: "astlabum"</note>, and add this altitude to that one. Multiply it by 60, but by 200 minutes to this which is in the limit of the sine <note>original: "algeib" - from the Arabic 'al-jayb', the source of our word 'sine'</note>, from which the diameter is measured. Divide the product by the chord of the arc of the total midday altitude, and what you wish to know will result <unclear>...</unclear> If a remainder is left, multiply by 60 and divide by the aforementioned divisor, and the minutes will result. To this, with the minutes, is the chord. In whatever chord the sum of the things is multiplied by the divisor... Divide those into minutes by the greater and lesser. <margin>note</margin> The degree of the chord will result. Here take the arc of the degree for each 15 degrees; take one hour up to the top, and this will be equal <note>original: "parales" - likely referring to equal/parallel hours</note>. If it is by proportion, the rest of the true sum multiplied by 4 produces the minutes of the equal hour. If there are minutes of degrees here, make the arc from which the minutes of the hours are drawn out. Where the altitude of the sun before midday will be the hours passed. If for the whole remaining part, subtract from 12, and the remainder is the hours of the day that have passed. And after the hours, then add the arc of the chord to these eastern ascensions. And with the sum, enter into the tables in the customary way, by which we find the rising sun.

### Concerning the form of the astrolabe.

There are two kinds of astrolabes: the **right-handed** and the **left-handed**. The left-handed is larger than the

<sig>iv.</sig>

<column-break/>

right-handed. We distinguish them in two ways: first, that in the **left-handed** instrument, the northern fixed stars are depicted inside the zodiac and the southern ones outside; in the **right-handed** one, it is the opposite. Second, that in the left-handed one, the largest of the circles is **Capricorn** and the smallest is **Cancer**; in the right-handed one, it is the reverse. The <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note> is the middle between both. Some astrolabes are "perfect" and others "imperfect." Furthermore, some are simple and others composite. Of the imperfect ones, some are divided by halves, some by thirds, others by fifths, sixths, or tenths. They are distinguished because the ninety degrees of the quadrant of the circle are divided by these parts; for example, by twelve parts... It happens that both kinds of astrolabes, however they are distinguished, have **plates** <note>original: "tablat̃" - the climate plates or tympans placed inside the instrument.</note> under the **rete** <note>original: "rethiclo" - the pierced framework of the astrolabe representing the stars and zodiac.</note> which it includes. The border <note>original: "marginẽ"</note> is divided by the number **360**. On the back, a ruler is placed which is called the **alidade**. Its two ends have protruding **sights** <note>original: "pinnulat"</note> which are called "the tables." In each of these, there are holes—in some, two, one larger and one smaller. ### On the Latitude and the Meridian Altitude of the Earth.

The sun at noon on the 14th day of March <note>This was the date of the Vernal Equinox in the medieval Julian calendar.</note> is said to be at the altitude of the "head of Aries" <note>The point where the sun crosses the equator into the northern hemisphere.</note>; because the sun then is precisely at the beginning of the head of Aries, subtract that altitude from 90, and the remainder is the latitude of our path <note>meaning: "of our current location."</note>. Thus, on whatever day you wish to take the meridian altitude of the sun, find its declination <note>term: <term>declination</term>, the distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note>, which you will find in whatever table you wish. If the astrolabe is "left-handed," and the sun is in the corresponding signs, place the sun's location upon the line of the midheaven and see the distance of the almucantar which is between the circle of Aries and Libra and the sun's location. That is the sun's declination. If it is "right-handed," simply see the distance from the circle of the sun to the equinoctial circle <column-break/> which is lower than the sun's location, and that is the declination of the sun, with the sun always placed upon the line of the midheaven. If the sun is "right" and the instrument is "left," see the distance from the sun's location to the equinoctial circle which will be below. If the instrument is "right" and the sun is "right," count from the equinoctial circle to the sun's location, which is the sun's declination. If the sun is in the "left" signs, take its altitude at whatever noon you wish, and subtract the declination of the sun from the meridian altitude, and the remainder is the altitude of the head of Aries. Once you have the altitude of Aries, subtract it from 90, and the remainder will be our latitude. If the astrolabe is missing a plate, take it according to the altitude of the plate provided. This is what must be done:

### Knowing the Latitude, How to Supplement the Lack of a Plate.

If you have plates in the astrolabe for which it is necessary to operate in a land where you want to take a plate larger than the one you have and one smaller than it—namely, of a greater and a lesser latitude—and you wish to work with the aforementioned instructions to find the eastern wood <note>original: "lignum orientis," likely referring to the eastern horizon or a specific structural part of the instrument used for alignment.</note>. If the "east" of the smaller plate is less than the "east" of the larger plate, find the difference between them. Multiply that by the difference of the smaller plate's latitude to your own latitude, and divide the product by the difference of the smaller plate to the larger one. The result will be the degrees to be added to the time of the "east" of the smaller plate, and the total will be our "east." If, however, the degree of the "east" of the smaller plate is greater than the "east" of the larger plate, multiply the difference of the smaller plate's latitude to your latitude by the difference of the eastern degrees of the larger and smaller plates. Divide the product by the difference of the latitudes of the smaller and larger plates, and subtract what results from the "east" of the smaller plate, which is the meridian altitude of the sun.

When you wish to know in **On Finding the Daily**
<margin>Daily</margin> **Altitude** of the sun, find the altitude for the day in your location with a known latitude. You should know the declination <note>term: <term>declination</term> (declinatio), the angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the sun through the <term>astrolabe</term> <note>term: <term>astrolabe</term>, a historical astronomical instrument used for solving problems relating to time and the position of the sun and stars.</note> or through very helpful tables. And if the sun is in the northern signs <note>The signs of the zodiac from Aries to Virgo.</note>, add the declination of the sun’s degree to the altitude of the "head of Aries" <note>The altitude of the celestial equator at your location.</note>. The resulting sum is the true altitude. However, if the sun is in the southern signs, subtract the aforementioned declination from the aforementioned altitude, and the remainder will show the predicted altitude. 

When you wish to know the arc of the day <note>The total length of time the sun is above the horizon.</note>: place the sun's position on the first eastern <term>almucantar</term> <note>term: <term>almucantar</term> (almu-cantarah), a circle of altitude on the astrolabe plate.</note> (the horizon). Mark the "head of Capricorn" <note>A pointer or specific mark on the astrolabe's rotating star-map used for measuring degrees.</note> and see the distance between the two marks of the head of Capricorn on the portable sphere. That is the arc of the day. Divide this by 15, and the result will be the arc of a seasonal hour <note>term: <term>seasonal hour</term> (hora temporalis), one-twelfth of the daylight period, which varies in length throughout the year.</note>. But before this, you will work to find the arc of the seasonal hour for the eastern parts, and you will work with the sun's position in the 12th degree. 

**On the Division of the Houses.**
The degree on the eastern horizon is the beginning of the first house <note>The "Ascendant" in astrology.</note>. The degree that touches the midheaven line <note>The vertical meridian line on the instrument.</note> is the beginning of the tenth house. See which sign that degree is in. Whether it be the tenth or eleventh sign from the rising sign, the position of this tenth house varies according to different lands and latitudes. The degree that is opposite the beginning of the tenth house—because the midheaven line touches it at the end of the sixth hour—is the beginning of the fourth house. The degree found on the western <term>almucantar</term> opposite the eastern one is the beginning of the seventh house. Then, move the head of Capricorn by two seasonal hours of the eastern side; whatever part of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>term: <term>zodiac</term>, the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note> the midheaven line touches is the beginning of the eleventh house. See if this degree is the eleventh or tenth sign from the rising sign. For the 12th house, move the head of Capricorn by two more seasonal hours, and whatever part of the <term>zodiac</term> the midheaven line

<column-break/>

touches is the beginning of the entire twelfth house. Note whether it is in the 12th sign, the 11th sign from the east, or in the rising sign itself. For here, whatever distance in degrees is between it and the 7th sign from the east is recorded. Thirdly, move two more units, and thus the eastern mark is found upon the midheaven line; if so, the work is correct. 

Next, subtract the double seasonal hour from 12 equinoctial hours <note>Standard 60-minute hours.</note>, and the remainder is the double seasonal hour of the night. Move the head of Capricorn by as much as that remainder is, and what the midheaven line touches is the seat of the 10th house <note>The text here seems to be calculating the subterranean houses.</note>. It touches its space in the third sign from the east, or within the eastern sign itself, according to its distance from it. Then move it again beyond where the <term>zodiac</term> is on the midheaven line; that is the beginning of the sixth house, and it touches that beginning in the third sign from the rising sign according to the seat of the signs. Opposite this seat is the beginning of the eighth house. Opposite the [third] is the beginning of the ninth. Opposite the eleventh is the beginning of the fifth; opposite the twelfth is the beginning of the sixth. And this is the distinction of the houses according to the ancients, Ptolemy and Dorotheus <note>note: original: "ptholomeu et dorotheus". Referring to Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century AD) and Dorotheus of Sidon (1st century AD), foundational authorities in Hellenistic astrology.</note>. 

**On the Ascensions of the Signs.**
Those wishing to have the table: place the beginning of the sign upon the midheaven line which is the diameter of the plate. Then place that beginning in the eastern aspect upon the horizontal line between which the other diameters lie. Mark the "head of Capricorn" in the margin, and upon that diameter place the end of the same sign, and make a mark at the head of Capricorn. Whatever the distance is between the marks, such are the ascensions of the other sign. Work the table correctly: place the beginning of the sign according to the line of the first <term>almucantar</term> and mark the declination; however great the distance of the sign is, such are the ascensions of the fifth. If you do not find the table for the latitude of your land, you can know the ascensions of its sign in this way.

# On Determining the Equal Hour

**B**y means of the moon, take the altitude of the moon at that time with its full light, and find the position of the moon in the tables of equations <note>Tables used to correct the moon’s irregular motion to find its true position in the zodiac.</note> for the time before that which we gave for the equation of planets at any hour. This gives you the moon's position in the night hour. Locate that position in the zodiac and place that mark upon the <term>almucantar</term> <note>term: <term>almucantar</term>, a line on the astrolabe representing a specific degree of altitude above the horizon.</note> of the moon’s latitude, whether in the east or the west. Then see what part of the zodiac touches the first almucantar (the horizon) and that is the rising point. See at which hour the position of the sun touches [the lines]; that is the hour of the night. If the position of the moon in the zodiac is not found correctly except in the total altitude on the almucantar, do not proceed until you have accounted for the movements of the zodiac. If you work from the position of the sun at the beginning of the hour, use the art which we gave above concerning the sun. If you have the table for your city, perform the art as we taught there. What we have said is correct if the moon is on the [ecliptic] zodiac; but if it is away from the zodiac—either greater or lesser in latitude—we would be deceived if we did not adjust for it.

**T**ake the highest altitude of the moon in the night. If it is ascending, place the moon where it is; if the moon is past the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>term: <term>mid-heaven</term> (medium coeli), the point where a celestial body crosses the local meridian; its highest point in the sky.</note>, set it there. You will see that as the almucantar touches it from the east, that degree [is recorded]; it is the altitude of the moon.

<column-break/>

Let those almucantars be equated as if the moon were in the zodiac. If the moon's altitude is greater, the moon has "left" (northern) latitude; if it is smaller, it has "right" (southern) latitude. Whatever the difference is from the almucantar that the moon's position touches to the actual altitude of the moon, that is its latitude to the right or to the left. And it should be known that just as we work with the moon, we can also work with the stars and the signs, provided the calculation is performed correctly.

**T**ake the highest altitude of some star near the pole, and take its lowest depression <note>The star's lowest point as it circles the celestial pole.</note>. Add the elevation and the depression together, take the half of the sum, and that result will be your sought latitude <note>This is the classic "circumpolar star" method for finding one's geographic latitude.</note>.

**T**ake the altitude of a star seen through the sighting holes, either in the east or the west, and place the pointer <note>original: "auē" (avem), literally "bird," referring to the pointed "beaks" on the astrolabe's rete that indicate star positions.</note> designating it upon the almucantar of its altitude. See what degree of the zodiac touches the eastern almucantar; this is the rising point. See which hour or part of an hour the sun's position touches: that is the true hour of the night.

**P**lace the pointer designated for the star upon the line of the mid-heaven, and see what degree of the zodiac touches that same line, and in which sign and degree that fixed star resides. By this art, you can know whether your <term>astrolabe</term> <note>term: <term>astrolabe</term>, a handheld model of the universe used for timekeeping and observation.</note> is true or not. See if the degree of the sign or the star matches the calculation of the tables for the time you are searching. If they disagree by some degrees, compare it over a period of ten years.

**P**lace the star’s pointer upon the line of mid-heaven. If the almucantar that touches that pointer is greater than the almucantar that touches its position in the zodiac, its latitude is "left" (northern); if it is smaller, it is "right" (southern). Whatever the difference in the almucantar is from the position of its degree in the zodiac to its pointer, that is its latitude—that is, its distance from the zodiac.

### Calculation by the Astrolabe

The location of the hour is in the **zodiac**, and with it placed upon the eastern <term>almucantar</term> <note>Circles of altitude on the astrolabe plate used to measure the height of celestial bodies.</note>, let the sign of **Capricorn** be taken. Let it be called the "median sign." Then place the beginning of the house upon the eastern almucantar and mark the <term>denticulum</term> <note>original: "denaclm" or "denticulum," the small 'tooth' or pointer on the astrolabe's rete used to indicate degrees on the outer scale.</note>; let this be called the "first sign." Then let the same be placed similarly toward that almucantar and let it be called the "second." Multiply the distance of the first sign to the middle by 60, and divide the product by the distance of the first [point]; the <term>lemma</term> <note>A subsidiary proposition or intermediate mathematical result.</note> will result. 

Then place the beginning of the house in which the temporal [hours] are sought upon the eastern almucantar, and mark the pointer at the end of the same house at the 18th almucantar. Multiply the distance between these two signs by that same lemma, and divide the product by 60; the degrees will result. If there is a remainder, take half of it and diminish it. Add these degrees and minutes to the beginning of the house in which the aspect is [sought], and you will have the location of the aspect.

### On the Division of the Houses

Regarding their boundaries, there is one method of equal degrees in which all **astronomical** authors agree, and it holds great weight in the "judgments" <note>Judgments refers to judicial astrology, the practice of predicting earthly events via the stars.</note>; and the weight of judgments is attributed to it. Others differ according to the latitude of the region, in which are held the views of **Hermes**, **Dorotheus**, **Ptolemy**, **Metalla**, **Andruzagar**, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer in the Latin West.</note>, and all the other ancients who do not disagree with them, except for **Avennonaulh**, **Al-Khwārizmī**, and **Al-Anunzi**; but the others follow the ancients.

<column-break/>

...brought the parts to the plate of the **astrolabe**. If the part is between the tenth house and the East, it serves to lead it to another plate. For example: the **Midheaven** <note>original: "mediū celi"; the highest point in the sky that a celestial body reaches.</note> in the zodiac. If it has the East, then place the marked location in the zodiac upon the first eastern almucantar, and let all the calculation be handled as it was during the day. Then take the time there.

But concerning the temporal hour, take the result in minutes. Then place the mark of the Midheaven which is in the zodiac upon the Midheaven line. Then mark the pointer. Then place the location of the leading part upon the Midheaven line from the same side, and mark the pointer there. Then divide the distance of the two signs of **Capricorn** by the temporal hour, and that which results will be the minutes of the removal of the leading part from the Midheaven line. 

Then place the leading location upon the Midheaven line, then the pointer, and note the distance of the two signs of the pointer in the margin; these are called the **Right Ascensions** <note>original: "ascēnsiones celi rec"; the distance of a point measured along the celestial equator.</note>. Then place the leading location upon the first eastern almucantar and note the pointer. Then place the leading location upon the same almucantar, and mark the pointer. The distance of the two signs of the pointer is called the **Oblique Ascensions** <note>original: "asēnsiones t̄re"; the arc of the celestial equator that rises with a degree of the zodiac in a specific latitude.</note>. 

Take the difference of these ascensions—the Right Ascensions and the Oblique Ascensions—and take a sixth part of that distance. Multiply the minutes of the ratio by it, and add the product to the Right Ascensions if they are smaller, or subtract if they are larger; you will have the degree brought forth. For each degree, consider each year. If any minutes remain beyond the degree, see what proportion they have to 60, and take that portion for one year. This remains for the years and the **Fortune of the Birth** <note>Refers to the "Pars Fortunae" or Lot of Fortune, a specific mathematical point in a natal horoscope.</note> into which we are led. Through this, the aspects of the birth are found, which lead to the person's mastery.

# Sophon

<margin>
[Bin uad f] <note>likely a scribal reference or shelf mark</note>
</margin>

Take the measurement. If the distance is to the right or the left, note that measurement. Then adjust the **alidade** <note>The pivoting sighting bar on the back of the astrolabe.</note> until the marked rod is seen through the sighting holes. Nearby, take the height of the shadow and operate as described above. Then multiply by 12 <note>Original: "p. 12"; 12 is the standard number of "digits" on the astrolabe's shadow square.</note> the space that lies between the two previous locations—whether it be forward, behind, or to your right or left. Then divide by the difference of the two shadows that resulted. From the resulting number, subtract your standing position; the remainder is the distance you seek. And if you are in a place where it is not possible to move forward or backward, take a rod in the ground and determine its shadow and height. Then take the height of the other rod in the earth through the **hypotenuse** <note>The diagonal line of sight.</note> by the rising of the **gnomon** <note>The vertical pointer that casts the shadow.</note>, and determine its height and shadow. There is a fifth distance between two signs that can be nearly equal; multiply that by 12 and divide by the difference of the two resulting shadows. Then subtract your standing position, and the remainder is what you seek.

¶ Just as you might easily find the width of a river elsewhere: take the instrument in your left hand and adjust the alidade until you see the far bank through the upper sighting hole. Take the height and the shadow's proportion to 12. Multiply that proportion by your distance from the bank, and the result will be the width you seek.

¶ If, however, you seek the depth of a well: take the instrument and adjust the alidade until the far edge of the bottom is seen. Note the height and its shadow, and see what proportion 12 has to that shadow. Multiply that proportion by the diameter of the well's width. Subtract your standing position from the result, and thus you will find what you seek. 

¶ If you see two fires or mountains and wish to know which is less distant from you: take the height of each. If the height is greater, it is the one that is closer to you.

<column-break/>

¶ As **Philo** <note>Likely referring to Philo of Byzantium, an ancient engineer.</note> says, wherever the measurements of **Abraham** <note>Likely referring to Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century mathematician, or the tradition attributing geometry to the patriarch Abraham.</note> are required more for distances than for heights, they accept this reasoning as inviolable. Taking the height and shadow on a double-scaled astrolabe is impossible if the reading decreases from two points. This is because one scale is for height beyond the distance (namely 12) where the alidade falls on the **shadow square**. <note>The "shadow square" is a grid on the back of the astrolabe used to solve surveying problems using similar triangles.</note> The other is used when the height is less than 12, where the **right shadow** <note>original: "umbr' recta"</note> is produced by the height of the two. The remedy then is to take the shadow for the height as treated above. Do as was said: subtract the height obtained from 90 degrees and find the remaining arc. Multiply that by 12 and divide by the difference in height; the result is in **digits**. <note>Units of measurement on the shadow square, usually 1/12th of the gnomon.</note> If there is a remainder, multiply it by 60 and divide by the same divisor, which will give the **minutes** of the digits. This method shows the shadow in the land without error. To convert this shadow into **Ptolemy’s shadow** <note>Refers to the coordinate system used by Claudius Ptolemy.</note>, multiply the digits you have by 9, ignoring the minutes; the result is Ptolemy's shadow. For those who wish to convert Ptolemy's measure back, multiply it by 9 and divide by 40; add the result to Ptolemy's shadow which was cast. If the remainder is less than 40, ignore it; if it is 20 or more, round the minutes up or down accordingly. 

**The end.** <note>original: "explicit"</note>

# Whoever wishes to know the rules of the astrolabe by Adelard.

First, let one learn what kind of thing it is. Know therefore that the signs...
It is a flat and round brass instrument which is suspended in equilibrium by a small bronze chain. One surface is called its face, while the other is called its back. And on the face indeed is seen the central axis, beneath which certain plates are contained within one another; some [rotate] with the center, while others are fixed in a stationary position. On the back, however, is a worked surface, which is called the [measuring scale] for the hours. Like those perforated tubes, it has two [sights] at the ends, specifically perforated along the diameter. Its **alidade** <note>The pivoting sighting bar on the back of the instrument.</note> is joined in the middle by a certain screw which in Arabic <gloss>that is, perforated</gloss> joins with a certain pin, the *alcorob* <note>original: "alcorob"; the wedge or pin, often shaped like a horse, that holds the components together</note> of its own small measure, which he calls the "horse" [equum]. Thus, what the astrolabe is has been said.

What it intends to signify must now be told. It should be believed regarding what pertains to its understanding: namely, through its division into Latin demonstrations which are proven by figures... through two chapters of notes. In the first place, for each day and each hour, how great the sun's position is, which in Arabic is *azusa* <note>original: "azusa"; a corruption of an Arabic term for height or position</note> and is called "altitude" by us; and through this, the hours of the night and the stars. Second, also, the sign and degree in which the sun acts each day. Third, the measurement of any given body below: its length and width, and also height, distance, and depth; the discovery of other figures is also seen. Fourth, the relationship of each body to one another. Fifth, the length and latitude of any given climate. First, therefore, to examine the known line... sixty days... ninety [degrees]... it shows the meridian section. When therefore [he wishes to know] the ascent of the altitude...

...inscribed with the names of two shadows. Of these, two are lying flat, called *elmobzore* <note>original: "elmobzore"; from the Arabic *al-mabsūṭah*, meaning "extended" or direct horizontal shadow.</note>, which are called "plane" shadows; and two are upright, called *elmanbuz* <note>original: "elmanbuz"; from the Arabic *al-mankūsah*, meaning "inverted" or vertical shadow.</note>, which are called "indirect" shadows. Each of these is divided into 12 parts, which they call **digits** <note>The standard unit for shadow scales in medieval science, where a gnomon is assumed to be 12 units high.</note>. Therefore, when we intend to know the length or width of any object, whether it is flat or upright, direct the sighting ray of the **alidade** <note>The pivoting rule on the back of the astrolabe.</note> toward the summit of the thing to be measured, and then consider how many digits the alidade occupies. From this, the measurement is deduced. For example: Let the surface to be measured be **b.c.** Let the height of the observer be **a.b.** If the number of indirect digits is four, which represents a fourth part of twelve, then **a.b.** will be a fourth part of **b.c.**, as demonstrated in the subject example.

But if you wish to measure the height of any upright body placed before your sight, you should know that such a thing is either **accessible** <note>An object you can walk to, like a building in an open field.</note> or **inaccessible** <note>An object whose base you cannot reach, like a tower across a river.</note>. Then consider how many digits on the side of the quadrant the ray occupies, and compare those to twelve. For whatever proportion exists between the occupied digits and twelve, that same proportion will undoubtedly be found between the height of the object and the flat ground that lies between the measurer and the thing being measured. One must only add the height of the measurer and the height of the astrolabe above the ground to the final calculation of the distance.

If one considers the difference between the first and second number of digits in relation to twelve, it will undoubtedly show the proportion between the object being measured and the distance between the two sighting points. If the difference is one, the height is equal to the distance between the points; if two, it is double; if three, it is triple, and so on for the rest. It must be spoken of in its proper place. Therefore, the double state of bodies is clearly shown and revealed. From this, we see that one type of body is that which is erected **orthogonally** <term>orthogonally: at a right angle (90 degrees) to a surface</term> upon any surface. Another type is when a body is joined or suspended orthogonally to such an erected object.

Because of this double state of bodies, it is necessary that the form of their shadows is also double. For the first, we take the **direct shadow** cast upon a flat plane. In Arabic, this is called *al-zill al-mabsut* <note>original: "helelmobzata"</note>, which means the "plane shadow." The second is when a body is joined orthogonally to an upright one; its shadow is cast down from the head or top of the object. Therefore, in Arabic, it is named *al-zill al-mankus* <note>original: "helelmaratū"</note>, which means the "indirect shadow." 

To lay down the teaching of these mutual proportions, **Ptolemy** <note>original: "acholomeo", a common medieval misspelling of the Greek astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note>, the master of geometry, described a **square** <term>square: the "quadratum umbrae" or shadow square often engraved on the back of an astrolabe</term> beneath the two diameters of the astrolabe that intersect each other at the center. The upright side of this square corresponds to any upright body along the vertical diameter. The horizontal side, however, designates the shadow of that same body. That side which is joined horizontally to the vertical diameter represents any such suspended body, while the other side declares its shadow. This is not indicated in the same way for the measure of degrees, since the shadow

occupied at the side of the square: the same proportion of the body’s shadow to its own body will be found. Wherefore, whatever digits of the indirect shadow on the astrolabe the ray occupies, it will be

indirect. But it also declares the plane shadow. When the ray decreases, it declares the indirect shadow. For the sake of clarity, I have not omitted the figure below.

Each side of the designated shadows is divided into twelve parts <note>original: "duodenat", referring to the 'digits' or 'points' used in medieval shadow squares</note>, just as any body is considered to be divided into twelve parts. When anyone wishes to estimate the shadow of any body—whether direct or indirect—by applying the astrolabe to the sun, I consider how many **digits** of the astrolabe’s shadow the sighting-ray occupies. For whatever proportion those numbers have at that hour, such will the shadow of the body obtain. For example, if it shows three of the twelve parts, it means the shadow is one-fourth the length of the body.

It is to be understood similarly for the direct shadow. If the ray occupies the corner of the two shadows, then the shadows are equal to the bodies themselves. I say this is the case if the bodies are equal. This is certain and manifest every day when the sun reaches **forty-five degrees of altitude**. When this happens, whatever height is to be measured is found to be equal to the measurement provided on the side of the shadow square.

Furthermore, when the indirect shadow presents itself to the ray instead of the plane shadow, the plane shadow cannot be seen before the sun reaches forty-five degrees of altitude. When you wish to find the plane shadow from the indirect one, consider the digits of the indirect shadow: divide the whole square <note>meaning the square of 12, which is 144</note> by that number, and the result determines the plane shadow. It is understood that one arrives at the indirect shadow from the plane shadow in the same way.

I have more to say about shadows, but since enough has been discussed here, I will close this little book and proceed to other matters.
