<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for using an astrolabe, shifting from measuring physical objects to calculating geographic coordinates—latitude and longitude—based on celestial observations. It relies on the medieval concept of "climates" or geographic zones.</meta>

The **latitude of the climates** <term>climates: horizontal zones of the Earth’s surface, categorized by the length of their longest day</term> is determined no differently than by the measurement of the hours and eclipses, just as it has been understood by our masters until now. They wish to determine the **latitude** of any region by the meridian altitude of the sun recorded on the day of the equinox. Whatever number of degrees this might be, let it be subtracted from ninety. The remainder, whatever it is, necessarily demonstrates the latitude of that climate.

But if the sun is working through other signs that are not equinoctial, one must know that some signs are to the "left" and others to the "right," which the Arabs call *shamaliyya* <note>original: "semelia", from the Arabic 'shamal' for North</note> and *janubiyya* <note>original: "genubia", from the Arabic 'janub' for South</note>. Those are called **northern** <note>original: "schemeleia"</note> which incline their face from Aries to Libra on the side of Cancer, as seen in the east. The others are **southern** <note>original: "genubia"</note>. Therefore, one will investigate the obliquity <term>obliquity: the angle of the sun's path relative to the celestial equator</term> in the right-hand middle. If it is northern, it shall be subtracted from the meridian altitude. If it is southern, they shall add the same to it. Then subtract the remainder from ninety, and do not doubt that the result is the latitude of the climates.

Furthermore, this must be understood in another way. For at night, it must be shown through the **astrolabe** how high the **pole** <term>pole: the celestial pole, around which the stars appear to rotate</term> rises in the given region. Without a doubt, that height must be announced as the latitude of those climates. The altitude of the pole is to be obtained in this way: for any star of those which I say never set <term>never set: circumpolar stars that stay above the horizon all night</term>, having noted its maximum and minimum altitude, one must take the exact middle of that measurement. Thus, having found the diameter, the midpoint is known to be the pole.

If anyone seeks the reason for all the things simply explained above, let him understand that it is found in **Euclid** and in the fifteen books of the art of geometry, which was translated from the **Arabic** language into **Latin**. These things were said concerning the latitude of the climates. Now, those things concerning their **longitude** are taken up as we received them from the masters; then, those things which by human

<column-break/>

ingenuity must be added. For they have found a way to calculate it: let it be carefully considered at what hour any eclipse, whether of the sun or the moon, occurs at the **meridian of Arim** <term>Arim: a mythical city or mountain on the equator, believed by medieval geographers to be the exact center of the world</term>. Then, let the hour at the present location be noted.

<margin>here the third. Arim</margin> 

For example: if the meridian hour <note>original: "midiana", i.e., noon</note> occurs at Arim, but in **Bathoma** <note>original: "bachoma", possibly referring to a specific geographic location like Bactra or a corruption of another name</note> the third hour is completed. Since fifteen degrees are assigned to each individual hour, it is clear that our noon differs from the noon of Arim by three hours. It is taught that the place differs from the other place by **forty-five degrees** in longitude. For this location is moved toward the west. Let this be the rule: the present climate is at 145 degrees. We do not doubt that it occupies 145 degrees of eastern longitude, or 45 degrees of western longitude. Therefore, following this reasoning, they assert that the longitudes of the climates can be denoted solely by the observation of eclipses.

However, it seems this can be understood differently and more easily. For any planet, whether the moon or another, let an examination be made at any hour over the meridian of Arim, and let that same examination be shown and clarified in the present climate. For if it precedes or follows the determined hour, the difference in the longitude of the climates will be indicated. For example, regarding the **moon**: let the examination be made at Arim on the coming fifth day; suppose the moon is at the first degree of Aries at the noon hour. If, however, in Bathoma it occupies that same degree at the third hour—which can easily be distinguished through the course of the preceding night—then the difference between the present climate and the climate of Arim is three hours, resulting in a longitude of forty-five degrees.

Similarly, it will be permitted to travel through the examination of hours and their changes. Furthermore, this is investigated in another way: for the noon hour of any climate, with the ray of the **alidade** <term>alidade: the sighting rule or pointer on the back of an astrolabe</term>...

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the astrolabe, moving from the mathematical theory of geographic climates to the physical components of the instrument—specifically the alidade, the limb, the climate plates, and the revolving rete.</meta>

One should generally position the astrolabe and the **alidade** <term>alidade: a pivoting sighting rule used for measuring angles</term> in wait until the following night. When the astrolabe is illuminated <note>Likely referring to using the instrument by starlight or artificial light to see the markings</note>, direct the moved alidade toward the **pole** <term>pole: the celestial pole, the fixed point in the sky around which the stars rotate</term>. If you can see the pole through that same degree, it may be **Arin** <note>original: "arin"; in medieval geography, Arin was considered the center of the world, located on the equator</note>, the most northern point, yet the longitude is undivided. But if it is necessary to move the alidade to see the pole, however many degrees that motion occupies, the **climate** <term>climate: a geographic zone defined by its latitude</term> will require that much difference in longitude by its own estimation.

<margin>The **alidade** <note>original: "alhidada"</note> is the ruler that turns upon the back of the astrolabe.</margin>
**I** shall now join the part concerning the back of the astrolabe to what we have said about the face. First, however, let us see how it should be handled. On the face, a certain **limb** <term>limb: the outer rim or edge of the astrolabe</term> stands out, occupying the outer circumference: its raised side presents itself to the view. This is divided into 360 degrees in equal proportion to the diameter. It is marked in the slope <margin>The **almustac** <note>original: "almustac"</note> is the equinoctial circle on a plane.</margin> of the **almustac** <note>original: "almustac", likely from the Arabic 'al-mushtarak'</note>, which is the equinoctial circle <term>equinoctial circle: the celestial equator</term> cast onto the flat surface of the astrolabe’s world by the logic of its operation. Beneath this limb, a certain circular plate represents the Earth. This "wheel" is divided by two diameters intersecting at the center. One serves the regions of the East and West; the other shows the markers for the Southern and Northern regions. In these, individual cultivated lands are described as equidistant. The outermost of these, which limits the limb, is fixed to the winter space. The second inside it is fixed between the North and the middle equinox. The third and smallest space is bound to the summer.

There are, furthermore, on the same plate, certain circles reaching upward, almost all of which <margin>**Almucantars** <note>original: "almicantaraz"</note> are the circles of progress in the hemisphere.</margin> are called in Arabic **almucantars** <term>almucantars: circles of altitude on the celestial sphere, used to measure how high a star is above the horizon</term>, meaning "progresses." These are applied to distinguish the horizontal upper hemisphere for any climate by equal division.

<column-break/>

As for the fact that the number of these is divided differently in various astrolabes, here is the reason. For the true and universal portion, as we discussed above, must consist of ninety degrees. But for easier operation, they insert divisions of those ninety degrees by skipping certain numbers. Hence, every such description is completed by points: there may be ninety, or twenty **almucantars**. They are shown clearly by twos (forty-five circles), by threes (thirty circles), by fours (twenty-two and a half circles), by sixes (fifteen circles), and by nines (ten circles).

<margin>The **alchemutch** <note>original: "alchemutch"</note> are the lines of the hours.</margin> Against these, others are noted reaching downward on the instrument, which in Arabic are called **alchemutch** <note>original: "alchemutch", referring to the unequal hour lines</note>. We may also call them the lines of the day. These demonstrate the same proportion on the same horizontal line, descending from the top to the bottom. The space behind those, which lies open across the aforementioned small circles, is universally divided into twelve to mark the distinction of the hours. For each climate is prepared with these, and he who follows the lines diligently will not be ignorant of the passage of the hours. Thus, in some places, the plates are called "climates" because they demonstrate the various geographic zones.

<margin>The **alcankabuz** <note>original: "alcankabuz"</note> is the revolving wheel.</margin> **U**pon these aforementioned plates, another open, inverted plate is placed, which geometricians distinguish by light. An eccentric center is located among the centers. On one side, it touches the winter space; on the other side, it does not fail to reach the summer space. In the excess of this, a certain tooth-like prominence is raised. This plate is called in Arabic the **alcankabuz** <term>alcankabuz: from the Arabic 'al-’ankabūt' meaning 'the spider'; the rete or skeletal top plate of the astrolabe</term>, or more clearly, the revolving plate. On it, the stars are found, whether they are in the **zodiac** <term>zodiac: the band of sky through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move</term> or outside it.

As a precaution, if any point falls between two **almucantars** <term>almucantars: circles of altitude marked on the astrolabe's plate</term>, the **almueri** <term>almueri: a pointer or "indicator" found on the edge of the rotating rete</term> will determine the value by calculation of the proportion.

## Following is the demonstration of the arc of light and night through the almucantars.
First, let us speak of this, because it is extremely necessary for opening up the subjects that follow. Therefore, when you wish to find the arc of light <note>The length of the day from sunrise to sunset</note> using the face of the astrolabe: place the degree of the sun upon the first **almucantar** and mark the position of the **almueri**. Then, move it until it reaches the last [almucantar] and note the position of the **almueri**. Between these two marks, you will find the arc of light you seek. Whatever remains of the circle you shall assign to the arc of night.

## Again, I say, once the light is thus found: if you desire to know how much of any hour of light has passed,
place the degree of the sun at the degree of its altitude upon its own **almucantar**, and mark the **almueri**. Then, [look at] the same degree through the first **almucantar** and note the **almueri**. The interval found between those two marks will determine exactly how much of the light has passed. If you use this and the following instructions diligently, you will also be able to do this for the day and the side of the hours.

## If, therefore, you wish to know in every island <note>In medieval geography, "islands" often referred to specific regions or "climates" of the known world</note> through these steps of the art:

In whichever climate you are, take the arc of light and night—demonstrated above—and collect the solstitial arc of light, for example, whether it be for the summer or winter of the year. Finally, divide this solstitial arc by twelve; and it will undoubtedly be clear how much that arc relates to the artificial hour. For by comparing each of the twelve parts of the artificial arc, you see how much each of the twelve parts of the natural arc relates to it, because it is always thus;

Twice therefore in this interval, it follows that all things reach their conclusion by defining the **radiation of the planets** <note>the "aspects" or geometric angles between planets, such as square or trine</note>. It must be known that one radiation is to the right and another to the left. It is assumed that you place the degree of the planet upon the meridian line and mark the **almon**. Finally, the **almon** itself shall be moved for a hexagonal radiation <note>a sextile aspect</note> so that it precedes by 60 degrees; for a tetragonal radiation <note>a square aspect</note> by 90 degrees; and for a trigonal radiation <note>a trine aspect</note> by 120 degrees. These are the degrees of the hours of the mid-heaven, for that is the first place of the radiations. 

Then, place the aforementioned degree upon the eastern **asofok** <note>horizon</note> and mark the **almon**; let it precede by the rightward movement of the **almon** for the hexagonal radiation by 60 degrees, for the tetragonal by 90 degrees, and for the trigonal by 120 degrees. From these results, the horoscope positions will be found and must be grasped; for that is the location for the time of the radiations. Therefore, to define the radiations of the hours of life, let one place the degree of the mid-heaven upon the meridian. Let the **almon** be marked, and let it precede with a rightward movement until the aforementioned degree sits in the view of the meridian. Let a mark "y" be made, and let the interval between the two marks be drawn into the difference of the radiations. If in producing this upon the arc of light it divides it, the aforementioned was above the earth; then [calculate] below the earth upon the arc...

...distance. — Let a point be placed in the middle of the center. And let the ruler <note>original: "regula", referring here to the sighting arm or alidade</note> be aligned so that whichever height you take is recorded: and on the other part, let a point be noted in the middle, and from those points let the middle point be found, so that a diameter may be made and afterwards the degrees.

---

**Direct shadows**, whether standing or flat, exist when the bodies of the objects stand orthogonally <note>at a 90-degree angle</note> to the earth. An **indirect shadow**, or a "lying" shadow, is one where the body is parallel to the earth. Therefore, there is always a ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of the lying or indirect shadow to its body: just as the body stands to its shadow. This is proven as follows: Let a body stand orthogonally to the earth at points *a* and *b*. In this figure, let *e* and *f* be similarly orthogonal to the earth, and let *f*, *a*, and *c* be equidistant <note>parallel</note>. Let the indirect shadow fall upon *a* and *b* at point *d*, and let *a* to *d* be the diameter of the shadow *c* to *d*. I say, therefore, that whatever the ratio is of *a* to *d* and *a* to *c*, the same is the ratio of the body to its flat or direct shadow.
Let the direct shadow of the body *a* to *b* be taken, which is *b* to *e*. The diameter is *d* to *e*. Let it be taken parallel to *b* and *e*, and it is proved that *a* to *d* is as *a* to *e*, and *f* to *d*. Therefore, *d* to *f* is the direct shadow of the body *a* to *d*, just as *b* to *e* is the direct shadow of *a* to *b*. Because whatever the ratio of *a* to *b* is to *b* to *e*, the same is *a* to *d* to *d* to *f*, because by the tangent it is similar. *a*, *b*, *e* and *a*, *d*, *f* are similar, but the tangent is *a*, *c*, *d*, namely the tangent *a*, *d*, *f*, because the angle *c*, *a*, *d* is the same as the angle *a*, *d*, *f*. But because the line is parallel, the angles *a*, *d*, *c* and *d*, *a*, *f* are equal. For the remainder, the angle *f*, *a*, *d* and *d*, *a*, *f* are equal. Therefore, whatever the ratio is of *a* to *d* (the indirect shadow) looking toward the increase of *e* to *a* to *c*, the same is *a*, *d*, *f* (the body) to the shadow *d* to *f*. But because the ratio of *a* to *d* to *d* to *f* is the same as the body to its upright shadow on that diameter. It follows therefore:

<column-break/>

that whatever ratio the shadow is seen to have to its body, the same is the ratio of the shadow of an upright body to its own shadow in the same diameter, as was proposed.

<margin>¶</margin> Note that in the **shadow square** <term>a mathematical grid found on the back of an astrolabe, used to solve height and distance problems using trigonometry</term> of the astrolabe, the lower side signifies the **flat shadow** <note>original: "umbra plana", the horizontal shadow cast on the ground</note>, and the opposite side of the descending diameter signifies the **direct shadow** <note>original: "umbra directa", the vertical shadow cast on a wall or scale</note>. Through the flat shadow one has the base; the height is found by looking through the astrolabe. Whatever the ratio of the shadow is to its body, the same is the ratio of the base to the height in that instance, determined by the height of the line called the **hypotenuse** <term>the diagonal line of sight from the observer's eye to the top of the object</term>, which descends from the highest point to the earth through the two sighting holes of the astrolabe, and subtends the height and the base. If the **alidade** <term>the pivoting sighting bar on the back of the astrolabe</term> marks the flat shadow, use the base; if it marks the indirect shadow, use the flat shadow. In this way, the base is calculated from the diameter of the astrolabe. Having the ratio of the base to the height, and the measurement of the base, the height will become known. If the distance cannot be measured directly, let the height and base be taken by moving toward or away from the object, so that by subtracting the smaller ratio from the larger, the ratio of the difference of the base to the height remains. The difference being measured, the height will be obtained. For example: if the first ratio of the base to the height is double, and the second is triple, and the difference between the base measurements is 30 feet, subtracting the double from the triple leaves a ratio of 1. Thus, the 30 feet have the same ratio to the height, just as if the height is compared to one base as double and the other as triple, and the difference is 30 feet, I will have 30 feet as the height...

...altitude. That which is placed below the things themselves, if it is also taken from the middle. For it is a straight line that is left: 30 feet to 6 [units] of altitude. Geometers have two ways of proving this same thing alternatively. Just as in the astrolabe, where the altitude is *ab*, the flat shadow is *bc*, and the other shadow is *bd*. So, as the altitude to be measured is indicated by the sides <note>original: "ossibus", literally "bones," likely referring to the legs or frame of a measuring instrument</note> *ef*, the first base is *fg*, and the second is *fh*. The ratio that *ab* has to *bc* is the same as *ef* to *fg*. But because the ratio of *bd* to *ab* is the same as *fh* to *ef*, then by the 4th proposition of the 5th book of Euclid <note>Euclid's *Elements* was the foundational textbook for medieval geometry</note>, the ratio of *bd* to *bc* is the same as *fh* to *fg*. And since whatever ratio *bc* or *cd* of the parts taken has to *bc*, the same is *fg* or *fh* of the parts taken to *fg*; and the distance, which is the ratio of *cd* to *bc*, is the same as *gh* to *fg*. But because the ratio of *bc* to *ba* is the same as *fg* to *ef*, then again by the 4th proposition of the 5th book of Euclid, the ratio of *cd* to *ab* is the same as *gh* to *ef*. That is, just as the ratio of the difference of two flat shadows to their altitude, so is the difference of two bases <note>horizontal ground distances</note> to the altitude being measured. In the astrolabe, therefore, the ratio of the difference of the shadows to the altitude can be made manifest, because the indirect shadow can be reduced to a flat one. And the ratio of the difference of the bases to the height to be measured is clear; and once the difference is measured, the height to be measured will be clear. Certainly, the base is also clear. In measuring a plane, whatever ratio the body has to the flat shadow, the same the observer has from below the eye

<column-break/>

to the earth to the thing being measured. That is, whatever the ratio of the body to the indirect shadow, the same is the ratio of the thing being measured to the observer. For the observer must take the place of the altitude, and the flat shadow takes the place of the base; and it is the reverse if it is an <unclear>indirect</unclear> shadow.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical tables for eclipses. While the previous page calculated solar eclipses at the furthest distance (apogee), this page provides data for lunar eclipses occurring at the lesser distance—when the Moon is at its perigee, or closest point to Earth. At perigee, the Moon appears larger, which affects the duration and magnitude of the eclipse.</meta>

<note>Glossary of terms used on this page:</note>
**Right Ascensions of the Right Circle:** Calculations for the celestial equator.
**Aries, Taurus, Gemini:** The first three signs of the zodiac.
**Degree (G):** A unit of angular measurement.
**Minute (M):** 1/60th of a degree or 1/60th of an hour.
**Hour (H):** Time-based measurement of celestial longitude.
**Right Ascension:** The astronomical term for the distance along the celestial equator.

# Solar eclipse when the <gloss>Moon</gloss> is at the farther distance.
<note>original: "Longitudine longiori." This refers to apogee, the point where the Moon is furthest from Earth. Because the Moon appears smaller in the sky, it often results in an annular eclipse, where a ring of the Sun remains visible.</note>

### Left Column

When you wish to know the **parallax** <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "diversitate aspectus," literally "diversity of aspect." This is the difference in the Moon's apparent position when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> of the moon: take the time that has passed between the hour of midday and the hour you desire. Enter with these values into the tables of the parallaxes of the moon, and take what you find there for the sign in which the moon was, regarding the minutes of **longitude** and **latitude**, and write each one down separately. After this, according to the portion of the moon, [look] in the table of equation, and take what was directly opposite it in minutes. Multiply those by the minutes of longitude and latitude respectively, and keep the result.

Then see if the equated portion fell in the upper half of the circle: subtract the result of the multiplication from the minutes of longitude and latitude, each according to its own kind. If it fell in the lower half, add the result of the multiplication to the minutes of longitude and latitude with the greatest certainty. 

And know that what was between the position of the moon and the **ascendant** <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> in degrees... <unclear>qd lib' min'</unclear>... the parallax in longitude is increased if the position of the moon [is before the meridian?]. If it was more, subtract it from the position of the moon, and the position of the moon will be [calculated] as you wish.

There is a certain table made for the parallax according to the latitude of the place. That latitude is **36 degrees and 50 minutes** <note>This specific latitude corresponds to the island of Rhodes, a major center for ancient Greek astronomy.</note>, and it happens that the longest **artificial day** <term>artificial day</term> <note>The period from sunrise to sunset, which varies in length throughout the year.</note> of that city is 14 hours and 51 minutes of an hour. Moreover, that table was made for the first degree of any sign, that is, for the first point of the degree of the sign. There are noted in the individual tables for the individual

### Right Column

signs: in the first line, the hours; in the second, the parallax in longitude; in the third, the parallax in latitude. If therefore you wish to calculate the parallax in longitude and latitude, do thus: Having found the **true opposition** <note>The exact moment the Sun and Moon are opposite each other, signaling a full moon and potential lunar eclipse.</note> of the sun and moon, find the longitude of the opposition from midnight; that is, calculate how many hours the eclipse is before midnight, or how many hours after midnight. 

Consider in which sign that opposition is. Let us say it is in **Cancer**, and suppose that the moon is in opposition at the first degree of Cancer, at the first point. If therefore you find that the eclipse occurred some hours before midnight—let us say two hours—enter into the table of Cancer with the entry [number] in the first line and take the number which you find noted there under the **recess** <note>original: "recessu." If, however, the true opposition should be three hours after midnight, the moon's entry must be sought under the recess. Having found, as we said before, the entry for the recess which notes three hours before midnight, you will take directly opposite it the parallax in longitude: 25 minutes; and the parallax in latitude: 49 minutes. 

If you work in other signs, always enter the table according to whether you have hours before or after midnight. But you must work thus if the moon was in opposition in the middle of the first degree of any sign. <margin>at night, i.e., in the table</margin>
At night, i.e., upon the retreat <note>original: "recessu." Then consider the difference <margin>Sign</margin> between the first longitude and this second longitude and take that excess. Write it down separately. Then, let a certain proportional part be found for that difference, just as was said <margin>in the table</margin> before, according to how it relates to the whole sign. Add this found value to the first longitude if the second was larger; subtract it from the first if the first was larger than the second. <margin>longitude</margin> In the same way, the latitude is to be equated <note>Calculated or adjusted for precision.</note>. When these values are thus equated, you will have the parallax in longitude and latitude for when the moon was in **opposition** <note>The Full Moon, when it is 180 degrees away from the Sun.</note> at the 10th degree <margin>mean</margin> of Cancer, three whole hours before midnight. Act similarly if the moon was in opposition in any degree of another sign three whole hours after midnight. <margin>If</margin> But if the moon was in some specific degree and some specific minute of another sign, find the parallax in longitude and latitude by the same reasoning. <margin>parallax</margin> However, if the moon was at a certain number of hours and a certain number of minutes of an hour in opposition before midnight: then <margin>of the moon</margin> first [look] in the tables for the whole hours upon the retreat. Then, add one hour to the three hours, and take the parallax for the 4th hour. Find the excess of the first longitude compared to the second and write it down separately. And find the proportional part for that excess, as the aforementioned minutes relate to one hour. Add this found value to the parallax in longitude that you first found for three hours before, and you have your goal. Do the same for the latitude. And what we have just said regarding the parallax in opposition for the whole moon, the same method must be used for the true **conjunction** <note>The New Moon, when the Sun and Moon are aligned; the necessary condition for a solar eclipse.</note> of the whole moon regarding the parallax, whether before midday or after. If the parallax is done this way, it is as if the moon were

<column-break/>

in its mean distance <note>original: "longitudine media," referring here to its average distance from Earth.</note>. But if it was further or closer: enter with the **argument** <term>argument</term> <note>The specific position of the Moon in its elliptical orbit used to look up corrections.</note> of the moon into the table of the equations for that argument. Take the proportional minutes which you find directly opposite it. Multiply those by the minutes of longitude and latitude separately. Then, subtract the product from each of its kind—that is, the longitude result from the longitude and the latitude result from the latitude—if the argument was in the upper half [of the circle]; and add it if it was in the lower half. Thus you will have the minutes of longitude and latitude for the moon's parallax at that same hour. Then, when the distance between the position of the moon and the degree of the **ascendant** <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at that moment.</note> is less than 90 degrees, add the moon's parallax in longitude to the equated position of the moon. And if it was more than 90 degrees, subtract it from it. The remainder will be the apparent position of the moon in true conjunction.

But if you wish to find the hour of the apparent conjunction <note>The exact moment the eclipse appears to happen from a specific location.</note>: add a twelfth part to the moon's parallax in longitude. Divide the total by the equated hourly motion of the moon. Subtract the resulting parts of whole hours from the hours of the equated conjunction, if the distance between the ascendant and the moon's position was less than 90 degrees. If it was more: add it. What remains or results is the hour of visible conjunction calculated for the city. You shall do similarly when you wish to have the moon's parallax for any hour. It differs, however, in this: that when the distance between the ascendant and the position of the moon is less than 90 degrees, add the parallax in longitude; if it is more than 90, subtract.

The altitude at Toledo is 40 degrees.
The altitude of the sun at Hereford in the winter time is 13 degrees <note>original: "gd," abbreviation for "gradus."</note> minus 38 minutes <note>original: "xxxviij gd," though likely "minutes" in context of solar altitude.</note>.
At the **Solstice** <note>The summer solstice, when the sun reaches its highest point.</note>, it is 66 degrees. The **latitude** is 52 degrees. The maximum day is 15 hours with 80 points <note>original: "bisce lxxx punctis." Points were a medieval subdivision of the hour, often 1/60th or 1/10th.</note>. **Capricorn**: 13 degrees.

These are the judgments of Hereford in the tables which are well-stated.

The collected years of all the parts composed by Master Roger <note>Roger of Hereford, an English scientist active around 1176–1198.</note> based on the years of the Lord at midnight at Hereford, in the year from the **Incarnation of the Lord** <note>A.D.</note> 1178, on account of an eclipse which the Master of Hereford saw in that same year by his own calculation.

Indeed, this eclipse of the sun and moon [was timed] at **Al-Arin** <term>Al-Arin</term> <note>original: "Arim." A mythical city in medieval geography located at the center of the world, used as a reference point for longitude.</note> on the 13th day of September at 15 hours and 1 portion <note>original: "pr. ḡ."</note>; at Marseille on the 13th day of September at 14 hours and 1 portion; at Toledo on the 13th day of September at 13 hours and 50 minutes; at Hereford on the 13th day of September at 11 hours and 1 portion.

Therefore, between Al-Arin and Marseille there are 46 degrees, which is three hours. Also, between Marseille and Toledo there are 26 degrees, which is one hour and a fifteenth part of an hour. Furthermore, between Marseille and Hereford there are 32 degrees, which is one hour and two-fifths. Between Toledo and Hereford there are 5 degrees, which is 11/6ths of an hour, which is a portion of one hour.

Hence, since the longitude of Al-Arin is 90 degrees and minutes, and the longitude of Toledo is 28 degrees and minutes, of Marseille 45 degrees, and of Hereford 32 degrees and minutes. And thus the distance of Hereford from Al-Arin is 66 degrees and minutes, that is, 4 hours and three-fifteenths of one hour.

And if the longitude of each city is placed toward the West from Al-Arin, its distance from the West is the same as from Al-Arin, that is from the eastern and western extremity. Thus, the aforementioned eclipse or **midnight** occurs later at Hereford than in other provinces or cities. Therefore, it was necessary to add to its **mean motion** <term>mean motion</term> <note>The average speed of a celestial body, used to calculate its position before applying corrections for its elliptical orbit.</note> because of the aforementioned calculations, which has been done in the present table according to the manner of Marseille, using the leap years of the Lord, as practiced by many Romans. For I have no other [tables] than the Arabic years, which I have changed because of the difficulty of the whole matter, as they are unfamiliar to our people.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Philosophia" (also known as *Liber de Naturis Inferiorum et Superiorum*) by Daniel of Morley. It follows the previous page's astronomical tables, which served as a technical supplement to the scientific knowledge Daniel describes acquiring in Spain.</meta>

## The Philosophy of Master Daniel of Morley to John, Bishop of Norwich.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'C' at the start of the text, rendered in red and green ink with internal foliate and vine scroll decoration and external penwork flourishes.</image-desc>

When, some time ago, I had departed from England for the sake of study and had stayed in Paris for a while, I saw certain "beastly" men occupying seats in the schools with a heavy air of authority. They had two or three benches placed before them, and displayed heavy books representing editions in gold letters or painted illustrations. They even held lead styluses in their hands, with which they would draw asterisks and obelisks in their books with a certain reverence. Although they occupied their places like statues <insert>indeed</insert> because of their own ignorance, they also wished to appear wise through silence alone. But when such men attempted to say anything, I found them to be completely infantile. When I realized that things were in this state, I considered with careful deliberation that I should not merely greet the arts that illuminate the scriptures in passing—skipping over them briefly—lest I incur a similar loss of knowledge. But because the doctrine of the Arabs, which consists almost entirely of the <term>Quadrivium</term> <note>The four mathematical sciences: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>, is most celebrated in these days at Toledo, I hurried there in haste so that I might hear the wiser philosophers of the world.

Eventually, however, being called and invited by friends to return from Spain, I came to England with a precious multitude of books. When it was reported to me that in those parts the liberal arts were silent, and that Aristotle and Plato were utterly consigned to oblivion in favor of <note>original: "p̄ p̄ciosa & scio penit⁹". Likely "pro pretiosis" or similar, suggesting a trade of deep knowledge for something superficial.</note> less valuable pursuits, I was deeply grieved. And so, lest I remain the only "Greek" among "Romans" <note>A metaphor meaning a man of learning among the unlearned.</note> where I had learned that such study flourished, I set out on a journey. On that very path, I met this lord of mine and spiritual father, John, Bishop of Norwich <note>John of Oxford, Bishop from 1175–1200.</note>, who, receiving me honorably as was fitting for him, rejoiced greatly at my arrival.

Therefore, as happens at a first gathering of friends, when I had been sufficiently questioned by the Lord Bishop about the wonders and teachings of Toledo, he finally turned the conversation toward astronomy, inquiring searchingly about the movements of the celestial bodies. Among other things, he added certain points about these <term>sublunary</term> <note>Referring to the Earthly realm "below the moon," which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> matters, which seem to serve their stations with a certain obedience to necessity. Since the brevity of time did not allow me to satisfy his questions at present, I decided that this present treatise should be presented to his discerning examination. The first part <gloss>part</gloss> pertains to the lower part of the world; the second to the upper part. He must therefore be pleaded with and exhorted in many ways: that even though nothing here may be found obscure, he should not hasten to despise the plain and clear opinions of the Arabs in what is said. Instead, he should notice that the Latin philosophers, laboring uselessly in such matters, have put forward obscure and ignorant fictions wrapped in certain ambiguities, so that under the shadow of ambiguity...

<summary>Daniel of Morley introduces his treatise, explaining his journey from the "ignorant" schools of Paris to Toledo to learn Arabic science and his subsequent return to an intellectually "silent" England.</summary>
<keywords>Daniel of Morley, John of Oxford, Paris, Toledo, Arab philosophy, Quadrivium, Aristotle, Plato, Astronomy, 12th-century Renaissance</keywords>

--- Page 186 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page where Daniel of Morley describes his return from Spain to England with a collection of Arabic scientific books, expressing his disappointment with the stagnant state of learning in the Parisian schools and his desire to introduce the 'doctrine of the Arabs' to his home country.</meta>

<margin>The pagan philosophers as witness</margin>
...lest the error of fear should cover [the truth]. Let no one be disturbed that, concerning the creation of the world and specifically regarding those things said about it, I do not present Catholic authors but call the **pagan philosophers** <note>original: "gentiles philosophos"</note> as witness. For although such men are not numbered among the faithful, some of their words, being full of faith <note>Daniel likely means "full of truth" or "trustworthy content" here.</note>, are to be held for our own teaching. Whence we, who have been miserably delivered from Egypt and from dominion, are commanded to borrow from the Egyptians **vessels of gold and silver** so that we may enrich the Hebrews. Let us borrow, then, at the Lord’s command and with His help, wisdom and eloquence from the philosophers of the gentiles, and thus despoil them in their infidelity, so that we may be faithfully enriched by their spoils.

<margin>All the world for the sake of man... concerning the world... concerning religion...</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' in red and blue ink with foliate patterns inside, set within a red square frame.</image-desc> But let it not be hidden how the **Divine Wisdom**, bringing forth every good into common use, shines forth beautifully. The distributor of all goodness wished His goodness to shine forth no less beautifully; but this would be impossible unless it appeared in its most beautiful form. He ordained two rational creatures to exist—namely, the **angel** and the **human being**—who would wonder at the Divine goodness with reason and intelligence; in wondering, they would understand; in understanding, they would praise; in praising, they would love; and in loving, they would imitate it as much as they were able. For before the formation of man, divine providence created the world and those things in the world necessary for man. Furthermore, man was created as if into a prepared house; he was led as the master of the household into the midst of the world. He placed him in the center so that all other things established on every side, as if common to man for whom they were created, might serve him as their worthier master.

<margin>Wisdom of the one God for the sake of man; the world in the middle; man not to be prideful</margin>
<insert>paragraph marker</insert> He did not do this so that man, becoming a world unto himself, might be puffed up and act proudly against his Creator; but so that, having been made more humble as one not ungrateful for so great a benefit, he might tremble before the Creator and Giver of all things. These things can be weighed from the *quantity*—namely, of the worldly workmanship—the power of the worker; from the *quality* of the creation: the wisdom of the designer; from the *marvelous beauty*: the immense goodness of the one who willed it. So that in what He was able to do, He might be feared; in what He wonderfully arranged, He might be marveled at; in what He willed, He might be loved, and truly loved. Since He lacked nothing, out of goodness alone, so that He might make us participants in His goodness when we did not yet exist, He deigned to build an ample house capable of holding the entire structure, which is now called the **palace of the world** <note>original: "aula mundi"</note>. But because a wise craftsman does nothing without counsel, He consulted His own wisdom. For whatever exists, exists as an image of a non-existent thing (such as a chimera that is painted though it does not exist) or as an image that represents the form of some existing thing. Therefore, the Supreme Builder sealed those things He disposed to be made in the <term>Nous</term> <note>original: "noï", a Latinization of the Greek word *nous*, meaning Mind or Intellect.</note>—that is, in the **Divine Mind**—as if in a golden sphere, with the seal of perpetual memory. This world, therefore, represents the image of the supernal will, as we read in a certain Arabic book called the *Book of the Triple World*. The first world...

Because of this, man is joined to the angels by kinship; let him reach them through holy religion. The angels also look upon and guard human actions with pious affection. Indeed, in the creation of man, the **provident dispenser** <note>God as the one who organizes and provides for creation.</note> was there, blending nature into one, and mixing as much as was necessary, He balanced the human being from equal parts—except that He perceived man to be such that he could satisfy both sides of his origin. 

On one side to wonder at and grasp celestial things; on the other: to inhabit and govern earthly things. Hence it is that since man is a single bond of soul and sense, of spirit and reason, he may be said to be **divine**, as if fashioned from the superior elements. Thus, through these superior faculties, he seems able to ascend into heaven. Yet in his worldly part, which consists of fire, air, and water, he remains a mortal marvel. 

But because God covered His image with a **corporeal house** <note>the physical body</note>, it happens that some of the world's vices remain mixed into these bodies. Furthermore, many discomforts come to the same because of the belly <note>the physical needs and hungers of the body</note>, which we necessarily have in common with all animals. From both these things it is necessary that the laziness of desires and other vices of the mind settle into humans. Hence it is that the soul is wounded incurably, which, infected by sins and corrupted, swells up as if by a draft of poison. But for these diseases, **discipline and understanding** are the highest cure. 

For since man is called an **incarnate mind** <note>original: "mens incarnata"</note> until, being deified, he flies free from the corporeal flesh, he is greatly stripped of the dignity of his origin while he is corrupted through the delights of carnal pleasures, while he is puffed up by the swelling of pride and envy, and while he is defiled by the stains of luxury and uncleanness. 

Whence these virtues of the soul are turned to perverse use, while man does not remember that **reason** <note>original: "rone" (ratione)</note> was attributed to him so that he might discern good from evil; **irascibility** <note>original: "irracibilitate"; the spirited or assertive part of the soul in Platonic thought</note> so that he might resist evil; and **concupiscence** <note>original: "concupiscibilitate"; the desiring part of the soul</note> so that he might desire the good. Hence it is that, from the corruption of the affections which are naturally in the soul, the aforesaid things are so varied and changed into their opposite. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the human soul's faculties—the rational, the desiring, and the spirited—and how their corruption leads to specific vices. ...for [rationality] <note>original: "bilitas", the suffix of "rationalitas" from the previous page</note> when corrupted, gives way to pride. It must then be seen by what and how many vices the inner man is subject.

It is established, therefore, that the human body consists of four humors, just as it is formed from the four elements of the world. For **yellow bile** <note>original: "colera"</note> derives its property from fire; **blood** from air; **phlegm** from water; and **melancholy** from earth. Therefore, when fire—that is, red bile—is disturbed, a man becomes **paralytic**. When air—that is, blood—is disturbed, a man becomes **polypous** <note>original: "polipus"; likely referring to growths or tumors of the nasal passages or skin</note>. When water—that is, phlegm—is disturbed, a man becomes **dropsical** <note>original: "ydropicus"; suffering from edema or internal swelling</note>. When earth—that is, melancholy—is disturbed, a man becomes **leprous**. Other corrupted humors generate the aforementioned diseases.

In the same way, the "house" of the body is, as was said, compacted from the four elements. From fire, because natural heat originates there; from this comes the light of the eyes. From air, the spirit <note>the breath</note> is formed into words. From earth comes the corpulence <note>the solid mass</note> of the body. From water comes the abundance of natural moisture. When these indeed exceed the boundaries of measure, other vices grow out:

Because it does not befit a wise guest to be ignorant of the composition of his own house, concerning this spacious and universal house—so that the mind of the listener might be more firmly held—that which I learned from the [work] of **Agalupo Mirta** <note>likely a garbled reference to an Arabic authority or a specific translation source from the 12th-century Toledo school</note> in the **Toledan language** is here written down in Latin.

Thus, in common philosophy, there is no doubt that this visible world was fabricated according to the exemplar and likeness of the eternal world. I call that true world the **archetypal world** <note>original: "mundum archetypum"; the "blueprint" of the universe existing in the mind of the Creator</note>, which remains always like a certain art within its craftsman, immutable. Yet it is not necessary that this visible world, composed according to that image, should lack the borrowing of its essence from that one. For example: if by chance a craftsman wishes to build a chest, he first arranges the width, length, and depth in his mind. The chest, indeed, can fail through age, but the art in the craftsman can neither fail nor perish.

Therefore, with the greatest effort, we must investigate if this fabric of the world ever emerged from an order—as if it were made by someone—or if it exists through itself. Some say that this world was made from **chaos**, and such people say that this chaos was **hyle** <note>original: "ylen"; the Greek term for primordial, unformed matter</note>, which they call primordial matter. <meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of primordial matter (hyle), specifically addressing whether this matter was a "body" and how it relates to the four elements. The author is navigating the potential contradictions between Aristotelian and Platonic physics, particularly regarding the properties of light, celestial bodies, and the inherent order of creation.</meta>

<margin>d a</margin>
<margin><unclear>Parts</unclear></margin>

Matter <note>original: "yile"; from the Greek *hyle*</note> was once the four elements. And the same reasoning can predict that the four elements were matter: that matter was indeed matter. And if matter generated the four elements, it would seem that it contained itself. Which is plainly false, since nothing entirely contains itself. Therefore, a figure of speech is observed in this expression. Because although I may say that a universal thing is produced in the world—which, when gathered together, is nothing other than the world—nevertheless, I do not concede that the world is contained by the world. If it is granted as stated above: matter was a body, and it was the four elements, each of which was a body. It would then follow that that one body was actually several bodies. 

But why is this surprising? For in any single body, there are infinite bodies. For any part of a body is itself a body; yet one body, in terms of its wholeness, is not many. Just as fire is not many, but is conceded to be a single element—even though every part of it is fire—so one body is not said to be many, even though every part of it is a body. By this comparison, it is proved that although matter was the four elements (each of which was a body), it was not many bodies, but one.

Still, perhaps Aristotle says: "It was a body, therefore it was colored." For he treats "body" and "colored" as equivalent properties. I, however, depart far from this assertion, for I know that there are celestial bodies <note>original: "stellaria corpa"; the stars and planets</note>, yet I do not dare to presume they possess color. Since a solar ray is a body, let the logician say with what color it is colored! As for an airy body, I do not know how to assign it a color. But so that "the Philosopher" <note>A common medieval title for Aristotle</note>, whom some do not understand, may be explained: we must understand that he was speaking of solid bodies that are subject to sight and touch. Such things are corporeal and colored, whereas the elements themselves are not affected by colors at all. 

For every color, as Hippocrates says in his book *On the Change of Airs*, arises from the four qualities <note>The primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. Therefore, an element—which consists of only two qualities—is not colored. Although the Philosopher, in his book on lights, called water "white," he did not intend for us to understand it as elemental water <note>original: "aquam elementatam"</note>; perhaps he preferred in this instance to be understood by common people rather than to follow strict philosophy. Similarly, a certain philosopher recently describing water called it "white and dry." Even though it is not truly white, the water is resolved through its dryness into fire, which is lit in a wick so that it might feed like wax and provide the power of burning. This will be clear to anyone who doubts, by looking at wax candles wrapped in snow. 

Finally, someone will argue and investigate the nature of the underlying thing according to Plato. This was a body; therefore, Plato would say it was either matter or an elemental composite <term>elementatum: a thing made of elements, as opposed to the pure elements themselves</term>. It is clear that it was not a composite, because such composites did not yet exist, even as a possibility. But if it is conceded that it was an element, one might conclude: "Therefore it was fire, or air, or water, or earth." Yet it was none of these; therefore, it was not an element. What, then, should be said? That it is certain matter was neither a pure element nor a composite, and yet I concede it was a body. Indeed, I know of infinite bodies of this kind. Such are all the celestial bodies, as will be determined in what follows; but now let something be said about the primary ordering of the elements.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical state of the early universe, moving from the definition of matter as a single "body" to the specific qualities of the four elements during the dissolution of chaos. It also introduces a classification of different types of "works" (divine, natural, and human) and begins a survey of ancient Greek philosophical opinions on the "first principle" of all things.</meta>

So it was that the earth was covered by the waters. The air was somewhat more corporeal <note>thicker or more physically dense</note> than it is in itself now. In its breadth, it extended for the most part into the fire. The fire was similarly somewhat thicker. These were the visible arrangements of the elements, which are now called the elements. But chaos was well dissolved when the earth began to appear and be adorned. I believe this was done through the operation of nature, in a slow and orderly fashion, and that it would be described as having been ordered. I prove it thus: Who denies that there are three types of works?

For every work is either the work of God, the work of nature, or the work of a craftsman imitating nature.
**The work of God:** He makes the world out of matter that pleases Him.
**The work of nature:** To procreate like from like.
**The work of man:** Because of the harshness of the weather, to artfully compose clothes; or to shape the inanimate into the likeness of a living soul—in which things he imitates nature.
Each work, however, draws its quality from its maker. Therefore, the work of God draws its quality of being "ordered" from God.

But lest I pass over the assertions of the philosophers like a rooster hopping over hot coals <note>original: "gallus insiliens per carbones"; a Latin idiom for rushing through a subject too quickly or skipping the difficult parts</note> with suspended feet, since we must discuss the beginning of the world's constitution, let me briefly touch upon what their ancestors held to be the true principle.

Hesiod <note>original: "Esiodus"; the 8th-century BCE Greek poet</note>, a professor of natural science, said that all things come from the earth, as if from the first principle, because she bore the mother of the universe. This follows what Plato asserted: that the earth was the oldest of the goddesses and the nourisher of all. For Hesiod considered that all things return to the earth as to a mother; and since he said all things come from her, he was the first who ordered that dead men be buried in the earth. He did this so that they might more quickly return to their origin, and have the end of their existence where they received its beginning.

Democritus and Thales of Miletus <note>original: "Tales milesi"</note> asserted that [water] was the principle of all things, because it seems that nothing vital can exist without moisture. This is especially true since an animal lives through the humors <note>The four bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament</note>, which physicians call **melancholy**, **phlegm**, **choler**, and **blood**. Furthermore, herbs and trees rejoice in moisture. Therefore, nothing vital can be sustained in them by its own power—since such an abundance of heat flourishes in those celestial bodies—unless intervening moisture can resist it; for Thales affirmed that life could subsist within that moisture. This is why some still say the fire of the sun is nourished by water; whence in their fables it is read that the gods were invited to a banquet <note>A reference to the classical belief that the sun and stars "fed" on the vapors rising from the ocean</note>.

Aristotle also held that the bodies of the planets were of a fiery nature. Burning comes from fire. Therefore they said that if moisture is lacking, the planets will consume the lower regions with their fires. As for what remains, since fire always seeks matter to consume, it will eventually consume itself. For fire, since it is never idle, always acts either upon itself or so that it consumes something.

<margin>Anaximenes</margin>
Anaximenes judged **air** to be the principle of all things. For every animal desires air; otherwise, it would not breathe. And so, in the airy spirit of the earth, nothing corporeal can live without it. Furthermore, in air alone is found that balance <note>original: "tempuries"</note> which is the seat of nourishment for all things. For air itself is the receptacle of heat and cold. It is the spirit that receives and joins all things in itself. It is that which

<meta>This page continues the survey of ancient philosophical opinions regarding the first principles of the universe. Having previously discussed the "work of God" and the "work of nature," the author now contrasts the views of the Epicureans, Stoics, Platonists, and Aristotelians before asserting a Hermetic view of a single, divine source.</meta>

...whatever moves, colors, and clothes. The poet touched upon this who said: "Jupiter is whatever you see." <note>original: "Iupiter quodcumque vides"; a quote from the Roman poet Lucan, suggesting the divine is present in all things.</note> 

From this, indeed, all things are brought into existence by the Lord's design. For from fire comes heat, and from heat—through the power of form—the procreation of things is born. For just as cold is the effect of death, so heat is the principle of life. Also, since the earth is cold, if the benefit of fire did not reach it, it would never sprout. For the "soul of the world" was called a spark of fiery substance. 

Empedocles established four divine principles: namely, the four elements, which when mixed with others, each would hold its own best quality. Epicurus said all things consist of the most basic atoms. He called "atoms" the smallest indivisible bodies. An opinion which the Stoics and Geometers asserted was nothing; for they grant that every body has three dimensions <note>length, width, and depth</note>. The "void" indeed was called the empty space lying between the conjunction of atoms. He affirmed that every body is porous, and that individual things happen by chance. He proved that the world was moved through the fortuitous clashing of atoms in this way: Whatever moves changes place. Whatever changes place moves into that which occupies a place. Therefore, whatever moves, moves something else, because from the movement of a single atomic body, the motion of the entire universe follows.

Plato established four causes in the principles of things. The first he named the **efficient** cause; the second, the **formal**; the third, the **final**; and the fourth, the **material**. He asserted the **efficient cause** to be God himself; the **formal** to be the wisdom of God; the **final** to be divine goodness; and the **material** to be the four elements. 

Pythagoras and Aristotle, however, said there were two principles of all things: unity and "otherness," <note>original: "altitatem," likely a scribal variant of "alteritatem," referring to the Pythagorean Dyad</note> that is, nature. By this <margin>h</margin> nature they understood **hyle** <note>hyle: the Greek term for primordial matter</note>. Pythagoras called it "otherness"; Aristotle called it "possibility" <note>potentiality</note>, because from it the form of various things was produced. 

Concerning this multitude of opinions, there is enough in the sacred writings. For they multiply words, but not toward a full understanding of the matter. If some were asked whether these principles are bodies—giving only words in return—they respond that it was an "incorporeal body." If asked whether they are "substance," they assert it was somewhere between having substance and having no substance. If it is said they were substance, they respond that this is too much of an affirmation. If it is said it was not substance, they say that is too vehement a negation. These things can indeed be said in this manner, but they can in no way be understood.

---

Perhaps someone might think I am disparaging these errors, but I see myself as simply enumerating the authors themselves. I hold to the unassailable opinion of the great Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy</note>: I boldly concede with him that there is only one principle. I do not assert it exactly as Heliodorus wished, but I affirm it to be far removed from all generation of elementary nature. The aforementioned authors perhaps speak well according to their own understanding. Yet it seems that many are deceived in this: that they hold "having a principle" and "being a principle" to be the same thing. Since there is as much distance between "the principle" and "that which has a principle" as there is between the "begetter" and the "begotten." For I call that which receives its beginning from another a "man" [or a created thing], but that which gives a beginning I call the principle. And it is rightly called a "beginning" because it gives a beginning. For that is established as the true principle which is not from elsewhere, but is in itself.

**Further**, two opinions of the philosophers remain, which I think should not be passed over. Some assert that the world never had a beginning and will never have an end, and they call it "eternal." Others affirm the world had a beginning, but will never have an end; they call it "perpetual." This must be dealt with briefly. Because if it is shown that the world will reach an end, then it will be shown to be neither eternal nor perpetual. For every body which is by its nature <term>passible</term> <note>capable of being acted upon or changed by external force</note> can also be corrupted. That which is corruptible in and of itself cannot stand with eternity. For no part of eternity is inherent in it. Therefore, since this world flows incessantly through hidden and manifest corruptions, and certain parts pass away while others succeed them, it cannot possibly be eternal, as it knows itself to be established in a nature of change. But this must not be defined rashly, as disagreements are found among authors of great name. From these, let two excellent witnesses be brought forward: one I shall call the great Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes</note>, the other Trismegistus, the grandson of the aforementioned Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom</note>. He says then: the great Mercury in the Book of Eternals states that there are things which, though they act, suffer in no way, nor are they diminished in their substance. Some act as bodies participating in nature, which however suffer the loss of themselves and are not eternal. For example, to use one case for many: A knife acts by cutting and suffers by becoming dull. Those things which are subject to generation and corruption, increase, decrease, and dissolution, eventually come to a fatal end by failing entirely. All reason testifies that changes are found in these lower movements. But since every kind of alteration is governed by regions far removed from the higher things, it does not seem that a nature so firmly established could ever be dissolved by any reason. Unless he who made such things sees otherwise; let us hear what Trismegistus wishes to encounter.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the origin of the world. ...have been recorded. Earthly <term>time</term> <note>original: "Terrenum tempus"</note>, however, is distinguished by its sharp quality: by the variation of heat and cold. But celestial time is marked by the returns of the stars to the same places in their temporal rotation; this enlivens the world as a vessel of time and governs its course through its movement. Time comes from the order of status. Order and time work together in the renewal of all things that are in the world. For all things being so, nothing is stable, nothing is firm, and nothing is immobile—whether among things born, celestial things, or earthly things. Only the Holy One is truly immortal; He alone is in Himself, from Himself, and with Himself, entirely full and perfect. To Him belongs His own firm stability; He is not moved by another’s impulse, nor changed in place, since all things are in Him, and He alone exists out of all things.

Therefore, with the above determined in this manner, the path is prepared to approach the creation of the world. To explain this better, four types of things must first be established, without which no hope of understanding the lower world can be found. These are: **matter**, **form**, **composition**, and the **composite**.

**Matter** consists of water, air, earth, and fire. **Form** is that by which each thing is distinguished within its own kind, just as a human is distinguished from a donkey. **Composition** is the harmony <note>original: "consonantia"</note> of the elements within physical bodies. The **composite** is that which is fashioned by such a composition. For as <term>Albumazar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886 AD), a Persian scholar whose works on astrology and philosophy were central to medieval science</note>, the son of Al-Balkhi—who followed the nature of celestial things after Ptolemy—says: in all these bodies where the signs are found, first is the composition; second, the composite; third, the nature; and fourth, the species <note>original: "Anarci" / "species"</note>.

With these arrangements, since it has been proved above that every generated thing has a generator older than itself, it follows that the sustainer is older than the thing sustained (just as the earth is older than earthly bodies). Thus, the composition of matter would be older than the matter itself; for the genera and species of animals, grains, and metals existed in the potential of nature before they finally came forth into action or succeeded as a composite. For what composition could exist without someone to compose it? And it is a truth of matter that it does not compose itself, nor does it impose a form upon itself.

Since things are so, it is necessary that every generated thing has a generator, and every composite has a composer who distinguishes between the genera and species of all things. Such a composer can be called nothing other than the life-giving Creator <note>original: "genitor vivificator"</note>, who by His wisdom reached all individual things at once. He created from nothing two primordial matters—the lower and the higher—for the sake of distinction. To ensure they kept the law of their established condition inviolate, He animated them at the very moment of creation with an eternal breath of divine inspiration. This law I call "Nature," which assigns motion or rest to each physical thing according to the properties of its subject. 

It is designed so that it does nothing without reason; it takes its constitution from the Soul, yet in such a way that neither operates against the other. These are the two instruments of the Great Artisan, which have learned from their Master how to compose every composite through a certain harmony in these lower regions, and likewise to dissolve them through a certain dissonance—though all this is ascribed to the Artisan, from whom they took the lead of their origin. Though a certain craftsman...

**P**redicted Nature, as a skillful servant, finally purified the elements and separated them from one another so that she might brighten the perfect world. **C**onsidering this, provident Nature, seeing that two extremes cannot be joined without a middle ground, placed <term>Water</term> <note>original: "aquam"</note> and <term>Air</term> <note>original: "aera"</note> in between. However, she tempered them so they would not intrude more into the junction of one than the other, wishing the two aforementioned elements not just to be mixed, but joined, so that each would remain what it is. For if she had placed only Water between them, this connection would not last, as it relates as much to Earth as to Fire. Water shares <term>corpulence</term> and dullness with Earth. Similarly, if she had only put Air in between, such a bond would not suit them, for Air shares subtlety and mobility with Fire. But since Earth and Air each have two qualities: let Earth be cold and dry; Water cold and moist; Air shares this moisture with Water and heat with Fire. Between both, this alone suffices. The arrangement of the elements is such that Earth holds the lowest place, then Water, then Air, and finally Fire surpasses them all. Water is placed next to Earth because, being of a natural kind, it could occupy a similar place, even if not as dense as Earth. Then comes Air, which is joined to Fire; it is subtler than Earth, though it is placed lower.

**T**here are, however, three distances between the elements: first, from Fire to Air; second, from Air to Water; third, from Water to Earth. <term>Physicists</term> <note>original: "phisici"; in this context, refers to students of natural philosophy rather than modern physics</note> call the first "Obedience," the second "Harmony," and the third "Necessity." Through these, nothing should be lost in the joining of the elements. The first interval between Fire and Air is called "Good Obedience" because those higher things act upon the lower through a certain obedience, mixing with them through free choice; namely, they conceive in the Earth and Water and create offspring. The second interval, between Water and Earth, is called by some "Necessity," because these two suffer by necessity from those higher elements. For this reason, <term>mythical astronomy</term> <note>original: "fabulosa astronomia"</note> imagines some elements to be called by feminine names and others by masculine <note>Earth and Water were traditionally viewed as passive/feminine, while Fire and Air were active/masculine.</note>. However, the joining of the middle elements is rightly called <term>Harmony</term> <note>original: "armonia"</note>, which is to say, the agreement of divided things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physical and philosophical composition of the universe. While the previous page established Nature as an artisan arranging the elements, this page defines the specific physical properties—such as density, compression, and visibility—of the four elements and explores the distinction between pure elements (accessible only to the mind) and "elemented" composite bodies (accessible to the senses).</meta>

Harmony is also a concord of differing sounds reduced into one. In this bond, however, there is a cause: one part acts and the other receives.

It is common to ask why the earth is more solid than other things. From this, a probable opinion is given: that thickness and solidity arise from compression. This is why <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: "phisici"; referring to scholars of the natural world or "physics" in the medieval sense</note> say the earth is thick because it suffers the greatest constriction. This is both because it is bound by the first surrounding of water, and because it is compressed on all sides from above by the descent of fire and air. From this, a measure is made: the earth [is at the center], water is twofold, air is single. Fire, being superior, is constrained by no compression. This is why air, which produces a medium <term>diffusion</term> <note>original: "fusionem"; likely referring to the way light passes through it</note> to the sight, resists the touch [scarcely at all]. Water, more gathered to the sight, resists the touch more effectively. The earth, however, being intensely congealed by things pressing from all sides, resists both sight and touch.

Natural philosophers also, when dealing with the creation of the world, do not insist on the individual natures of bodies that seem to distinguish the elements of the world, since there is none of these things that is not made from the four elements. This can easily be proven by example. In the earth: there is something of water, since a degree of moisture is found in it. In the same earth: something of air, which smoke proves during evaporation. The same can be seen in the others. However, since elements are of the purest essence, they are the kind of bodies that are not subject to the senses, but only to the <term>intellect</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "pure" elements are theoretical building blocks; the "dirt" or "water" we see is always a mixture.</note>. Therefore, these four compose the body of this world in such a way that, while those components exist in every single composite thing, they never appear to the senses as themselves. Rather, the composite thing itself is called by a "false assignment" by the common people using its simple name. No one, as the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Usually referring to Aristotle.</note> says, has ever touched earth as [pure] water, nor has anyone seen air as [pure] fire. These things we grasp with the senses are composites, not the elements themselves. Truly, they exist through them; therefore, because one element abounds more in a specific thing, each thing falsely receives its name [from that dominant element].

What has been said here regarding <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "yle"; from the Greek "hyle," meaning the fundamental raw material of the universe.</note> and the elements is theoretical, because Matter did not exist except while the elements were pure. Since these were quickly corrupted [mixed] so that the generation of things might occur, Matter—which in Greek defines the one <unclear>sphere</unclear> of the world—ceases to be [in its pure state]. Similarly, the elements, having been somewhat alienated from their principles through the aforementioned generation, then persisted in the essence of "elemented" things, in which nothing remains except the properties of the elements. Yet these "elemented" things are said to be generated from elements just as bread is from flour and water. For we ought not destroy the principles of the disciplines; indeed, every single discipline has its own subject matters and certain <term>foundational concepts</term> <note>original: "ficciones"; here meaning conceptual axioms or postulates</note>, such as a "point" (which has no part), a "line" (length without width), and things of this sort. It is not necessary to prove these, because a reason for a first principle should not be demanded, just as if one were testing a rule. Such is the case in the study of nature regarding "elemented" things.

An element is a simple body, placed beneath the lunar globe, contained by two qualities. This is so that an "elemented" thing [a composite] may have more than two qualities. "Simple" means that which is the same in essence and has all parts similar to each other. For any part of elementary fire is fire. In every description, an element is said to be "placed beneath the lunar globe" because nothing above [the moon]...
