<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physical and philosophical composition of the universe. While the previous page established Nature as an artisan arranging the elements, this page defines the specific physical properties—such as density, compression, and visibility—of the four elements and explores the distinction between pure elements (accessible only to the mind) and "elemented" composite bodies (accessible to the senses).</meta>

Everything below the moon is subject to corruption as well as generation. For there is a reciprocal <term>generation</term> <note>The cyclical process where elements transform into one another, a core concept in Aristotelian physics</note> of the elements. For indeed, the earth is dissolved into water; water thins into air; air thickens into water; water densifies into earth; and earth is massed into a solid body. Fire is described in this way: Fire is hot and dry; it is sharp, fleeing the lowest depths by its own lightness and bursting forth into higher regions by its <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: "subtilitate"; referring to the "fineness" or lack of density that allows it to rise</note>; and it is hot in the highest degree, retaining a quality that has movement away from the center. Air is a moist and hot body, thin and mobile, retaining a quality that has movement away from the center and being moist in the highest degree. Water: cold and moist, flowing and heavy, retaining a quality that has movement toward the center, and being moist in the highest degree. Earth: cold and dry, solid, immobile, and heavy, retaining a quality that has movement toward the center, and dry in the highest degree.

Now, that is said to be hot "in the highest degree" which is naturally and principally hot, such as fire; for it is impossible for fire to exist and not be hot. Likewise, air is said to be moist in the highest degree because nothing is more naturally moist than it; and water, because nothing is more <term>substantially</term> <note>original: "subalr'" for "substantialiter"; the essential nature of the thing</note> cold. So too is the earth: because nothing is more potentially dry; hence it is called "arid" by some.

It should be noted that two qualities, as mentioned—namely heat and moisture—since by their nature one has the power to dissolve and the other to relax, they cause movement away from the center toward the circumference; that is, they have a tendency to move from the lower parts toward the higher. Therefore, fire and air, in which these two qualities dominate, occupy the higher regions. The other two qualities, however, move toward the center: namely cold by constricting, and dryness by thickening and contracting. 

<margin>They teach the motion from the middle to the extremes. Motion toward the center is motion...</margin>

Whence it is that water and earth, in which these two qualities predominate, are located below. This is the motion from the extremes to the middle. For earth is, as it were, the center of the elements. For in every spherical thing, only the middle is the lowest part.

This arrangement is made after the likeness of an egg: earth is in the middle, like the <term>yolk</term> <note>original: "vitellus"</note> in an egg; around this is water, like the white around the yolk; around the water is air, like the <term>membrane</term> <note>original: "panniculus"</note> containing the white. Outside, enclosing all things, is fire, after the manner of the eggshell.

But it must be known that although these four elements are joined in one, each has two qualities, of which one is substantial and the other is <term>accidental</term> <note>original: "accidentalis"; a property that can change without the thing losing its identity</note>. For example: Earth is potentially dry in itself, but it is actually cold as if by the influence of water. Water is naturally cold of itself, but it has an accidental moisture from the air. Air, while it is moist of itself, also has heat from fire; in it, moisture prevails. Fire, however, since it is in the higher place, is not held by the necessity of a strict law; elements must give [qualities] to those subjects below them, but fire could receive nothing from others. And if it were to receive from anything, it would be from the first thing below it, namely air, or it would acquire it from nothing. But what would it receive? Moisture. In what then would it differ from air, which is moist and hot? Indeed, since moisture is heavy and dispersing, it would have no place in fire, which is sharp; nor would coldness have a place, since it is the contrary of heat. Therefore, only dryness joined to heat was suitable for it. Because when supreme dryness in some way assists the heat, it sharpens the heat of the fire. And so, since fire is hot and dry, it has heat from its substantial part, and from that heat it derives dryness, which the effect of heat generates. But since fire is naturally always in motion, the motion which belongs to it by kindling in a spiral...

</margin>
They cannot descend, because it would be against their nature. One would not find them ascending, since all the lower places are occupied by the lower elements. Just as above the moon there is nothing that can ascend, for it would instantly vanish because of the violence of the rapid motion of the firmament and the planets. These planets, while they move with natural motion and revolution by the mass of their bodies, produce among themselves a proportional **harmony** <note>This refers to the "Music of the Spheres," an ancient philosophical concept that the movements of celestial bodies create a divine, mathematical harmony inaudible to human ears.</note>, although it cannot be heard by us due to the excessive distance. When, therefore, [the element] ascends almost to the first circle of the moon, it is by such a great explosion of motion somehow beaten back and it reverberates and is gathered into itself; and once gathered, it bends obliquely, and although not voluntarily, it moves nonetheless into a cavity. So turning back into the cavity, it covers the other elements and always naturally tends upward. Air, however, extends itself sideways. Just as through fire it has a wider <term>sphere</term> <note>original: "sphaeram"; referring to the concentric layers or "shells" of elements that make up the universe in medieval cosmology</note> than the other elements, it encloses, hides, and sustains water and earth from every view. Indeed water, although it naturally moves in length <note>meaning horizontally across the surface</note>, yet as if by some indissoluble bond it surrounds and binds the neighboring earth. Earth, however, since it is heavy, tends downward in a straight line; not that it moves at any time since it is immobile, but because it has by nature the tendency toward the lower parts. Just as fire always
<margin>
etc. on the other side
</margin>
tends to the heights; not that it is always tending [moving], but because it has such a property from its own nature. Even if it be immobile, what then should be said of the **earthquake**? Because sometimes it happens that the earth is moved perceptibly. But this is called movement in a specific sense, just as one of the elements is prohibited from entering into another, since no element can enter totally into another. The earth moves, therefore, particularly <note>i.e., in specific parts</note> and not universally. The cause of this motion is trapped air, which, since it encloses the earth on all sides with itself, is found deep within its bowels. This is because air, trapped by entering beneath the earth, strives to break out to its own origin <note>The "origin" or natural place of air is above the earth and water.</note>. For since every nature loves its like, it likewise flees its opposite. Whence therefore air, trapped in the aforesaid manner, hastens to exit with great effort toward the outer air as if to one calling it; gathered into itself, it fills the cavities of the earth with greater intensity. And while it finds an obstacle, it [shakes] it with great weight and makes a large part of the earth tremble. If it allows it to rest, it finds an exit through the back [surface]; this eruption is shown to be dangerous to those who are nearby. Because while exiting it separates the surface of the earth, it absorbs all the heavy things it finds into an irrecoverable abyss. For that earth which receives them closes its mouth: after the air is forcefully excluded, the earth resides again in its own place.

<margin>On the opinions of the philosophers</margin>
**S**ince I must treat the constitution of the higher realms according to the Arabs, first it must be known that they do not approve of the opinions of certain philosophers who claim that the celestial bodies were composed from the purer part of *hyle* <term>hyle</term> <note>original: "yles"; a Greek term used by medieval scholars to refer to the primary, unformed matter of the universe</note>. Others say that the lighter parts of the elements, which were carried through our air, were those from which the stellar bodies were constructed and joined by divine wisdom. Clearly, from the fiery parts they were made bright; and from the corporeal parts, they rendered them solid. Some, however—which is absurd—affirm that the stellar bodies were dark in the beginning, being compacted from three elements, but were afterwards illuminated by the ascent of elemental fire, just as a candle is lit by a brought flame. But since my intention tends toward another matter, I should not care which opinion they prefer for the present; let these other things be set aside. Yet it is right to mention this:

<meta>This page continues the discussion on celestial and terrestrial physics, specifically addressing the extent of the heavens and the distinction between the eternal celestial realm and the "corruptible" world of the four elements. ...to the extent that it stretches from the circle of the moon even to the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the outermost sphere of the fixed stars in the medieval geocentric model.</note>; such that everything is thus enclosed. In this branch of knowledge, this is what the Arabs call the "heaven." It is agreed that the aforementioned philosopher <note>Likely referring to a commentator or Aristotle himself mentioned on the previous page.</note> said that Moses <note>original: "Moysen"</note> declared that the Lord in the beginning created heaven and earth. Here, they marvel at him because he explained the manner of creation: indeed, he sets out the works of the six days. Whence even Plato calls him a "rude philosopher" <note>original: "rude philosophu"; "rude" here implies unrefined or lacking in technical dialectic, though Plato still respects the underlying truth.</note>; and yet this same Plato testifies in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "timeo"; Plato’s dialogue on the origin of the physical world.</note> that the works of men follow one after another, but they are not made by the observation of a set order. Therefore, it is necessary for us to speak of the works of God in a human manner. In human acts, our speed ensures that before the first work is finished, one can pass to the second; but it is not so with divine works. For the Father did not arrange them one after another, but all at once in one eternal Word. Whence in the Psalm: "My tongue is the pen of a writer" <note>Psalm 45:1. In medieval theology, this was often interpreted as a metaphor for the Trinity's role in creation.</note>. The Son is called the "tongue" because the Father speaks through Him; and He is likewise called the "pen of the writer" because the Father works through Him. For just as words are imprinted and formed by a pen—in the manner that a mechanical pen writes and the scribe writes with the pen—so it is not that the Son works in the Father, nor the Father in the Son, but they act as one. It follows: "of one writing swiftly." Because He wrote all things at once; because "He spoke and they were made; He commanded and they were created." <note>Psalm 33:9 and 148:5.</note> Therefore, they were created as was revealed through the preceding words: namely earth, water, air, fire, and heaven.

However, the heaven, which is moved by its own nature, is mixed with and shapes the aforementioned four elements. If the heaven did not exist, they would undoubtedly not be moved, nor would they be mixed. And by the motion that is shaped by it, the substance which is below the circle of the moon is shaped as "mixable" <note>The "sublunary" realm—everything below the moon—was considered the region of change, decay, and mixture, whereas the heavens were eternal and unchanging.</note>; and it is changed from accident to accident, from form to form, from figure to figure: from a triangle to a quadrangle, from earth into water, from white into black, and such things. In either case, the higher things are demonstrated to be the causes. For so says Aristotle in the book *On Assigning the Reason for Knowing One thing* <note>likely a reference to the *Posterior Analytics* or *De Caelo* regarding the hierarchy of sciences</note>: the greatest division of the sciences will be made into the science of the heaven and the science of all things contained under the heaven. However, the matter of the substance which is contained by the heaven—that which is below the circle of the moon—is tiny compared to the air, water, and earth. Although in regard to its elements it is always one and the same, its "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property (like color or temperature) that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note> are nonetheless changed by the four qualities. These are: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. For example: the juice of food which is turned into blood, and afterwards that same thing into flesh; and though it is the same substance, it is fixed in another figure and colored with another color. Similarly, the palm tree itself and its dates, and man himself and the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note>—these are changed in figure and accident. And for this reason, the substance which is below the circle of the moon is called "corruptible" <note>term: <term>corruptibilis</term> (subject to decay and change)</note>. But the substance of the heaven is not changed except in its location; it does not depart from its own nature unless by some troublesome external case occurring, which would be to receive increase or diminution. But if it should seem that there is an increase, it will be easy to recognize that all those things are diminished; and it would easily happen that the heaven does not have increase, and thus no growth

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical properties of the heavens, transitioning from the theological discussion of creation on the previous page to a technical analysis of "augmentation" (growth) and the spatial limits of the cosmos.</meta>

...disposition. That which was congealed is now dissolved; that is, this is not called augmentation <note>original: "augmentum"; in medieval physics, this refers to a specific type of increase in size where the substance remains the same.</note>. For when something grows in such a way, it ought to remain in its own disposition and not be changed. Nevertheless, in the contemplation of the world <note>original: "contemplatione mundi"; here "world" refers to the entire physical universe.</note>, that which while it extends, it hardens; it is changed into a cord. We find that the length has increased while the width and depth have decreased. This is not called augmentation, because augmentation is described thus: the increment of length, width, and depth. However, if we look at a bladder that is inflated, we will see its length and width increase; but we find its height — that is, the thickness of its body — diminished. Because the more it is extended, the thinner it becomes. Therefore, we would not say that it has grown. But if we consider an oblong pool full of water, into which more water is poured from above, there is an augmentation in the dimensions because the water is not changed from its first disposition; this remains even if other matter is added. Now we have established what augmentation is.

The heaven, truly, since it is such a body that in no part of its division can it be increased or diminished, does not receive any other body into its mixture or beneath the subjection of its parts. Indeed, it is a marvel if anything of a celestial nature should be found nearby which might be added to the celestial body for the increase of generation, or if anything should remain beneath it which its impassible nature <note>The "impassible" nature of the heavens means they were believed to be incapable of suffering change, decay, or physical impact from the lower elements.</note> would admit for the detriment of corruption. Rather, since it is equal in all its parts, such that more of it is not found in one place than in another, it does not differ in its three dimensions; since it is entirely similar to itself through a total uniformity of a simple nature, it does not decline from its own state. It is clear from these and other necessary arguments that the heaven does not admit growth or diminution, generation or corruption. Since these things are established, it is now manifest that it is not changeable from one disposition to another, because it is eternal — that is, it lasts with all time. Furthermore, since the heaven is a body, it must be investigated whether it is a finite or an infinite body; whether it is heavy, or light, or neither. Or whether color happens to it, and if it has color, whether it is a bright or obscure body. Whether it is simple, or composed of diverse natures. What its motion is when it moves; whether it is spherical, or oblong, or of some other figure. All these things concerning the body of heaven ought to be inquired into.

In the premises, it was given that the heaven is a body. But the definition of a body is that it has length, width, and depth. However, length with width makes a surface; and a surface is the limit <note>original: "finis"; literally the end or boundary.</note> of a body. Therefore, it is necessary that a body be finite. Because it is a body, it must have length, width, and thickness. Since a surface is nothing other than length and width, it follows from this that every body has a surface. If it has a surface, it has a limit of the body. Therefore every body without doubt has a limit, because it is not possible for a body to be without a limit. But the heaven is a body; therefore the heaven is without doubt finite. 

After it has been proved that the heaven is a finite body, that which follows will be to show that it is neither light nor heavy. That this may be better understood, it should be known: every body is either heavy or light, or a medium. A medium body is that which participates in equality between the heavy and the light. But such equality cannot exist unless it is in the elements, according to the dominant quality in the body. Therefore, in the equality of a complexioned body <note>A "complexioned" body refers to one made of a mixture of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water), where the "complexion" is the specific balance of those elements.</note>, such a thing can be imagined, but it cannot be found in reality.

<summary>This page defines "augmentation" as an increase in all three dimensions and argues that the heavens are a finite, eternal body that cannot grow, decay, or change. It concludes by beginning an inquiry into whether the celestial body possesses weight or color.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the physical analysis of the heavens, moving from the concept of augmentation (growth) discussed on the previous page to the specific material nature and natural motion of the celestial body.</meta>

<margin>If you should say the heaven is a light body</margin>
<margin>The heaven is not composed of qualities</margin>
If you truly say the heaven is a light body <note>original: "corpus leve"; in medieval physics, "light" elements like fire and air naturally move upward, while "heavy" elements like earth and water move downward.</note>, then it certainly moves upward like fire and air. Likewise, if it were heavy, it would move downward like earth and water. Because it is not a heavy body, it must be "equal" <note>original: "equale"; meaning balanced or impartial, not dominated by any one earthly element.</note>; but an equal body does not consist of several distinct natures. Thus it is proven that the heaven is not composed of qualities <note>original: "complexionatum"; referring to the "complexion" or mixture of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. Through this proof, one is led to prove that the heaven is not colored, since this was made manifest in the previous treatise: every color proceeds from the four qualities. Therefore, because the heaven is not qualitative <note>not made of the four qualities</note>, it is denied to be affected by any color.

<margin>Aristotle’s *On the Senses*</margin>
<margin>The brightness of the stars</margin>
**I**t is usually asked whether the heaven is a bright body or a dark one. But Aristotle demonstrates this in the book *On the Senses and the Sensible* <note>original: "de sensu & sensato"</note>: that the heaven by its nature possesses splendor, but its parts differ in clarity according to "the more and the less." For in the stars there is more splendor, and in the remaining parts there is less. And for this reason, the light of the stars is seen, but the light of the body of the heaven is not seen. In the same way, the light of the fire that is below the heaven is not seen, except perhaps as ignited air. We see that by day the smaller stars are hidden because of the radiation of the solar splendor.

<margin>The heaven is a simple body</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
<margin>The wheel</margin>
<margin>The sublunary world</margin>
<margin>Two motions</margin>
<margin>Composite body</margin>
<margin>Simple</margin>
It remains yet to see whether the heaven is a simple body or a composite one. Just as it was predetermined that the heaven is not composed of qualities, it is clear that it is not composite. There is another proof that leads us to the same conclusion, which Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated medieval science.</note> teaches thus: it is impossible for a composite body to move circularly except by force, like a wheel; and this motion is "beyond its nature." For we find that all bodies in the sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, consisting of the four changing elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> move by their nature toward their center or away from their center. They also have two motions: "straight" and "natural." That is, the motion which is away from its center is upward; truly, that which is toward its center tends downward. From these things, it is manifest that every composite body naturally moves in a linear motion. Therefore, since the heaven does not move linearly, it is not a composite body; it is, therefore, simple. But it should be noted: a "simple body" in this field of study is not said to lack parts (which would be nothing), but that in its parts it has nothing diverse. For this body, the heaven, is within a likeness of the nature of air, so uniform <note>original: "indifferense"</note> that it is called simple. Truly, if it is proposed to be simple or similar according to nature, it is for this reason the body of heaven is called simple. But now, let something be said concerning its motion.

<margin>On the Heavens and the World</margin>
<margin>Two natural motions</margin>
<margin>Albumazar</margin>
<margin>Circular motion</margin>
<margin>Aristotle’s *Natural Hearing*</margin>
**S**o it is declared in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>Aristotle's *De Caelo*.</note>: some bodies are simple, some are composite. And where there is a composite, the motion ought to be according to the nature dominant in it. And where it is simple, the motion ought to be simple and pure. But since there are only two natural motions, one of which is straight and the other circular—and the straight belongs only to a composite body—it is impossible for one body to have two natural motions. Therefore, the body of simple things naturally moves circularly. Whence Albumazar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a famous Persian astronomer and astrologer.</note> says of the celestial things: "it was apparent only as circular." This motion is the most perfect of all, because it lacks both a beginning and an end; I know not what else it might admit. But although it is said that circular motion lacks both an end and a beginning, let no one therefore estimate it to be infinite. Because circular motion is unceasingly revolved from one place back to the same place. And again, Aristotle manifests this in the book *On Natural Hearing* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>: the motion of a finite body must be finite, because the space in which it moves is finite. Otherwise, it would happen that its space would proceed into an infinite length.

**C**oncerning the fact that the heaven is of a single nature, it is similarly proven by other means. Since for all figures, it was necessary for its nature to be a figure that was a finite body, the spherical figure was the most fitting for it among all figures. This is because among all figures, the spherical figure is the most similar to unity. If it had been formed in another shape, the circle on the surface would be more or less dissimilar <note>to the center</note>. Of other figures of bodies, none is as suitable for the heaven, because in all of them being divided, they are not similar to the whole. Therefore, from these things which have been said, it is clear that of all shapes, the sphere is the most fitting for the heaven. Likewise, from these things it is proved that it is a simple body, and its shape must be spherical. For the sphere alone among all corporeal shapes is bounded by a single surface. The circle likewise is the most simple among shapes bounded by a line or surface, because it is bounded by one line. Unity is closer to the simple, because that which is composite is more than one. No other shape consists of one continuous thing except the circle and the sphere, as has been said. Thus, since the heaven is a simple body, no other shape is more suitable than the sphere. If these solutions do not satisfy the seeker, let him seek the book of Alfraganus <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer</note>. He will find there that no division exists among the wise regarding the heaven being in the likeness of a sphere, since it revolves with all the stars that are in it, like a sphere that moves upon two immobile axes. One of these is toward the north, and the other toward the south. ->¶<- Now we have established this: that the heaven is a finite body, simple, bright, neither heavy nor light, in the middle <note>of the cosmos</note>, colored by no color, moving with circular motion, and spherical.

**I**t should next be known that the heaven is of the same nature in all its parts. It is clear that since the stars are parts of the heaven, they are of the same nature as the heaven, although some may tell fables otherwise. To these people, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astronomer and astrologer</note> openly opposes with trust and reason in this manner. He says: By the authority and reason of all philosophy and heavenly investigation, it is established that the substance of the bodies of the stars is made neither from any of the elements nor from the qualities of all things that are generated. For if they were made of these elements, they would be subject to the necessity and laws of the elements; namely, to being born and dying...

Since these are foreign to that place <note>the celestial realm</note>, they are subject both to the celestial eyes <note>original: "oculorum celestium"; likely referring to the stars as observers or the sight of the heavens</note> and to the substance of the stellar bodies, from which our own nature is known to stand apart. Consequently, so that no one should believe the stars are composed of **complexions** <term>complexions: the medical and philosophical theory that all things are made of a balance of four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</term>, he adds: "The quality of the stars, however, is in the form of their bodies." Therefore, they are spherical bodies, and so on. As if to say: Do not seek in the stars exterior qualities like color, or interior qualities, that is, complexions. Others receive this through the quality of being spherical and bright bodies, worthy of their natural motion, and such is their nature. Some, however, relying on the authority of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note>, wish to prove that the stars generate their natures from the four qualities: heat, cold, dryness, and moisture.

### The arguments of Ptolemy are indeed at hand; but because there were many named Ptolemy, whose lengthy writings are accompanied by doubt, it must be asked: who is this Ptolemy?

<margin>
concerning Ptolemy of Philadelphia
</margin>

### Thus the history of the Egyptians tells us that after the death of Alexander, King of the Macedonians, ten kings reigned successively and ruled over Egypt, and all were called by the single name of Ptolemy. 

Among these, one originating from **Philadelphia** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, though the author is here conflating the Hellenistic kings with the later astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note>, reigning in Egypt, wrote a certain book in which the whole body of astronomy is contained, called the *Almagest* <note>original: "almagesti"; the foundational text for medieval astronomy</note>, written in the Ionian <note>Greek</note> language. In it, speaking of the natures of the stars as if to beginners, he affirms that the Sun is hot, asserting that by its approach it kindles heat, and by its receding it leaves behind cold. The Moon is said to be moist, because of its proximity to the surface of the waters, which, as vapor rises, affects the disk of the moon. They maintain that Saturn is cold and dry, since it is far removed from the heat of the Sun and from us. Mars, however, is hot and dry, as the color of fire testifies. Jupiter is temperate, because it is situated in the middle between Saturn and Mars. From the immoderate cold of Saturn and the immoderate heat of Mars, the temperance of Jupiter is born. Venus they assert to be hot and moist, both because of its proximity to the Sun and because of the office of the star which serves the luxurious. For Venus abounds in moist and hot things. Mercury, however, is neither dry nor moist, insofar as it neither rises to the Sun nor to the Moon <note>referring to its orbital position or balanced elemental influence</note>.

<margin>
to
</margin>

### However, some who have examined the natures of things more deeply turn their eyes away from Ptolemy; yet they cannot pass over the assertion of such a great man without admiration. 

For if the stellar bodies generated these qualities, it would be necessary for their substance to be capable of containing those qualities within itself. But since these are elementary qualities, it would follow that the substances of the stars are composed of these elements—which is not to be understood as true, for the bodies of the stars are never within themselves [composed of elements] <insert>(this was rejected above)</insert>.

### It must be known, therefore, that the bodies of the stars are in no way within themselves hot, dry, cold, or moist. Rather, they assert such qualities are of their nature according to how their influence is compared to those qualities. 

Thus, for example, the Sun is said to be hot and dry by nature, because when it is in its own "house"—namely, in Leo <note>The zodiac sign of Leo is the astrological 'home' of the Sun, where its power is greatest</note>—heat is generated along with dryness. Likewise, Saturn is found to be cold and dry, because when it happens to be the **Lord of the Year** <term>Lord of the Year: the planet believed to exert the primary astrological influence over a specific year</term>, it signifies cold and immoderation. Indeed, immoderate cold leads to dryness. In this way, they say Saturn's nature is cold and dry, and by this reasoning, the investigation of the stars classifies them as hot, cold, dry, moist, masculine, feminine, diurnal, and nocturnal.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of celestial bodies, moving from the identity of Ptolemy to the physical properties of the stars—specifically addressing the debate over whether stars are made of fire.</meta>

...determined concerning the heat. Are they something of this kind? But their effect among us is established as being constant.

**P**erhaps sometimes they do not prefer me in this place, having established their own obstacle, when one exclaims with wonder at what precedes: "What? Do you deny that the stars are hot when all are of a fiery nature? Are not brightness and the ability to heat properties of fire? If these two are found in stars, it follows then that the stars are fiery." Here, however, is our path. To this it is said: a thing seems to be of a fiery nature in this way, but it does not seem sufficient to simply have brightness and heating power. For these two properties should be in it by nature, not by accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a property that a thing happens to have, but which is not essential to what it is</term>. In fire, heating occurs because its nature is hot; here, however, it is assumed that everything which heats must be hot by nature. Yet we find many things that heat accidentally whose nature is not hot. Such is motion, which we ought not to call "hot," even though it generates heat. We find cold things that heat, such as stone and iron in the section from **Aristotle** <note>likely referring to *De Caelo* or *Physica*</note>, which becomes hot and heats others through the motion of a wheel. In that case, for the sake of the heating, it would have to be naturally hot <note>which iron is not</note>. Likewise, we find many things having brightness in themselves by which they illuminate, such as fragments of rotten oak <note>original: "quercus putride"; referring to foxfire, the bioluminescence of certain fungi on decaying wood</note>, and the animal called the glow-worm <note>original: "noctiluca"; literally "night-shiner," usually referring to fireflies or glow-worms</note>, and mirrors, and other similar things. Their nature is not said to be fiery. Hence it is manifest that although the stars agree with fire in heating and in brightness, they are not, however, of a fiery nature.

Likewise, <margin>The nature of fire</margin> the nature of fire is to disperse and to come to rest in the higher place. It is established, however, that the stars are capable of being carried around and revolved. It is not probable, as was made clear above, for anything to have two natural motions <note>in Aristotelian physics, fire moves only in a straight line upward; circular motion belongs only to the heavens</note>. It follows, therefore, that since the stars revolve, they do not have this motion of ascending higher, nor of resting in the higher place. From this it follows that they are not fiery. But if someone should say that the stars are fire because they move like glowing iron or hot coals, which are not themselves "pure fire," this is attested here: fire moves upward, while coals and glowing iron move downward <note>because they have "earthy" weight</note>. Although these two receive heat and brightness from fire, they do not remain so for long, but return to their own nature. From this it is clear that if the stars were fiery, their brightness and heating power would diminish. But it does not happen that they are diminished in heat; because of this, the stars are not fiery like glowing iron or hot coals.

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*</margin> Aristotle demonstrates aptly in the book *On Sense and the Sensible* concerning this: that the heat we feel is not from their nature in the way the heat of fire is, but they heat us by their motion. Indeed, it sometimes happens in a hot region that a lead arrow-tip melts from its motion, which is also a remembered fact. Therefore, the stars heat the things below them by their motion, <margin>solar heat</margin> and they have a more powerful effect.

**F**or every round and voluble <term>voluble: capable of rotating or rolling easily</term> thing is moved more quickly than something less round. <margin>it reaches</margin> Just as a "rare" <note>low density, like air</note> body is cooled the more it is moved—which is apparent in the fanning of air—so also every firm body, which we call "solid," the more it is moved with great force, the more it is heated, or indeed it heats both itself and its surroundings.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> **H**ere it can be asked why we receive heat from the stars in this way, but not from the sky itself, since the sky is a luminous, round, and voluble body. But it is found in the book *On the Heavens and the Earth* that the light of the sky does not reach us, <margin>see the manner</margin> but the light of the stars does. Therefore, we do not receive heat from the sky, but from the stars. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Since in the sun these things are joined... because the stars are nearer to us than the fixed stars, <margin>Aristotle, the Moon</margin> and faster...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical properties of celestial bodies, moving from the debate on whether stars are naturally fiery to how we perceive their motion, color, and number according to authorities like Ptolemy.</meta>

...motion in the heavens is not the cause: for as **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptholomeus"; the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> proves, a star is equal in its quantity <note>size</note>, since it precedes the better-known circle that is above it. If there are any stars of faster motion than that one, they are nonetheless further away from us; as for those below it, if they are closer to us, they are far smaller and of slower motion. It is necessary, therefore, that they receive greater heat from the sun than from other stars.

However, it must not be kept silent that there are some who assign the colors of various metals to the planets, whose motion has been examined by philosophy. To **Saturn**, they attribute the color of lead. To **Jupiter**: silver. To **Mars**: golden. They say the **Sun** is gilded, although one cannot discern its color in the middle <note>of the sky</note> since the sight fails because of its immense splendor. To **Venus**, they assert a whitish color. To **Mercury**: they assign a black color. To the **Moon**, they hand down the color of tin. But since every color arises from the four qualities <note>the Aristotelian qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, as is taught regarding mixed bodies and so forth, the greatest authority of all denies that they have color. It should be known that because they are at a great distance from us, they never appear to our sight as they truly are. Great things are seen as small. They are not colored, but are thought to have color. For sight is often deceived, as in the case of a staff that appears broken in water; so often things that are not colored are seen to be affected by color. 

Regarding color, the philosophers say that it is seen in the elemental fire; a blackness is ordained in the sea. In the same way, the stars are said to be colored when it is not their own color, but rather that of the underlying air, which, being infected by various vapors, is illuminated and feigns colors, just as a window <note>original: "fenestrum"; likely referring to stained glass</note> represents the smell <note>perhaps "scent" or "visual aura"</note> through which the visible species will be met. We also see sometimes that the sun, at the time of its rising and setting, appears very red and large. Likewise, we often judge the moon to be ruddy when we look at it during its rising. This increase in the magnitude of the sun and moon in the east and west does not happen because they are closer to us there than in the middle of the sky; rather, it happens to our sight because of the vapor that rises from the earth. This shows them to be larger to us, especially when the air happens to have a vapor of great humidity, as happens on winter days, especially for the moon. If, as they say, the sun is colored since, according to them, it is of a fiery nature and incomparably hotter than the other stars, no one doubts—if color belonged to its nature—that the sun would be redder than Mars. 

Likewise, it often happens that from the reverberation of the solar rays, a luminous splendor is drawn out. If anyone wishes to prove this, let him put water in a basin; if the rays of the sun reach it when it is moved, a certain irradiation occurs which, with a shadowy splendor, presents a greenish color. We see that a great shadow proceeds from a snow-white body; this air many times represents other colors which flow from no subject, as appears in the rainbow <note>original: "iri"</note>. If those colors were similar to those in the sun, the sun would undoubtedly be called multi-colored.

But according to the preceding mode, it must still be known—and no one doubts that there are others—that **Ptolemy**, since the stars are innumerable, collected from the entire multitude the 1,022 <note>original: "m̄. xxii"</note> most notable ones in the quantity of their light. Out of these, seven are faster: **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, the **Sun**, **Venus**, **Mercury**, and the **Moon**. These, because they are carried in a rapid course before the eyes, are called the erratic stars <term>erratic stars: from the Greek "planētēs" (wanderers), referring to the planets that move against the background of the fixed stars</term>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial bodies and their influence on the terrestrial world, moving from the classification of fixed stars to the specific powers of the planets, particularly the Sun and Moon, over nature and human health.</meta>

But as for the remaining **1,022** fixed stars—since they all share the same motion and the same visual magnitude—each one completes its cycle in nearly a hundred years. All of these **1,025** <note>The text specifies 1,022 then 1,025; this may include the planets previously discussed.</note> are arranged into six orders <note>levels of brightness or "magnitudes"</note>; whoever wishes to learn more about this should read the ***Almagest*** <note>The influential 2nd-century astronomical manual by Ptolemy.</note>.

Since, therefore, among the multitude of stars, the **seven planets** excel with more pleasing leadership and greater power over things, it is sufficient for us to treat them. These move from sign to sign <note>through the zodiac</note>, and all of them set according to the lower world, where the effects of their motions reach fulfillment. For example, the sun’s power is clearly manifest in itself: as in the **sunflower** <note>original: "solsequio"; literally "sun-follower," likely referring to the heliotrope or marigold</note> and the crystal, which testify to the sun's effect. This same power appears in the heliotrope gem, and likewise in certain <gloss>pearls</gloss> known as "unions" <note>large, unique pearls</note>, in which the solar force and effect are manifest. There is no doubt among the common people that the sun changes these lower things according to the seasons of the year. See how in nature plants and trees, deprived of their innate heat in winter and impoverished of their nourishing benefit, wither and lose their leaves in the cold. But as spring approaches, they feel the beneficial heat; soon they are restored by nourishing grace, and they begin to sprout leaves and branches, producing their flowers and fruit. Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in his book *On Generation and Corruption*: "The sun generates by approaching and destroys by receding." 

If one asks why certain trees, such as the boxwood and the laurel, flourish in both summer and winter by some special privilege and never lose their leaves: to this it is said that the nature of the laurel is "disobedient" to the sun's effect. For in order for such an effect to occur, two things are necessary: the active nature of the agent and the receptive nature of the patient <note>the thing being acted upon</note>. Because if the nature of the patient cooperates with the nature of the agent <margin>it is impossible for a third thing not to proceed from the two</margin>, it is impossible for a third thing [the effect] not to proceed from the two. Therefore, although higher things act, if these lower things do not cooperate with the actions of the higher, the effect of the higher is either removed or delayed. Since the nature of the laurel, which is a viscous, cold, and moist tree, resists the winter cold, it is not affected like other trees in which the moisture is dried up and winter burns them. For coldness joined with viscosity always preserves moisture in the laurel. Indeed, cold alone can preserve moisture, as occurs in the middle of mountains; because the air there is cold, ice forms through excessive coldness, which is nothing other than water preserved in a frozen state. But when the sun's heat arrives, they resist by overwhelming the cold, though they are helped by it.

Whence, if the testimony of the **moon** is added to this, women's menstruation proves it. The ebb and flow of the sea affirm the same. Fittingly, the primary cause of things being born exists within these: in the natural revolution of places, in the condition of waters, and in the motion of the moon. Wherefore **Albumazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer</note> treats everything he reads with probability. Indeed, he is so trustworthy that it is said one is powerless in medicine <note>original: "medicina"</note> without him, specifically regarding the knowledge of **critical days** <note>specific days when a disease was thought to reach a turning point</note> in which the changes of illnesses are understood; he claims all this for the moon. Hence it was pleasing both to **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, as well as other doctors, to calculate the critical days according to the motion and various "mansions" <note>the 28 positions of the moon's orbit</note> of the moon. Therefore, he who condemns astronomy necessarily destroys medicine <note>original: "phisicam"</note>; for he who is ignorant of the causes of things cannot easily cure them. When the astronomer foresees who must be cured, and why, and when...

...finally the physician approaches his work usefully. But these things about the effects of the moon still occur to memory, which must not be passed over. <margin>For there are many kinds of things</margin> For there are many kinds of things that, as long as the moon is waxing, indulge more largely in growth; but while it is waning, they withdraw their growth. Thus, for instance, with the moon waxing: humors <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> abound in the bodies of animals; when it is waning: they are thinned. Whatever is cold and moist in animals—namely the brain and the marrow—abounds with the waxing moon; with the waning moon: it is thinned. These things, according to the teachings and edicts of all [the wise], are more abundant in the first half of the lunation. I shall immediately begin to narrate one of the virtues of the moon that is even more admirable, lest I omit it through delay.

<margin>At Toledo on the Tagus</margin> Outside the walls of the city of Toledo, next to the Tagus [river], in a certain elevated place, two fountains were constructed, devised by the ingenuity of the ancient pagans. To these, water flows through subterranean paths by an artificial conduit; at last, breaking out through two narrow openings, it is received by two stones, which the people of Toledo call by the common name <term>conchas</term> <note>original: "conchas"; literally "shells," referring here to large stone basins or reservoirs.</note>. When the moon reveals its full orb, the aforementioned basins are found filled to the top; so much so that not a single drop of water overflows, nor would any greater abundance of water cause an effusion, as the basins suffice to retain it. If anyone should draw water for cleansing, or even if they did not, one would always find the basins filled with abundant water during the full moon. But when the moon is shortened with imperfect light, so that it shows itself half-full, the water is held back within itself; it does not rise beyond the middle of the basins. Indeed, if one were to try to pour the whole Tagus river into them little by little with a small pitcher to force them to fill or at least increase the water within them, the water would be found to falsely [refuse the increase] <note>This describes the famous "Water Clocks of Toledo" built by the astronomer Al-Zarqali, which synchronized with the lunar cycle.</note>; although the sea is at least six days' journey from Toledo. <margin>fountains</margin> And elsewhere before the city are other twin fountains of sweet water, which were fashioned with similar artifice, which likewise increase and decrease according to the waxing and waning of the moon. These fountains flow at the foot of a certain precious rock, upon which is marvelously built:

<margin>Galiana</margin> And the stupendous palace of Galiana <note>The *Palacio de Galiana*, a mudéjar-style villa on the banks of the Tagus, named after a legendary Moorish princess.</note>.

<margin>the sun in the middle of the world</margin> Because for our sake the sun is placed in the middle of the world. For if the sun were raised up to the aplanetic sphere <note>The outermost sphere of the fixed stars.</note> or lowered down to the lunar orb, the world could never endure, either because of the cold [of the heights] or the heat [of the depths]. Wherefore the provident Creator of all things placed the sun, like a universal fuel for the body [of the world], in the middle region of the world, and gave it just motions. Because he does not allow it to happen by necessity that heat should always be upon the face of the earth in one and the same way, since living things sometimes have need of cold, sometimes of heat, and sometimes of a moderate temperature.

<margin>moon and sun</margin> Regarding the moon and the sun: why it alone among all the stars runs in such a cycle, wherefore it is called the "star of the sun," because it receives its splendor from the sun. If the moon had innate light, it would be harmful by its heat; for it would burn up the fruits, dry up the springs, and set the earth on fire with its proximity, reducing it to dust. The excellent providence of the Creator guarded against these things...

In the first creation of the world, the sun, the moon, and the other planets began their movements. The earth was warmed, and by the command of God, it brought forth diverse animals. But since the face of the earth was still placed under the water and veiled by it, soon from the heat, the water of the earth bubbled and was turned somewhat into mud, and the diverse kinds of animals were created. Of these, certain ones which had more of the higher elements <note>The "higher elements" refer to air and fire, which were believed to be lighter and more spiritual than earth and water.</note> are the birds. Others, however, in which water was superabundant, are the fish; and these are able to live in this element alone and in no other. Thus were the fish and birds created. Whence it is written: "O God of great power, who out of the waters brings forth a race, sending part back to the abyss and lifting part into the air." <note>original: "Magne d’t’ potencie qui ex aq̃s ortū genus partī remittis gurgiti, p’tē leuas in aera"; this is a quote from the Vesper hymn for Thursday, "Magnae Deus potentiae."</note> Then, when the earth was somewhat dried and solidified, the other animals were brought forth. If fire was more abundant in any, they were made **choleric** <note>The temperament associated with yellow bile and fire, characterized by a hot, dry nature—symbolized here by the lion.</note>, such as the lion. If dry: **melancholic**, such as the ox. If however water: **phlegmatic**, such as pigs.

But perhaps some who consider the released course of nature deny that animals can be procreated by themselves through mating. Instead, they think that those things happening daily are not procreated from the teaching of another's seed, but rather that those coming together from matter give birth, as happens in crystals and other gems, which are frozen from various vapors. For animals are now produced as much from airy and watery vapors as from earthy ones; such as, for instance, flies, frogs, fleas, and that kind. All of these follow certain patterns of the elements and the changes of the seasons, yet they were not procreated in their own nature from any seed of their own kind. There are those who deny the movements, powers, and efficacy of these things; indeed, they are so shamelessly foolish that before they can drink in the discipline of science, they begin to disparage its teaching.

Whence certain people, from the name alone, hold **astronomy** in hatred. If they would only attend to how much dignity and how much utility it holds, they would never again disparage it with such insults. Concerning its dignity, it is found that it stands at the head of what the wise call the eight sciences. These are: the **science of judgments** <note>Astrology, or the interpretation of celestial omens.</note>, the **science of medicine**, the **science of necromancy** <note>original: "nigromancia"; in this context, it refers to natural magic or the study of hidden forces in nature, rather than modern "black magic."</note> according to physics, the **science of agriculture**, the **science of prestidigitation** <note>The art of creating illusions or "miracles" through natural means.</note>, the **science of alchemy** (which is the science of the transformation of metals into other species), the **science of images** (on which a great and universal book exists, published by Thoz the Greek <note>original: "thoz grec’"; likely Toz Graecus, a legendary figure associated with Hermetic talismanic magic.</note>), the **science of mirrors**, and a science more wide and broad than the others, as Aristotle manifests in the book *On the Burning Mirror*. <note>A work on optics and the physics of light reflection.</note>

The utility of astronomy, moreover, ought to be weighed as not being small. For when the astronomer has foreknown the events of future things, he can better repel their harm or avoid them; such as, for instance, a public war, a general famine, a universal earthquake, eruptions, floods, or a common pestilence of men or beasts. If, however, he is entirely unable to flee these things, yet the endurance of a foreseen event is much lighter through foresight; it is those who are ignorant whom an unforeseen and sudden strike hits more surely. For this reason, these things had to be set down in the middle, so that the errors of men who calumniate astronomy might be destroyed. Now let this digression return to the proposed matter. But before the effects of the planets are said—which they have equally in human bodies—let us discuss their spheres and the dwellings which they hold in the signs.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap initial 'S' in green and red with intricate foliate and interlacing patterns inside the curves of the letter.</image-desc>

The **spheres** <note>The celestial orbits or shells in which the planets were thought to reside.</note>, which it is not fitting to number as eleven (as some do), but rather as eight (as we are taught in the book of Al-Farghani <note>original: "alphragani"; Al-Farghani was a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose work was a primary source for medieval European astronomy.</note>), are witnessed by life itself. The first, and the one closest to the earth, is the sphere of the **Moon**. The second: **Mercury**. The third: **Venus**. The fourth: the **Sun**. The fifth: **Mars**. The sixth: **Jupiter**. The seventh: **Saturn**. The eighth: the **Fixed Stars**.

It is equidistant in all its parts from the two poles. At these poles are fixed the two ends of a conceptual line which, passing with an equal division through the body of the heaven,
divides the sphere of the world into two parts. Each of these halves is named a "hemisphere," and this line is called the **axis**.

</margin>
the **Arctic** is that which, from our region, never sets, but is always seen by us. The **Antarctic**, however, is seen in the lower

hemisphere: it is never presented to our sight. Let us return here to the equinoctial circle. This is said by the Latins to be the "equinoctial" because when the sun touches it, it makes the days equal to the nights in all climates.
It is called *almustakim* by the Arabs, that is, "straight," for the reason that its motion differs in no way from the motion of the bodies of the planets. The *aplanon* moves in such a way that within the space of one day and night, it revolves entirely. **B**ut the second

where he says: "The Zodiac encompasses the living." <note>This may refer to a theological interpretation of the constellations or a citation from a medieval astronomical authority like John of Sacrobosco.</note> Indeed, the Zodiac is named from "animals" because animals are imagined within it, 
such as **Aries** (the Ram), **Taurus** (the Bull), and the other signs that represent the likeness of animals. The Zodiac is likewise called *metnor* <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic term for "the path."</note> after the manner of the Greeks; in Arabic it is named *felek elberug* <note>original: "felek elberug"; from Arabic *falak al-buruj*, the "sphere of the constellations/towers."</note>, the circle of the towers. It is called the circle of towers 
because it contains the twelve signs, which are called "towers" by them. <gloss>that is, twelve</gloss> Whence it must be noted: that since the eyes of the [zodiacal] animals are only weighed down by linear length, the Zodiac does not lack the passage of the planets.

</margin>
Whence it is fit to receive celestial forms. In the middle of the circle, it is said to be the "path" <note>original: "per cammea"; likely referring to the ecliptic, the sun's path.</note>, because an **eclipse** always occurs there. Therefore, since an eclipse always happens either at the **Head** or the **Tail of the Dragon** <note>The "Dragon" (*Draco*) refers to the lunar nodes—the two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the Sun's path (the ecliptic). Eclipses can only occur when the Moon is near these points.</note>,
the Dragon never leaves the boundaries of this line, so that such a failing [an eclipse] never exceeds this line. Thus an eclipse occurs when the moon is joined to the sun near the Head or the Tail of the Dragon, and there 
is no latitude between them; then its motion in our sight will cover the sun, since that shadow of the earth will take away the light of the sun from it; hence an eclipse is suffered here. **A**fter speaking

It is called the "summer" tropic because at the summer solstice which occurs in it, the sun ascends no further but turns back. The winter **tropic** is so called because at the winter solstice which happens in it, the sun revolves toward the equinoctial 
circle; by ascending, it increases the days. Whence one lies above **Cancer**, the other above **Capricorn**.

<summary>This page describes the primary circles of the celestial sphere, including the Equator (Almustakim), the Zodiac, the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, and the Colures, explaining their Greek and Arabic etymologies and their roles in eclipses and seasons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of the equinoctial circle and the celestial poles to the remaining major circles of the sphere, followed by an explanation of planetary motion and the concept of epicycles to account for retrograde motion.</meta>

the **horizon**, which in each climate distinguishes the upper hemisphere from the lower; and the **meridian**, which divides the aforesaid circle into two equal parts. There are also some who describe other circles, but since they pertain more to the division of geographical regions than to the motion of the stars, it is certain that for the present they should be passed over. **I**t is therefore noted that there are eight major circles, of which the first is the **equinoctial**. The second is the **zodiac**. The third and fourth are the two **tropics**. The fifth and sixth are the two **colures** <note>The colures are two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that pass through the poles and either the equinoxes or the solstices.</note>. The seventh and eighth are the **meridian** and the **horizon**.

**A**fter the enumeration of the circles, it would be appropriate to persist with the climates of the world, were it not like "helping the sun with torches" <note>original: "solem facib; iuvare"; a Latin idiom meaning to do something redundant or unnecessary.</note>. Because Alfraganus <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a famous 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were translated into Latin and became standard textbooks in Europe.</note> treats these climates clearly in his book, I do not wish to disturb his work. Instead, since mention was made above regarding the circuits of the planets, it must be explained according to what path they travel their circles, so that they might not be judged as stationary, nor progressive, nor retrograde <note>Planets sometimes appear to slow down, stop, or move backward in the sky; the author is about to explain this using the theory of epicycles.</note>. In this matter, almost all Latin authors have erred. And the Arabs have put forth the knowledge of these things to us so obscurely that it is said they scarcely understood it themselves. **T**o understand the root of the matter and the evidence of the thing, it must be understood that each of the five planets has twin circles, of which one is called the "fuller" [larger] and the other the "shorter" [smaller]. Understand, therefore, a circle placed upon a circle, with the smaller circle cutting the larger one. The larger circle, for example, in the case of **Saturn**, is called that because Saturn measures the *aplanon* <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> in a space of thirty years. The smaller circle placed upon it is called **elchedur** <note>original: "etchedow" / "elchedur"; the Arabic term for an epicycle, a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the deferent).</note> in Arabic; by the Latins it may be called the "brief circle" or the "promoting circle." Thus, let Saturn be carried in its larger circle until the angles of the circles mingle together; let there be a certain conceptual "station" there <note>a point where the planet appears to stand still</note> until it exits and ascends the brief circle. When it ascends, its height increases; thus there is a certain progression, and it seems to exit more swiftly, because its motion appears greater in the brief circle than in the full one. This is why even the **moon**, by reason of the shortness of its circle, appears swifter than the other planets. When the planet descends in the brief circle, again at the opposite angle which it touches while descending, it is found to be "stationary," until it reaches the lower part of the brief circle. There it eventually ascends when it reaches the intersection of the circles, and turns away from the brief circle; and thus, while it follows a line through the center, it is judged to be **retrograde**. Because we are unable to distinguish the space between the circles (which cannot be seen), it is thought by us to be returning by the same path it previously traveled in the brief circle. This must be understood similarly regarding the other planets and their circles, with the exception of the **sun** and the **moon**, which, because they lack the **elchedur** circle, never become stationary or retrograde. Lest a spark of doubt remain for anyone, that which the preceding text narrates, the figure below declares.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the celestial sphere, moving from the eight major circles (equinoctial, zodiac, tropics, colures, meridian, and horizon) to a detailed analysis of the twelve signs of the zodiac, their elemental properties, their classifications, and their influence on the human body.</meta>

It now remains to treat the twelve signs, each of which occupies thirty degrees; thus the entire **zodiac** is divided by physical consideration into three hundred and sixty degrees. The names of the signs are these: **Aries**, **Taurus**, **Gemini**, **Cancer**, **Leo**, **Virgo**, **Libra**, **Scorpio**, **Sagittarius**, **Capricorn**, **Aquarius**, and **Pisces**. It is also pleasing to know which dignities the planets obtain in these signs, namely their houses: **Saturn** holds the houses of **Capricorn** and **Aquarius**; **Jupiter**: **Sagittarius** and **Pisces**; **Mars**: **Aries** and **Scorpio**; **Venus**: **Taurus** and **Libra**; **Mercury**: **Gemini** and **Virgo**; the **Sun**: **Leo**; and the **Moon's** house is **Cancer**.

Furthermore, **Aries** is fire, **Taurus** is earth, **Gemini** is air, and **Cancer** is water; having found the beginning, the order repeats. **Leo** is likewise fire, **Virgo** is earth, **Libra** is air, and **Scorpio** is water. Repeating the order again, **Sagittarius** corresponds to fire, **Capricorn** to earth, **Aquarius** to air, and **Pisces** to water. Therefore, there are signs that are fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some aquatic. Specifically, the fiery signs are **Aries**, **Sagittarius**, and **Leo**; the earthy are **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**; the airy are **Gemini**, **Libra**, and **Aquarius**; while the aquatic are **Cancer**, **Scorpio**, and **Pisces**. Although the signs themselves are not literally made of fire, they are called such because while the Sun travels through them, it brings greater heat. Likewise, they are called earthy when the Sun, existing within them, works coldness with dryness; and the airy and aquatic are named by a similar logic.

No less diligence should be used in observing that some of the signs are **tropical**, some are **fixed**, and some are **bipartite** <note>These classifications are now commonly known as Cardinal, Fixed, and Mutable signs.</note>. **Aries**, **Cancer**, **Libra**, and **Capricorn** are **tropical**. **Taurus**, **Leo**, **Scorpio**, and **Aquarius** are **fixed**. **Gemini**, **Virgo**, **Sagittarius**, and **Pisces** are **bipartite**. A sign is called **tropical** <note>original: "tropicum"; from the Greek 'tropos' meaning 'a turn,' referring to the points where the sun appears to turn back toward the equator.</note> for this reason: when the Sun enters it, the season is changed into another quality. For example, when the Sun ascends to the first degree of **Aries**, it rises in the circle and brings an increase to the day; therefore we call this a tropical sign. The following sign, which is **Taurus**, is called **fixed** because the Sun, entering Taurus, firms up the state of that same season. A sign is **bipartite** <note>original: "bipartitum"; literally 'divided in two.' Modern astrologers call these 'mutable' signs.</note> when the Sun travels through it and the weather is rendered a mixture of two different qualities; just as in Autumn, where one half holds to the preceding summer and the other looks toward the following winter.

However, it must not be overlooked that the **Arabs** <note>The author refers to Arabic-Islamic astrologers, whose sophisticated systems were being integrated into Latin science during this period.</note> hunt for the virtues of the signs in such a way that they divided the whole body of man among them according to their powers. In the first place, they say that **Aries** governs the head and face in the human body. **Taurus**: the neck and throat. **Gemini**: assigned the shoulders, with the arms, forearms, and hands. **Cancer**: holds the chest with the lungs, the esophagus, the spleen, and the ribs. **Leo**: according to them, possesses the base of the stomach—which they call the *merim* <note>original: "merim"; likely a Latinization of the Arabic 'mari,' referring to the esophagus or the cardiac orifice of the stomach.</note>—as well as the heart, the liver, and the sides with the back. **Virgo** is allotted the belly with the intestines. **Libra**: the navel and the pubic area, continuing down to the loins. **Scorpio**: the private parts from the loins to the buttocks. **Sagittarius**: the buttocks and thighs. **Capricorn**: the knees with their joints. **Aquarius**: the shins down to the ankles. **Pisces**: the feet with their joints. Likewise, since the spleen is **melancholic** <note>One of the four 'humors' or bodily fluids thought to determine temperament.</note>, they give it to **Saturn**. The liver to **Jupiter**. The bitter gall with its **choler** to **Mars**. The heart to the **Sun**. To **Venus**: beauty of form. To **Mercury**: the mouth and tongue. To the **Moon**: the bulk of the body. With these things thus arranged, they claim to have from **Saturn**: slowness; from **Jupiter**: temperance; from **Mars**: anger; from the **Sun**: the power of ruling; from **Mercury**: wisdom and eloquence; and from **Venus**: pleasure.

It also introduces "melothesia," the astrological practice of mapping the signs and planets to specific parts of the human body and temperament.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial influences, transitioning from the houses of the zodiac to the specific temperaments and characteristics of the seven planets and how they name the days of the week.</meta>

...from the **Moon**: since it is the mother of the <term>humors</term><note>The "humors" were the four primary bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note>, it brings an abundance of moisture.

From these seven **planets**, the seven days of the week take their names. The first is the day of the **Sun**. The second, the **Moon**. The third, **Mars**. The fourth, **Mercury**. The fifth, **Jupiter**. The sixth, **Venus**. The seventh, **Saturn**. Why the days are not ordered according to the physical order of the planets in the heavens is a long question to solve; therefore, let it be set aside for now.

Having listed the opinions of the <term>mathematicians</term><note>In this period, "mathematician" (mathematicus) usually referred to astronomers and astrologers who calculated planetary movements.</note>, it must be known that where the aforementioned Arabs treat the constellations, they call the planets the "lords of births." Starting from **Saturn**, they are called "Saturnine," from **Jupiter**, "Jovial," and so on.

Whoever is born under **Saturn**, since **Saturn** is dark in its aspect and appearance, will be <term>melancholic</term><note>The temperament associated with black bile, characterized by being somber, analytical, and prone to sadness.</note>, greedy, and a wanderer in distant and cold places. He will say one thing with his mouth and hold another in his heart. He is diligent in evil, envious, deceitful, and a traitor. He will be a solitary person, a compeller of others, a jailer, and a <note>original: "leuifer"</note> bearer of light. He will acquire the inheritance of his fathers and grandfathers, yet he will be silent, slow, and dull; however, once he has gained knowledge, he will not easily lose it.

**Jupiter**, however, since it is a royal star—prosperous, sweet, and temperate—creates kings, religious men, the wise, and the honorable. It makes those who are moderate in legal matters, law-givers, the obedient, explainers of visions, truth-tellers, and the constant. It makes men generous, powerful, wealthy, and lovers of women (and pleasing to them), as well as fathers, <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking clergy members like bishops or abbots.</note>, watchful, merciful, joyful, and clean.

**Mars**, since it is sharp, bitter, and harsh, makes violent kings, the inhuman, and the unmerciful. It creates judges, migrants, and those who love <note>original: "celā"</note> concealments, destructions, battles, and slaughter. It produces plunderers, oppressors, robbers, waylayers of travelers, searchers of graves, and those who hang the dead. It makes men diligent in strife and wars, ministers of crimes, clever, deceptive, inconstant, shameless, insatiable, bold, and proud.

The **Sun** is a royal star, the light and eye of the world. It makes men beautiful and life-giving. It creates emperors, royals, supreme pontiffs, and prelates, as well as the religious, those profound in divinity, and contemplators. It makes the wise, the intelligent, dreamers, rulers, counselors, the wealthy, the worthy, and the eloquent. It produces philosophers, hiders of counsel, and those who sustain both the good and the evil with a patient spirit.

**Venus**, being benevolent, is called the "star of women." It makes a man generous, charming, and affable; handsome with women, luxurious, a drunkard, and a gambler. He will be one who desires gold, silver, musical instruments, pleasures, and joys. It makes him delightful and idle, an admirer of sculpted and painted images, one who walks about markets and tents, and one who frequents temples.

**Mercury**, since it is of a mixed nature, appearing with hesitation and ready to agree to every mixture, accords with all planets and signs. This star makes men cunning, busybodies, teachers of the arts, <note>original: "compotatores," likely meaning "computatores"</note> calculators, geometers, astrologers, augurs, and explainers. It makes abductors of women, scribes, and historiographers. Such men are capable of all sciences, but they flee pleasures, are men of little joy, and are despicable in their dress and habits.

<meta>This page continues the astrological descriptions of planetary influences on human character and fate, specifically focusing on the social and professional outcomes of those born under benevolent alignments.
