...with the just they are just; with the kind they are kind. Sparing in payments, vigorous in eloquence. Businessmen, merchants, seeking and losing riches, distributing and sharing the things they possess.
<margin>and presiding</margin>
Together with a benevolent planet, which is called the "sister star" <note>This likely refers to Venus or a specific beneficial aspect of Jupiter.</note>: it makes princes, leaders, defenders of the law, and justices, consuls, counselors, protectors of mothers and sisters, envoys, those bringing honest decrees, not hiding secrets, affecting the form itself, pardoning little, friends to the prosperity of fortune. Since this leadership of the stars is never joined all together in one body: so it is not that they arise from one simple star, but are gathered by mixing from a conjunction. For the malevolence of fate could be mitigated by the respect <note>original: "respectu" — in astrology, this refers to an 'aspect' or the geometric relationship between planets.</note> of another benevolent star, or its benevolence could be augmented. Whence it happens that some are raised in happiness, and some in misfortune. Indeed, [it is better] if the benevolent stars should regard the birth <term>trigonally</term><note>A "trine" aspect, where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered very harmonious.</note>, or <term>tetragonally</term><note>A "square" aspect, 90 degrees apart, usually considered challenging but powerful.</note>, or by region, and if they 
<margin>are not regarded by the malevolent ones.</margin>

All the aforesaid and other such things were being taught as necessities in this manner to their listeners by the <term>mystagogues</term><note>Teachers of secret or initiatory knowledge.</note> and "Zaphars" <note>Likely a reference to the Arab astrologer Sahl ibn Bishr, known in Latin as Zael or Zaphar.</note>. **Gerard of Toledo** <note>Gerard of Cremona (c. 1114–1187), the most prolific translator of scientific works from Arabic into Latin in the Middle Ages.</note>, who translated the *Almagest* <note>The definitive astronomical manual by Ptolemy.</note> into Latin while **Galippus the Mozarab** <note>A Mozarab was a Spanish Christian living under Muslim rule; Galippus was Gerard’s primary linguistic collaborator.</note> interpreted: I was amazed. 
And to those readers who sat by him, I—being a bit of a nuisance or rather indignant—offered the homily of the **Blessed Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), who famously argued against astrology by citing the different lives of twins born under the same stars.</note> in which he disputes against the <term>mathematicians</term><note>In the medieval context, "mathematician" (mathematicus) was a common term for an astrologer.</note>. 
But he said: "I understand your tricks. 
You say that he who is born under **Aquarius** will be a fisherman. But **Getulia** <note>A region in North Africa, synonymous with the dry interior of the Sahara.</note> precedes it, and Getulia has no fish. Finally, it is cold. How then will he who is born there under Aquarius be a fisherman? To this I say: man is a rational animal, mortal, walking, two-footed. Just because a man is born [without the use of] his feet, he is no less a 'two-footed' man by definition, although in his state he may not be able to walk. So also he who is born under **Aquarius** is called a fisherman, not because he always exercises the art of fishing, but because he will have a greater aptitude for fishing than if he were born under another sign."

I, indeed, admiring the depth of his genius and yet pretending not to, replied: "It will not escape thus, because it is often seen that the son of a king and the son of a peasant have the same constellation. Yet one remains in his peasant state; the other is raised to be a king." 
But he, waiting patiently, finally said: "Have you ever read **Julius Firmicus**?" <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the *Mathesis*, the most extensive Latin handbook on astrology.</note> When I replied that I had read him, he said: "Look where we have the treatise on **Births** [Genituris], where two things must be inquired into for a birth: namely, the constellation and the nature <note>original: "nata" — referring to the inherited social status or physical lineage.</note>. If the nature does not suit the constellation, or the constellation does not grant to the nature, the constellation will not follow its effect in every way. If therefore, as it is said, the son of a king and the son of a peasant are born in the same constellation: both will indeed be kings, but not in one and the same way. For the son of a king has it from his nature to succeed his father in the kingdom. However, the son of a peasant, although it does not detract from his constellation, will rule among peasants over all who are in his lineage; he will be more powerful and stronger. Why do you wonder? Even I who speak am a king, as I was born under a royal sign, with the **Sun** dominating, and other things concurring." 
And when I asked him ironically where I might reign, he replied: "In the soul," which to no mortal...

...to serve. If by chance there are those who say this, in this way kings can be called servants. Because they are humble in heart and serve God: what should these servants be considered? **O truly venerable Duke of the Normans and Count of the Angevins,** the magnificence of whose deeds is far loftier than the renown of riches. This is the true cause why you wish for a teacher and a student to be in agreement within them. For there are two things in which the success of teaching is achieved: namely, when one cannot be deceived by the other, and the one does not wish to deceive the other. Let that be known by necessity: one is worked by knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>, the other by justice. For knowledge teaches what is true, guards against the unfairness of words, and unmasks the tricks of sophists <note>Sophists were ancient teachers criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments; here, the author means anyone who uses logic to deceive.</note>; through study and doctrine it works, and it establishes the outcome from the beginning: so that neither in the matter nor in the words can the teacher be deceived. Justice, however, which is that divine power that renders to each his own, expels the will to deceive from the person and impels them toward instructing everyone. Because, therefore, both of these duties of teaching are joined together in your lordship, it is for this reason that I am better trusted.

Students, however, are not without fault; they have abandoned the form of Pythagorean teaching <note>Pythagoras was said to have required his students to maintain silence and listen for several years before being allowed to speak or ask questions.</note>, which decreed that a student should listen rightly for seven years, and only in the eighth year should he ask questions. Instead, as soon as they have begun their schooling, before they even sit down, they ask questions; indeed, they even judge those who are better than themselves. Having studied neglectfully for the space of a single year, they think they have attained the whole of wisdom. They depart from the threshold of their teachers full of wind and noisy chatter, but they leave empty of the weight of reason. And because they are such, they are heard by their peers: then, from their own hearing, nothing of utility is found. Immediately they are accepted as teachers by others; but through this, the authority of the teacher is diminished.

It is clearly evident that this fault is greatest in the work which they do; for they decree that the goods of the churches should be given to these people. The wise and the noble are excluded from the churches; and lest the place remain empty, fools and ignoble shadows of clerics—not true clerics—are included. Already, those who excel in science are considered as nothing else but objects of hatred and envy; they endure because they have no other place to go. They seek one thing while following a diverse way of life: they labor to enrich their coffers while bringing nothing of value to others. This is a very harsh thing, through which the dignity and authority of the teacher perishes, and all knowledge vanishes into hope. In such a matter, some hope is cherished in fools, whom you have devoted to the game of dice or the study of wrestling in your tender age, and you will long preserve the scent of those youthful idleness. Because of this, this hope excites both the young and the foolish; they wish themselves to be considered as belonging to knowledge.

Because it has pleased you that in our agreement the judgments of others should be adorned. I would not dare to disapprove of what I heard, nor to approve of such things. But since all knowledge is either about things, or about the names of things, or indeed about the accidents <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has (like color or size) which is not essential to its nature.</note> that happen to things, they are done by philosophy. For of this matter, they are able to discuss through Dialectic <note>Logic</note>, Sophistry, Rhetoric, and Physics. To judge whether a thing is unique or whether it is something else belongs to the Dialecticians; to prove that a thing is worthy of promotion or punishment is the role of the Rhetoricians; to prove what a thing is, or to discuss its habits and duties, is the concern of the Physicist. Therefore, Dialectic is the wisdom of the orators and the physics. <insert>It is, however, to be known: it is for his own concern.</insert>

<meta>Continuing from page 19, where the author, William of Conches, began his dedication to Duke Geoffrey of Anjou. This page contains William's formal "retractions," where he corrects errors from his earlier work, *Philosophia Mundi*, to align with Church doctrine before starting the main scientific dialogue of the *Dragmaticon*.</meta>

...considering the same matter in a divided way, they presume to dispute. Because they do not understand certain things, they have drawn them out from sophistical disputation in dialectic, yet they have adopted their names. They have preached that those things alone are true or individual. They find God to be foolishness, they who do not include the names of things and reduce almost every disparity to light. However, that one sect which was not of God failed by its own weight. Regarding physics, which we have arranged to treat concerning **substance**, whoever seeks it diligently will find it useful for knowledge and necessary for the reading of the philosophers.

There is, however, a little book of ours on the same subject which is called *Philosophy* <note>William refers to his earlier work, *Philosophia Mundi*, written in the 1120s.</note>, which we composed in our youth, imperfectly in an imperfect body, in which we mixed some false things and omitted many necessary ones. It is therefore our plan to place here what is true in that book, to condemn the false, and to supply what was omitted. As for the false words which seem to us in that book to be against the Catholic faith, we have deemed it worthy to condemn them before the beginning of this present work. Whence we ask all who have that little book that they condemn and cast those words out along with us. For words do not make a heretic, but the defense of them does.

In that book, we said that in the divinity there are these: power, wisdom, and will; that power is the Father, wisdom is the Son, and will is the Holy Spirit. But because what was said regarding power being the Father and will being the Holy Spirit—even if it was said in some spirit of defense—since we do not find it in the Gospel or the writings of the Holy Fathers, we condemn it according to that saying of the Apostle: "Avoid profane novelties of words." <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:20. William is retracting his attempt to explain the Trinity through logical categories.</note> Concerning wisdom being the Son of God, we do not condemn that, since the Apostle says "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God."

In the same construction, we attempted to explain how the Father begat the Son, according to that which is said: "Who shall declare his generation?" <note>Isaiah 53:8.</note> Therefore, it is to be condemned, because it is difficult, if not impossible, to explain. This we condemn, and we pronounce that no other explanation should be sought.

<margin>
x
</margin>

When in that same book we spoke of the creation of the first man, we said that God made Adam in ecstasy, and that He made Eve not truly from a rib, but from the clay that was joined to Adam’s side, from which the body of the man was fashioned; and therefore that the breath of life was shared. This, however, we now judge must be condemned, consenting to the Holy and Divine Scriptures which say: that God, having cast a sleep upon Adam, took one rib from his ribs, from which He fashioned the body of the woman. These then are the things which we condemn in that earlier book, marked here; we signal those things as false or trifling so they are not added to this work. But let us attend to this: provided we remain in the substance of the truth we have established. 

But because the similarity of our long speeches might cause boredom <note>original: "fastidium"</note>, we shall distinguish our discourse *dragmatically* <note>original: "dragmatice", meaning in the form of a drama or dialogue. This gives the book its title, the *Dragmaticon*.</note>. You, therefore, most serene Duke, shall ask the questions; and let the Philosopher respond to the questions in your name.

<meta>Continuity with page 104: This page transitions from William of Conches’s personal corrections of his earlier work (*Philosophia Mundi*) into the first major topic of the *Dragmaticon*: the nature of "substance." Following the medieval tradition of "faith seeking understanding," he begins by defining the term and then provides a profession of the Catholic faith (a Creed) to establish his theological grounding before discussing the physical world.</meta>

...which is composed of both is called substance. However, various descriptions of substance are given by different authors.

Substance is a <term>thing subsisting through itself</term> <note>original: "res per se subsistens." In medieval philosophy, a substance is something that exists independently, unlike "accidents" (like color or size) which must exist within something else.</note>. Sometimes the cause, for the sake of which things exist, is called their substance. At other times, it refers to the means of living; this is how we understand substance as sustenance, or something similar. Generation is the entry into substance. Corruption is the departure from substance. Sometimes it refers to physical presence; because it helps a person to exist, it is called substance. For example: "Give me the portion of **substance** that falls to me" <note>A reference to the Parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:12, where "substance" means property or inheritance.</note> in the Gospel. [And:] "He consumed his **substance** with harlots, living luxuriously."

**D.** <note>D stands for "Discipulus" (The Disciple).</note> Since "substance" is used in so many ways, tell me in which sense it is to be understood in this work.
**P.** <note>P stands for "Philosophus" (The Philosopher/Teacher), representing William of Conches.</note> Let it be understood in this work according to the first definition: as something subsisting through itself.
**D.** Since we agree on the name, proceed to the matter itself.
**P.** Substance is a thing subsisting through itself. But one type is created, and the other is uncreated. Regarding the uncreated substance—because it is the most worthy according to our faith—a few things will be said briefly, lest we be thought to disagree with the Catholic faith. You, however, should defer the task of questioning for a time, so that you may read the reasoning according to which it is said to be eternal. For <term>faith has merit where human reason provides no proof</term> <note>This is a famous maxim by Pope Gregory the Great, suggesting that faith is most valuable when it accepts truths that cannot be proven by logic alone.</note>.
**D.** Let it be so.
**P.** We believe
<margin>the Catholic faith concerning God the Father and the Son</margin>
that there is one substance of the deity, like something of equal length, breadth, and depth; immense without any physical application or boundary; wise according to its own nature regarding all things; merciful and pious; the highest movement acting upon all things; essentially existing in every place by its own extension and distribution. It is not past, but always present; omnipotent; omniscient. We believe that in the divinity and the person of God, there is the first-born Son, the only-begotten of the Father—not by <gloss>cutting off or withdrawal</gloss>, but born by <gloss>procession</gloss>. We believe in the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. We believe that none of them is the other; all three are one. All are of the same power, wisdom, will, and operation. God is able to do much that He did not will; however, He chooses nothing that He does not first intend. Each of these is a person: <term>the individual essence of a rational nature</term> <note>This is the classic definition of a "person" established by the philosopher Boethius.</note>. All are one substance, one Lord. 

We believe that one of these persons—that is, the Son—took on flesh from the Virgin, so that he who was the Son in divinity might also be the Son in humanity. He is our true Lord, a man subsisting in two natures from true flesh and a rational soul, without carnal corruption. He remains the same through that which he was before—being and essence—and what he was made to be. It is true that he was unchangeable before. He is both Creator and created, because he is also a man. One should not rashly deny that the Creator is a creature, because it is said that the man was born. Truly, in the form of a man, he created heaven and earth. We say that this one died; yet he was not a man when he was doing those [creative] things; he was God when he died. 

We believe that this true God and man suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, and died. His body remained in the tomb with his soul's divinity. His soul, with that same divinity, descended to the underworld. On the third day, having taken up his soul, he rose from his body. He appeared to the apostles with many proofs. On the 40th day <insert>on the mountain</insert> he ascended into the heavens. On the 50th day, he sent the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. He shall come to judge the living and the dead.

-> It is finished. <-

On the five regions of the world.

our faith.

**P.** Plato, the most learned of philosophers, divided the world into five regions: into heaven, ether, air, the moist region, and the earth. They call "Heaven" that where the stars are fixed. "Ether" from there down to the lunar circle. "Air" from the upper half of the ether. The "moist region" is the lower part of the same. He wished none of those rational animals to be lacking.

<margin>
On the five kinds of animals that live in the regions of the world.
</margin>
There is, therefore, in heaven an animal that is visible, rational, immortal, and impassible <note>original: "impassibile." In medieval philosophy, this means it cannot be changed or affected by external suffering or physical decay.</note>—namely, the stars. On the earth, however, there is an animal that is visible, rational, passible <note>original: "patibile." Able to feel, suffer, or be changed by external forces.</note>, and mortal—namely, man. In the three middle regions, it is said there are animals which, while they agree with the two extremes in some ways, differ in others. We shall set down their common distinction; let the prudent reader weigh in which things they agree with the extremes and in which they differ based on the distinction. The middle animal, which resides in the three regions, is thus defined by Plato: it is rational, immortal, invisible, and passible, just as it differs from men themselves. For the two higher kinds, through the goodness of the Son, love humans; they rejoice in their prosperity and suffer with them in adversity; they are in peace. For joy and pain are not "passions" as they are commonly thought, but knowledge; for they have greater knowledge and dignity...

<column-break/>

[The following circular diagram illustrates the hierarchy of beings in the five regions:]

| Region | Description of Animal | Identity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Outermost Ring** | Celestial animal: rational, immortal, impassible | The stars |
| **Second Ring** | Ethereal animal: rational, immortal, passible | Angels |
| **Third Ring** | Aerial animal: rational, immortal, passible | Demons |
| **Fourth Ring** | Aquatic animal: rational, mortal, passible | Fish |
| **Innermost Ring** | Terrestrial animal: rational, mortal, passible | Humans |

...although at times unequal in desire. The aerial [spirits], however, are called "mediators" between God and man; they represent the will of God through imaginings and visible signs revealed to men. They report the prayers of humans to God—not because He is ignorant, but by His will. Whence they are called "angels," that is, messengers. The humid animal <note>Referring to the spirits of the lower, moist air or "aquatic" region.</note>, however, is differently passible; it is full of wickedness, hatred, and envy, and it tortures good men and rejoices in evils. Because it fell through pride, it [hates] man who ascends through humility. It suggests hopes and thoughts, and sharpens tongues for quarrels, detraction, or false testimonies; it sharpens them against honest actions and hinders all good things.

<margin>D.</margin> **D.** Since Plato divides the good angels into two, but the Divine Page <note>original: "divina pagina". Authorities that seem to contradict themselves are explained thus: Air is sometimes called "spirit," as in: "The Spirit of God was hovering over the waters" <note>Genesis 1:2</note>. Thus a demon dwelling in the ether is called "spiritual." Therefore angels are spirits, that is, substantial ethereal or aerial bodies. Whence they move with such speed that they are here one moment and elsewhere the next; just as a ray of sunlight—which no one doubts is a body—is in the east and immediately in the west, touching the sun and the earth in almost the same moment. This is also why some claim that demons have knowledge of the future. <margin>That demons are said to have knowledge of the future.</margin> When people ask them about something they do not know, [they find out] just as souls that dwell abroad quickly return; in the blink of an eye, they arrive at the place where the thing has happened. It might seem that they have already begun to speak with assurance before the thing even arrives, and they could do the same...

...found in those writings. **Master.** Your will must be complied with. <margin>
Description of an element.
</margin>

is found first in the construction of a body, and last in its breakdown; it divides other things but is not itself divided. How is it then that just as every body is divided into two largest parts, it can likewise be broken down into infinite smallest parts? For every body has a boundary and is contained. Also, how "infinite" is spoken of in two ways.
</margin>

"Infinity" is spoken of in different ways: in number, in measure, and in kind. For in one way, things are said to be of a certain finite number. Again, things are called "infinite in number" which never remain in the same number. Thus also Plato says that individual things subject to birth and decay are said to be infinite; though then they are partly fewer. Other things are called infinite in number not because they do not have a total number, but because their number is scarcely or never certain to man. All things, therefore, exist in a specific number, but some exist more in one way and some in another. Some are always in the same state. These exceed human conception and are called "infinite in number." When therefore we said that a body can be broken down into infinite smallest parts, and since Boethius says magnitude decreases into infinity, this "infinity" is placed at the end of the process. There is another physical line of thought that says: just as a multitude grows toward infinity—though it does not follow that anything is said to be infinite in a single thing where it has a limit—so magnitude decreases toward infinity. Not that there is such an actual part, but because no part is found so small that nature cannot make it smaller than it was. **Disciple.** What you are saying, say more clearly. **Master.** Every part is smaller the larger the number it is named by, and larger the smaller the number. Whence, as the number of parts goes down, the quantity grows, and conversely it decreases. For a half-part <note>original: "media pars," meaning 1/2</note> is larger than a third, and a third is larger than a fourth. Magnitude therefore decreases toward infinity not in regards to the actual number of parts, but in regards to their names <note>The Master is explaining fractions: as the denominator (the "name" of the fraction) increases toward infinity, the size of the part decreases toward zero.</note>. **Disciple.** Return to the point. **Master.** There are, therefore, in every body the smallest parts, which when joined together constitute one large thing. These are called and defined by us as 

<margin>
How the bodies are generated.
</margin>

elements. Constantinus <note>Constantinus Africanus (c. 1020–1087), a physician and translator of Arabic medical texts into Latin.</note> agrees with this opinion where he says: "An element is a simple and minimal particle of a body." Of these particles, some are hot and dry, which are called fire; some are cold and dry, and these are earth; some are cold and moist, and these are called water; some are hot and moist, and these are called air. **Disciple.** Since these particles are...

It concludes by identifying the four classical elements (fire, earth, water, air) through their primary qualities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Master's investigation into the physical composition of matter. Having previously discussed the infinite divisibility of magnitude and the authority of Boethius, the dialogue now moves to the specific nature of "particles" and "atoms," comparing the building blocks of the physical world to the letters and parts of speech in grammar. The Master addresses the classical Epicurean theory of atoms and attempts to reconcile the existence of invisible particles with the visible world using the authority of Macrobius.</meta>

<margin>
Master. No. Brother. Also Master.
Concerning the particles of the elements.
</margin>

**Master.** It is clear that infinitely divided bodies consist of divisions, since it is possible to state that what has been said also applies to the four elements, and that all things consist of those same elements. Just as every sentence is composed of the eight parts <note>original: "partes octo," referring to the eight parts of speech in Latin grammar (noun, verb, etc.), a common medieval analogy for the "grammar" of nature</note> and the letters are the individual components of speech, so we must say that every single particle is an element. **Master.** It is also true that they are contained within four types. For when someone reads these two sentences, the philosopher <note>original: "r[et] pto," likely a contraction for "ratio" (reason) or "Plato"</note> argues that they consist of the same principles of speech, but not of the same specific particles. Rather, these four types of particles are produced by the generative divisions of the particles themselves, and they are called "bodies" for the reason we stated above. **Disciple.** 

<margin>
Concerning the opinion of the Epicureans.
</margin>

In the opinion of the Epicureans <note>The Epicureans were ancient Greek philosophers who taught that the universe was composed of atoms and void; medieval scholars often viewed their "materialism" with suspicion.</note>, it will be revealed that they say the world consists of atoms. **Master.** There is no false sect that does not have some truth mixed in, but the mixture of falsehood obscures that truth. Regarding those who said with Epicurus that the world consists of atoms: this is true, as we have said. But when they say those atoms existed so in the beginning, and were divided and flew through a "great void" <note>original: "magnū mane," likely "magnum inane," the vast vacuum of Epicurean physics</note>, and were then forced into four large bodies—this is a fable. Nothing can exist by itself in a specific place and beginning. These divided particles exist simultaneously as a single joined unit and as things divided, just as nature has provided in all things. For nothing could exist as a whole by itself. **Disciple.** Regarding these particles that constitute everything: 

<margin>
Query: whether all particles of elements are visible or invisible.
</margin>

should they be called visible or invisible? If they are only visible, they would lack all further division; if they are only invisible, they can be perceived by no sense. How then can this be maintained? For one should not believe that the visible is born from the invisible, according to Macrobius <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century author whose "Commentary on the Dream of Scipio" was a primary source for medieval cosmology. He argued that qualities in a result must exist in the components.</note>. Every quantity, when doubled, never works against its own nature. Therefore, the invisible mixed with the invisible will never produce a visible thing, for it preserves its own nature. **Master.** 

<margin>
The Determination.
</margin>

The invisible is that which can be perceived by no bodily sense, neither alone nor mixed with others of its kind. An example is the soul: one can perceive neither a single soul nor a multitude of souls by sense. But if one particle cannot stand by itself, it might stand when mixed with others. For what else is a body but particles joined together? 

<margin>
Whether they are also bodies or not.
</margin>

**Disciple.** If these particles are invisible, are they also bodies? If they are bodies, they must also have division—namely, length, width, and depth. Thus, a final "body" would be found possessing these divisions. **Master.** This troublesome swarm of questions flows from this: the one asking does not know the definitions of the names he uses. He applies the name "body" to something constituted from the four elements which is visible to the eyes. But words have different meanings. The Logician <note>The "Logician" here refers to the scholar of the *Trivium* concerned with formal definitions, as opposed to the "Physicist" or "Philosopher."</note> does not call something a "body" based on its constitution from the four elements. But the philosophers trace names back to the first principles, calling the first principles of bodies "bodies"—but to distinguish them from composite things, they call them "simple." Just as a simple sound <note>original: "prola"</note> exists before it is joined into a composite word, so there is a "simple body" and a "composite body." As it has been said...

<meta>This page continues the Master's (P) and Disciple's (D) dialogue from the *Dragmaticon Philosophiae*. Having established that the universe is made of tiny particles, the text now explores the primordial state of these particles—the Chaos—and distinguishes between the works of God, Nature, and Man (Artifice).</meta>

Bodies did not achieve these three dimensions <note>Length, width, and depth.</note> on their own; hence, it is not unfitting to say that the first imposition of the name "body" comes from physical observation. Let "bodies," therefore, be things perfectly realized through physical observation, yet not solely by dimension. <margin>So prepared also to create together.</margin> **D.** Since he says those divided particles previously existed on the day in which the things that were created came to be. **P.** The Creator established those particles in one great body; they were divided not by spatial distinction, but were mixed throughout the whole mass, so that none of these particles existed outside this body. They truly occupied every place because they occupied all bodies. <margin>Regarding this chaos.</margin> This is noted by physicists, through this mixture of particles, as "chaos," which is interpreted as *confusion*. Truly, the hot and dry resisted each other within it by their own proportion and middle rest; similarly, the moist resisted the dry. Hence **Ovid** says: *A raw and undigested mass.* <note>original: "Rudi indigestaque moles," from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, describing the state of the universe before the elements were separated.</note> Then he adds: *The moist things also fought with the hot, and the dry.* <note>original: "Etia pugnabant calidis humida siccis."</note> But because from that great body God immediately created four bodies—which today are spoken of by some—apart from the first mass from which they were led out into diverse places. **D.** The Creator, who created all things by his word alone and knows all things before they happen, purposed that there should be four, because he knew that the initial state would not long remain. 

**P.** What you ask is fitting for no one to know. You have seen our works established, yet he created them despite our ignorance; yet if they possessed any reason, it was from him, because reason in us seems to speak of God. <margin>Concerning the plural work.</margin> Let us hear what others say of the same. Every work is either the Creator’s, or it is natural, or it is artificial. The work of the Creator is the creation of souls from nothing, the resurrection of the dead, the virgin birth, and <margin>Concerning Nature</margin> justice. **D.** Before he shows our work, let him define the name. **P.** It is difficult to define the power and nature of "Nature." But let us say this according to a second interpretation: Nature is a certain force implanted in things, through which like things produce like from themselves. <note>This "force" (vis) refers to the biological and physical laws that allow plants and animals to reproduce according to their kind.</note> The work of nature, therefore, is that humans are born from humans, or reptiles from other animals. But artificial work is what is set forth by man to meet a universal need, <margin>How nature does not work.</margin> such as clothing against the cold, or ropes as for a house of works. Namely, when they [artisans] work at something, they first produce a certain raw beginning. Then, bit by bit, it forms and divides; for dust is worked into that [form], and then because it is observed in it, it is placed congruously in an infinite place on the earth; because truly the light element escapes upward while the mediocre stays in the middle place. Just as it is created as a sign in the world, afterward, in its substantial quality, man separates it, not by office but with help. Those who could not reach the operation of the Creator among the artisans, the Creator willed to descend to their operation. Just as there would be weakness here if one thought that they were created by some changed things they perceived, but as others say, he created it silent lest the confusion of things be too great, so that he might rule and order it by his own direction. **D.** This is now sufficient; but <margin>Chaos was immobile in the beginning.</margin> tell me, in this world-mass, was it mobile or immobile? **P.** Reason proves that it was immobile. Since it filled every place by name, it did not move visibly from place to place, because it could [only] be moved [if there were space to move into]. Therefore, it was silent regarding every kind of movement. **D.** After he decided that the things should be united, it happened that they acted. He says now that every bodily thing is moved by an inopportune motion.

<margin>
Every element received its name from the quality that dominates within it.
</margin>

...called, and so on. Therefore, following from the aforementioned things, the **Philosopher** says: He gathered the hot and dry particles, which were mixed with others, to a higher place. And from those, joined with certain others of the same kind, He established one thing, which is called "fire" from the parts that dominate in it. But the cold and dry particles He led down to a lower place. And from those, joined with certain others, He composed one corporeal and robust thing, which is called "earth" from the parts that dominate in it. From the hot and moist particles, joined with others, He made "air"; and from the cold and moist, "water." 
**Duke.** If earth, which is said to be cold, is actually made of hot particles, then in a cold thing that is effective, there is no heat. Therefore, two contraries are in the same thing, and a certain thing is both cold and hot. 
**Philosopher.** It is impossible for two contraries to exist in the same whole and in the same part at the same time. However, we see with our eyes that they can exist in different parts of the same whole. As for what is said regarding its being hot—judging by that from which it proceeds—it is nonetheless called "hot" in common speech when heat dominates. Since, therefore, the quality of cold dominates in earth, it is called cold, not hot. Just as wax is named not from everything within it, but from those qualities that dominate in it, so are general names applied. Yet I do not deny that part of the earth is hot. 
**Duke.** Moreover, I perceive water to be hot to the touch <note>The Duke is likely referring to hot springs or water heated by the sun</note>. I feel that a part of the air is earthy when the North wind <note>original: "boreas"</note> blows. But whether there are cold and moist particles in fire, or dry ones in air or water, I do not know. 
**Philosopher.** He judges like a beast who judges only by touch. Therefore, a man who surpasses beasts by reason should judge things by reason, not by the accident of how they feel.

<margin>
Its consistency is in the dry.
</margin>

**Duke.** I wish to hear the reason from you. 
**Philosopher.** No one who philosophizes correctly doubts that fire is composed and mixed, unlike the other things that exist. But since a part of fire is especially thickened in winter and changed into air, and since such a thing is consumed from fire at one time by another, it must be restored in another. In summer, therefore, parts of water are changed into air... There are some who say fire is nourished by moisture <note>A common ancient belief that the sun and stars "fed" on vapors rising from the sea</note>; but it is more that the air does not retain them and they are ignited. They are not merely transformed. All philosophers agree that coldness and dryness perform the "retentive power"; heat and moisture perform the "digestive" power. Heat, although it consumes things, finishes them. Cold, although it freezes things... Cold and moisture dissipate. Only moist heat digests. To "digest" <term>digere: the process of transforming one substance into another through heat, likened to boiling</term> is to transmute something into another through boiling <note>original: "ebullitione"</note>. In the same category is the "expulsive power" which expels waste, consisting of cold and moisture; and the "attractive power" which comes from heat and dryness. If therefore in fire there are certain particles where hot and dry dominate, the rest must be proved. Since air and water retain, there is in them an <unclear>att</unclear>ractive power, which cannot exist without cold and dryness. 
**Duke.** This is a hard manner of reasoning. For how can one conclude those things? I have [difficulty]; but if this thing which is made into fire has anything cold and mo<unclear>ist</unclear>... it has another... it must be that... another argues that it is more fruitful.

</margin>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Duke and the Philosopher regarding the physics of the elements. In the previous page, they discussed the qualities of earth and fire and how they interact. Here, the Philosopher explains the mechanism of vision and the necessity of the two intermediate elements (air and water) for the stability of the world and human life.</meta>

...better in nothing than what is mixed and obscure; for this same reason, it is sent to the eyes. Therefore, fire prepares the eyes for something better. 

**Duke.** I understand how fire operates in vision. But I ask whether fire acts by its rays alone. 

<margin>Fire operates through rays.</margin>

**Philosopher.** As the philosopher says, nothing is perceived by the senses except through an instrument that mediates between the sense and its utility. What is called an instrument there is a certain airy substance which the soul sends from the brain through the nerves to the exterior. <note>original: "aeriam substantiam"; this refers to the 'animal spirits'—a refined, airy fluid believed by medieval thinkers to carry sensory information through the nerves.</note> We shall speak of this in the following sections. Therefore, when we apply this "instrument" to a hand that is well-disposed to feeling, and it touches a hot object, it becomes heated. Along with that heat, it returns to the brain, which is the seat of the soul. It is not only those things that run about there that are retained, but if the soul perceives heat through that instrument. There are sparks when it touches anything cold; <note>The text is likely discussing the friction or interaction of qualities.</note> but fire, which is always in motion, is the principle of movement. This is the reason why this instrument runs out to the exterior and returns. 

**Duke.** I no longer doubt the cause of the creation of those elements <note>fire and earth</note>; but I desire to know the cause of the creation of the intermediate elements <note>air and water</note> that change their forms. 

<margin>On the cause of the creation of the intermediates.</margin>

**Philosopher.** Two extremes could not exist without a middle. <margin>Reason.</margin> Because if they were placed together, a vacuum would remain in the space between them, or if one descended to the earth and the earth ascended to the fire—but a place cannot exist without being filled by a body—the earth would have to ascend toward the heavens, whereas it is inclined to move toward the center, falling to the bottom. And if fire were to come to the earth, it would struggle with a similar motion to ascend away from the center. If this were to happen, the great machine of the world would be dissolved. <note>original: "machina mundi"; a common medieval metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely ordered structure.</note>

**Duke.** If the earth were so large that it extended to the middle of the space, <margin>Supposition.</margin> and fire extended to the same point, then a vacuum would not exist and this evil of dissolution would be solved. 

**Philosopher.** See that in fleeing Scylla, you do not run into Charybdis! <margin>Response.</margin> <note>A classical idiom meaning that in trying to avoid one danger, you fall into a worse one.</note> If these bodies touched each other without an intermediate: fire, by the power of its substance, would send its heat and motion into all parts, dividing part from part. Whatever it encountered, it would consume by drying it out. And because this is the case, man—for whom all things on earth were created—would not be able to live; nor would brute animals, nor would there be trees which exist to serve man. 

**Duke.** It is clear that it would not be suitable to be without a middle; <margin>Why there are two intermediates.</margin> but why God created *two* intermediates is a wonder to me. 

**Philosopher.** If only air were in the middle, it would have more in common with the fire above than with the earth below. Because of this, it would gradually be changed into fire, and the earth would be burned up before the fire reached it. Likewise, if only water were placed in the middle, because it has more in common with earth than with fire, it would be changed entirely into earth, and thus the earth would be joined directly to the fire. 

**Duke.** This is clear and provides a consolation; these high laws would be inconvenient if only one of these were placed in the middle. <margin>Why a single intermediate was not created that was equal to both extremes.</margin> But I want you to tell me why God could not have created some other body in the middle of these which would relate equally to both extremes. 

**Philosopher.** I place no limit on Divine Power; but I say that if He had done this, there would be no air, without which man cannot breathe. From which he would not be able to live for even an hour. Likewise, water is necessary for the use and benefit of man. 

**Duke.** If God wished man to be able to live without these, would one intermediate between these extremes be sufficient? 

**Philosopher.** With things remaining as they are, no.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Duke and the Philosopher regarding the natural philosophy of the elements. Having established the roles of fire and earth, the Philosopher now explains the necessity of the two intermediate elements—water and air—using the logic of geometric proportion and shared qualities to explain how the universe is bound together into a cohesive whole.</meta>

<margin>
For the earth to remain stable, a single medium between it and fire would not be sufficient, even if it were possible.
</margin>

Earth is a solid body that serves as a foundation through its qualities. For earth is **dense**, **blunt**, and **immobile**. Fire, however, is **subtle** (refined or thin), **sharp**, and **mobile**. <note>The Philosopher is using a set of three pairs of opposing qualities: density vs. subtlety, bluntness vs. sharpness, and immobility vs. mobility. These were standard categories in medieval physics derived from Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> If there were a single medium between them, it would have to receive only one quality from each of those aforementioned six qualities, or perhaps two from each, or one from one and two from the other. If it shared no qualities with them, it would not be a proper medium between them. Every medium must participate in the qualities of the extremes; but let us see what would follow if it took only one quality from each.

<margin>
Read these correspondences: if one medium were to have from each side either a single nature/quality, or two from each, or one from one and two from the other.
</margin>

Suppose that this medium took **density** from the earth; in that case, it could not also have **subtlety** from fire. Or if it had two differences, and it took from fire only the quality of being **sharp**, it would then be **dense** and **sharp**; but it would then be either **mobile** or **immobile**, which the logic does not allow. <note>The argument here is that a single element cannot bridge the gap because it would always leave some qualities in total opposition.</note> The reader should understand this as applying to the other qualities as well. Since there are immediate pairs of qualities regarding bodies—**dense** and **subtle**, **blunt** and **sharp**, **immobile** and **mobile**—if that medium took only one quality from each extreme, two immediate differences would remain that the medium would lack. 

**Duke.** And if it were asked what would happen, I want to know what kind of mixtures could be made by sharing only one quality from each side? Let this be explained briefly.

**Philosopher.** Two contraries cannot exist in the same thing at the same time. If the medium took only one of the six qualities from earth and one from fire, it might be **dense** and **sharp**, yet it would lack a state regarding **mobility** or **immobility**. Or it would be **dense** and **mobile**, and thus be neither **blunt** nor **sharp**. Or it would be **blunt** and **subtle**, and thus never be **mobile** or **immobile**. Or it would be **blunt** and **mobile**, and thus neither **dense** nor **subtle**. Or it would be **immobile** and **subtle**, and thus not **blunt** if it were **sharp**. Or it would be **immobile** and **sharp**, and thus neither **dense** nor **subtle**. Thus, whichever of these it were, it would lack two of the essential qualities required for a body. But if it took only one of these six from each side, it would have a duality of traits; yet each would be held so weakly by the extremes that it would not function as a proper medium, nor would it preserve that connection.

**Duke.** I see why it could not take only one from each. But show me what happens if it took two from each, or one from one and two from the other.

**Philosopher.** If it took two from each, it would have four qualities; but it cannot have four because it is only permitted to have a duality of qualities in this sequence. If it took one from one and two from the other, it would be more similar to the one from which it took two; thus the proportion among these things would be unbalanced, and the mutual bond would be dissolved.

**Duke.** I agree: I judge that one medium followed here could not have been sufficient.

**Philosopher.** Two elements are placed in the middle. Each of them properly receives two of the aforementioned qualities, while being removed from one. There is <gloss>water</gloss>, which is **dense**, **blunt**, and **mobile**. **Air**, however, is **subtle**, **mobile**, and **blunt**. In this way, these bodies agree in "solid conjunctions." <note>original: "solida coniugia"; this is a reference to the *Timaeus*, where Plato argues that two mean proportionals are needed to connect solid numbers (cubes), just as two elements (air and water) are needed to connect the "solid" elements of fire and earth.</note> For those elements that are neighbors share two qualities in common, while differing in the third. They also agree in "plane conjunctions": Earth is **cold** and **dry**; water is **cold** and **moist**; air is **hot** and **moist**; fire is **hot** and **dry**. Thus they agree in the aforementioned ways. For as much as earth is denser than water, so much is water denser than air, and air than fire. But consider more carefully what has been said.

<summary>The Philosopher explains why two intermediate elements (air and water) are mathematically and physically necessary to link the extremes of fire and earth. <margin>
On the motion of the elements.
</margin>
**Philosopher.** Some have defined motion in substance through "generation and corruption" <note>The process of coming into being and passing away</note>. Others defined it in quantity through increase and decrease. Others in quality as a change from one contrary to another. Others as motion in place. Since, therefore, these elements are moved at least in their parts regarding their substance, and since they change in their quantities and are altered in their qualities, why do you doubt that they are mobile? **Duke.** It is the Aristotelian way to say that the aforementioned things move. But tell me in what way they move in their parts through generation and corruption.

<margin>
On the reciprocal mutation of the elements.
</margin>
**Philosopher.** In a certain part of the year, the two upper elements <note>Fire and Air</note>, which are subtle <note>thin or light</note>, are thickened by accident and transmuted into the two lower ones <note>Water and Earth</note>. In another part of the year, the two lower elements, which are corpulent <note>dense or heavy</note>, are accidentally refined so that they are transmuted into the two upper ones. **Duke.** Explain the cause, if you please, why the upper ones are thickened and the lower ones are refined, and the manner in which this happens. **Philosopher.** No one of sane mind doubts that the Sun is the source of heat for the lower things. Therefore, when the Sun reaches Cancer <note>the summer solstice</note>, which is our time of summer... it rises through the air with power. The air, undergoing its change, refines the water and changes the water into itself. But when the Sun is in Capricorn <note>the winter solstice</note>, which is farthest from us, the water is thickened by the cold. The thickened water cools and thickens the upper element, namely the air which it touches, and changes it chiefly into itself. The thickened air then thickens the fire and transforms a part of it into itself. In summer, therefore, through the presence of the Sun, the lower elements are refined and changed into the upper ones; conversely in winter. By this cycle of mutations, the world remains indissoluble. **Duke.** You have satisfied me by saying this much. I see that the four aforementioned elements are generated and corrupted in their parts, increased and decreased, and altered. But what is asserted regarding their "local motion" <note>movement from one place to another</note>?

<margin>
On the local motion of the elements.
</margin>
**Philosopher.** Local motion is a transformation within the same place. A thing moves in the same place when it remains in the same location but its parts move... <note>The text here describes rotation or internal movement</note>. Change of place, however, is when the whole thing is in one place, and then in another. There are seven types of this motion: upward, downward, forward, backward, right, left, and toward the center.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion on the nature of elements. <margin>Concerning the waters that are above the firmament and the waters that are below the firmament.</margin>
...nothing that divine and human philosophy <term>philosophia; the study of all knowledge, including what we now call science</term> contains [contradicts] what says that the heaven rules all things. It says the firmament is that in which the stars are fixed, and that waters are above the heavens, as it is written: "Bless the Lord, you waters that are above the heavens" <note>original: "benedicite aquae quae super caelos sunt domino"; a reference to Psalm 148:4</note>. It says the firmament is in the middle of the waters; hence it is necessary that waters be above it and below it. And likewise, He divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament. **Philosopher.** Air is sometimes called "heaven," as in the phrase "the birds of heaven that play" <note>a common medieval reference to the "volatiles caeli" or birds of the air</note>. Sometimes the ether, which is called fire, is called "heaven." Sometimes the outermost part of heaven is called the "firmament" because it strengthens <note>the word "firmament" comes from the Latin *firmare*, to strengthen or make firm</note> the two lower elements. When it is said that "heaven rules all things," it means the stars are embedded in the firmament. They call the outermost part of the air both "heaven" and "firmament." But when it says that waters are above the heaven and above the firmament, it calls the air "heaven" and "firmament," and it is true that in the lower part of the air there are watery vapors suspended in the clouds.

<margin>Concerning the authority of Bede.</margin>
**Duke.** Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (d. 735), an influential English monk and scholar</note> says that the waters are frozen, appearing to us like a shell of crystal. **Philosopher.** In those matters which pertain to the Catholic faith and the instruction of morals, it is not right to speak against the authority of such holy fathers as Bede. However, in those matters which pertain to philosophy, if they err in any way, it is permissible to affirm a different view. For reason holds a greater power for us in these matters. **Duke.** Since the knowledge of the lesser [should] follow the reason of the greater, let it be shown why it ought to be otherwise. If you wish to be believed, even if you cannot prove Bede's words to be false, let a true or plausible reason be brought forward.

<margin>The opinion of Bede.</margin>
**P.** All water is naturally heavy; when it is frozen, it approaches even more the weight of earth, and thus by its own weight it is pushed toward the center. If, therefore, there were water above the ether, its weight would cause it to descend to the depths.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**D.** We see that an arch <note>original: *arcus*</note> is held up at the top and never descends; therefore, waters frozen in the manner of vaults are suspended and cannot descend.

<margin>Response.</margin>
**P.** An arch whose shape is not connected to something solid at its base must immediately collapse. These arches of yours, since they are not fixed to any solid base, are nothing but a lack of solidity. It is necessary, therefore, for them to have a base to hold them up, otherwise the whole structure would be raised up with no lightness.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**D.** If they are not sustained in that way, they can be sustained in another. We see that fire lifts and sustains certain solids by its own force. Since fire is placed under these waters on all sides, does it not sustain them by its force?

<margin>Response.</margin>
**P.** You have indeed found a way to flee from blame, but it lacks skill. If the waters are sustained by fire, is there something between them and the fire, or nothing? If something were between them, whether it be air or something else, it would be a body. But every other element is below the fire. If there were something else, it would be visible; why then is it not seen? If no body is between them, and fire and water are joined, all things would be mixed in the middle. There would then be conflict and discord in the heavens, and thus the fire would consume the waters.

<margin>How they extinguish the fire.</margin>
**D.** Some think the waters are placed there to moderate the heat of the stars. They say they are frozen together in the likeness of crystal; hence, even if they are touched by fire, they cannot be dissolved.

**P.** Crystal is dissolved even by the smallest fire. What then would happen in that intense heat? For when crystal was water, the water first bubbles on the surface, then in the middle, until it becomes ice. Then, by long cold...

<margin>On the creation of the stars.</margin>
It appears to differ from the visible heavens. On the first day, out of that great mass of the four [elements] which today are also called seeds <note>original: "seminalia"; the fundamental building blocks of matter</note>, the earth was everywhere covered by waters. The water was indeed raised up to a great part of the air; the air was thicker near the fire than it is now. This thickness was produced by the presence of the earth and the waters that had entered within it. And so, the first state of things was ignited in the air, while God created those round, splendid, and moving bodies which are called stars. Although the bodies of the stars were made from the four elements, there is no proof at hand by visible reason for this.

<margin>That the stars are made from the four elements.</margin>
It could be that they are visible: because that is easily granted by sight. But because they are visible, they are generated from visible things. Yet, as was said at the same time: nothing produces its own light from its own body alone. They have what is seen from visible things.

<margin>This</margin>
Only earth and water are naturally visible; fire and air are invisible. There is, therefore, in the stars some earth and water so that they may have substance; but there is in them a dominant rule of the higher elements. They are solid, yet they are not of the same solidity as the earth. Furthermore, whatever does not change among its own kind is stable; but the bodies of the stars are nourished by the moisture of the ocean <note>A common medieval belief held that the stars "drank" or were sustained by rising vapors from the great world-ocean</note>. This liquid is common to all, providing water to the bodies of the stars. Those stars which are splendid and mobile possess these traits from splendid and mobile things; therefore, they consist of fire and air. Thus, they are made from all four elements. But the qualities of fire dominate in their upper parts, and water in their lower parts. Since in the air there is moisture,

<margin>Whether the stars were created in the region of the air.</margin>
thicker than in fire, it is asked why their bodies were not made in the air. Perhaps the air was the occasion for this, being an earthy world, wherefore he could not, by drying what was in itself, thicken it and create a lucid and visible body. This can be judged from common things: water placed under fire thickens and is changed into a stony substance <note>The author uses the analogy of minerals forming or liquids hardening under heat to explain how stars became solid bodies</note>. But if it is placed under some heat and moisture, like boiling water, it becomes hot but does not thicken. Indeed, in these four elements, they have binary qualities: one they have from themselves, and another from another. Fire is hot by its own nature, but dry from the earth. Air is moist by its own nature, but hot from fire. Water is moist from the air, but cold by its own nature. Earth is dry by its own nature, but cold from water. Therefore, there is in the air, besides its own moisture, a heat born from another; because of that moisture, he could not create the bodies of the stars by drying it. Or what is more likely: it was not the Creator's will to create stars in the air. When the stars were in his hand, or in God's plan, they were not of the earth. While the stars were in the air, they were nourished by the ocean. But what is to be expected from the alteration of heaven? Because the bodies of the stars were thus created as fiery things, they do not cease to move, and by the movement of the air, they are subtly heated, which is further heated by the mediation of water. From this, through the boiling of fire, various other things were made. Of which some, which have more

<margin>On the creation of animals.</margin>
moisture and lightness, are the birds of heaven. Because of their lightness and ability, they are suited to the air; yet because of their weight, they descend to the lower earth. Those which have more of the moisture of water are the fish. In this, the power of God alone is seen. While in reason and authority...

<meta>This page transitions from the physical formation of humans and elements to a philosophical and astronomical debate regarding the timing of the world's creation and the nature of the celestial spheres. It contrasts the views of Virgil and Macrobius with those of Aristotle and Plato regarding the "quintessence."</meta>

<margin>
The creation of the world occurred, according to the Egyptians, in July.
</margin>

The world began to exist according to its being. Whence Virgil, speaking of the days of spring, says: "I believe that such were the days that shone at the first dawn of the world's origin; it was spring, and the great world was keeping spring." <note>original: "ver illud erat: ver tpe agebat." This is a reference to Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book II), where he argues the world must have been created in the gentle climate of spring to allow life to survive.</note> This is because everything that arises is found in a state of balance. Just as everything that moves out of balance and into intemperance moves toward death. No time of the year is more temperate than spring. Thus, the first creation of things was done in that season, according to a consistent belief in a new creation. For autumn is stormy, and the rains and cold of winter are not fully suitable for life; as we see, if frost reaches new growth, it brings death. 

However, the Egyptians say that the creation of the world occurred in July. Regarding this, Macrobius <note>Macrobius (5th century AD) was a Roman provincial and author whose work on the *Thema Mundi* (the world’s birth chart) was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> says: "On the birthday of the world, the moon was in Cancer and the sun was in Leo." This occurred for a reason. In the first creation of the world, there was such a great amount of moisture that the earth was covered by water. This moisture was so vast that it could not be dried and tempered except by the greatest heat; therefore, the creation of the world happened at that time of year in which the heat is greatest.

<margin>
The opinion of Aristotle regarding essence.
</margin>

This will be clear if we weigh the following opinion: every terrestrial body is composed of one of the four elements, and fire is located above the lunar heaven, while the other elements are below it. This is not my opinion, but that of Plato. Since, however, he is considered more severe than all other philosophers, it is said that they agree with him in this. Philo <note>Likely Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who harmonized Greek philosophy with scripture.</note> attempts to explain these lights, though some of our own people fear these things; they complain about their origins, yet they fashion themselves to be their sons. They treat philosophy and the science of the stars like a foreign household, engaging in so many quibbles that they obscure the matter further. They fight for their own glory rather than the truth. False lights must be explained, and they are divided under a common heading: what is in the heavens, and what is condemned. Whence Solomon says: "He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will not reap." <note>Ecclesiastes 11:4. The author uses this to warn against over-analyzing natural signs instead of trusting in divine providence.</note> One waits for the word of the Lord, while the tongue of the talkative moves easily in those times. A rude seat is easily moved and rolled; I show nothing less than what is alive. And let no one judge such a portent. She will give a good response in that name; for vanity and ignorance conquer the weak and join themselves against them.

Aristotle wanted there to be one essence <note>original: "essentia," here referring to the *quinta essentia* or quintessence—the fifth element that makes up the heavens.</note> which he called the "fifth." The four elements are found from the moon downward, while the fifth essence exists from the moon upward. All things that are below the moon are elements and consist of them. All things that are above the moon consist of that fifth essence. Just as those things below the moon have the four qualities—namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—nothing of these qualities applies to those things above the moon. There is no birth or death there; they do not move toward or away from the center, but rather *around* the center. Whence the sun, placed in the middle of its path, neither ascends nor descends in its nature, but moves according to its being. It is for this reason that the stars revolve at an equal distance from the center. 

Know that those who hold this opinion believe that above the moon there is no heat, nor cold, nor moisture, nor fate. That place which is under the moon is where there is lordship <note>original: "dominical," perhaps referring to the sublunary world as the realm of chance or mundane rule.</note> and change. This essence is divided into the ethereal and the firmament. From this same essence, eight splendid bodies called planets are formed in the ether; in the firmament, there are innumerable bodies, which are the fixed stars. Therefore, all stars shine because of the quintessence, not because they consist of the four elements. And because the sun is not of this [sublunary] nature...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the celestial bodies, moving from the timing of creation to the specific physical qualities of the planets and the mechanics of the firmament’s rotation.</meta>

8.

<margin>
On the motion of the seven planets
</margin>

The sun is the hot source of all heat. <note>original: "calidus sit fons totius caloris"</note> Saturn is cold in itself and generates cold in the air. Mercury is moist in itself; we call it the god of moisture. Mars is hot and dry. The moon is cold and moist. Those who have understood this theory—indeed, the truth of the elements—even if it is understood by effort, let us speak of another thing among those we allow. One such visible figure lies before our eyes. I have spoken of the invisibility of the variety of the stars. Therefore, one discusses their natural motion. Through those things which are reported today in the lessons of the schools, I will allow the rest to be said about them. The bodies of all seven stars are judged to move from place to place, which are generally called **planets**, that is, "wanderers." <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek "planētēs," meaning wanderer, because they appear to move against the backdrop of the "fixed" stars.</note> Beyond these, existing in a higher place, they are rotated in the perpetual firmament and also against the firmament; whence again they are called "in the firmament." I call the firmament that celestial part in which the fixed stars are set, not like a gem in gold or a nail in a wheel, but it works so that they are held fast within it by their own nature. <note>original: "non ut gemma in auro, nec ut clavus in rota." This was a common medieval debate: whether stars were attached to the surface of the spheres like jewels or embedded through the thickness of the sphere.</note> They are divided so that fire is also in all things that move from the center; as the eccentric <note>original: "eccĩa," likely referring to the *eccentrica*, the off-center circular paths used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note> says: they move around the center.

<image-desc>
A circular cosmological diagram drawn in red and black ink. The diagram consists of eight concentric outer rings and four inner rings. The outer rings represent the celestial spheres, labeled from the outermost to the innermost: "firmamentum" (appearing twice), "circulus saturni" (circle of Saturn), "circulus iouis" (circle of Jupiter), "circulus martis" (circle of Mars), "circulus solis" (circle of the Sun), "circulus veneris" (circle of Venus), "circulus mercurii" (circle of Mercury), and "circulus lune" (circle of the Moon). The four inner rings represent the elemental spheres: "ignis" (fire), "aer" (air), "aqua" (water), and "terra" (earth) at the very center.

He made these stars run about. If one were unmindful of what has been said, one would call it by three names. First, consider this turn of motion carefully. This mode of fire is from the center; but because from the light itself there is no weight, it has an acute motion upward. For it is the nature of all things to stand or to descend downward. Because that which stays in the same place, the eccentric does not move. From the center there is another mode of fire, kindling around the whole. They are led from the east around the center...

<margin>
On the motion of the firmament
</margin>

...the central motion and lateral motion joined to the horizontal path from the east through the southern pole to the west, returning toward the north to the east, and again from the east through the midday <note>The word "meridies" means both midday and the direction of the south.</note> to the west. If the eccentric is recognized as being led again to the east, it moves obliquely around each in turn; but they move the firmament together. The firmament is seen to move from the east through the west back to the east, as if the sphere of the zodiac signs moves into the west joined to the horizontal path. Just as a star moves, it appears rising in the morning in the east; at midday, it is in the southern region; in the evening, it sets; at midnight, it is in the north. This does not happen if it moves around the summit. One part is seen from the poles through the middle of the earth, the other from the opposite side, which we do not see with our eyes. Therefore, the firmament moves by ascending from the east to the south, then through the west to the east. If any eccentric sphere were situated in the middle of the earth with the firmament rotating over its head, or if it were figured as equivalent. Where he speaks of those who live below the **torrid zone**, <note>The "torrid zone" refers to the tropics, the earth's hottest central belt.</note> he says of the signs: "Man travels obliquely if Taurus or Scorpio, but more surely if Aries is right." Around both habitable zones, the firmament moves obliquely by ascending, which you will see by looking at those stars whenever they rise; you will see them somewhat before the sight is oblique...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics, shifting from the nature of the planets to the fixed points of the heavens—the poles—and the "intelligible" lines that define the movement of the stars and the paths of the Zodiac.</meta>

...ascending, and by slanting toward the west, they come to evening. On this side, place the pole...
<margin>But this is the pole which is called the **Arctic**.</margin>
**Question:** What is a pole? **Answer:** It is answered that the pole is a star that remains immobile. Among the vast multitude of stars, only one exists in our interior hemisphere that is always in the same place, and another is in the opposite hemisphere. Between both of these is an **intelligible line** <note>an imaginary axis understood by the mind rather than seen with the eye</note> drawn from pole to pole through the center of the earth. Since the earth, the habitable part of our world, sits in the middle—not on its own horizon—it is understood that this is so. It is established that the slanted firmament <note>the celestial sphere</note> moves around our habitable land just like a **wheel on a chariot**, because it is moved by itself. Just as those who stand in the middle of it are moved toward the setting or the rising sun, so too the things around the pole, where the planets are always seen, would not be hindered by the brightness of the sun. Where it says that in the interior parts there are no physical bodies, but they subsist by themselves in their own motion. Is the firmament some kind of solid thing, as some say the earth is solid? Tell us then, are these stars held up by anything?
<margin>On the motion of the fixed stars.</margin>
Their motion is not because they are supported by anything. Let it be that the Lord of the heavens is moved by his own motion toward blessedness, and the stars sustain themselves in the same place. Others say the stars move from place to place by the heat of the planets' motion, while the earth has no motion; so it seems to our eyes. Because they consume such a vast space in the journey through their heavens, the life of a man who lives forever would still not see the sphere complete its circuit at such a speed. **Student:** Yet, regarding what is now said: **Teacher:** The heavens move from place to place. It is also said that they move like **a man in a ship**; though he stays still, he sees the land move. What is this? This whole manner of motion is not a mobile thing running through a perverse time. When one thing moves, another thing that is not moving seems to move. Just as when we look through a nearby opening, if it moves, it seems smooth. But if nothing from those things is immobile, only the mobile part is seen, in a smooth manner, as when a ship goes through a part of the sea. **Teacher:** The manner of the stars, however, is that they are moved by the "first mover" <note>the *primum mobile*, the outermost sphere that moves all others</note>, being led around under it. By their positioning, we never speak of their motion through the signs as we do with the planets, as if one were looking at wood beneath another thing. Beyond the aforementioned stars, nothing else is visible, and it is not their own motion that runs through them. They are always moved, but they do not shine. **Student:** It is sufficient to speak of the fixed stars; but before I speak of the planets, tell me of the **celestial circles**. **Teacher:** The philosophers said there are twelve circles. Two of these are invisible and two are visible. 
<margin>On the twelve celestial circles, and first on the zodiac.</margin>
Regarding the invisible ones, let us speak first. The first of the invisible circles is the **Zodiac**. This ascends from Capricorn through Aries to Cancer, and descends from Cancer through Libra to Capricorn. To descend or to ascend is to understand its own name. This constitutes the third degree in the present figure.
<image-desc>A diagram of eleven concentric red circles. The innermost circle has six radiating lines dividing it like spokes on a wheel. The diagram represents the celestial spheres or circles described in the text.</image-desc>
If one wished to bring back the water, it was divided by the Egyptians. They are called "signs" because when the sun and other planets are properly in a sign, it indicates the logic of what ought to happen. They are titled with the names of animals, such as **Aries** (the Ram), **Taurus** (the Bull), and so on. Because of this, it is called the **Zodiac**. Five divisions are commonly called <term>parallels</term> <note>From the Greek *parallelos*, meaning "beside one another."</note>. Regarding the shadows, no particular property is attributed to them.
