<margin>On retrogradation and the station of planets.</margin>
Our ancestors affirmed many things about this. Some say the Sun is the cause of this action; when the planets precede the Sun, they are drawn or pulled back by it, acting like a diamond or a magnet <note>Original: *adamantis et magnetis*. This is a fascinating medieval attempt to explain gravity or orbital mechanics using the known force of magnetism.</note>. In their receding, they seem to stand still for a time. Others say they never truly stand still, but only appear to do so. Since they are in constant motion, it is not necessary that they should stop. It appears, however, that they stand still and move backward. These "stations" <note>The point where a planet appears to stop moving before changing direction.</note> occur, according to astronomers, when a planet moves through its usual path but at a different "height" or altitude, or when it descends lower than usual, which confuses the observer’s sight. Sometimes a star is elevated at one time and depressed at another. Through the Sun, it has this heat; sometimes it is called "higher" or "lower." Hence, bodies naturally rise when they are light. When they move toward the moisture of the Moon, they are made heavier and thus appear to descend. This happens because of the curvature of the heavens; in certain places they are depressed, and in others exalted, sometimes directly and sometimes obliquely. When they are seen at the peak of their "exaltation" or "depression," they are said to "stand still" (at station). When they move obliquely, they are said to be "retrograde," especially when they appear to move behind their usual lines. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers, often cited in the Middle Ages as the ultimate authorities on the stars.</note> give another reason for this retrogradation.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary movement begun on the previous page. Having introduced the cold nature of Saturn and the tempering influence of Jupiter, the author now shifts to the geometric explanation of planetary "loops"—the stations and retrogradations—using the model of epicycles. This transition moves from the astrological character of the planets to their physical-mathematical behavior in the geocentric cosmos.</meta>

<margin>An analogy of a racetrack regarding the stationary point and retrogradation of the planets.</margin>

In each of these orbits, one part is more remote and the other is nearer. This is because the sky, which is called the <term>firmament</term> <note>In ancient and medieval cosmology, the firmament was the sphere of the fixed stars that formed the boundary of the universe.</note>, is where the planet itself moves with this kind of motion. It is not the firmament itself that moves the planet; rather, it is shown to move by the motion of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent). This was used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to explain why planets sometimes appear to slow down or move backward.</note>. Therefore, this motion is like this: Just as before a wheel <note>Original: *rota*</note> begins to turn, it must run along certain measurements so that it moves from the West toward the East. If that wheel is perceived to be moving swiftly, it seems to the eyes to move toward the East. Yet, when it descends along that same path, it appears to the eyes not to go East, but to move toward the West. Then it seems to stand still; and on that same lowest path, it appears to move from East to West directly before the eyes. When, however, it ascends along that same path, it seems to stand still. So it is with each and every one of these planets. For example, there is a place of <term>station</term> <note>The point where a planet appears to stop moving against the background of the stars before changing direction.</note> or <term>retrogradation</term> <note>The optical illusion where a planet appears to move backward in the sky because of the relative positions of the Earth and the planet in their orbits.</note>. To understand this matter, I shall make a certain visible figure, in which we place the Earth in the middle, and around it the <term>zodiac</term> divided into twelve signs. Below this, however, is the sky that touches the Earth, and above the Earth is the epicycle—that is, a circle made of nine parts, ascending at the top and in two middle points—with a single line designated by human measure directed toward four locations.

->**[DIAGRAM]**<-

<note>The diagram illustrates the geocentric model. At the center is Earth (**TERRA**). Around it is the "concentric circle" (**circulus egrocentris**). A smaller circle, the "epicycle circle" (**circulus epiciclus**), is placed on the larger orbital path. Labels on the epicycle include: **Statio I gradus .a.** (First Station, point A), **Retrogradatio .B.** (Retrogradation, point B), and **Statio .II. gradus .D.** (Second Station, point D). A radial line lists the celestial bodies from furthest to nearest: **Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Moon**. The outermost ring contains the names of the twelve Zodiac signs: **Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces**.</note>

In each movement of these epicycles, when the planet resides there, it is seen to be in front of the eye. Its course is seen to move toward the West. When it reaches nearly to **B**, which is the descent, it seems to stand still because it appears to go backward and seems to be in Taurus. This is the **first station**. When, however, it reaches **C**, it is seen to move from East to West; in that same place which we previously observed, we say it is in the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; planets are usually seen near this line.</note>; this is its **retrogradation**. When it comes to **D**, the third place, it will be thought to stand still; it will be seen in Pisces, even though it was originally seen in Aries. In that same way, it is thought to be allowed to come through that sign. Just as with certain understandings, there are diverse opinions regarding what is read about the station and retrogradation of the planets. I affirm none of these specifically, but I lay them out. According to Plato, the planets do not move by chance. A star is everywhere described as "benevolent" or rare in its timing.

<margin>On Mercury.</margin>

**D.** Regarding what is said of **Venus**, just as we mentioned regarding the opinion of Plato, let it not be otherwise elsewhere. The **Egyptians** said something different: that the Sun stands above the Moon, Mercury above the Sun, and Venus above that. The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers known for their advanced celestial observations.</note>, however, following their own tradition, place the Moon first, then Mercury above it, then Venus, then the Sun. ...nothing could be concluded regarding its entity. This is how it stands regarding the Sun: it has Mercury in the middle of the Sun’s [path]; Venus is above the middle. So that this might be better understood, let a figure be drawn. In this drawing, the Sun is shown, then the <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circular orbits whose centers move along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> of Venus and Mercury are depicted in two locations, namely the highest and the lowest. When Venus and Mercury are in the inner degrees of their circles, they are then above the Sun. And when Mercury is at its farthest point from the Sun, or when they are in the outer degrees of their circles, then the Sun is above them, in both cases being further from the Sun. 

The <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A term often used in medieval texts to refer to ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers renowned for their observations.</note>, looking at this, saw that whenever they are below the Sun, they appear as lights. For the Sun does not hide the light of that which it is placed beneath. They concluded the Sun was lower than all of those. By observing the heights to which the planets are able to rise, they saw that the Sun does not rise as high as Venus or Mercury. They judged the Sun to be lower than Mercury and Venus. Ptolemy, however, depicts the order of all the planets in the margin of the page. This similar equality of the Sun being above or below Venus and Mercury is more easily accepted. 

Furthermore, since the Moon is cold and humid, it was necessary for the Sun to be its "doctor" <note>The text uses a medical metaphor here; the Sun's heat "treats" or balances the Moon's cold nature.</note>. Just as here on Earth, the heat of the Sun illuminates the Moon and makes it appear; out of dryness, humidity is balanced. It is known in the world that if things are not governed by it, and if its untempered rays reached the Moon, the Moon would be destroyed. But because the Moon lacks its own splendor, it is illuminated only by the Sun. It is necessary, therefore, for the Sun to be the substance in the middle of the lights.

## Regarding eclipses, the location of the planets, and a review of their motion.

**J**ust as the orbits of the planets move from the West to the East, the force of the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars that carries the planets in a daily rotation.</note> carries them all back toward the West daily. Thus, the Sun is balanced so that Mercury does not move more than 32 degrees away from it, and Venus does not move more than 45 degrees. If they reach that distance, they return to the Sun. Mercury circles the zodiac roughly in a year. Venus also takes a year, though it remains in its circle for 20 months. In another year, when it is at a different distance, it moves through the Martian or first orbits. When they are near the Sun, they are hidden by its splendor; returning, they begin to be seen in the morning before the Sun, which is called the **morning shining** <note>Original: *matutina effulsio*, referring to the heliacal rising.</note>. If they follow the Sun all day, it is called the **morning setting**. From their rising, they are seen to be a certain distance from the Sun. Venus is seen on one and the same day before the Sun, and then it is called <term>Lucifer</term> <note>The "Light-Bringer," or the Morning Star.</note>; at the end of the day, it is seen after the Sun, and then it is called <term>Hesperus</term> <note>The Evening Star.</note>.

**Q.** Since the astronomers say the planets move quickly, and since Venus is seen at the beginning of the day before the Sun and at the end of the day after the Sun, it is demonstrated similarly: Venus is sometimes lower than the Sun, which is why it is positioned further from the Sun locally. Yet by its height, it is seen above the Sun in the evening and before the Sun in the morning. Likewise, at the beginning of the day, it is seen to precede the Sun locally, but by its height, it is seen above it. This can be understood through a visible figure.

If, therefore, the Sun moved [only] from East to West, it would pass from Aries into the sign placed to the West, namely into Pisces. In the third [hour], it would then pass from Aries into the signs placed to the East... then into Gemini. This delay is a clear proof that the motion is truly from West to East, because that is how it moves. 

However, since the <term>firmament</term> <note>In medieval cosmology, the firmament is the outermost sphere of the stars that rotates once every 24 hours.</note> returns from East to West, if those planets held [only to that direction], there would be such a great impediment <note>The author suggests that if the planets didn't "push back" against the firmament's rotation, the friction or speed would be destructive.</note> that nothing could stand or live there. It is clear that they resist the force and momentum of the firmament's rapid motion, being drawn back by the gravity of their own motion. If the firmament moves all things at once, every day it draws everything with it toward the sunset. 

**D.** [Disciple]: I believe it was necessary for the planets to be moved by the firmament; yet if it was natural for them to return to the sunrise, I do not see why they are carried back by the firmament. 

**P.** [Teacher]: When the Sun moves from West to East in a day, resisting the force of the firmament, it would be [as if it traveled] eight thousand miles... <note>The text here uses "milibus" (thousands) to describe the immense speeds or distances involved in celestial mechanics.</note> for the benefit of the course of the night. If it ran with the firmament at eight thousand miles a day, would not the fire consume the life of the firmament... and the color of the water... nothing would remain. 

Therefore, since the Moon is in the <term>ether</term> <note>The "fifth element" or celestial substance that makes up the heavens.</note>, which is called the firmament, it would be subject to that motion of the pole... the momentum of which is frequently questioned. If you remember, it is the common opinion of all philosophers that the light of the planets moves against the firmament. In which matter, another [view] is found.

<margin>
The opinion of the Arabs regarding the motion of the Sun.
</margin>

I shall explain their opinion, though it is not troublesome. 

**P.** [Teacher]: The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> say that the light revolves above the Moon alone... They say, therefore, that all things are carried around the center. They conclude that as much as the planets [move] in their own natural course, they are returned daily to the East and West by the foreign motion [of the firmament]. 

**D.** [Disciple]: I dared to speak regarding the arrangement of the signs according to the aforementioned philosophers. 

**P.** [Teacher]: The "fox has its hole." <note>A metaphorical way of saying everyone has their own specialized place or theory.</note> The Peripatetic scholars, who recognized philosophical truth, said that the Sun truly passes to the signs placed to the East... Whence they came to the Sun. Where, therefore, we place the Sun as having risen today in the first part of Aries, the firmament and the Sun are followed for the whole day and night... because the firmament is faster than the Sun...

And then, when the spring Sun comes to Aries, all things follow through the region of summer; from which it will appear to us that the Sun stands upon it. Thus, constrained by the prior motion of the sphere, they follow the Sun. Hence, the Sun is thought to move toward the east. But whenever they are in the presence of the general assembly of the most learned philosophers, they concede this to him. Therefore, the Sun and the other planets move from west to east, not in a straight line but obliquely; descending toward the southern parts and ascending toward our habitable land, according to the aforementioned arrangement of the spheres.

<margin>
How the four seasons of the year are distinguished by the Sun moving obliquely.
Concerning Winter.
</margin>

Concerning this, it is necessary that the Sun, which always moves as one, should produce variations through the four parts of the year by moving obliquely. For if it followed a straight path, it would not have these variations of the year. When, therefore, the Sun comes to Capricorn, which happens on the <term>Kalends of January<note>January 1st in the Roman calendar.</term>, the Sun reaches that sign... <note>The text here contains a difficult reading regarding the 15th Kalends of June, likely discussing the solar cycle.</note> because that time is most remote from us, our habitable land freezes with cold. Thus, indeed, it is a cold time; the air then thickens into clouds above the earth, because they dissolve into rains. Thus, that part of the year is called **winter**.

<margin>
The time of winter according to the Greeks and Romans, following Isidore.
</margin>

The composition of the winter season begins for the Greeks and Romans on the <term>7th Ides of November<note>November 7th.</note></term> and lasts until the <term>15th Ides of February<note>February 13th.</note></term>. <term>Isidore<note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose encyclopedic works were foundational for medieval science.</note></term>, however, says it begins on the 7th Kalends of December <note>original: "vij. kl deccẽb[ris]"; November 25th.</note> and ends on the 15th Kalends of March <note>original: "xv. kl marti"; February 15th.</note>. In this time, the pores of the earth are closed by the cold; in which [earth] the heat, which used to evaporate, remains inside. They hold their rays and the trees are nourished; from this, many plants come forth. Since in this season there is no heat in the moisture—which is the quality of the <term>blood<note>Latin: "sanguis"; one of the four humors.</note></term>—growth is produced in the trees through the cold as mentioned before. Whence in this season there are many storms and rains, rather than lightning and thunder. The end of this discussion on what is generated: to this season is compared the humor <term>phlegm<note>Latin: "flegma"; the cold and moist humor associated with water and winter.</note></term>. In the same season of winter, those who suffer from <term>colic<note>Severe abdominal pain.</note></term> will find it persists; they will find it at its worst during the daily <term>quotidian fever<note>A fever that returns every day, often attributed to an excess of phlegm.</note></term>, which is a sickness arising from the cold.

<margin>
The state of the blood and the day during winter.
</margin>

At that time, the blood is greatly increased because the pores of the human body are closed by the cold; so the heat, instead of evaporating, remains inside and produces an abundance of blood. This generates a loss of vigor and affects the external governance of the body. In the same season, one’s strength is such that <insert>it requires caution</insert>. Concerning drink: in this season, it ought to be diminished. But the drinking of wine, which is "hot and dry" <note>In medieval medicine, substances were classified by their "complexion." Wine's heat was thought to counter winter's cold moisture.</note>, is said to resist the nature of winter. For if a man is too "moist" in his habits, it increases the moisture within and extinguishes the internal "fire," just as a lamp is put out by too much oil.

<margin>
Concerning Spring.
</margin>

When the Sun, in its descent, reaches Aries—which is completed around the <term>15th Kalends of April<note>March 18th, near the Spring Equinox.</note></term>—it moves closer to us from its remote position, being placed in the middle of the <term>Torrid Zone<note>The central part of the earth according to ancient geography.</note></term>. Whence our habitable air becomes both warm and moist. This is the first of the four seasons of the year, which is called **Spring**. Spring begins for the Greeks and Romans on the 7th Ides of February <note>February 7th</note>; according to Isidore, on the 8th Kalends of March <note>February 22nd</note>. In this time of year, the pores of the earth, which were closed by the cold of winter, are opened by the heat. The Sun reaches the roots and the trees begin to grow; the moisture that was gathered in the winter is processed, and the trees take on their green clothing. And the earth...

<margin>
The inconveniences that would follow if the sun always declined along the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator</note> in winter would be obvious even to a commoner.
</margin>

**I**nconveniences would follow if the sun were always present to us in the same way as in summer, or if it were always remote from us as in winter; this would be plain to anyone of the common people. But if it ran strictly along the equinoctial line, then those things in which all things rejoice would occur at the proper time: things which follow the orderly pattern of the world.

<margin>
Concerning the accidental motion of the Sun.
</margin>

**F**urthermore, many evils would occur in the world if the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> were recognized only in turn. For a certain gratuitous humidity would persist under the Moon, whereby water would be lacking on the earth when the sign of Cancer <note>The zodiac sign associated with the summer solstice and the element of water</note> begins; there would be nothing thereafter to dry it out. The fruits which a man might use in the snow would not reach a state fit for chewing. And they would lack all the good things of the elements—even gold—for the lack of winter.

**T**he true reasoning of the [heavenly] constitution acts by ascending and descending obliquely in latitude. Regarding the animals, enough has been said previously concerning the accidental motion of the same sun.

**F**or the sun, by its own motion, moves from west to east through the firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>. It is then turned by the firmament and returns to the west. Because of the splendor between the sun and the earth, it is called "day"; in the same way, entirely beneath the earth, it is night.

<margin>
On the distinction of one day from another, and the usual day.
</margin>

**I**t should be noted that one kind of day is "natural" and the other is "usual." The natural day <term>naturalis dies: the full 24-hour cycle of day and night</term> is generally a space of 24 hours. The usual day <term>usualis dies: the period of daylight from sunrise to sunset</term> is divided differently. From the ninth part of the night until the third part of the "usual" day, they say it is warm and moist <note>associated with the humor of blood</note>. From the third part of the usual day until the ninth, it is hot and dry <note>associated with yellow bile</note>. From that point until the third part of the night, it is cold and dry <note>associated with black bile</note>. And from that until the ninth part of the night, it is cold and moist <note>associated with phlegm</note>. This is why certain illnesses fare better in different parts of the day, according to the aforementioned distribution of times and qualities.

<margin>
Concerning the usual day.
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning the elements found.
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning the texture of days.
</margin>

**A** usual day is the space in which the sun is carried from sunrise to sunset. In the first part of it, the sun is red; in the second, there is splendor; in the third, heat; in the fourth, it is tempered as it descends. Note these properties in the following names of the sun's horses: the first is **Cruthe** <note>original: "cruthe," a corruption of the Greek *Pyroeis*, meaning fiery or red</note>, which is called "red." The second is **Acche** <note>original: "acche," likely *Eous*, meaning of the dawn</note>, meaning "shining." The third is **Lamp** <note>original: "lamp," from *Aethon*, meaning burning</note>, meaning "burning." The fourth is **Philogen** <note>original: "philogen," from *Phlegon*, meaning loving the earth</note>, meaning "loving the earth." In these usual days throughout the year, there is diversity. Sometimes they are equal, sometimes shorter, sometimes longer. This is obvious when the sun is in the winter signs; the "swelling" <note>The arc or height of the sun's path</note> which is in the middle of the torrid zone—where we are situated—is closed off, which is why we see it briefly. It sets quickly and there is less light and longer shadows. But when it is in Cancer and other summer signs, that "swelling" is reborn; the sun is seen early in the morning and sets late, providing more light and shorter shadows.

<margin>
Concerning Autumn.
</margin>

<margin>
† The beginning of Autumn.
</margin>

**I**n the same way, in Aries and Libra <note>The signs marking the spring and autumn equinoxes</note>, they are constitutionally at an equal distance from us. Light and shadow are then equal. There are two equinoxes <term>equinoccia: the two times a year when day and night are of equal length</term> in the year: one in March, on the 15th day before the Kalends of April <note>March 18</note>; the other in September, on the 16th day before the Kalends of October <note>September 16</note>. There are also two solstices <term>solsticia: the points where the sun appears to "stand still" at its highest or lowest point</term> in the year: one in December... and the other in June... The first is called the winter solstice because the day is shortest, lasting 8 equinoctial hours and a half, while the night is long. From this point until the summer solstice, the day increases, until the day is 15 equinoctial hours and a half.

**W**hat we say regarding equinoctial <term>hours that are of equal length regardless of the season</term> appears to be evident. <unclear>P</unclear> If you wish to know how many hours in a day are pronounced without [considering] length—though he who knows should listen: an hour is the space of time in which half a zodiac sign rises. Truly, the equinoctial hours 
<margin>But for the hours</margin>
of the day are twelve. The equinoctial hours of other days are unequal; yet every day [as a unit] has twelve hours, and every night has twelve hours. If 
truly six signs rise during the day, another six rise in the night. This is distinguished by the distance of the zodiac, which is 
divided into twelve equal parts called "signs." Then, certain disparities exist: some [signs] participate in the day, others in the night. 
Where [the signs] rise directly <note>original: "rre", likely "recte"</note>, six signs rise in the night and six in the day, which is seen 
only on the equinoctial day <note>The day of the spring or autumn equinox</note>—by this law they rejoice. Or, where the signs are not equal, or in the shortest night and day, if six signs rise [they do so at different rates].

<margin>Concerning the rising and setting of the signs.</margin>
**B**y error, some wish for the signs to be equal because while one sign lingers in its rising, another does not. It is certain that 
all [signs] set directly or obliquely <note>at an angle to the horizon</note>; some rise obliquely and set directly. Because where they rise directly, they linger longer than those that rise obliquely. This common [measure] of length can be weighed according to the opposite habit of the season. And just as 
arithmetical scales <note>A metaphor comparing the rising of stars to the balance of a scale</note> begin to ascend: first, they are seen entirely obliquely; in their beginning, they are 
entirely oblique as they ascend. Immediately, the whole will appear. This shows the gift of 
the spear-shaft <note>original: "hastale"</note>, to hold from its own end at the last; but they will linger through the oblique [path]. 
This is how it is with the signs. The signs of the summer day rise directly. But the signs of the summer nights rise obliquely. 
Wherefore, in those times when many signs rise, the nights appear shorter than the days because of their rising. But in 
the signs of the winter days and nights, the signs of the day rise obliquely, and the signs of the night rise directly. 
Thus, the day is shorter and the night is long. Truly, the signs of the equinoctial days and nights rise and set equally. 
So that one may better understand, I shall say how long each sign lingers in its rising 
and setting. Cancer, Scorpio, and the Martian sign <note>original: "marcianus"; likely a scribal error for another sign or referring to a sign ruled by Mars</note> rise in two equinoctial hours and a third part of an hour [2 hours, 20 minutes]. They set in one hour and eleven-twelfths <note>original: "deuncc", meaning 11/12 of an hour</note> [1 hour, 55 minutes]. Leo rises in 2 hours and a third part; it sets in an hour and a half <note>original: "semis"</note> and a sixth part of an hour [1 hour, 40 minutes]. 
Virgo rises in 2 hours and a half and a sixth part of an hour [2 hours, 40 minutes]. So too Libra. It sets in seven parts [of an hour]... and with a trembling 
mutation. [Virgo/Libra] sets... [and] rises in 3 hours... 4 and a third part of an hour. It sets in 5 hours and a third part of an hour. 
Sagittarius rises in 2 hours and a third part of an hour; it sets in one hour and eleven-twelfths. These are the six signs that 
rise directly and set obliquely. Others rise obliquely and set directly, whereby each lingers in its rising. 
Capricorn rises in one hour and eleven-twelfths; it sets in 5 hours and a fourth part of an hour. Aquarius rises in an hour and a half 
and a sixth part of an hour; it sets in 5 hours and a third part of an hour. Pisces rises in an hour and a third part of an hour; it sets 
in 5 hours and a half and a sixth part of an hour. So too Aries. Taurus rises in an hour and a half and a sixth part of an hour; 
it sets in 5 hours and a third part of an hour. Gemini rises in an hour and eleven-twelfths; it sets in 5 hours and a third 
part of an hour. If this belongs to the matter of opinion, the day has 12 equinoctial hours directly, 
but the third is the smallest: it is seen as a half and a third part of one hour. This repeats until the end. 

<margin>Concerning the Solar Eclipse.</margin>
**C**oncerning the eclipse of the sun, I shall speak. It announces that in its length, the zodiac is divided 
into 12 equal parts. Its latitude is also divided into 12 equal parts, which is called the *enagone* <note>possibly referring to the *evagatio* or deviation of the planet from the ecliptic</note>; it has all twelve parts 
of latitude with whichever moon. But the Sun travels through the middle of the latitude where the description of the moon's mass occurs.

Since, therefore, the sun is always carried along the center line of the zodiac <note>The ecliptic, or the Sun's apparent annual path</note>: if on the day of **conjunction** <note>The New Moon, when the Sun and Moon align</note> the moon is in that same mid-point of its latitude: then it is so positioned at that time, being between the sun [and us], that the line from the solar vision to the eye is directed straight through the middle of the lunar body. <margin>Whether a total eclipse occurs.</margin>

**B**ut if on the day of conjunction the moon is in the middle of the zodiac's latitude <note>This refers to the "lunar nodes," the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path</note>. This one can see in this figure: for the descent of the sun's rays is hindered by the moon: then it happens that a solar eclipse sometimes becomes total, and sometimes partial. If indeed on the day of conjunction the moon is positioned exactly in the [node] of the zodiac's latitude, then a total eclipse of the sun occurs. If, however, it is only partially in the middle, it is a partial eclipse. But note that whenever a solar eclipse occurs, because the moon tends from the east toward the west <note>relative to the Sun's disk from our perspective</note>, first the splendor of the sun fails from the western side little by little, until the whole splendor is taken away from us. But as the moon passes across from the western side, the solar body begins to appear to us like a <term>new moon</term> <note>original: "noue lune", referring here to the thin crescent of the Sun reappearing</note>, until the moon passes entirely from the solar body and then the whole sun appears. And note that although the conjunction occurs in the view of the hemisphere, the solar eclipse may not be seen by us; just as it occurs on earth, it does not happen at the same hour for all peoples. Hence, the time will be found differently in every single habitation.

<margin>Proof that the sun is larger than the earth.</margin>

**P**hilosophers assert that the sun is larger than the earth, even though it seems not to exceed the width of a shield. This is due to a <term>fallacy of sight</term> <note>An optical illusion caused by extreme distance</note>, for it is well known that when large things are viewed from afar, they appear very small to us. Hence, because of the height of its location, the sun appears small. Many learned men prove by necessary argument that it is larger than the earth; for if the sun were not larger than the earth, how could it present itself to inhabitants in different parts of the world at once? It is said to be sufficient that the sun is called larger than the earth in the writings above. Because the sun is larger than the earth, during the night it is necessary for the earth [to cast a shadow]. If it were not equal to the earth—if it were smaller than the earth—it would be different. But it happens that the sun is concluded to be larger than the earth.

<margin>of the moon</margin>

If the sun were equal to the earth, the shadow which exits from the earth's hemisphere would be sent upwards [in a straight cylinder]: then the earth would divide it... the moon would always remain in the same condition. Then not only the moon, but even the planets and stars would be overshadowed; but an eclipse of the sun always generates its own [shadow]...

Likewise, if the sun is not smaller than the earth, but you make it larger than it, it creates a **conoid** shadow <note>A cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point</note> which does not transcend the lunar eclipse <note>The text reads "mcurẽ," possibly a contraction for Mercury, but contextually refers to the reach of the shadow toward the lunar orbit</note>. <image-desc>Three geometrical diagrams demonstrating shadow projections from a light source (Sun) past an object (Earth). The leftmost shows a diverging shadow (opening wider) labeled "Calachoid, that is, a tyboid shadow." The middle shows a converging shadow (tapering to a point) labeled "Conoid shadow." A **cylinder** is a round figure with equal ends <note>A tube shape</note>, if the lines are drawn together; hence the shadow is called **cylindroid** because it is in the form of a cylinder. A **top** <note>original: "turbi," referring to a spinning top or whirl</note> or **calachus** is a figure extending from a sharp point to a wide base; hence a certain more pure tube <note>or trumpet shape</note> is so called. Thus, a shadow which is in the form of a top or calachus is called **tyboid** or **calachoid**. A **cone** is a figure extending from a wide base to a sharp point; hence its shadow is formed as a **conoid**.

### Concerning the Moon

<margin>
The reason why one lunar month has 29 days and another 30 days is revealed.
</margin>

Following what has been sent before, I shall proceed concerning the moon. The **Moon** is the closest of all the planets, positioned in the lowest ether or air. Hence, it possesses an eclipse. In 27 days and 5 hours, it traverses the zodiac. Where, for example, it is ignited <note>aligned as a New Moon</note> in the highest part of Aries, in 27 days and 5 hours it returns to the first part of Aries; but it does not find the sun there. Therefore, it is ordered by a recurring law to receive light so that it can be seen; for it leaves the sun behind for 2 days and 4 hours. Then the conjunction is made... from the sun it is ignited. A straight lunar calculation, therefore, has 7 hours of the 29th day, which pass through the middle of the day; wherefore it is necessary to compute one day. In that lunation, one whole day is computed from two halves. Thus, from these, 13 hours are made, which for one lunation make a 29-day month, and for another, 30 days. The wise men [calculate] from September, because of the occurrence of the Egyptians, who begin their year... in the lunar <insert>zodiac</insert>. But since we say the moon is 27 days and 6 hours... from 6 hours there remain 8 **degrees** <term>moira: a Greek term for a degree or a 30th part of a zodiac sign</term>, which are all collected proportionally; through 22 years they propose one day. Hence, in the 22nd year of the lunation, they subtract one day... Thus, it traverses in 5 days and 4 hours that which the sun passes through. It is for this reason that it is never ignited in Gemini twice in the same year, in which the sun dwells for 26 days; but in the opposite sign, that is, in Sagittarius, it dwells for 28 days. If the moon is ignited in the first degree of Gemini, it leaves it behind in 26 days and 6 hours; yet it will not be ignited there again, because the sun will still dwell in that sign for 50 days. If the sun dwells in Gemini for 26 days, and in Sagittarius for 28, between the signs the sun is seen to err more in one than the other... but which of these is chosen... I choose none of these. I shall find something else more profitable, if I may be worthy to speak of the moon. As it is said... they unite their opinion, and the philosophers who stand in authority. Let me be worthy to speak...

<margin>
Why the sun lingers longer in certain signs and less in others.
</margin>

Since this pertains to the sun <note>original: "hylio," a Latinization of the Greek *helios*</note>: The Earth is the center of the zodiac. Above it is the center of the heaven through which the sun runs, which is a single path; however, due to its distance from the earth, it is as if it passes through a point. While the zodiac is divided into thirty degrees, the sun stays longer in some signs than in others because of its **eccentric** <note>original: "eccentros"; a path where the center of the orbit is not the same as the center of the Earth</note> orbit. This is clearly shown: if we place a circle in the middle, with the zodiac at an equal distance from the earth on every side, the arc of the sun’s eccentric path—through lines directed from the zodiac toward the earth—would divide the solar heaven. If one were to observe the sign where the sun is furthest from the earth, under Gemini, the sun would appear to linger for thirty days <note>In the medieval model, the Sun is at its furthest point (apogee) in Gemini, making its motion appear slowest to an observer on Earth</note>. Under Sagittarius, however, it is at its nearest point. Although the sun travels its own path at a constant rate, because of the distance of its heaven, the segments of the zodiac that are enclosed by these lines appear different. Thus, the sun is said to be "in Gemini" for a longer stay of thirty days in that upper part of the orbit. Conversely, the arc under Sagittarius is the shortest, and therefore the sun is said to pass through it in fewer days <note>The transcription reads "xv" (15), likely an exaggeration or specific geometric example to illustrate that the sun seems to move faster when it is closer to the Earth</note>: judge the other signs according to this principle.

<margin>
Why the brightness of the moon increases and decreases.
</margin>

<margin>
The moon has its light from the sun.
</margin>

<margin>
When the moon is "monoeides," when "dichotomos," when "amphikyrtos," and when "panselenos."
</margin>

Pliny and others say that the moon has no light of its own, but rather reflects brightness. For when it is in the same sign as the sun, it is darkened by the sun's excessive splendor. When it moves away from the sun, its brightness begins to appear to us, and the further it is removed from the sun, the more its brightness appears; the closer it is, the more it diminishes. This is indeed the case. It does not begin to appear from the western side because it is being lit from a further distance by the sun, but it is always lit on the side opposite the sun. Some have wisely said that the moon has a body like a mirror, made of the density of earth and water, which all stars possess. Hence, it does not have light from its own heat or brightness. Rather, it has its own inherent nature, just like the earth, and it ascends to Cancer and descends to Capricorn, passing through the heat of summer and the cold of winter. Just as a mirror or water reflects light, so the moon, positioned in its path, is illuminated by the heat/light from the sun, though it does not always appear equal to us. When it is positioned under the sun, that part of it is much colder, and it casts a shadow toward the earth; hence it is not seen by us. When it moves away from the sun, a small part of its splendor begins to appear in the shape of a horn; this is called <term>monoeides</term> <note>original: Greek "monoeidēs," meaning "single-form" or crescent-shaped</note>. As it moves further from the sun, more splendor descends upon it, and on the seventh day it is called <term>dichotomos</term> <note>original: Greek "dichotomos," meaning "cut in half"</note>; that is, it is seen divided through the middle. And note that as much as the splendor descends, so much the shadow ascends. From the seventh day until the fourteenth, it is called <term>amphikyrtos</term> <note>original: Greek "amphikyrtos," meaning "curved on both sides" or gibbous</note>, which means it is seen as more than half full. On the fourteenth day, when it is removed from the sun across the diameter of the sky, it appears in its fullness as the sun sets and the moon rises. Now the shadow has completely ascended and the splendor has completely descended. This is the <term>panselenos</term> <note>original: Greek "panselēnos," meaning "all-shining" or full moon</note>, which is the full moon. Afterwards, it begins to approach the sun again, whereby the shadow descends and the splendor ascends. It first descends through the *amphikyrtos* phase, then *dichotomos*, and finally *monoeides*.

If the new moon appears larger at one time than at another.

...all things would be suitable with such a figure placed before the eyes. **From this, it is asked why the splendor of the moon appears greater in one lighting <note>original: "accensione"; referring to the "kindling" or first appearance of the new moon</note> than in another.** If the moon is seen by us as soon as it is lit, its size appears to us [in a certain way]. **If it is lit in the morning before the sun rises, or in the evening; if it appears on a day when it is waning in Aries, then by the Ganges <note>The Ganges was often used in medieval texts as a metonym for the farthest East</note>: it appears most great. <margin>What kind of lunar eclipse occurs.</margin>
**And so it is said that on this day it is lit; the closer it is lit to the sun at its setting, the smaller it appears.** An eclipse of the moon happens in this way: When the Sun and the Moon are positioned on the ecliptic line <note>The path the sun follows through the sky; an eclipse can only happen when the moon crosses this line</note> such that the sun is in the lower hemisphere and the moon is in the upper, they are distant from each other by the diameter of the circle. Then the mass <note>original: "rumor," likely a transcription of "moles," meaning bulk or mass</note> of the earth, being directly opposite, directs its shadow all the way to the moon itself. From this it happens that the rays of the sun cannot light it, and it enters into the shadow for a partial eclipse. To see this, one should subject a figure of it to the eyes: the moon undergoes a partial eclipse on its eastern side when it touches the shadow of the earth, and as it touches the shadow from that side, it begins to appear darkened. A partial eclipse occurs not only on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the lunar month—at which time the moon is positioned diametrically opposite the sun—but also whenever it moves through the middle of the width of the zodiac. For if on the 14th day the moon is positioned near the middle of the zodiac’s width, the shadow of the earth is directed straight back toward the moon. If it is here, and as if between wings <note>referring to the geometric shape of the shadow cone</note>, as seen in the illustrated figure, an eclipse of the moon occurs. If, however, on the 14th or 15th day the moon is in a part touched by the shadow, it is darkened in that part. But an eclipse of the moon occurring in the day is not seen by us. What shall we say of the shadow seen in the middle of the lunar body? For it is not the case that the entire body of the moon is obscured, but rather some of its parts are smooth like a mirror, and some are rough and as if rusty <note>original: "rubiginosum"; referring to the reddish tint seen during a lunar eclipse</note>. One part is positioned to reflect the rays of the sun, but the rough part retains the darkness; however, they do not show themselves today in a quantity greater than usual. This is what is stated by all.

It is advised that wisdom should, as it were, flee from the envious; but they cloak themselves in their own laziness. The chaste person holds hope for this philosophy; to this, no wickedness is an obstacle, for no power is able to take this from us.

**Disciple:** Since the honor of the Church has been led astray for a long time—not by the pious, but by the ignorant—I see the care of souls being hindered. Regarding this, I look upon the soul’s small sparks, wondering what might be said of the power of its judgments. But I look with contempt upon the vanity and the wide sleeves of the clergy, and the long hair of those who should be tonsured <note>The tonsure is the practice of shaving the top of the head as a sign of religious devotion; William is criticizing monks who let their hair grow long against regulations</note>. **Philosopher:** Woe to a divinity that is made of wood and not of reality! For the Gospel says otherwise: **By their fruits you shall know them,** <note>original: "a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos"; Matthew 7:16</note> not by their clothes, nor by their shortened hair. Oh, what a hollow religion that a single tonsure and a single razor can perfect! Indeed, as long as they can go without these things, they can claim to be religious; yet this is only because the multitude of the leadership deserves to have its highest secrets hidden. Such a hypocrite is seen as a monster.

**Disciple:** Let these things be. But now the sun is rising; it is necessary to proceed with our begun task. And since you have discussed the remaining matters of the Church—which pertain to the merit of your stewardship—it is now necessary to speak of sublime things.
<margin>What wind is.</margin>
Tell me of those things which differ in the air.

**Philosopher:** In the air, there are certain aerial things like the origin of winds; certain watery things like clouds, rain, snow, hail, and the rainbow; and certain fiery things like flashes, lightning bolts, <term>coruscations</term> <note>sudden flashes of light or heat without thunder</note>, various forms of fire, and comets. I shall discuss these in order. Wind is a current of air, standing or flowing, generated by some cause of movement in the air.

**Disciple:** Why is it that these aerial movements are generated more in one time than in another?
<margin>The opinion of Democritus.</margin>

**Philosopher:** Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 460–370 BCE) famous for his atomic theory</note> says that air is something emanating from the evaporation of water and earth. This happens when minute bodies <note>atoms</note> are gathered in a narrow part of the air, and when one collides into another, they are moved by the blow into the wider expanse of the air, pushing others out of the way. This is proven by the breadth of the wind; when few particles are in the path, they move slowly, but when a crowd of them rushes into a narrow space, the rush of some against others occurs. This is why on a cloudy or foggy day, the wind is less; for when many bodies are gathered into one, there is a thickness and darkness. Indeed, no time is more lacking in wind than a foggy one. There is also a view that winds are created from the reflections of the ocean or the enclosure of the tides, about which the laws of nature differ.

<margin>Another opinion.</margin>
Another view is that vapor evaporates from the earth, or that which is generated from the earth and water is raised up. These vapors, by their own motion, wish to descend from the heights, or they ascend with force, or they move in a circuit. From this fluctuation of the air, it is moved and seethes in some parts; this is the cause of winds. Also, because the earth is cavernous and its pores are not dry, a great weight of air enters the caverns of the earth and struggles to escape; from this fluctuation of moved air, wind is generated.

<margin>A third opinion.</margin>
This is why Aeolia <note>The mythical home of the winds in Greek mythology</note> is said to be a cavernous region of winds. From a third source, wind is sometimes generated from the clouds.

<margin>The truer opinion.</margin>

**Disciple:** What are these "subterranean clouds"?

**Philosopher:** Water is diffused through the cataracts of the earth where it stands; there, the subterranean air is stirred. From the friction of the water, the air...

**D.** I delight to hear the reasoning of these things from you.
**P.** Winds of this kind are especially created from marshy places. Then it fills the valleys, and the rays of the sun move and drive it.

<margin>On certain winds proper to specific regions.</margin>
**Regarding** all winds, it is sufficient in these places to explain them according to their regions. A "scorched" region is one that has a pure breeze. Wind is air flowing in some part; hence it is seen that every wind is hot and humid, although the North Wind <note>original: "boreal"</note> is called cold and dry.

<margin>On the qualities of the winds.</margin>
For the nature of the earth is such that it is hot or humid. Wherever the heat of the earth moves, wind is born. There is a region that is hot and humid, from which hot and humid winds are born. The Western region is dry, from which cold and dry winds are born. Two bodies of the earth, the dry and the humid, give birth to winds. Philosophers say that the South Wind <note>original: "austru~"</note> is hot and humid, and the North Wind <note>original: "borea~"</note> is cold and dry. The South Wind is in a humid region, yet because it comes to us through the middle of the Torrid Zone <note>the belt of the earth between the Tropics, then thought to be uninhabitably hot</note>, it reaches us with intensified heat, driving away clouds to that corner of the earth where it produces rain; thus it indicates humidity. But the North Wind, though in

its origin it may be humid, it is perceived by us as driving away clouds. Whence it is called "dry" by its effect. **If** it is affirmed that a wind is humid, why is it that every wind dries the rain-water that is on the surface of the earth, or dries trees? **For** a wind that is humid, like the South Wind, is also hot; heat works with dryness. A wind that is cold is also dry. Thus it either moves or dries the matter which was in that place. For bodies that are loose <note>original: "sola", likely *soluta*</note> are resolved or changed from one form to another. <margin>On the whirlwind.</margin>
but regarding the whirlwind <note>original: "tūine", for *turbine*</note>, it is so called because of the multitude of waves, for a great and powerful disturbance is made. When the waves find no hindrance, they are turned back upon themselves. This conflict of water and air creates a "whirling" effect, which swallows things into itself. These winds, when they meet no obstacle, follow their own outflow. Just as a sound is repeated when it rolls back upon itself, a similar image is made by the water. This whirlwind is a circular revolution of the air in a place of disturbance, which by this conflict revolves and generates an "inflaming" force <note>referring to the friction-based heat or lightning often associated with storms</note>.

The causes of rains are therefore diverse. For sometimes a thicker exhalation of earth and water evaporates upwards. It is noted that some believe the sun attracts its moisture to the cloud, so that what is liquid there is transformed into the fire of the cloud; this, whatever it is, falls downward.

## On the Heavenly Arch

<margin>
On the heavenly arch
</margin>

Regarding how the multicolored arch <note>the rainbow</note> appears: they say it is like a crystal in which all these colors appear. The first opinion was of those who said that some colors exist in reality, while others are not real but are created in the image of the sun in different colors; and they do not exist except by opposition and position. 

<margin>
The First Opinion.
</margin>

This, which through much quality changes the air, is made subtle and clear in that form to us... <note>The text here discusses technical optical qualities like "ochre" and "bright forms"</note> for it is naturally dark. They later say it exists in this way: in the rain, all the droplets are in themselves both dark and bright. That which shines from the opposition of the sun—because they are distant from the sun—appears there. Of these things which appear from the body in the likeness of an arch: the more splendid the droplet shines out of the dark and black, the more it takes a middle color from the twin mixture of these, just as the sun takes color in the mixing and lessening of light.

<margin>
The Second Opinion.
</margin>

They say it is the image of the sun; and just as every image of the sun is, so it is the image of the sun... in which a round figure appears. And although it is an image, it has colors just as on earth in its whole likeness. Just as by the density of the cloud in which the image of the sun appears to the sight, the image appears in various colors.

<margin>
The Third Opinion.
</margin>

Just as they say it is nothing other than our cloud, partly dark and partly very bright. From the four elements come the four principal colors: from fire, red; from air, purple; from water, blue-grey <note>original: "glaucum"</note>; and from earth, the green of grass and trees <note>original: "herbam et arbor"</note> that you see.

To signify the arch.
</margin>

Moreover, the arch is bound differently in different places. From the south, it signifies a great way... <note>likely referring to a weather pattern or a "path" of storms</note>. If it has risen from the sunrise, calm <note>original: "lena"; likely "serenitas" or "lenitas"</note> is promised. For in summer at noon, the sun is very hot and consumes the clouds; it destroys its own image and splits it apart. But in the autumn time, when it flourishes and the setting sun is not as hot...

<margin>¶ Why the rainbow is not made in the polar regions.</margin>
The philosophers say <note>original: "p. deim"; likely a contraction for "philosophi dicunt"</note> that the rainbow is not accustomed to appear except to the sight of those for whom the clouds are positioned when the day is clear, or when a cloud is oblique to the sun. Therefore, whatever can be said elsewhere, it is most certain that in the winter days there are other clouds that can be brought to the sight. However, in the summer times, it happens above the clouds <note>original: "super itice niri"; likely "super vertice nubis" referring to the top of the cloud</note>. Therefore, at midday, the sight of the vineyard <note>original: "vinea"; possibly a corruption of "linea" or "vision"</note> is most excellent. This is useful for clouds at that time... <unclear>occinni</unclear>. If, however, it is another thing, so many images appear in the cloud of the sun's power. For there is one sun which never fails to rule the world in this image we see. The sun is far higher than the clouds and, because it is brighter, it casts a shadow. In that image, it impresses its light. Note that the closer the sun is to its rising or setting, the larger the rainbow appears.

<margin>¶ On the circle around the moon.</margin>
When the moon is at its most splendid, it is seen that, not rarely, she makes a second rainbow; though the night air is darker, it is no less splendid with rays. Then a circle is formed which is perfectly round, like a green <note>original: "viridam"</note> or colorful thing included within itself. This is seen then... <unclear>caget range</unclear>. This image is formed far from the center. But the sight is deceived by its own weakness around the moon and thinks it to be the thing itself, because it does not bend in the middle. These forms are made from thick bodies like the sun; in subtler things they do not have the same cornered shape, which is the rainbow. It is most clearly formed before a fall <note>of rain</note>.

<margin>¶ What is said concerning the signs <gloss>of the air</gloss>.</margin>
The sky is a thick thing. If this circle happens to fall equally, it lightly vanishes, which indicates the tranquility of the air. If it remains in one part as if there were rocks, then it truly indicates a splitting. If rocks <note>metaphorical for thick cloud formations</note> occur in many places, it signifies a suddenness of ships at sea. These circles appear at night around the moon and the stars. For this reason, it is rare. The sun makes the light of the air warm, and from it alone is the heat. The moon's power is weak. Therefore, its composition is more easily dissolved. Similarly, the stars themselves cannot break through the air with their own light. Therefore, their image is received in a more solid matter and is revealed in the same way. Moreover, the air is so thick that it excludes, rather than removes from itself, that humble light, not coming as strongly as the sun's. Thus, it offers a shadow to the coming rays. This happens at night when the air is gathered together and the stars shine, and it becomes thicker than when the sun is present. However, this does not happen at night except very rarely, because the moon does not have such strength and does not shine in the clouds so as to pour heat into them. For they receive the sun's light more excellently. But they are hindered from seeing the multi-colored form of the rainbow, because some parts in the clouds are brighter, others are softer, and some are more clear where they are illuminated by the sun. Others are weaker where they are excluded. This inequality of light and shadow is mixed together and that wonderful appearance of the rainbow is folded back. And it happens that halos <note>original: "coronal"</note> and rainbows are made unstable by the proximity of wind. For these things, which are like the air, are fixed in some form but not by what flows. They are not made where things resist, nor are they formed where the image is quickly dissipated. This can be understood by throwing a stone into a pond <note>original: "lagno"; likely "stagno"</note> and seeing the circles made in the water; there the shapes of the paths are formed.

<margin>On the rod.</margin>
They are seen to be similar in color, but they differ in shape and location. Just as the shape of the rainbow is held opposite to the sun, the rod <note>term: <term>virga</term> (an atmospheric phenomenon where a streak of light or "sun-dog" appears)</note> lies in that way and has the same colors. If the cloud is moist and is stretched so thin, the halo <note>original: "corona"</note> is around the light. The rod or the rainbow is in the opposite position. The halo is the circle of the rainbow.

These will be either "rods" <note>virgae: vertical streaks of light or "light pillars" often seen near the sun or moon</note>, or solar and lunar crowns <note>halos</note> which are accustomed to arise.

<margin>Just as by logic many suns or moons appear according to their appearance.</margin>
**I**n history books, it is read that many suns have appeared, and many moons as well. For it is only then that the year is deceptive, due to the doubling of the sun. It is not truly that the sun or moon is seen in each individual image, but just as one is seen in many mirrors. For in some figures the sun is seen, and in others the moon. <margin>On hail and snow.</margin>
**¶** Therefore, enough has been said concerning clouds, the rainbow, the "rod," and the crown; see, we shall now speak of hail and snow. **¶** When faint moisture is raised into the highest regions of the winds and dryness, the water drops are frozen by their own coldness into a stony hardness. This is clear because water, through its round shape, strikes less [forcefully], and because the hail becomes round through the constant falling of the water's weight. These would be like stony drops and snow if they were thickened and frozen.

<margin>In summer there are no snows.</margin>
**D**espite hail being produced at the end of spring and in summer, snows do not occur at those same times. **¶** In summer, humidity is raised higher by the heat of the sun. And while it is raised, because it is in a greater volume and higher up, it is frozen and produces hail. In winter, however, because of the coldness of the earth and the small amount of water, snow is found before it can be raised to the very highest points due to the coldness of the earth.

<margin>In the lower parts of the air there is greater cold than in the higher parts.</margin>
**D**uring times when there is heat in the lower parts of the air, there is cold and vigor in the interior parts of the air, because the coldness of much water and earth does not touch them in summer. **¶** I say, however, that snow and hail reach the mountains and are reflected by the heat of the sun before they reach the summit, since they descend through colder places. This is seen in the water that is in them because of its irregularity, for while it is solid, it can stand by the strength of treading <note>The author refers to the way snow packs down under pressure</note>.

<margin>Why snow is on the mountains and not in the valleys.</margin>
**E**t because in the rivers and first in the mountains, the cold of the sun and the earth is reflected in the mountains, while the heat is in the valley, it results in snow. **¶** There is a double vapor from the water. Since fire does not ascend into itself in this world, the thinner <note>original: "resperis"; likely meaning dispersed or thin air</note> the air is, the colder it is; and the colder it is, the thicker it is. The sun's rays touch the valleys and the earth's motion, and the reflection of the rays recoils upon itself with mixed rebounds, from which a doubled heat is made. Thus, all evaporation, however it originates in a dangerous <note>The author may mean a "constricted" or "intense" place</note> place, is so much hotter. Regarding these vapors, the thicker the air is, the hotter it is, because the power of heat is removed from it <note>The author is describing the medieval concept of "antiperistasis," where heat is concentrated by surrounding cold</note>.

**D**e Regarding hail and snow, I will not say more, since I shall now explain about the fires that are produced from the air. **¶** From here, I will speak briefly; namely, I will recount various points about lightning, just as I will explain about thunder and the flash of lightning that precedes the sight.

<margin>On thunder, flashing, brightness, and lightning.</margin>
In the highest part, since the moisture ascends to the upper parts from the lower by the wind, and reaches the lower parts through the air, it gathers the motion of the air from the pushing of the moisture. The striking together of waves from the divided parts generates fire and makes thunder. From this motion, the air grows hot, becoming a fiery cause in itself: namely, brightness <note>original: "fulgore"</note> and flashing <note>original: "coruscatione"</note>. This fire reaches us more quickly because sight is faster than hearing. This can be seen in common work: look from a distance at a fuller or some woman washing clothes; you will see the stroke raised before you hear the sound. Therefore, when it is created in the upper part for the sake of the eye and appearance, if it happens above, it is brightness or lightning. If, however, it falls downward...

For it is a fact that they reach as far as an obstacle, unless it is a lightning bolt. When it reaches an obstacle, it cleaves through the things standing in its way; but because of the manner of its descent, it appears to move upward, though it retains no truth in the crossing <note>The author is likely describing the visual illusion where a lightning strike seems to move from the ground up, even though the "truth" of the phenomenon is a descent</note>. Just as on the ground, it gathers fire. If, however, it is of this kind of air, then it establishes this air with that impetus so that it neither— <margin>Here I note what lightning is, what thunder is, [and] what the dance <note>original: "chorea"; likely referring to flickering or jumping lights in the sky</note> is.</margin> by this fact that the lightning cleaves, it does not burn. Therefore, lightning is caused by the collision of air, sometimes coming with impetus as far as an obstacle. Thunder is the small sound of air rushing against itself with impetus. Heat, indeed, is sharp, and from the impetus it shines forth ignited. This lightning is therefore stony, as some assert <note>A reference to the "thunderstone" (lapis ceraunius), a common medieval belief that lightning bolts were physical stones that fell from the sky</note>. But since it is a certain light, lightning is a stony substance, and it is not through ignorance that I might see that those things have occupied India <note>The mention of India may refer to the source of precious stones or specific meteorological legends</note>; we shall briefly set it down after it has fallen. From this it takes its cause when its light ascends to the earth. And indeed, it is raised toward the wind thereafter, because the stony substance is thickened by the heat of the sun. <margin>Response: Not every origin [is of] lightning and thunder.</margin> And it is gathered in the clouds; it generates a cloud in its home and is enclosed by chance, from which the stone descends with impetus. Another [theory] distinguishes this: that lightning and thunder might ascend at every time of year, since not every origin is of lightning and thunder. How? Namely, as this smoke is ascending, such was its nature until it reached the highest part of the air. Wherefore, just as the sea through seven years... when the sea is moved by the smoke then ascending from the bottom. In its thickness <gloss>from which</gloss> no one is filled by this; gathered at the <margin>Toward evening it begins to go out from the bottom.</margin> summit, that force drives it here and there. Hence come storms, since a storm begins from the bottom of the sea. And this is done in various ways, because through this, heat is seen, and we see water in the air before a storm. Rain is also seen. Hence it is said at night: the smokes from afar will have been gathered from the depths and they ascend all around. Seeing this, the sailor grows terrified, etc. That is placed at the first storm. It appears already beginning in the depths of the sea, just as flocks lie down. While also the internal smokes are thrown against another; through their own thickness they will push against this and that, and they reach the upper regions. Then, however, from their own readiness, they move there. Hence also come thunder and lightning. In winter, however, it is rarer, because the air is thick and there is not such great heat that it might raise the thick smoke upward to the summit. It remains therefore in the lowest parts; it generates the winds and rains of the air. In summer indeed, when the sea is boiling, it is raised to the summit; thus there is a long tossing of a small amount of air, from which it generates lightning and thunder. In autumn, however, it is sometimes similar to <margin>A certain opinion on thunder. The opinion of others.</margin> winter, since it raises it, yet there is no heat to allow it to be raised. But when the clouds lie heavy, it falls, whence the crash of thunder is generated. Most, however, say it is an impetus that descends from the upper regions, which is lightning. Others say a thin spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; meaning a gas, breath, or pressurized vapor</note> enclosed in a hollowed cloud immediately wishes to scatter through the clouds; it claps <note>original: "plodit"; related to "explodit," to clap or strike</note> the clouds against one another like <gloss>and so forth</gloss>. Just as water which is in enclosed places breaks out with impetus, so it descends to the lower regions and strikes an obstacle. This is lightning. While therefore the clouds thus release the spirit, the sound forces out and renders a groan and a lowing sound. This is thunder where the cloud is thickest. Hence it is that the cloud dashes against itself and claps, and a sound is made.

<margin>The opinion of Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle sharply asserts that what is produced is of a similar nature to both the grammate <note>likely referring to "grammata" or lines of fire</note> and the lightning, which are distinguished by their intensity. If not previously existing, the exhalations are divided into parts as they evaporate: some are dry, and some are moist; but the dry exhalations, through the movement and the striking of the sun's rays, conceive fire. If this fire is thin and spreads out until it descends through the air, it is called a **lightning-flash** <note>original: "fulgatio"</note>. If, however, it is thickened 
<margin>The difference between a lightning-flash and a lightning-bolt.</margin>
and reaches down to the earth, it is a **lightning-bolt** <note>original: "fulmen"</note>. Therefore, the lightning-flash and the lightning-bolt are the same in their nature, but they differ in their impact. For while the lightning-flash is more diffuse as it reaches toward the earth, the lightning-bolt is a contraction reaching into the aforementioned place. Thus, a lightning-flash is almost a lightning-bolt, and 
<margin>Still another opinion.</margin>
a lightning-bolt is something more than a lightning-flash. Others say: that the path of heat lasts for a long time. When, therefore, watery clouds ascend to the shores of the earth, two kinds—namely fire and water—meet. Whence a very great movement and sound is generated. If a piece of fire falls into the water, a very great tumult is produced, just as it is thought that if a fire should touch a watery cloud, a sound is generated by the strike of the fire in the manner mentioned before. In the air it is a lightning-flash; on the earth it is a lightning-bolt. Here, therefore, are two very light and highest types of comets: the flash and the bolt, which, although they may be seen, 
<margin>On the wondrous effect of lightning bolts.</margin>
do no damage. The effect of the lightning-bolt is a hidden thing that is placed upon us; but it is feared because of its power in some things. For among those things worthy of being found is that which the lightning-bolt does in various places: it leaves the scabbard unharmed while melting the sword within. It causes the iron of a cask to drip while the wood remains intact. It causes wine to stand firm in a dry vessel because that vigor of the blow provides a sudden cold that hardens it, and many other things. 

V. It seems, however, that the stars flow toward the lower parts, 
<margin>It seems, however, that stars are seen to fall.</margin>
and I desire to hear the reason from you. 
P. It is clearly taught that a star does not fall from heaven. Since they are fiery, it is not possible for the starry place or the celestial tracks to fall to the earth; for if any of them were to fall, being so large, it would occupy the whole earth or a great part of it. 
As **Seneca** says: It is a most foolish thing to estimate either that the stars fall or that they leap out of their tracks, or that anything is taken or scraped away from them. For if that were so, the finished sciences would be destroyed for us. Those stars, however, which do not seem many nor long-lasting, are led away; but before they are accustomed to be found in their places, their magnitude is shown through their light. 
D. Since Seneca himself was convinced of this, tell me of the light which seems to fly across the sky. 
P. But that is prepared from the fire of the air. For either that fire falls in the air by the reason that it flashes, or because of the clouds of the mountains colliding and striking it, or from those exhalations which, being suitable for catching fire, are struck by movement and then fall; or having been breathed upon, they catch fire, but since they lack a foundation, they quickly fall and are extinguished. 
<margin>Why the fires flying at night are not seen by day.</margin>
D. Why are these fires not seen during the day? 
P. They exist, but they do not appear during the day because of the sun's brightness. If, however, such a great flash or burst of light should pour out its brilliance on a cloudy day, they might appear. We read in histories of "daylight torches" appearing, some moving from east to west, others from the setting to the rising sun. Sailors think these fires are signs of storms when they are seen flying in different directions. If, however, they come from one side, the wind will come from that direction. Because these fires are visible in the air, they are signs 
<margin>Whence these fiery places appear by divine providence.</margin>
of the winds in the air, for their vigor depends on the air. Concerning these fires, the common people wonder at the many images generated in them, and that stars appear to leap in diameters. Also, that when they appear as twins, they are called **Castor and Pollux** <note>A reference to St. Elmo's Fire, which sailors historically associated with the Gemini twins; two lights were seen as a good omen, one as a bad omen</note> and are said to be of better hope to help against shipwrecks, and from these, the winds are predicted. Otherwise, these fires are seen in the air as an increase of light.

<margin>That the aforementioned fires appear in various forms.</margin>
On the spears of soldiers, lights appear like candles, which are often seen in the clouds on both sides. In this manner, history records that when Gylippus <note>A Spartan general; this refers to an account in Seneca’s *Naturales Quaestiones*</note> was receiving money, a star was seen staying upon his spear. In the camps of the Romans, spears were seen to burn. These fires flow down and settle upon trees and branches, and they cling to the trunks. Whence arises the error of the common folk, who believe they have seen the "candles of the dead" <note>A folk belief regarding *ignis fatuus* or "will-o'-the-wisps" as spirits of the deceased</note> being struck out of the clouds. Sometimes they appear when the air is clear, if the air is suited to expressing these fires; but sometimes they are seen in lower regions. This heat is in the lower parts, and it is a wonder that these fires fly toward us when the air is clear. Sometimes the air is thinned. These fires differ in various quantity, figure, and color. If the matter <note>original: "materia"</note> that is ignited is large, the fire appears large. Sometimes, because of the brightness of this fire, the sky never truly <note>original: "nunquam vero"</note> appears to burn; sometimes a middle part appears, sometimes a smaller part, and sometimes the smallest. Certain figures are seen according to how the fire is disposed in the air. Sometimes it is like a crown, sometimes like a great sun. Sometimes it is like a hollow cave <note>original: "spelunce"</note> dug out in a circle. Sometimes it is of an oblong and round magnitude of fire, similar to a jar <note>original: "dolio"; the Latin *dolium* refers to the *pithos* or "jar" shape of atmospheric phenomena</note> staying in one place; and then it is called a **pithos** <note>original: "phron", likely a corruption of the Greek *pithos*</note>. Sometimes it appears in the form of a shield <note>original: "clipei"</note>, and is shown to the eyes of men. These fires appear with the magnitude of the moon, and shortly thereafter they portend a full war. Sometimes they appear in the form of beams <note>original: "trabes"</note>, or in other forms this fire appears. Their heat and the sharpness of the fire are divided. In truth, as the matter itself is ignited, the light in the middle of the fire is great, and because of the diverse matter in which it is ignited, the heat varies. Because of this, if it ascends into the celestial regions, the fire then descends from there.

<margin>Why this fire descends.</margin>
This fire falls for two reasons: namely, the pressure of the air and following its own matter. The fire, having been ignited at the summit, follows its matter by descending.

<margin>Concerning comets. A certain opinion.</margin>
Concerning comets, I wish to discuss whether those fires are stars or whether they are established as something else. Indeed, the opinions of the ancients regarding these things are discordant. For it pleased some philosophers to say that a comet is a gathering of planets that have applied themselves to one another. The space between them is illustrated by the solar rays, and they are reputed to be a single star by those watching. To confirm this, they say that a comet appeared in the time of Esson <note>Possibly a corruption of a historical name like Aristoteles or a specific ruler</note> which, under the gaze of the people, was seen to have descended into individual stars. This is not impossible; for it is nothing if not the positions of the planets. Astrologers call these positions "stations," which occur in the upper hemisphere. But if a comet were merely a conjunction of planets, it should appear to all people; therefore, it is not merely a conjunction, nor does it arise solely from that. If it were from a conjunction, they would arise very frequently. If they were seen, they would soon be dissolved, just as stars coming together are separated, which can be seen after an eclipse. But if this were so, the planets would not exceed the zodiac, and comets would appear only in the zodiac; however, they frequently appear outside of it. They say that in the time of Esson a comet divided into two stars, but no one living has seen this, and it is difficult to find any witness who saw a comet dissolve and exceed the known stars.

<margin>The opinion of others. The difference between a beam and a comet.</margin>
Others say that every comet is an aerial fire from the same formation as those called "beams" <note>original: "trabes"</note>. These are divided in the clouds; for beams descend from the higher to the lower parts, but a comet ascends from the lower to the higher. However, it is not a general rule; for comets last up to a year. Therefore, a certain type is called a comet. Furthermore, comets frequently appear in the northern region, because the air there...
