<margin>Why comets appear so rarely, and why they last so long.</margin>

In this light, because the fire is produced from a cause outside of itself, it is consumed more quickly when it finds suitable matter for catching fire. Why then does it appear so rarely? It is because it exists in the same hemisphere in which the sun is located, and because of the sun's brightness, it is not seen; it is rarely seen at night. Therefore, there are those who say it is rare because such a cause is rarely orchestrated in time. And as to why that fire lasts so long: by what reason does the fire draw nourishment to itself so that it does not cease? It remains in the same place for a long time, as has been seen in the times of Nero <note>original: "nerol"</note> and during the royal droughts. Whence one might ask if comets are forbidden to represent "woodenness" <note>likely referring to the density or fuel-like nature of the material</note> since they are prepared there. But it is difficult, most illustrious ones, to say whether they are fused from the air...

<margin>Concerning the ocean and other waters.</margin>

...or made from water. These things suffice for now, as we remember in the first cause that the earth was entirely covered with water. But the thinner part of it was dried out by the heat of the celestial bodies, especially by the power of the source of water being opposite to the source of heat—that is, the sun. Let us take this from divine wisdom: nothing is more pleasing to the union than the moist and the dry. The earth was not so dry as to be completely unified, but because the sun did not heat the earth equally, we place it in the middle. But because of the external heat, it was not unified in the middle of that same earth, but was placed under the heat of the moisture. 

Because of these two things, the earth is tempered here and there. Thus the sun makes the "Torrid Zone" <note>original: "torrida zone"; the region between the Tropics</note> in the middle, surrounding the earth at the celestial equator <note>original: "equinoccial' celi"</note>, which is so named by the ancients because it reaches the very peak of heat. By the necessity of what was said before, it must be called the sea.

<margin>Concerning the ebbs and flows of the ocean.</margin>

This sea flows toward the west, and there occur two "reflections" <note>original: "reflexiones"; referring to tides</note> upon the face of the earth, one toward the south and another toward the north. Similarly, it seems there are two reflections toward the west and the east. When that western reflection occurs, it is driven toward the north, and by that repulsion, it is held back; hence arises that famous "access and recess" <note>original: "accessio r recessio"; the high and low tides</note> of the ocean. Similarly, there are two others at the other end of the earth in the west. Some say that there are mountains under the sea that are the cause of the ocean's tides. And the sea reaches all the way to them and recedes. Others say this is different: that before they are explained, they live...

As we have said, the aforementioned western reflux joins at the seventh zone and at Mount Atlas <note>original: "achalantē mōtē"</note>, or it is called "Achalatum" in the Adriatic Sea. Below this lies England <note>original: "anglia"</note> and the sea shines <note>possibly "Mare Mortuum" or a specific coastal reference</note>, and through the eastern reflux it joins at the seventh zone. The Indian Sea and the Caspian Sea are born there. There are also other refluxes joining towards the south, from which divided seas are born. However, these should not be described here because they come to us from unknown places across many intervening locations. We must now discuss how the winds are born from these refluxes of the ocean. Since two refluxes, as I said before, are in the west—one at the seventh zone and the other at the source of all moisture—and one is divided toward the south...

<margin>Why winds are born from the refluxes of the ocean.</margin>
<gloss>in that part of the vast earth</gloss>
Through the separation of such a vast amount of water, the air is moved. Then it is pushed forward until it reaches us. Thus a wind is generated, which is called **Zephyr** <note>the West wind</note>. Two other refluxes divide toward the east; by their motion, they generate the wind named **Eurus** <note>the East wind</note>. When the western zone and the seventh zone join together in the west, the air is moved by that repulsion. That wind is the "Seven-Zonal" wind, which is called **Boreas** <note>the North wind</note>. Because it is born within the cold zone, it is rightly called cold. Just as it drives clouds from the corner of the earth toward the center, it is therefore rainy in the Torrid Zone <note>the tropics</note>; but where we are, it brings little or no rain. When it is in the Torrid Zone, it is hot; but when it comes from the cold zone, it is cold. Similarly, when the two refluxes join in the south, the wind called **Auster** <note>the South wind</note> is generated. In the Torrid Zone, it is cold <note>the author's theory of displacement</note>, but among us it is the "North wind's" opposite; because it is born near the Torrid Zone, it arrives to us heated and warm. It drives the clouds toward this corner of the earth where we live, and thus generates rain. It is therefore accidentally warm and moist, though in its origin it is cold and dry.

If, in the two refluxes joining at the seventh zone that generate Boreas, the motion of the western ocean is faster than usual, a collateral wind is born between Boreas and Zephyr. If the western and eastern oceans move beyond their normal measure, collateral winds are born between Boreas and Eurus. These are...

<meta>Continuity with previous page: Following the discussion of the four major ocean currents and the map of the world, the text now explains how the interaction of these tides creates secondary winds and addresses the scientific mystery of why the sea is salty while its source waters can be sweet.</meta>

Two other ebb-tides, meeting each other in the middle from here and there, give birth to two side-winds <note>original: "collatale ventos"</note>. One arises from the **East-South wind** <note>original: "eura i austrū" (Eurus and Auster)</note>, and the other from the **South and West wind** <note>original: "zephirū" (Zephyrus)</note>. Just as the eye tracking a figure will find through its labor a similar result, they produce this effect. In the middle, where the ebb-tide itself occurs, it meets the primary winds, while outside the cardinal points, these side-winds reach out. Just as one might show more than two on a single diagram, the same should be understood for the others. These principal tides generate the winds; they are divided and then meet, witnessing the daily flow of the sea which generates winds every day.
<margin>Thus, conveniently, the tides occur just as the daily winds do.</margin>

<margin>Why the sea is salty.</margin>
If these winds are generated daily, why is it that their cause is sometimes so rarefied <note>original: "rarasẽ"</note> by the time they reach us? It is often because when we have one wind, there is another blowing in different regions. This matter is demonstrated both through illusions and through reasoned principles. Regarding the actual flavor of the wind, it is tasteless <note>original: "insipidum"</note>, just like the water it contains. Therefore, since the wind is tasteless, why is the sea from which it originates salty? Because when the sea is mixed and composed of heat, it becomes thickened and salty. It is certain that water is turned into salt through the intensity of heat. Just as the sun draws wind directly from the water, the testimony of **Solomon** confirms this when he says: *Unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return, to flow again* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:7. This was a standard medieval explanation for the hydrologic cycle.</note>.
<margin>How some waters are sweet even though they are salty at their origin.</margin>
This must be explained: the waters return to the sea just as they were enclosed. How then, from the same beginning, are some sweet and some salty? In this life, other waters are distinguished; there were common waters that are called "waters of bitterness" <note>original: "amarrudī" - likely a reference to the bitter waters of Marah in the Book of Exodus</note>.

<image-desc>A circular diagram positioned in the right margin area. It consists of a large circle with a serrated or toothed outer edge. A horizontal line, also serrated, bisects the circle. Inside the center of the large circle is a smaller, simple circle drawn in red ink.</image-desc>

The origin is salty and bitter because the sea itself is salty and bitter. But because the earth is full of caverns <note>original: "cauinosa"</note>, the water slips through the earth into the sea. As it flows through <term>cataractas: underground channels or filters within the earth's crust</term>, it is filtered, thinned, and takes on the quality of the earth it passes through. If it flows through stony and sandy earth, it acquires a sweet flavor; if through salt beds, it becomes salty. If it flows through muddy earth, the water is vapid. If it flows through sulfurous stones or lime, it becomes bitter. Thus, according to the diverse nature of the earth, the water receives a diverse flavor. If the water descends through these underground channels but the path is blocked by the thickness of the earth, it cannot proceed further and instead breaks out, making the earth "boil up" <note>original: "ebullir̄"</note>. This is why water bubbles up in certain places; the quality of the water is determined by these channels, which is a great proof that the earth's composition produces the flavors of the waters.

<margin>Concerning Wells.</margin>
Regarding the water in **wells**: they have their beginning from these same underground channels <note>original: "cataractal"</note>, and they have a pure beginning because the water flows there in abundance. Just as these channels provide a source, so the well generates a channel within itself that flows here and there. This is why the water in a well boils upward. There are some wells that do not have these earthen channels but are simply dug into a hollow, yet they do not lack water. For in such a place, they have another type of moisture which falls into the well drop by drop, like the sweat of men <note>a medieval metaphor for seepage or condensation</note>. In those wells, since they are not fed by the channels, the water will be stagnant, appearing like river water but purer. Often, one well is created near another, and the second takes the water away from the first...

<meta>Continuity with previous page: Having discussed why the sea is salty due to the sun's heat, the text now turns to the behavior of subterranean waters—wells and springs—and how the interaction of heat and cold within the earth leads to seasonal temperature changes and, on a larger scale, the Great Flood.</meta>

Well water in winter may appear to "sweat" <unclear>flow</unclear> because the porous earth, which is filled with cracks internally, receives the well water from all sides. ¶ Regarding the cause of water being warm in the earth [in winter] and cold in summer: this occurs because of the state of the earth, whereby well water is inversely warm in winter and cold in summer. ¶ First, it should be known that in the winter season, the pores of the earth are tightly closed; hence the moisture and heat <note>This refers to the medieval scientific theory of antiperistasis, where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite.</note> that remain inside warm the water. In summer, however, the pores of the earth open wide, the surface evaporates, and the heat is diminished. For everything rejoices in its own similar quality and flees its opposite. In winter, since the surface of the earth or the air is cold, the heat increases in the interior of the earth, hiding itself as it flees its opposite; thus well water is made warm. In summer, the heat of the sun affects the earth, and the cold retreats to the interior to find refuge; thus well water in summer is very cold. However, the water of rivers and rain, which is much more exposed, behaves differently. Therefore, river water is more subject to the rains, and water that comes from the force of the winds is received back into the earth.

<margin>
On the Flood and the final retribution.
</margin>
The "floodgates" <note>original: "cataractae," a reference to Genesis 7:11</note> in the lower depths are thick with salt, forming what are called the "seas." Now we must discuss the <gloss>diluvio</gloss> Flood, its cause, and the arrival of the <term>conflagration</term> <note>original: "exustione," the periodic destruction of the world by fire, contrasted here with the flood.</note>. First, water is drawn from the lower pores by celestial heat <gloss>as if</gloss> by a gradual drawing out of moisture. This heat thins the water until it reaches such a quantity of moisture that it pours back over the land and submerges it. When the earth is saturated by this heat and moisture, it gradually thins and expands until those depths are overwhelmed. We see this in small ways when moisture is dried up in summer and extinguished in winter; thus we can envision the great conflagration. ¶ If the water and heat were balanced, no flood would occur; but because the heat is sometimes greater, it consumes the moisture until it turns to vapor. Then, in the following winter, from the great cold, it turns back into water. This moisture, accumulating over many years, continues until a <term>cataclysm</term> <note>original: "cataclis̃m̃," a universal deluge.</note> occurs. If the winter season is very cold and humid for a long time, a great flood follows. When great floods flow into the hollows of the earth, the time comes for them to be restored to the surface as vapors, creating a deluge. When the water on the surface transfers itself to the interior, it resists the exterior heat. But when the time comes that the planets, through their rising and falling, cause these changes: if all the planets are elevated and far from the earth, the moisture is consumed. But when the water passes through the earth and spreads, a flood results. If two or three planets are elevated, the moisture is diminished by that same amount. If they are all depressed, their proximity to the earth causes a burning <note>original: "adustio"</note>. If two are depressed, they cause an effect according to their distance. Thus a general flood occurs when the planets align. There are two general types of destruction, but many particular ones.

<margin>
By what reasoning the ocean rises and falls.
</margin>
These inundations are witnessed in the ebb and flow of the tides. Within a period of days, following the lunar cycle, the waves of the ocean decrease. In some seven-day periods they rise, and in the third week they decrease, and in the fourth they decrease further. If one understands this universal movement, they have the means to grasp these great events. ¶ For the valley is closed...

It is seen that two things occur at once. It is like the occurrence of a half-full pot placed over a fire with no water added <note>The author uses the "pot" (olla) as a scientific model to explain how heat causes displacement and movement in fluids.</note>. It is the same in the ocean. When the sun is generated in light or when its splendor approaches, it is able to thin out what is placed under it as its own, which then draws the spirit <note>original: "spiritum," here likely referring to air or vapor</note> into the moisture of the water. generally, the spirit is moved to flow by its own nature. The tide <note>original: "fluxus"</note> therefore grows until the new moon. In the first week it is cast down. Then in the second it grows with the kindling and is cast down; in the third it kindles and in the fourth it is cast out again, because the radiation which deletes the spirit provides it very lightly, because we, as human bodies, gradually fail.

Those things which are said more forcefully are heard very lightly in the voices and all things are returned <insert>Book 5</insert> even to the middle of memory, not yet firm, nor are the words irrevocable <insert>Proem</insert> coming to Nola <note>Possibly a reference to St. Paulinus of Nola or a specific academic setting.</note>. Never would there be reason in pure water. It is difficult for him if it was shown that he does not understand, yet he prepares to teach others. If one could be universal, not born of humans but of angels in the flesh, I would estimate such a man to be a god or an angel. I promise all these things not to a god but to an angel, as if they would swear by a little grain. <meta>Continuity with previous page: Having discussed the physical influences of the sun and moon on the tides and the atmosphere, the author now transitions to a geographical and cosmological argument regarding the physical shape of the Earth, moving from the properties of elements to geometric proofs of its sphericity.</meta>

First, I shall lead to an end that which I have begun. For it was said that what had been conquered remains in a part of the earth.

As stated above, the earth is an element <note>In the medieval worldview, Earth is one of the four fundamental elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) and occupies the center of the universe.</note> positioned in the middle, and therefore it is at the lowest point in the midst of its entire spherical whole. Because the middle is there, it remains there, since there is no lower place to which it might descend. There is nothing to support it, although some say there are gaps; I shall remain silent on those points. That which is said—that the earth is carried by the air like a ship—is a silent point, but what is said is certainly seen to be true.

The opinion that it occupies the lowest realm is most fit to refute those who disdain a leap in logic. I do not care for the perversions of the stubborn, but let us take up the matter of the earth’s form. <margin>On the shape of the earth.</margin> I ask, then, as much as has been sensed by the learned: did Bezalel <note>original: "bethalel," likely referring to the biblical craftsman Bezalel, often associated in medieval lore with the architecture of the world.</note> play more of a game than he showed by saying the earth was flat? Therefore, they may remove fear from themselves when they do not support this opinion, but I shall move to destroy it through probability. <margin>Proof that the earth is not flat.</margin> If the earth were flat, the water surrounding the world would not be distinct, but would gather in one place. If the earth were flat, a city positioned in the east would have its noon at the same time as the middle of the world. Although this appears to be the case, it would be in its presence. Likewise, a city positioned in the west would have noon in the evening. Thus, if there were cities in the east and the west, they would have the same space of noon. But since noon and evening are seen at different times in the western climate, you may better understand this by the visible figure depicted here, in which I place a line across the flat plane of the earth. On its two heads [ends], I will curve two cities and the sun, and the sun will be depicted over both.

<margin>Proof that the earth is round.</margin>

<image-desc>

Since, therefore, it is established among all men that the space from morning to noon is equal to that from noon to sunset, it appears that the earth is not flat, but round. Hence, among the eastern cities, when it is noon for them, it is sunset for others. This is depicted here by four cities in one circle: one in the east, the other opposite in the south <note>original: "meridienē," though the geometry implies cardinal points around the sphere.</note>. The earth is in the middle, eastern and round, above those three... although the earth is opposite... the eastern city is A, the southern is B, the western is C, and that which is in the middle of the night is D.

When, therefore, the sun rises for the city that is A, it sets for the one opposite it, which is C. It is noon for that which is D, and midnight for that which is B. When the sun rises for that which is B, it sets for D, which is opposite. Then it is noon in A and midnight for that which was in the east. They set in the opposite, which is called A. And in the middle of the day for B, it is midnight in D. To the city which is D, it sets for that which is B, and here it is noon for that which is A; C is at midnight. If the aforementioned places of the earth were not cities, the same movement would be shown most clearly. For between the eastern and western cities, there are places located where the sun rises...

<meta>Continuity with previous page: The author continues the argument for the Earth's sphericity, moving from abstract logic about elements to physical proofs involving the stars and the sun's position, leading into the standard medieval division of the world into five climatic zones as described by the philosopher Macrobius.</meta>

...and let neither of these two things fall into doubt. Therefore, in every single hour, as the sun sets in a certain part of the globe, in another part it is midday and in another it is midnight. All of these occurrences are due to the roundness of the earth. There is also another argument, which is that stars <margin>The prophet Isaiah, since he speaks of the earth <note>This likely refers to Isaiah 40:22: "It is he who sits above the circle of the earth."</note></margin> that appear in one climate <term>climate<note>In ancient and medieval geography, a "clima" (plural climata) refers to a latitudinal band of the earth defined by the length of its longest day.</note></term> do not appear in another. The star Canopus, which is seen by the Egyptians, <margin>That mountains and valleys do not take away from the roundness of the earth.</margin> is not seen by us, which would never happen if the earth were flat. But because the earth is round and globose, despite the great depth of the valleys and the height of the mountains—which some say even exceed the clouds—they still maintain that it is round. Because of the scale of the earth's roundness, these mountains do not make it appear significantly different. Even mountains like Puelle <note>Possibly a corruption of a local name or a specific peak known to the author.</note> and Mount Olympus must be considered as nothing more than a tiny puncture in the total mass of the earth. Just as a ditch that can be crossed in a single step does not impede the rest of the earth's surface, so too would a skilled observer judge a valley or a mountain. If one considers the whole, the depth of the valley or the height of the mountain should not be judged as significant against the earth; thus, valleys and mountains do not take away the roundness of the earth, which must be perfectly round like a sphere.

<margin>That the earth is in a certain way rolling, and in a certain way not rolling; in a certain way mobile, and in a certain way immobile.</margin>
Regarding what we attempted to explain above, we shall be silent on how it is held. If the earth is round, it is not "rolling." Rolling occurs when a thing is not fixed, like a stone in the middle of a sea or in some other unstable place where it never stays still. But it is certain that the earth is immobile <note>The author is defending the Geocentric model, where the Earth stays fixed at the center of the universe while the heavens rotate around it.</note>. "Mobile" can be said in two ways: either as we see the earth here, or as the earth is moved by its own nature; yet the earth remains essentially immobile. Enough has been said here regarding all its immobility.

It is now established, therefore, that the earth is round. By comparison with the heavens, its dimensions are like a mere point. It occurs to me now to explain the sun and its light. First, there is the dry land, even at the center of the earth, which the rays of the sun scorch with perpetual heat. Those two ends, because they are so far from the sun, are constrained by perpetual ice and water. Between the scorched and the frozen lands, there are two regions which, because of their balance between the heat on one side and the cold on the other, are temperate and capable of being inhabited. There are, therefore, five parts or "zones" on the round earth: two frigid and two temperate, which have a certain width and encircle the earth on all sides. These second zones are called "circles" by us. I shall now describe their arrangement.

<margin>These five zones according to Macrobius <note>Macrobius (c. 400 AD) was a Roman provincial whose commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio" was the primary source for medieval knowledge of climate zones.</note> on the earth.</margin>
It is said that there are five zonal laws in the high heavens, which are perhaps attributed to the earth by some. Some assume these five zonal laws exist only in the heavens and deny they exist on earth; but in truth, there are five zones in the sky and five on the earth. The reason is the same for the air, which is here called "heaven." There is an echo here: just as the earth is high in one part where no habitation can exist, so there is habitable land, just as on the moon. Some places are uninhabitable because they are scorched, just as the earth and moon are. Where it is witnessed that certain things are not on earth, it is because the heat there cannot be endured. The reason for the elements is proven by the quality of heat and cold, which lie opposite each other according to the heat of the sky. In the central part of the earth, the inhabitants experience scorched land. Because of the air at the ends of the earth, the waters are frigid due to their distance from the sun. Between these extremes, the parts are temperate. So it is with the parts of the earth placed beneath the sky: just as there are five zones in the heavens, there are five in the air and five on the earth. Two are frigid and uninhabited; two are temperate because they receive heat from the air above; and two frigid zones exist on the earth's ends. The scorched zone is radiated by the sun, while the two temperate ones are located between the extremes.

After(?) the distinction.
</margin>
The former part is the one we occupy. There are, therefore, four habitable areas, but only two are inhabited. 

<margin>
Concerning the four inhabitants, a brief determination when they truly follow philosophical reason.

Some are inhabited, others are not. Whence, some of our people agree on certain things and differ on others. We and the Antipodes alike have summer and winter at the same time, as well as the other seasons of the year, but when we have day, they have night, and vice versa. **If**, however, summer is caused by the proximity of the sun, then winter is its removal from us. From the midpoint of the distance comes autumn. This is a sign where they have equal distance. Wherever the sun is located, summer is found where the sun produces its effect. There is, therefore, a distinction among the inhabitants, though they do not have day and night at the same time. Since day is caused by the brightness of the sun and night by the shadow of the earth, the shadow is always in the part opposite to the sun's brightness. **In** the upper part of the earth is the brightness of day; in the lower part is the shadow of night. There is no hour in which it is not day in some part of the earth and night in another. If we simultaneously have summer, yet when we have day, they have night. In summer, when the days are longest and the nights shortest, they have in their summer short days and long nights. For this reason, if we have day when they have night, it is not the case that their night is as long as our day. I shall show the quantity of the day when it is at its greatest in summer and at its greatest in winter for the night; by the property of the day, one will understand the night. **While** the sun is seen to be here in summer, if it is evening for them, it is morning for us. And the closer it is to our sunrise, the more day they have than us in our morning. When the sun begins to decline for us, it begins to be seen by them; they have morning while we have evening. The closer it is to our sunset, the more day they see...

...as is clear from what was said above. <margin>
**On the habitable earth**
</margin>

Which, although it is prepared for the sun, is part of the torrid zone near Libya and Ethiopia; it is hot and dry in the vicinity of the cold. It is cold and humid. In the East: hot and humid. In the West: cold and dry. Lydia is in an equally tempered part. This earth is divided into three parts: Asia, Africa, and Europe.

**On Asia, Europe, and Africa.**
</margin>

Asia begins and extends from the East, occupying the region from the [temperate] zone even to the torrid zone. It is bounded by the Ocean, the Tanais <note>The ancient name for the Don River, traditionally considered the boundary between Europe and Asia</note>, and the Nile. ...since the habitable mass is similarly enclosed by these boundaries. In this habitable mass, there are mountains on whose summits there are perpetual snows, but in the valleys there is the greatest heat. Since heat comes from the sun and the higher bodies, it is singular that it is not at the summits closer to the sun, but in the lower valleys. In those [summits] there is cold, while in the middle there is heat. According to this reasoning, we can say that the air above cannot be ignited into fire except in a thick and humid space. In the aforementioned mountains, the air is thin, and therefore cannot be ignited into fire; but because of its lightness, it moves here and there. It is cold. But in the valleys, the air is thicker and remains immobile. The rays of the sun, touching the side of the mountain, strike it and bounce back <note>original: "resiliēdo"—the author is describing the "reflection" theory of heat, where sunbeams heat the earth more effectively when they "bounce" off the ground in thick air</note>, from which heat occurs for everyone. If the air in these lower places is like a tube in a cloud, it is thickened there. Through that discussion, it is not just thickened, but is made humid by the vapors ascending from the valleys. The coldness of the higher mountains everywhere prevents them from being touched. For this reason, the nature of mountains is defined. <meta>This page continues the discussion of human development, moving from the moment of conception to the nourishment of the fetus, the dangers of premature birth, and the eventual development of the five senses. It reflects medieval medical theories—largely based on the works of Aristotle and Galen—concerning why certain months of pregnancy are safer than others.</meta>

<margin>When the fetus is fed.</margin>
Since every created thing lives by food, it follows that the fetus is nourished while in the womb. It is asked how it comes forth. Since the fetus must be fed, this is done through its **umbilical cord**, which adheres to the mother just as the roots of trees <note>original: "cauda sua arborum"; the text compares the placenta and umbilical cord to the roots or "tails" of a tree drawing nutrients from the earth</note> are placed in the ground. Thus, everything living is touched by this; they descend from the mother's blood which provides the strength of the mother. And it is worthy to note that it receives this through the movement of the vegetative soul <term>vegetative soul: the most basic level of the soul in medieval philosophy, responsible for growth and nutrition</term>, which flows through it. In all these things, according to the nature of the child, two things are joined: the separation of the mother and the child.

<margin>Why a child born in the eighth month does not live.</margin>
¶ When, however, the child is born in the eighth month, it often does not survive. The philosophers say that the **seventh month** <note>original: "vij. m̄s"</note> provides a sufficient way of living. Hence, if by chance a child is created and born then, it is healthy. This is because at that time the formation of the spirit <note>original: "formacor̄ ſpūalr"</note> is complete and provides a sufficient way of life. Thus the child moves.

<margin>Whether a child born in the eighth month dies.</margin>
But you who are weak, whose limbs are joined and whose strength is fragile, are not yet fit to be born. If a child is born in the seventh month, it may live. But if it is born in the **eighth month**, it ought to be larger and more perfect, yet it is often not. For the child in the eighth month labors to exit, and by that long labor it is debilitated. Hence, if it is then brought forth, it cannot live. It is said that it does not remain in the womb for that whole month because it seeks to move itself, and its fragile limbs are not yet fit for birth. But because the heat and moisture change, the child attempts to leave.

<margin>Why a child is born with a crying voice.</margin>
When it comes out into the world and the light, it emits a crying voice. This is because the first voice of a human is a **voice of sorrow** <note>original: "vox ē dolour"</note>. I do not know if this is from teaching or from nature, but physicians place the infant in lukewarm water so that it might be quieted and find delight in it. Other animals, from the moment they are born, have their eyes open and move about, whereas—

<margin>Why a child cannot stand or walk for a long time.</margin>
—the human, for a long time, cannot stand or move. This is because the blood and the mixture of the humors are still changing. Other animals lack such a long period because their flesh is soon firm and solid. But the human is very tender, and their flesh is soft and moist at the beginning. Other animals have flesh that is harder and suited for the labor they must perform. Thus the human body is found to be weaker than other animals. This time of life is called **infancy** <note>original: "infantia"</note>, which lasts until the seventh year. In this period, a person is healthy if they grow well. During this time, the child's senses begin to work: they see, hear, smell, taste, and touch. Reason then begins to govern them.

¶ Since therefore we have spoken of these things, we must now speak of the senses. In the first part, we ask what is the reason that diligence and reason are lacking in the first stage. <unclear>Solo q o il k mhia eng</unclear>. If therefore the wood is not... it does not make a long life. If however they are of such quality... it is useful. If they are few... it displeases for a long time. For the labor of the one who knows is derived from everything anew.

<margin>Whether there are senses.</margin>
¶ Because those things which I shall say are useful, may they please you, for they are mine. I do not make them yours... <unclear>xp g i sulul mera</unclear>. They are the ones who understand from the exterior—

<margin>Concerning the five senses.</margin>
—the movement of the soul. But because the soul's power is not changed, we shall speak of one thing at a time. Sense is divided into five: namely **sight**, **hearing**, **smell**, **taste**, and **touch** <note>original: "visus, auditus, odoratus, gustus, tactus"</note>. These differ from one another... which is seen in the similarity of things.

<margin>Whether the senses come from the spirit of healthy forms.</margin>
We must understand that they have one origin. I work so that the divine error <note>likely "divine order" or "operation"</note> may be recognized. In this place, the subtlety of the spirit is the cause of perfection. Truly, these are the spirits...

---

...spiritual soul.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the body’s functions, transitioning from the development of the fetus to the fundamental biological "powers" or virtues that sustain life: the four stages of digestion and nutrition. It draws heavily on Galenic medicine, which viewed the body through the lens of primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</meta>

<margin>
There are two aiding forces:
namely, the appetite.
</margin>

There is, however, a fourfold division of the bodily powers: the **appetitive**, the **retentive**, the **digestive**, and the **expulsive** <note>These "four virtues" were considered the essential mechanical functions of the soul according to medieval medicine</note>. The first, the **appetitive power**, works through heat and dryness. For in man, a great heat and long labor dry him out. He then seeks a "juice" or essence for nourishment: the marrow takes this juice from the flesh, the flesh from the intestines, the intestines from the liver <note>original: "epate"</note>, and the liver from the veins, which serve all members. Thus, every living thing has its own nature. The stomach, moreover, takes its own "attraction" through certain hot and dry nerves that exist in the mouth, which cause it to desire and seek food; this operation begins in the "fasting" state <note>original: "iaiuat", likely referring to the jejunum or the state of hunger</note>. But because food is sometimes soft and sometimes hard, it is necessary that it be properly processed. For this purpose, the teeth are prepared, for they must defend and resist while grinding and breaking down the food.

<margin>
Concerning the teeth:
the incisors, canines, and molars.
</margin>

And hard food is heavily ground. They are called "incisors" <note>original: "calozum"; likely referring to the cutting teeth or *incisores*</note>, and their task is to separate part from part. There are also the "canines," whose job it is to break apart hard things. Then there are the "molars" <note>original: "molaref"</note>, which are long and broad; their task is to grind the food into small pieces and reduce it to a slurry. From there, the food prepared in the mouth passes through the **esophagus** to the stomach. By this path, it is defended and carried down. If by chance the body cannot retain all that it has taken, it requires the **retentive power**. This work is performed in the stomach through cold and dryness <note>Medieval theory held that "cold" was necessary to contract the stomach and hold food in place for digestion</note>, for without this, the nourishment would not be held.

<margin>
The retentive power.
The digestive power.
Concerning the Stomach.
</margin>

Next is the **digestive power**, which works through heat and moisture. It is said that the heat of the stomach digests and "cooks" the food, transforming it into a liquid state. The stomach is not alone in this; for when a person eats more than usual, it takes longer to digest. This is because there is much in the stomach that must be softened. It is assisted by the heat of the **liver**, which is placed beneath the stomach like a fire placed beneath a cooking pot <note>The "stomach as a cooking pot" was the standard medieval metaphor for digestion, with the liver providing the external heat needed to "boil" the food</note>. If the fire is strong and the pot is well-sealed, the digestion is proper. However, if the heat is weak or the stomach is too cold, the food remains raw and does not nourish. In such a case, the person may feel the need to sleep or may even vomit; and this is the primary failure of digestion.

<margin>
The members of the stomach
are necessary for these
three functions.
</margin>

These three things are necessary for all: to have an appetite, to retain, and to digest. The stomach is naturally hot and dry so that it may desire and suck in nutrients. Every member of the body has its own appetite. From all the members, a desire arises for what they need. When the food in the stomach is fully transformed, it must move on to the next stage. What remains is passed through the **expulsive power**, which acts upon the intestines. First, it enters the **duodenum** <note>original: "duodenū"</note>, so called because it is the length of twelve fingers. Then it moves into the next intestine, called the **jejunum** <note>original: "ieiunū"</note>, which is called "empty" because at whatever hour a person is killed, it is found without any juice or nourishment. This jejunum is surrounded by thin veins that draw the essence toward the liver. The liver is the source of the veins, just as the heart is of the arteries and the brain is of the nerves. These veins carry that juice to the liver to be further refined. Thus, the essence is separated from the waste.

<margin>
The first flow or the first
stage of digestion.
</margin>

This is called the first stage of digestion. What remains of the nourishment, which reaches the liver through these thin veins, is "cooked" by the liver's heat. Here, the heat and dryness transform some of it into **red bile** <note>original: "cola rubā"; one of the four humors</note>, while other parts are sent through various veins to other organs without further change. Some of it is sent to the stomach to stimulate the appetite. Some, being cold and dry, is sent to the **spleen** to be transformed into black bile <note>original: "melanc̄"; melancholy</note>. These are the various paths through which the body is sustained.

<summary>This page describes the medieval physiological theory of the "four virtues" of the stomach: appetite, retention, digestion, and expulsion. It uses the famous "cooking pot" metaphor to explain how the liver's heat processes food through the digestive tract and into the various humors of the body.</summary>
<keywords>digestion, four virtues, stomach, liver, teeth, humors, medieval medicine, anatomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of bodily systems, moving from the mechanical "powers" of digestion (appetite and grinding) to the chemical transformation of food into humors and the processing of waste fluids like urine and bile.</meta>

<margin>
In the **liver** and **spleen**, the heat of this master—and the **humors**—is seen through signs.
</margin>

For what is **urine** but a "changed flame"? <note>original: "flamma mutata"; medieval physicians often viewed urine as a byproduct of the body’s "metabolic fire" or heat</note>. It is a settled residue that takes its form through the universal power of extinction. Because urine is essentially heat within matter, it is changed into **blood** by the heat of the liver. However, it does not possess the same heat as the liver itself. Why then does it draw back and produce this liquid? Because the liver possesses the liquid heat of the urine; it dries the **yellow bile** <note>original: "cola"</note> and the **black bile** <note>original: "mela"</note>, which are separated through this process. Urine is thus generated. The humors exist in a mixed state within the juice of the food; they are then separated. The heat does not stay in the yellow bile, but the yellow bile is sent to the **gallbladder** <note>original: "cistam fellis"</note>. From this, yellow bile is produced. 

If indeed the blood is generated from this mixture, it is because the humors are soon exhaled from the food and drink and are prepared. These humors are divided accordingly: the **yellow bile** in the gallbladder, the **black bile** in the spleen, and the **phlegm** <note>original: "lta", likely *pituita* or *flegma*</note> in the lungs. Those humors which are added to the blood are there for two reasons: to aid the life of the veins and to allow the blood to be drawn and led more easily.

<margin>
Concerning the stone and the flow of digestion.
</margin>

When these functions fail, the blood must be restored. The humors that were in the urine flow through the "pineal" vein <note>likely referring to the *vena cava* or a specific vessel thought to lead to the kidneys</note> and descend to the **kidneys**. Whatever is retained there is eventually transmitted to the **bladder** <note>original: "uesicam"</note>, which is the purging of the urine through the flow of digestion.

<margin>
How the urine is managed so that it enters and exits through one opening of the bladder.
</margin>

The **bladder** has only one single opening <note>original: "unus solus foramen"</note> through which urine both enters and exits, which it manages whether the flow goes downward, upward, or obliquely. If it goes downward toward the kidneys, the bladder manages it as it descends; if it goes upward or obliquely, it is handled the same way. This single opening of the bladder possesses a power that manages the urine drop by drop as it penetrates the bladder.

<margin>
Concerning the stone of the bladder.
</margin>

I wish to speak on the composition of the **stone** <note>original: "lapidis"; referring to bladder stones or *calculi*</note>. The stone is managed by three things: when heat dries out the moisture, it creates a stony substance. This often happens because of the **black bile** <note>original: "melar"</note> in the bladder. 

<margin>
This is the flux and the evacuation of digestion.
</margin>

This stone is also felt in the kidneys. This occurs through the veins where heat processes the digestion. If the heat is redirected, other things prevail: a "cooked" urine which is called **hypostasis** <note>original: "hypist"; the sediment at the bottom of a urine sample</note>. It is also useful to see what collects there, which is called **enyorema** <note>original: "encorima"; particles suspended in the middle of the urine</note> if it is in the middle, or **nephile** <note>original: "nephile"; a cloud-like suspension at the top</note>. If there is a heavy drink, it is because the heat has directed it toward the hypostasis. 

<margin>
But if the blood is separated from the yellow bile and others...
</margin>

If the blood is separated, as **Theophilus** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician whose work "On Urines" was a standard medieval textbook</note> and **Isaac Judaeus** <note>A famous 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> say, it is because the yellow and black bile are divided from the blood and sent to their proper places to be purged. It is a false claim to say otherwise. We see, however, that unclean yellow bile and black bile are generated with the blood. They are changed by heat and dryness, and this yellow bile is the cause of many conditions.

<summary>This page explains the medieval physiological understanding of how the liver transforms food into blood and humors, the role of the gallbladder and spleen, and how excess heat creates urine and bladder stones.</summary>
<keywords>urine, blood, yellow bile, black bile, liver, bladder stones, Theophilus, Isaac Judaeus, digestion, humors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of humors from the previous page, specifically how the balance of yellow bile, black bile, and blood was altered by the Fall of Man and the onset of human labor and mortality. It moves into a definition of the four humors based on heat and moisture before introducing the nature of sleep.</meta>

<margin>
Why is the **melancholic** <note>original: "melic̅"</note> state present with **jaundice** <note>original: "ialo̅", likely *icterus*</note>? Yellow and black bile are found in the **breath** <note>original: "sp̅ūtu̅", referring to the vital spirit or breath</note>.
</margin>

This arises from the flowing of the heart, where the cause of generation begins. Therefore, the same purification occurs in the **veins** <note>original: "uasa ierana", likely referring to the *vasa hyerana* or the sacred/principal vessels</note>. Similarly, black bile is purified. To this, the learned doctors provide a response. Since yellow and black bile are separated from one another, they do not remain in the blood. For no member of the human body could endure their change or restore its life if it were not so. When the heat in the members arises solely from the blood, it does not become inflamed. Just as in a long-standing **colic** <note>original: "colico"</note>, when yellow bile is not separated, another thing occurs. It is not that there is black bile, but rather that the blood appears more **melancholic**. This is because the operation of the humors must be viewed in their totality. After all, every excess in the breath is an action of these humors. This increase is perfected by the heat of **rheumatism** <note>original: "rh̅uo"</note>, which is contrary to the heat that nourishes human nature. If, therefore, there is an increase in this heat, it is in the judgment of things: heat in the highest degree, and moisture in the lowest. Where black bile is a flame that is elevated, yellow and black bile are dry in the highest degree. Furthermore, the human being was once hot and moist, more than any other thing. But the first man <note>Adam</note> was expelled from the pleasantness of **Paradise** into the **valley of tears** <note>original: "valle lac̅mar̅", a common biblical metaphor for earthly life</note> to labor with his hands, eating his bread through labor, vigils, and fasts. From this, the limbs were dried out by that excessive heat. Similarly, humanity is now in a corrupt state because of this. All who are born in this time are born from corruption and are themselves corrupt.

<margin>
Why [the discussion] regarding the health of the **spirit** <note>original: "phre san.", possibly *phrenis sanitate* (health of the mind/spirit)</note>.
</margin>

In man, it is found that blood is in all the members and the skin, and in all the organs. In these members, it is divided. It is a good thing that in all these members, there is a restoration of the spirit. When this harmony is broken, corruption is found in the body.

<margin>
What is **yellow bile**, what is **phlegm** <note>original: "flamā", literally flame, but used here for the humor pituita/phlegm</note>, what is **black bile**, and **blood**?
</margin>

What is more and what is less? What is heat and what is moisture? Where there is abundant heat and reduced moisture, there is **yellow bile** <note>original: "colia"</note>. Where there is abundant moisture and reduced heat, there is **phlegm** <note>original: "flamma"</note>. Where heat and moisture are both reduced, there is **black bile** <note>original: "melia"</note>. This is cold and dry. But where heat and moisture are in balance, that is **blood** <note>original: "sanguinei"</note>. Or if any other humor enters the body, it is through the labor of the human body or by a fall. From this, the humors flow in various ways, for some are long-lasting and some are short. **Yellow bile** acts quickly because it is kindled by heat. **Blood** and its vapors are long-lasting because they follow the moisture of the body. **Phlegm** <note>original: "flamma"</note> lasts for a moderate time according to the moisture of the body. **Black bile** is cold and putrid, and follows its own rules. These things arise from the sins and the various changes of the body. Yellow bile and black bile are both warmed by the heart's heat. Blood and phlegm are produced by labor and the movement of the limbs. If yellow bile and blood are putrefied, they cause various illnesses. Phlegm and black bile do the same.

<margin>
Concerning **Sleep**.
</margin>

Lastly, we should speak of **sleep**. Sleep is another state of the body. It is a rest for the soul and the limbs. While the person is asleep, the soul is quiet, and the senses are bound, saving only the spirit. In this state, the soul and the life of the body are restored.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the body's internal functions, transitioning from the balance of humors to the physiological causes of sleep, dreams, and the cooling mechanism of the lungs and heart. It draws upon the authority of Hugh of St. Victor.</meta>

Hugh says: memory <note>original: "memō."</note>, it is said, is moved voluntarily. Then an increase in the **animal power** <note>The "animal" power or spirit (from *anima*, soul) was believed to govern sensation and voluntary movement, centered in the brain.</note> occurs. Although this may be caused by an external reason, words operate within the mind. <margin>Why a human sleeps.</margin> And because this happens in relation to the high animal power, sleep is generated from heat and moisture in its own time. This moisture, diffused through the body, evaporates; as long as the senses are closed off from their normal state, it is the time for nourishment. Therefore, as the **fumes** <note>original: "fūmo"; medieval physiology taught that "vapors" or "fumes" rose from the stomach during digestion to the brain, causing sleep.</note> from the humors ascend to the brain, they fill it. If the brain remains full, it must be dilated, which is why those who are sleeping seem to hear things; while that smoke is being "digested" by heat, those things which descend are like foreign things being emptied out. <margin>How a person is awakened from sleep.</margin> And when they are processed, the person rises. When the sleep is digested, it no longer fills the senses in sleep nor is it held by the pulse. Sleep is a movement of the animal spirit, but not through the pulse of the humors; rather, air is moved through the openings of the head, and thus it is explained locally. This is how sleep is created. But in the movement of the body, which occurs more constantly, those who are cared for have sleep; some do not sleep at all, while others have a continuous sleep. <margin>On the signs that occur before waking or in sleep.</margin> Through sleep, they may have signs: some from good hours, or from many things which are easily known before they happen. The common cause of this is taught by the season: just as smoke arises from burning wood, so too in the body, fumes from food in the stomach rise to the brain. In the deep arteries, the signs are gathered from food or drink. This is why sleep is considered the time when the reason is at rest. In the same way, when a person is hungry or full, the stomach is either lightened or burdened by food; all of this comes from the smoke ascending to the center. 

### On Dreams
<margin>On Dreams.</margin>
While a person sleeps, they see certain things which are called dreams. Some of these arise from natural causes, such as the remains of thoughts, being full of food, or from the impurity of the soul and habit; all of these signify nothing. Others are born from the intervention of **angels** or from the judgments of the soul’s divinity; the causes of these are portents. Authorities have much to say on this, but let us leave it to the quiet of the mind and speak of the **spiritual power**. <margin>On the spiritual power.</margin> The spiritual power <note>original: "spūali uirtute"; the *spiritus vitalis* or vital spirit was believed to be a subtle substance that carried life throughout the body via the blood.</note> is that which is liberated while the air is drawn in. It is founded in the seat of the heart. 

<margin>What things are necessary for sleep in the intake of air.</margin>
The heart requires two kinds of heat so that it is not consumed by its own fire; therefore, air is necessary. It must be drawn in and expelled. This is the work of the **lungs**. <margin>The Composition of the Lungs.</margin> The lungs are composed in such a way that they act like a bellows, expanding to draw in air and contracting to expel it, so that the heart is not destroyed by excessive heat. Therefore, it is necessary to breathe to return the air. We should also discuss **transparency**. <margin>On transparency.</margin> <note>original: "diafinitate"; this refers to the "clearness" or "fineness" of the spirits, allowing them to carry light or images to the brain.</note> It is said that the heat and the fumes of the humors are drawn toward the heart, dilating it; from the heart, they are pulsed toward the brain, ascending upward. Then, by being refined, they reach the brain and make it illuminated. This power is led from the stars of the ether and has moved within.

<meta>This page transitions from the physiological mechanics of sleep and the animal spirit to the specific anatomy and qualities of the human head, focusing on the origin and characteristics of hair and beards based on the theory of humors and bodily heat.</meta>

Since, as we have shown, different **animal actions** <note>The "animal" faculty in medieval science referred to the functions of the soul (anima) such as sensation and thought.</note> are perfected in different locations, he does not wish there to be a specific soul in the face that acts differently than the soul in the rest of the man. In man, no soul is created separately from the others; rather, it is the same soul which, through dissolution, exists in the body. This soul, while it is dissolvable, is not destroyed like a physical thing; rather, it is like a drop of dew <note>original: "stilla roris aquae"</note> or like a fire. If the soul were merely a material fire, it would be subject to the **flames of Gehenna** <note>original: "flammal gehenal"; a reference to the fires of Hell, often used in theological debates about the soul's substance.</note>... [the text here becomes fragmented regarding the soul’s definition].

### <margin>On the head of man.</margin>
Regarding the human head, which extends from the **occiput** <note>original: "ocip’"; the back of the skull.</note> to the face, we shall speak further. The head is more noble than the rest of the body's form, obtaining a "celestial body" because the soul, in the likeness of the heavens, attains immortality through it. It is also the easiest part to move, as it is the property of the brain to be in motion. The skull is compacted from separate bones to protect it...

### <margin>Whence hair is born.</margin>
The hair exists for the purpose of beauty and decorum. It is asked how hair is born. Hair is produced throughout the human body because of **heat** and **smoky moisture** <note>original: "calorē r̃hı nıtātē ſuũ ſumoſū"; medieval physiology taught that hair was a "superfluity" created by vapors rising from the body's internal heat.</note>. Just as when a vessel is placed over a fire, it evaporates steam; if that vessel is covered, the steam or smoke adheres to the lid and thickens. Similarly, the heat of the body pushes these "smoky" vapors through the pores of the skin, where they solidify into hair upon contact with the external air.

### <margin>Whence hair receives different colors.</margin>
Hair receives various colors based on the mixture of the humors. A **choleric** <note>original: "solica" (likely cholerica)</note> temperament results in red hair. A **phlegmatic** <note>original: "flavia"</note> temperament results in white or flaxen hair. A **melancholic** <note>original: "melica"</note> temperament produces black hair. A **sanguine** temperament leads to a reddish or healthy hue. No one's hair color is determined by just one humor, but by the dominant one in their constitution. This is why some people have very thick hair and others thin, depending on the abundance of these vapors and the openness of their pores.

### <margin>Why women have little beard.</margin>
Women and children have hair on their heads but lack beards. This is because they lack sufficient internal heat. In men, the heat of the testicles and the overall temperament opens the pores of the jaws, allowing the "smoky" vapors to escape and form a beard. Because women are of a "moister" and cooler nature, these vapors do not project from the face in the same way.

### <margin>That certain women are nevertheless bearded.</margin>
There are indeed some women who are bearded. Do you not know that some women possess a **masculine form**? These women are of a "hotter" temperament than others and live a "warm, manly" life; hence they have beards, though they are not truly men, but women with masculine qualities.

### <margin>Why some men have no beards and why some are bald.</margin>
Regarding men who have no beards or who are bald: it is a matter of the dignity of the head's position. Baldness occurs because of a lack of moisture or an excess of evaporating heat from the "vessel" of the head, which prevents the hair from taking root...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human physiology, moving from the growth of hair and the causes of graying to the internal anatomy of the head, specifically the protective membranes of the brain and the three-cell theory of mental function.</meta>

[The vapor] can ascend through the head by itself. Whence in that part it has fewer openings, lest the smoke remain inside and generate **migraines** <note>original: "hiemesim," likely a corruption of "hemicrania."</note>. This can be observed in the skulls of those long dead. If, therefore, someone has [closed] pores because of excessive dryness, the smoke cannot adhere, nor can it generate hair. This is how one becomes bald. For this reason, **eunuchs** <note>original: "miqui," a shorthand for "eunuchi." Medieval medicine often noted that eunuchs did not go bald due to their lack of "choleric heat."</note> who remain so for a long time do not have those wide pores, and thus they do not go bald. <margin>On hair becoming gray.</margin> Enough has been said concerning hair; now it is said why grayness occurs, <gloss>that is</gloss> on account of the origin of **phlegm** <note>One of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note>. Phlegm is the cause of such a color. Whence generally old people, who have cold and moisture, turn gray. For if old people do not encounter that dryness [of youth], they abound in such crude and phlegmatic moisture. <margin>How the old turn gray.</margin> First, if they are chilled... by phlegm and phlegmatic moisture, which internally softens the **rheum** <note>A watery discharge or flow of humors.</note>, it makes them moist as if by a natural soul. If therefore the grayness of the head comes from phlegmatic moisture, why is it that a youth who is **choleric** <note>The "choleric" temperament was associated with yellow bile—hot and dry.</note> turns gray? <margin>Why adolescents and choleric people turn gray.</margin> Because the choleric [humor] which stays in the moisture of the brain is established in adolescence, and they turn gray in their youth. If the moisture of the choler itself is there, they turn gray in some summer. We see that many old people are very gray, but these reasons suffice for the cause. Regarding these things, [one finds] under the skull a certain membrane of the head... the **dura mater** <note>original: "dura m̄ra"; the "hard mother," the tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain.</note>, <gloss>hard</gloss> membrane, which is for the protection of the brain lest it be harmed. <margin>On the pia mater and dura mater.</margin> The softer one is called the **pia mater** <note>original: "pia m̄r̄"; the "pious mother," the delicate innermost membrane.</note>. From the "mothers" [membranes] of the body are born the nerves... but the pia mater is also born... <margin>From the membrane is born that hard one which is the tunic of voluntary motion, which tends toward the back of the head and there creates a certain swelling.</margin> Under these membranes the brain is located. <margin>The Brain.</margin> The brain is white and liquid. It is cold and moist, lest it be consumed by the continuous motion and heat of the body. To briefly distinguish: some do not turn gray because they have a certain complexion of the brain. Since the members of men are divided, they have different **complexions** <note>The specific balance of the four humors in an individual.</note>. Although every brain is cold and moist, some are more hot and less moist than others; these are said to have a **choleric brain**. Some are hot and more moist; these are said to have a **phlegmatic brain**. In some it is more cold and less moist; these are said to have a **melancholic brain**. In some it is more hot and more moist; these are said to have a **sanguine brain**. <margin>On the three cells of the brain: the fantastic, the logistic, and the memorial.</margin> In the head there are three cells [ventricles]: one in the front, another in the back, and a third in the middle. The first cell is called the **fantastic** <note>The "phantastica," where sensory images (phantasms) were processed.</note> or visual cell. In it, the soul is said to see and understand. This cell of the brain is hot and dry, so that by dry heat, forms [of things] are shaped... In the middle cell, which is called the **logistic** <note>The "logistica," the seat of reason and discernment.</note> or rational cell, the soul discerns... [the differences] between things. The [last] cell is called the **memorial** <note>The "memorialis," the seat of memory located at the back of the head.</note>, in which the soul exercises memory. Between the middle cell and the back one, there is a passage. This opening has a certain **caruncle** <note>original: "caruncula"; a small fleshy valve, often identified in medieval texts as the "vermis," thought to control the flow of thoughts and spirits between ventricles.</note> which acts as a barrier...

Many things here are to be committed to new memory or recalled to mind. It is noted how those openings are renewed. Forgetfulness occurs there. The **chamber of the brain** <note>The author refers to the medieval "Ventricular Theory," which divided the brain into three ventricles or "cells" responsible for different mental functions.</note> is dry; yet this chamber, as its nature returns, if the nature of the brain is loose, it will diminish the retention of things. If, however, the middle chamber of the brain is distorted, the person becomes demented. According to how much it is distorted, the person is less of a person. If the chamber is very moist, he is stupid; if it is dry, he will be of a slower wit. 

<margin>Whether a man be forgetful, demented, or stupid.</margin>
<margin>What kind of spirit exists for understanding, retaining, and remembering in the head, etc.</margin>

**This part** is accepted through many thousands of examples. When someone was of a powerful memory, a physician noted that having received a wound in the first chamber, he lost the power of understanding, yet he retained things in his memory. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), a Greek physician whose writings dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> relates that he experienced this with a certain man who, after receiving a wound, became demented. When Galen drew a figure for him, he pointed to a **pot** <note>original: "olla," a common ceramic jar.</note> that would immediately shatter it; then he smiled. He showed him a figure that he immediately wanted to penetrate. It appears that he still possessed discernment, for he distinguished the figure from the pot. It is established by **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a translator of Arabic medical texts into Latin who helped bring "Ventricular Theory" to Europe.</note> that he still had a memory of things previously known. Likewise, it has been seen at times that others, having received a wound in the first chamber, retained their intelligence and reason but lost their memory. It also varies in those who are "polluted" <note>likely referring to a corruption of the humors or a specific injury</note>; some, after a wound, come to such great forgetfulness that they do not even know they were ever human. Others have been seen where, with the middle chamber injured, they lost their reason, yet retained their memory and their **fantastic power** <note>The "virtus fantastica" or imagination—the ability to conjure images in the mind.</note>. Rightly, therefore, is it said:

<margin>of the eyes</margin>
In a certain book, it is said that the substance of vision is airy. Since every corporeal substance is substantial through its extreme subtlety and splendor, it is called "fire" by some, according to its proportion. Again, vision is now called that power which is born in the eyes; whatever arrives at the eyes is divided into two branches. These are flexible like a cord, arranged in this manner: the one on the right tends toward the right, and the left toward the light. The aforementioned substance is substantial and clear, and through itself it now comes to the eyes; exiting through the middle of them, which is called the **pupil**, it finds itself in the splendor and in the messenger air. It joins itself and proceeds until it reaches an obstacle in the form of a **visual cone** <note>original: "specie coni," referring to the ancient and medieval theory that vision travels in a cone-shaped beam with the point at the eye.</note>, which is a form of touching. Thus, through its substantiality, it perceives the shape and color of the surface it strikes. For when the messenger air is clear, it is ready to receive forms and colors into itself. When the form and color pass through the eye, they return to the **Chamber of Imagination** <note>original: "fantastica cella," the first ventricle of the brain where sensory data was thought to be gathered into images.</note>; then they return to the **Chamber of Logic** <note>original: "logisthica cella," the middle ventricle where the soul reasons and judges the information it receives.</note>, in which the sign of the color is represented to the soul. In this cell, everything that was perceived is weighed, and the judgment of the color is determined.

**Disciple.** Many things seem to occur to this sentiment.
<margin>On the speed of vision.</margin>
First, how—given that there is such a great distance between the sun and a star—is vision fixed upon them? We see them as soon as we open our eyes. Does that substance arrive there in such a brief moment and return to us? If that substance were moved by its own nature, it would never be known without doubt; it would be like a judge who indicates something with a slow mind, like a snail. But it is so fast that it exists in the world almost instantly.

**Scholar.** I understand this, and I believe it to be true.

**Scholar.** Tell me then, while someone looks at something for a long time, does this substance remain immobile, or is there a continuous transmission of it created? For everything that lacks weight cannot stand still.

**Scholar.** In this case, does it continue to run back and forth, or is it reflected?

**Professor.** A coarse objection befits a coarse mind. This substance is so fast that no distance between the viewer and the seen object is noted. But as a substance, it meets the object without being hindered. When it is directed from the eye to the star, is it all in the eye before it reaches the star, or is it in this place and that? And if it is in both, is it broken or continuous? If it were all in the eye and then all in the star, it would not be in the intermediate space at the same time, which is impossible. If it is in this place and that, it must be continuous; for since the space from the earth to the sky is filled with air, there is no empty place between them. If there were a vacuum between them, the things in the eye could not touch the color or the nature of the object; if we say it is in the air, then it reaches the object.

**Professor.** It is difficult to dispute this with someone who is ignorant. However, I will respond well to your zeal. This corporeal and substantial spirit can be equally fast in one place as in another. And because it is in the rays of the sun, the distance of that path cannot be measured. If, therefore, the ray is simple and reaches the body through its power, the distance between them should not be considered a hindrance. Listen now to my mind with all attention to what I say, and I will set forth the opinions of others on this matter.

**Professor.** There were those who said that vision is a single universal thing. Nothing comes to the vision from the outside.
<margin>Three theories.</margin>
They find that the air itself is formally filled with colors. Then it returns to the soul. When one object meets another, if they look at each other, the ray in the middle of the air finds the white color.

<margin>The reasoning why one who is in a dark place sees that which is in a bright place, but not vice versa.</margin>
In a dark chamber, if one remains for a long time, whatever is manifest is seen. Again, one thing remains that raises a doubt regarding the walls, where two certain points are distant from each other. A stronger and more powerful place will find you, but for viewing, it will be known by a rarer space and five times weaker. Clearly, the further a ray is from its origin, the weaker it is. For this reason, it does not proceed or join remote things as well as those placed nearby. Because of this, when going toward a glaring light, the eyelids of the eye are closed. One must, therefore, shield the ray of the eyes with the hands so that they may emerge more strongly from the parts. If you keep the eye fixed on a field <note>original: "agrol," likely referring to a bright open space</note> for too long, the sight fails. Therefore, when a ray enters from that which proceeds from such a bright place and reaches an object, the brightness is entirely dissipated, and it is weakened further from its origin; touching its own kind, it returns to the eye as if to report back. This proceeds from that which is in a dark place, which is more effective... coming from weakness, it reports back to the man the figure of that which sent it. It is divine wisdom then to consider how it differs in hearing. 

**Proposition. On Hearing.**
Concerning hearing, it happens thus: the air in those instrumental organs, just as in the mouth of the speaker, receives a certain form; then, through the movement of the air, an angle is generated which forms the shape of a thread <note>original: "fili formam," likely referring to a direct line of vibration or a sound wave</note>. These are then led to the ears, which are concave like a drum <term>tympanum</term> (the eardrum). They resonate in that concavity and excite the soul; it is moved as much as by the aforementioned airy force through numbers <note>original: "numeros," referring to the mathematical ratios of music and sound</note>, which from the middle extend out even to the ears. Therefore, the acting air, which it finds in the ear, shapes the form of a thread and recalls it to the soul in the **logic cell** <note>original: "logistica cella," the middle chamber of the brain where reason was thought to reside</note>. There, they weigh the figuration of the voice in the soul, and thus one hears, leading us to some former good. A real example: a stone thrown into the middle of a pond <note>original: "stagni," a pool or pond</note> creates bubbles... which creates many waves and a circle. It pushes another wave. This continues thus until it reaches the bank and peacefully fades away. Thus, drawn out by the movement of the air, it informs the shape of the thread for the ears of various people; then the voice falls into being nearby through the similarity already held. Whence it is that wherever the sound goes, people receive their hearing in the same way. Sometimes the lips compress the air, which they express well, <gloss>sustaining</gloss> the sound with enunciation. For which reason one compares sight to hearing. [Boethius] spoke concerning the figure of the voice which forms those present and the hearing. This is said. ¶ Therefore, one hears a different whistling sound <note>original: "sibilum," a hiss or whistle</note> when they whistle by pressing the lips together and narrowing the air. Therefore, the act is close to the ears of that person... <insert>according to the whistle heard</insert>.

<meta>This page transitions from the physical mechanics of the senses (concluding the discussion on hearing from the previous page) into the internal cultivation of the soul and the anatomical structure of the human being.
