That a part of the soul is to be cultivated within. Thus it is seen in the worthiness of knowledge. First among others, the <term>Manicheans</term><note>A dualistic religious movement that viewed the world as a struggle between light/spirit and darkness/matter.</note> wish for the principal [faculties] to be viewed as a tree, the remains of which [belong] to the King. Concerning these well-known moral reasons of man, man now needs intellectual strength for everything; it is necessary that those things which are driven from the depths are turned into necessary actions. But because he is often deceived, or often [mistakes] what is merely apparent when he desires something, it is necessary to have a means of repelling [error]. Toward this end, nothing shall pass by.

<margin>On the division of the human body.</margin>
The form is prepared from the hands up to the shoulder, which operates from all the mental ligaments. Let it be felt that while all things are well, they are also fragile; unless one can examine oneself. But it is unusual for every kind of limb to have the same flexibility; some parts cannot be bent at all. The soul, joined with a well-compacted [body], falls partly into the more remote areas of the body. Thus, it is seen as if in a broken arm; not that those bones are so prepared for work, but rather that the dissolved parts are joined by external ligaments. The hand is bent when the external parts are called upon, but the internal parts are the source of all motion. The hand is extended toward the internal living being when it is opened. Because of this, it is prepared for the delight of the neck, and then divided into the necessary branches. This occurs from the right hand and then to the left, each of which reaches the fingers and is divided into five. 

Another splendid part is divided into branches in the body toward the cut of the heart for delight; then it is divided into two around the thighs, of which one depends toward the right foot and the other toward the left. In the extremities, it is divided into five, just as man is like an <term>inverted tree</term><note>A common medieval philosophical concept (found in Plato and Aristotle) suggesting man's "roots" are in heaven/the head, unlike plants whose roots are in the earth.</note>. Wherefore it can be said:

<margin>Also, man is called "anthropos" in Greek.</margin>
Indeed, a true tree has roots that go downward into the earth, from which other things are chosen internally and the branches expand upward. I, a man, [perceive] the head as the root of God, an inverted root, from which the spirit is sent forth. From that root, all joints are produced, just as branches are adherent to a trunk. This is the path of the <term>nucha</term><note>From the Arabic 'nukhā'; a medieval term for the spinal cord.</note> which is located in the neck. It is for the soul to hold and to emit [commands] whenever it wishes to move a hand, or to hasten the feet. For whichever action is required, the living power is administered to the hands or feet, so that it may move whichever of them it wishes. Similarly, the head is the principle of those things which happen in animals.

<margin>On imagination.</margin>
It happens to animals that they possess what is called <term>imagination</term><note>original: "imaginario"</note>. Indeed, imagination is a certain power of the soul <note>original: "vis animae"</note> which is the source of figures and the color of a thing in its absence. Nature granted this to man so that he would not surrender things to oblivion. For even if we do not carry the actual figure or color of an individual within us, we immediately recognize them through imagination as soon as we see them. Even if we have not seen a thing for a long time, we have a likeness of the thing imagined within us. Therefore, it is said that imagination is born from sight. For we imagine those things which we have seen; we imagine them according to the likeness of the thing itself. Even while waking or [dreaming], one might see the likeness of a city they had imagined. For instance, I can imagine the <term>Red Sea</term><note>original: "Mare Rubrum"</note> in a corner [of my mind], which I have never seen, by using the likeness of other seas I have seen, but with a red color. This [faculty] is found in other "brute" animals as well. Indeed, through imagination, other animals recognize their masters when they see them; they flee from one and approach another. This they do out of affection or a certain attraction. Truly, this imagination is the leader of other actions, oh most serene [reader], which sounds differently in other animals; and in those things where it is separated from other [faculties], it is seen [clearly], as when a dog adores its master.

<summary>This page discusses the anatomical and spiritual composition of man, famously describing the human being as an "inverted tree" with its roots in the head. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the physical body and the soul. ...reads with a swift progress. <margin>These actions belong to the soul.</margin> If, therefore, nothing were to paint this unformed state with color, colors, and flavors, I would place it... 

...might be changed by the wintry <note>original: "brumali"</note> laws of the blessed. To the end which we have not added fear, with fate granting to man from a special grace to be more blessed; or rather, that he would be no man at all. If a man remains the same as a piece of wood, the soul lacks all sense, not only of human things but even of a small staff, and so on. Is it not that man, even the wisest, becomes better through old age? Just as it is fitting for the body or its works to be [refined]. Then it is asked: if the body lacks a soul, is it condemned by that fact? But if it is widowed of the soul, they do not have [suffering] inflicted upon them; for the body is known by the soul. If it is true that works are composed of both, then they have their special qualities together in their parts.

->**The Philosopher.**<-

<margin>Let them speak of corporeal things.</margin> These accidents of the soul are then condemned or the soul is crowned. For it is given safely by the reason of the body; because the soul does not operate without the body. The required merits of the body are filled; wherefore the soul is judged while it is in the body and operates it. Certain <term>accidents</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that can change without changing the essential nature of a thing (e.g., being tan or being tall).</note> which do not belong while the spirit is at rest, which make a man in his spirit [rise] from a man to something above man; of what quality he may be said to be. If few things are given to human beauty, let them be said here.

<margin>On the unique difference of man.</margin> **Power** is spoken of regarding the human soul in its species, which, being joined to the body, possesses the suitability for discerning and understanding the human <term>office</term><note>The "office" (officio) refers to the specific duty or function a human is meant to perform in the natural order.</note>. It is asked whether man consists of two things, namely the rational soul and the body. Since the soul has reason within it, it is human. The soul is <margin>The soul is fundamentally mixed with the body, not merely placed beside it, nor superficially mixed, nor generated.</margin> placed beside the body and mixed; touched and mixed. But if it were merely placed beside it, it would be [distinct from] it. For everything placed beside another either loses its own quality or has its own quality besides that which is mixed. Generally, things placed together are more [active]; for example, water placed beside something moistens it more, or the soul is more moved or has its own special and similar union. 

Man: [the soul] is placed beside the body, yet it is not merely mixed with the body. For if one were made from two, neither would remain as it was before. This is argued by the example of things which are mixed in the same choice. And so that in man this [nature] remains, the soul is not mixed [like a liquid] with the body. If it were generated from the body, it would have some corporeal quality; just as water has the quality of salt in a very small degree. Whence, if it were mixed from many elements, it would seek its own place and flee from this world. Why is it that the soul, in such an unclean world, loves the world? It is because the soul is neither merely placed beside, nor mixed, nor generated from the body, but **joined** to it. There are certain "chains" <note>This likely refers to the Platonic concept of the soul being bound to the body.</note> which unite it to the body and make it love it. 

If it were possible to say... the love of the soul is given through a proportion of reason toward God; whence in this [life], it loves those "feathers" <note>An allusion to the "wings of the soul" from Plato’s *Phaedrus*, which grow when the soul contemplates truth.</note> and wishes to leave behind those things which are many. It is said the soul is constituted of a spiritual dwelling. Free bodies are bettered by a proportional reason. All mortal things are [so] constituted. This proportion and concord allures the soul and unites it to the body; and by temperance and balance, let us say the soul is not the body. It is not a qualitative thing, but a proportion of concordant reason, which it prefers above all else that it loves; whence it seeks those things which preserve that proportion. <margin>That the soul is whole in any part of the body.</margin> And it flees from those things which destroy it. From this, [parts] begin to discord. The soul abhors the [decaying] body and is separated from it. If the soul were [purely physical], it would be in one part or in every single part as a whole.

->**The Philosopher.**<-

It is more [probable] that the soul is whole in any given place. But it operates the same in all parts. <margin>An objection regarding a severed hand, and the response.</margin> If the soul were entirely in the human hand, then when the hand is cut off, the soul would be separated from the body. If it truly were in the hand as much as [in the heart]...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical union of the soul and body, arguing that the soul is not just a passenger but is "joined" through a "concord of reason." It concludes with the classic scholastic puzzle of "totality," questioning how the soul can be present in every part of the body simultaneously, even if a limb is lost.</summary>

...even so: the whole offering is valid in another member. Just as in a hand which is entirely cut off, there remains with the rest of the body...

<margin>On the creation and infusion of souls.</margin>

## On the ignoble animal when it was through the whole. He says, however, according to what follows: those animals which are called "animals" are such from the character of the soul 

that which is called the "new creation of souls" to be cherished, by its own reason without external help. 

## When, however, it is said that God, 

the best creator, establishes new souls in nature, leading them into that grace. Only the mind is widowed from the reason of those things to be cherished. If anyone asks about the moment from which man is born: whether it is when the body is fit for the soul in the womb—the <term>formative stage</term><note>The "formative stage" refers to the medieval belief that the body must reach a certain level of physical development before it can receive a human soul.</note>—or on the day of movement, or at the hour of birth? I have not read a definitive answer. To which it seems contrary to say that it appeared to me as if in a moist and fluid body, then hidden as if for the soul. 

## The soul is sufficient in this. 

<margin>On the naming that brute animals have.</margin>

## This then follows: that brute animals did not have boldness concerning God. 

## Through that follow many earthly faculties: talent, opinion, reason, intelligence, and memory. 

## Talent <note>original: "ingenium"</note> indeed is that which a certain animal makes alive, prevailing by its own strength. Talent is a power of the soul made for perceiving quickly, according to what is understood by hearing. Good reason is talent, while a hard heart is dullness. 

## Opinion <note>original: "opinio"</note> indeed is not spoken of except as a habit in the mind. 

<margin>That opinion and reason come from the senses.</margin>

It comes from the senses, because the soul in the first time of the mind, like an unlettered tablet <note>This refers to the "tabula rasa" or blank slate theory.</note>, perceives color and figure; which the soul itself or reason does, whereby it is properly called a judgment of things while they are distant. In these, someone might be deceived by their own existence.

<margin>That reason stands toward both sides.</margin>

## That the animal itself, as much the material of the soul as the time in which it happens, stands between things. Opinion stands as a habit, or stands toward either side. 

Concerning something of the world in the perceived soul; but it fluctuates and does not know whether it is so or not; then that is called opinion. 

<margin>But the foundation of opinion.</margin>

## Opinion, therefore, is a false judgment concerning the reason of the soul, yet it fluctuates as if uncertain. If indeed this judgment is certain, it is called reason proper. 

<margin>But the foundation of reason.</margin>

From every sense it tastes and argues, but not conversely. For reason is called the proper judgment of the habit. Therefore, Adam observed that opinion runs into reason. If I say the soul judges through this: if it fails, it is a false opinion; if it does not fail, but still fluctuates, it is still opinion. 

## Thus, until <term>intelligence</term><note>original: "intelligentia", here meaning a higher form of spiritual or intuitive understanding beyond logical reasoning.</note> is confirmed. This, because it is an incorporeal thing, grasps the truth in a new way; it is a small thing that is high, then when in full, it is called intelligence alone, after the manner of a few men. 

<margin>Regarding reason and intelligence.</margin>

## He says that opinion and reason are in the nature of reason, but from opinion it seems to have intelligence—though the truth I do not know. 

## For intelligence is born from reason. For in what way reason becomes intelligence, this is the cause: intelligence prepares the man and leads him to contemplation, just as the body is led... 

...it could act upon bodies. Through perceiving it, what is received... that the body has this called spirit... talent... through it they have an opinion... it might fail if led by long labor... but because intelligence is born from the leading of reason: in intelligence there is a judgment called incorporeal. This intelligence, according to the true cause of <term>Alcasel</term><note>original: "Alcasel", likely referring to Al-Ghazali, the Persian philosopher whose works on the soul were influential in Latin translation.</note>... 

<margin>But here, intelligence.</margin>

...it seems to follow the philosophers who say that men and angels are able to know something of God, together with the invisible, while he meditates for a long time... what remains more boldly... I have read according to what is in the beginning of the Gospel... 

## Memory is a power of the soul by which things are remembered... 

<margin>Whether reason and intelligence should be said to be the same.</margin>

From this time, the pseudo-Albert <note>original: "pseudo. alb", referring to works falsely attributed to Albert the Great.</note> says... indeed Albert says intelligence... but in what way it is led, we do not say to have reason or total intelligence...

<margin>Whether infants, through a pure lack of the action of reason, do not possess intelligence.</margin>

For the body thus blunts the soul and holds it back like a reed in a bow. The body, which is a burden to the soul, weighs it down, and the earthly inhabitant thinks of many material things from which he wakes. For in these names the bodies are slowed down. 
The spirit, however, cannot be killed so that experience does not come from the doctrines of others. That which was here was hot and moist, so that from one it might appear to another. Because with the soul being present in the body, the duty of discerning and understanding is troubled. This happens due to the unsteadiness which is hot and dry, for it is dried out: the humor which a man has from the wind is in the lesser things. Not for a long time is the spirit moist, nor is it said to be good, just as a man is ready to discern because a perfect odor can be perceived. But in this, let them come to the doctrines of the fathers.
For the youth is as the old man, who is called foul and dry, departing from the soul and its color: so that they may have a vigorous memory. But in the young body they fail. From this is generated the artificial reason: or if it is great: it is memory. From the heat it makes an impulse, but in the strength of the body. Or the light: let this be given: because in that which was moist, memory is made.
